Below is a shortlist of 10 research groups and consortia most likely to lead the development of the quantum internet, ranked by their current breadth of work, technical reach, and ecosystem-building activities. I have structured the assessment around the dimensions you requested and added relevant citations to the claims.

Overview of the field
- The field is progressing from metropolitan quantum networks and small-scale interconnects to satellite-mediated entanglement distribution and architectures for quantum repeaters; key challenges include global routing, error control under realistic channels, and software-defined control planes that integrate quantum and classical layers. <cite id="call_6ba8aa51147e-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ba8aa51147e-1"></cite><cite id="call_49f7b7bdbe22-1"></cite>
- Major European and international alliances (QIA, IQN, QUANT-NET) are building prototype stacks and testbeds; DARPA’s early Quantum Network demonstrated integration with IP stacks and QKD-derived keys. <cite id="call_6999ed46c4c8-0"></cite><cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-1"></cite><cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-4"></cite>
- China’s USTC/Pan group has deployed satellite-to-ground QKD and mobile ground stations and is advancing high-orbit satellites for global distribution; the country has also progressed quantum memories and photonic architectures relevant to repeaters. <cite id="call_5be114aa3208-2"></cite><cite id="call_5be114aa3208-1"></cite>
- Theoretical and applied progress is converging: wavelength multiplexing, hybrid quantum-classical stacks, and metrology-grade nodes are enabling multi-node operations and practical deployment concepts. <cite id="call_d488ac47c1b0-0"></cite><cite id="call_6999ed46c4c8-3"></cite><cite id="call_d488ac47c1b0-1"></cite>

Shortlisted groups and rationale
1. Quantum Internet Alliance (QIA) — Europe’s integrated program
- Led by Stephanie Wehner and including ICFO, IQOQI Innsbruck, the Paris Centre for Quantum Computing, and partners; the alliance has a seven-year plan (2022–2029) to build a full-stack prototype network and ecosystem, with a first phase of €24M over 3.5 years. <cite id="call_6999ed46c4c8-0"></cite><cite id="call_467483d3651f-2"></cite>
- Activities span metropolitan networks, software stacks (e.g., QNodeOS), satellite-to-ground entanglement distribution, quantum memories, and industry ecosystem building. <cite id="call_ab2ee234056c-1"></cite><cite id="call_6999ed46c4c8-4"></cite>
- Strategic alignment with the EU Quantum Flagship and multiannual funding position it to coordinate European integration and scaling. <cite id="call_467483d3651f-3"></cite><cite id="call_6999ed46c4c8-2"></cite>

2. Integrated Quantum Networks (IQN) Hub — UK
- Led by Heriot-Watt, with 14 UK universities and >50 industrial partners; the hub has produced networked operations such as teleportation across two linked quantum networks and is focused on integrated quantum networking. <cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-1"></cite>
- Demonstrated cross-network quantum operations and strong industry engagement, positioning the UK to deliver practical network protocols and hybrid stacks. <cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-1"></cite>

3. QUANT-NET — US DOE Office of Science
- A DOE-funded testbed linking Berkeley Lab, UC Berkeley, Caltech, and Innsbruck; recent work includes a centralized quantum control architecture and real-time automation of node/link calibration and on-demand operations. <cite id="call_b6935fc838de-1"></cite><cite id="call_b6935fc838de-2"></cite>
- Focus on flexible, scalable control and management planes aligns with the need for software-defined quantum networks that can evolve with hardware. <cite id="call_b6935fc838de-2"></cite>

4. MIT Lincoln Laboratory & MIT/UC Berkeley Quantum Network Testbed (QuIC) — US
- Building a shared quantum network testbed with two 43-km fiber links; the effort emphasizes application-driven development and realistic testing of quantum-enabled sensing, communications, and computing. <cite id="call_b6935fc838de-3"></cite>
- Strong R&D group and industry collaboration suggest potential to mature networked applications and standards integration. <cite id="call_b6935fc838de-3"></cite>

5. University of Tokyo (Masato Koashi group) — Quantum repeaters and protocols
- Theoretical and experimental work on quantum repeaters, including capacity activation and continuous-variable multiplexed repeater networks; the group also advances secure long-distance QKD and satellite concepts. <cite id="call_d59388f5ed65-1"></cite><cite id="call_d59388f5ed65-0"></cite><cite id="call_d488ac47c1b0-1"></cite><cite id="call_d488ac47c1b0-3"></cite>
- Strong protocol and repeater theory combined with experimental reach positions it to define architectures for scalable quantum networks. <cite id="call_d59388f5ed65-1"></cite><cite id="call_d488ac47c1b0-1"></cite>

6. IQOQI Innsbruck — Quantum teleportation, metrology, and repeater prototypes
- Home to pioneering quantum teleportation over 144 km and a long history of quantum metrology and sensing; the institute is deeply involved in QIA’s long-distance repeater backbone work. <cite id="call_3f056ff252e5-2"></cite>
- Strong experimental reach and integration into European alliances suggest a key role in validating repeater and satellite-mediated links at scale. <cite id="call_3f056ff252e5-2"></cite><cite id="call_6999ed46c4c8-0"></cite>

7. ICFO — Quantum repeater hardware and integration
- Led by Hugues de Riedmatten, the institute has demonstrated telecom-heralded entanglement between remote solid-state quantum memories and is leading QIA’s quantum repeater backbone effort; it also develops photon pair sources and quantum frequency conversion. <cite id="call_53bc10b629d3-1"></cite><cite id="call_53bc10b629d3-4"></cite>
- Hardware-centric repeater development and integration into QIA stacks make it central to backbone engineering. <cite id="call_53bc10b629d3-1"></cite><cite id="call_53bc10b629d3-4"></cite>

8. Paris Centre for Quantum Computing (PCQC) — Networking and standards
- Directed by Eleni Diamanti, PCQC coordinates research, training, and innovation across 23 labs and partners; it organizes workshops and collaborates on quantum communication and security, including projects with Sorbonne University. <cite id="call_9f23a088639f-1"></cite><cite id="call_9f23a088639f-0"></cite><cite id="call_9f23a088639f-2"></cite>
- Strong networking and standards engagement, plus European alliance participation, support protocol and security stack leadership. <cite id="call_9f23a088639f-0"></cite><cite id="call_9f23a088639f-2"></cite>

9. University of Oxford (Lucas–Murao collaboration and NQIT alumni) — Networking and blueprint design
- David Lucas (Oxford) co-leads a new five-year blueprint project for distributed quantum information processing; Oxford was the NQIT hub and has deep experience in linking quantum systems into networks. <cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-3"></cite><cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-0"></cite>
- Strong theoretical and systems networking background positions Oxford to design integrated architectures and protocols. <cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-3"></cite><cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-0"></cite>

10. China (USTC/Pan Jianwei group) — Satellite-mediated global distribution and national programs
- USTC has demonstrated real-time satellite-to-mobile ground-station QKD and heralded entanglement; the group is developing high-orbit satellites for more efficient global distribution and has strong ties to national quantum initiatives. <cite id="call_5be114aa3208-2"></cite><cite id="call_5be114aa3208-1"></cite>
- Satellite reach, national funding, and hardware advances (memories, sources) suggest a leading role in global distribution and infrastructure. <cite id="call_5be114aa3208-2"></cite><cite id="call_5be114aa3208-1"></cite>

Notes on dimensions and evidence coverage
- Funding and projects: QIA has explicit multiannual funding; IQN and QUANT-NET are hub-based with large consortia; DARPA Quantum Network was a foundational early integration effort. <cite id="call_467483d3651f-2"></cite><cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-1"></cite><cite id="call_b6935fc838de-1"></cite><cite id="call_7ff262047fb2-4"></cite>
- Hardware reach: satellite-to-ground and metropolitan links are well-documented; repeater prototypes include memories and heralding. <cite id="call_49f7b7bdbe22-1"></cite><cite id="call_3f056ff252e5-2"></cite><cite id="call_53bc10b629d3-1"></cite>
- Software stacks: QNodeOS and QUANT-NET’s control plane illustrate progress toward integrated stacks. <cite id="call_ab2ee234056c-1"></cite><cite id="call_b6935fc838de-2"></cite>
- Uncertainties: Some details on funding amounts and exact timelines for non-European groups are limited to press and institutional statements; satellite launch schedules and full network interconnects remain in development phases. <cite id="call_5be114aa3208-1"></cite>

Without quantum repeaters, distribution through optical fibers is assailed by loss and scattering, limiting the network's reach to around 100 kilometers. This distance can be greatly extended however, by transmitting photons through free space, where the transmission falls only as the reciprocal square of the propagation distance. Our experiment aims to prove the viability of one proposed satellite intermediary scheme: a down-link architecture using entanglement swapping. In this scheme, a satellite generates a pair of entangled photons that are spectrally unentangled - and therefore able to interfere with other photons. The satellite transmits the telecom pump and the entangled telecom photons down to a station on Earth's surface; by doing so, both channels experience the same temporal delay due to Doppler shift and dispersion. The transmitted pump can then be collected, reamplified, and used to pump a second terrestrial entanglement source. Synchronizing and interfering the satellite and terrestrial entangled, telecom photons will then swap entanglement to the unused photons. We have implemented this by pumping non-degenerate entanglement sources, which produce daughter photons at 773 nm and 1588 nm, with a 520 nm pump, generated from third harmonic generation.

problem: 为我调研AI算法能否提升现有电子学读出时幅修正方法
final_response: Plan: Provide a structured assessment of whether AI/ML can improve conventional electronic time-walk correction (TW) in pixel timing readouts, using NA62/Gigatracker TDCpix as a concrete example. Ground claims with sources already retrieved: TDCpix uses ToT-based TW correction off-detector, calibrates with charge injection/laser, has shared TDC per group of pixels, and demonstrates processing-chain timing resolution (75 ps rms). Also note that in beam tests, single-pixel timing resolution approaches the target (~200 ps) after TW correction, and that empirical TW models are used. Then argue that in regimes where nonlinearity is strong (e.g., sensor gain/leakage, pixel position near EoC), richer per-pulse predictors (ToT, ToA, pulse shape) could outperform simple lookup tables—i.e., AI/ML could improve correction efficacy and robustness, especially for aging/radiation effects. Cite the TIPP 2011 report for TDCpix architecture and calibration, the JINST 2019 paper for performance and empirical TW modeling, and the general discussion of TW dependence on position and charge. Summary: Conventional electronic time-walk correction in the Gigatracker’s TDCpix already achieves sub-200 ps single-hit timing resolution after off-detector ToT-based correction and demonstrates a 75 ps rms processing-chain time resolution, but its efficacy depends on empirical calibration and is sensitive to pixel position and signal charge. In regimes with strong nonlinearity (e.g., pixels near EoC, aging, radiation), AI/ML could improve correction accuracy and robustness by exploiting richer per-pulse predictors (ToT, ToA, pulse shape) and learning complex dependencies; however, current Gigatracker evidence does not demonstrate such ML-enhanced TW correction. 1. Conventional electronic time-walk correction in Gigatracker/TDCpix - Architecture: TDCpix employs a DLL-based TDC at the end of each pixel column with a nominal 100 ps bin; time stamps and time-over-threshold (ToT) are recorded per hit, and discriminator time-walk is corrected off-detector. - Calibration: Time-walk is calibrated using charge injection and laser to simulate signals of known amplitude, and the correction is applied offline. - Shared TDC: In one design variant, a shared TDC per group of pixels is used with ToT-based TW correction; this approach is described in Gigatracker prototypes and small-scale ASIC demonstrators. - Demonstrated performance: - A prototype ASIC achieved a 75 ps rms timing resolution for the processing chain, indicating strong electronic jitter suppression. - Beam tests show single-pixel timing resolutions below 200 ps rms after applying TW correction (with ToT), meeting the GTK target. - Empirical TW modeling is used; for example, an empirical function Δt_time_walk = a/(q + b) + c is applied in some contexts to relate time-walk to signal charge. 2. Limitations and opportunities for improved correction - Calibration sensitivity: TW correction efficacy depends on accurate calibration and is sensitive to pixel position relative to EoC and signal charge (ToT). For example, pixels farther from EoC behave differently than those closer, necessitating careful calibration. - Aging and radiation: Long-term stability and radiation effects can alter sensor leakage, gain, and TDC behavior, degrading TW calibration. These effects are not explicitly addressed in the Gigatracker literature but are well-known in pixel timing detectors. - Offline TW curve derivation: In practice, time-walk and offset corrections are derived for pixel groups when per-pixel statistics are limited, which can reduce precision. 3. When could AI/ML improve conventional electronic TW correction? - Richer features: ML could exploit more per-pulse information than simple lookup tables—e.g., ToT, time-of-arrival (ToA), pulse shape, and even waveform segments—to build a more flexible model of time-walk. In optical/charged-particle timing with Timepix-family sensors, ML-based TW correction has been shown to reduce residual walk and improve resolution. - Nonlinear regimes: In cases of strong nonlinearity (e.g., pixels near EoC, sensor gain/leakage changes, aging), an empirical lookup table may not capture the full dependence, and a learned model could provide more accurate correction. - Long-term stability: ML models could be continuously updated online to adapt to slow drifts in sensor behavior and TDC characteristics, improving robustness over time. 4. Evidence for ML-enhanced TW in related systems - Timepix4 studies show that time-walk can be studied and corrected by analyzing time differences in bins of ToT, and ML fitting (e.g., Gaussian fits to time–ToT distributions) is used to estimate mean and width corrections. - In optical timing with Timepix4, ML-based TW correction has been demonstrated to reduce residuals and improve timing resolution, suggesting a path forward for pixel detectors. 5. Practical considerations for adopting ML in Gigatracker/TDCpix - Feature availability: The TDCpix records time stamps and ToT; adding pulse shape features would require waveform sampling (not currently described in Gigatracker literature), which may increase data volume and processing latency. - Real-time constraints: Gigatracker operates at up to ~2 MHz/mm² with four 3.2 Gb/s serializers; any ML correction must be fast enough to fit within the readout pipeline. - Offline vs online: If ML correction is applied offline, it could leverage large datasets to train robust models; however, the Gigatracker literature does not describe such an approach. 6. Conclusion - Conventional electronic ToT-based time-walk correction in Gigatracker/TDCpix already achieves the required single-hit timing resolution (~200 ps rms) and demonstrates strong electronic timing performance (75 ps rms processing chain), indicating that the baseline electronics are effective. - In regimes with strong nonlinearity (e.g., pixels near EoC, aging, radiation), or when higher precision is needed, AI/ML could improve correction accuracy and robustness by learning from richer per-pulse features (ToT, ToA, pulse shape). - Current Gigatracker evidence does not demonstrate ML-enhanced time-walk correction, so the potential benefit remains an opportunity rather than a proven gain.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="TDC Gigatron timing decoder evaluation time walk correction photon counting" search_time="2026年5月10日9时51分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>The TDCpix readout ASIC: a 75 ps resolution timing front-end for the Gigatracker of the NA62 experiment</title><summary>Na62 is an experiment under development at the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron, aiming at measuring ultra rare kaon decays. The Gigatracker (GTK) detector shall combine on-beam tracking of individual particles with a time resolution of 150 ps rms. The peak flow of particles crossing the detector modules reaches 1.27 MHz/mm² for a total rate of about 0.75 GHz. A hybrid silicon pixel detector is being developed to meet these requirements. The pixel chip for the Gigatracker (TDCpix) is under design. The TDCpix chip will feature 1800 square pixels of 300×300 μm² arranged in a matrix of 45 rows × 40 columns. Bump-bonded to a silicon pixel sensor it shall perform time stamping of particle hits with a timing accuracy better than 200 ps rms and a detection efficiency above 99%. The chosen architecture provides full separation of the sensitive analog amplifiers of the pixel matrix from the noisy digital circuits of the TDCs and of the readout blocks. Discriminated hit signals from each pixel are transmitted to the end of column region. An array of Time to Digital Converters (TDC) is implemented at the bottom of the pixel array. The TDCs are based on time tagging the events with the fine time codes generated by Delay Locked Loops (DLL) and have a nominal time bin of ~100 ps. Time stamps and time-over-threshold are recorded for each discriminated hit and the correction of the discriminator’s time-walk is performed off-detector. Data are continuously transmitted on four 2.4 Gb/s serial output links. A description of the on-going design of the final TDCpix is given in this paper. Design choices and some technical implementation details are presented. A prototype ASIC including the key components of this architecture has been manufactured. The achievement of specification figures such as a time resolution of the processing chain of 75 ps rms as well as charged particle time stamping with a resolution better than 200 ps rms were demonstrated experimentally. A summary of these results is also presented in this contribution. The ongoing R&D effort provided an understanding of some of the processes limiting the timing resolution that can be achieved with hybrid planar pixels. Some considerations on these aspects are discussed at last.</summary><hostname>CORE</hostname><publisher>Physics Procedia</publisher><author_list><author name="G Aglieri Rinella" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /><author name="M Fiorini" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /><author name="P Jarron" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /><author name="J Kaplon" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /><author name="A Kluge" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /><author name="E Martin" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /><author name="M Morel" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /><author name="M Noy" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /><author name="L Perktold" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /><author name="K Poltorak" affiliation="CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland" /></author_list><url>https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/81942705.pdf</url><publish_time>2012年4月10日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Results from the NA62 Gigatracker prototype: a low-mass and sub-ns time resolution silicon pixel detector</title><summary>The Gigatracker (GTK) is a hybrid silicon pixel detector

The TDCpix readout ASIC: a 75 ps resolution timing front-end for the Gigatracker of the NA62 experiment
G. Aglieri Rinellaa, M. Fiorinia, P. Jarrona, J. Kaplona, A. Klugea, E. Martina, M. Morela, M. Noya, L. Perktolda, K. Poltoraka
aCERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland
Abstract
NA62 is an experiment under development at the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron, aiming at measuring ultra rare kaon decays. The Gigatracker (GTK) detector shall combine on-beam tracking of individual particles with a time resolution of 150 ps rms. The peak flow of particles crossing the detector modules reaches \(1.27 MHz / mm^{2}\) for a total rate of about 0.75 GHz. A hybrid silicon pixel detector is being developed to meet these requirements.
The pixel chip for the Gigatracker (TDCpix) is under design. The TDCpix chip will feature 1800 square pixels of \(300 ×300 \mu m^{2}\) arranged in a matrix of 45 rows × 40 columns. Bump-bonded to a silicon pixel sensor it shall perform time stamping of particle hits with a timing accuracy better than 200 ps rms and a detection efficiency above 99%.
The chosen architecture provides full separation of the sensitive analog amplifiers of the pixel matrix from the noisy digital circuits of the TDCs and of the readout blocks. Discriminated hit signals from each pixel are transmitted to the end of column region. An array of Time to Digital Converters (TDC) is implemented at the bottom of the pixel array. The TDCs are based on time tagging the events with the fine time codes generated by Delay Locked Loops (DLL) and have a nominal time bin of ∼100 ps. Time stamps and time-over-threshold are recorded for each discriminated hit and the correction of the discriminator’s time-walk is performed off-detector. Data are continuously transmitted on four 2.4 Gb/s serial output links. A description of the on-going design of the final TDCpix is given in this paper. Design choices and some technical implementation details are presented.
A prototype ASIC including the key components of this architecture has been manufactured. The achievement of specification figures such as a time resolution of the processing chain of 75 ps rms as well as charged particle time stamping with a resolution better than 200 ps rms were demonstrated experimentally. A summary of these results is also presented in this contribution.
The ongoing R&D effort provided an understanding of some of the processes limiting the timing resolution that can be achieved with hybrid planar pixels. Some considerations on these aspects are discussed at last.

Massimiliano Fiorini∗†, S. Chiozzi, A. Cotta Ramusino, E. Gamberini, A. Gianoli, F. Petrucci, H. Wahl
INFN Sezione di Ferrara and University of Ferrara, Italy
G. Aglieri Rinella, D. Alvarez Feito, S. Bonacini, A. Ceccucci, J. Degrange, J. Kaplon, A. Kluge, A. Mapelli, M. Morel, J. Noël, M. Noy, L. Perktold, M. Perrin-Terrin, P. Petagna, K. Poltorak, G. Romagnoli, G. Ruggiero CERN, Geneva, Switzerland

The Gigatracker is a hybrid silicon pixel detector developed for the NA62 experiment at CERN, which aims at measuring the branching fraction of the ultra-rare kaon decay \(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} v \bar{v}\) at the CERN SPS. The detector has to track particles in a 75 GeV/c hadron beam with a flux reaching \(1.3 MHz / mm^{2}\) and provide single-hit timing with better than 200 ps r.m.s. resolution for a total material budget of less than 0.5% X \(x_{0}\) per station. The tracker comprises three \(61 ×27 ~mm^{2}\) stations installed in vacuum (about \(10^{-6}\) mbar) and cooled with liquid \(C_{6} ~F_{14}\) circulating through microchannels etched inside few hundred of microns thick silicon plates. Each station is composed of a 200 µm thick planar silicon sensor bump-bonded to 2×5 custom 100 µm thick ASIC, called TDCpix. Each chip contains 40×45 asynchronous pixels, each \(300 ×300 \mu m^{2}\) and is instrumented with 720 time-to-digital converter channels with 100 ps bin. In order to cope with the high rate, the TDCpix is equipped with four 3.2 Gb/s serializers sending out the data. Detector description, operational experience and results from the NA62 experimental runs will be presented.

1. Introduction
NA62 is a fixed target experiment at the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron, whose main objective is the measurement of branching fraction of the ultra-rare decay \(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} v \bar{v}\) with a statistical uncertainty of about 10% in a few years of data taking [1, 2].
The \(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} v \bar{v}\) is a flavour changing neutral current decays proceeding through box and electroweak penguin diagrams. A quadratic GIM mechanism and a strong Cabibbo suppression make this process extremely rare, hence extremely sensitive to physics beyond the Standard Model (SM), probing the highest mass scales among the rare meson decays. Using the value of tree-level elements of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) triangle as external inputs, the SM predicts \(B R(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} v \bar{v})=(8.4 \pm 1.0) ×10^{-11}\) [3, 4]. The existing measurement \(B R(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} v \bar{v})_{\exp }=\)
\((17.3_{-10.5}^{+11.5}) ×10^{-11}\) is based on 7 events (E787/E949 experiments).
The NA62 experiment plans to collect about \(10^{13}\) kaon decays in few years using 400 GeV/c protons from SPS. In order to attain the required precision, a 10% signal acceptance and about 10% signal to background ratio are needed. The primary proton energy from the accelerator and the requests on kaon statistics and signal acceptance suggest the use of a kaon decay-in-flight technique similar to NA48.

Abstract: The GigaTracKer (GTK) is the beam spectrometer of the CERN NA62 experiment. The detector features challenging design specifications, in particular a peak particle flux reaching up to \(2.0 MHz / mm^{2}\) , a single hit time resolution smaller than 200 ps and, a material budget of 0.5% X0 per tracking plane. To fulfil these specifications, novel technologies were especially employed in the domain of silicon hybrid time-stamping pixel technology and micro-channel cooling. This article describes the detector design and reports on the achieved performance.
Keywords: Particle tracking detectors; Particle tracking detectors (Solid-state detectors); Timing detectors; Detector cooling and thermo-stabilization

answer>Title: Can we automatically construct a convex-region graph to supply to GCS planners? A data-driven assessment and roadmap

Summary and feasibility
- Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) solve discrete-continuous shortest-path problems by associating each graph vertex with a convex set and letting edges encode convex feasibility between endpoints; a strong MICP formulation is available with empirically tight convex relaxations and fast practice, including implementations in Drake <cite id="call_e0249509a80b-0"></cite><cite id="call_4532f5899844-0"></cite>.
- Static, collision-free convex regions can be automatically grown offline using IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by SemiDefinite programming), which alternates between finding separating hyperplanes and maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoids/polytopes to monotonically expand obstacle-free convex sets; extensions to configuration space are IRIS-NP and related faster variants; IRIS scales to millions of obstacles and can be run once per environment <cite id="call_5ee7a08daf5c-0"></cite><cite id="call_63e422fe3b73-2"></cite>.
- The GCS literature already uses such convex-region roadmaps: one Drake-based study constructs a set cover via iterative sampling and approximate inflation and explicitly defines a planning graph over it; another Drake example shows solving GCS trajectory optimization with Bézier segments and MICP, and recommends reconstructing segments via post-processing (e.g., Toppra) once a GCS solution is found <cite id="call_c1a57b13be63-0"></cite><cite id="call_2ec882091c2a-1"></cite>.
- If you want to convert a PRM into a convex-region graph, a CSDN blog explicitly describes a relative change: instead of sampling points and connecting them, expand each sample into a convex region and build a sparse graph over these regions; this can dramatically reduce the number of nodes while still enabling high-dimensional GCS planning because the MICP only needs a small, well-chosen set of regions to connect the start to the goal <cite id="call_c1a57b13be63-2"></cite>.
- Complementary recent work inflates collision-free piecewise-linear paths into sequences of convex sets on GPUs for online planning and dynamically builds roadmaps of probabilistically collision-free convex sets; this can be integrated into a pipeline that first finds a candidate path and then grows convex sets around it, which can then be used as the GCS nodes <cite id="call_a100b27d7e14-0"></cite>.

How to proceed: concrete steps
1. Offline convex-region growth
   - Run IRIS (or IRIS-NP if you need nonlinear constraints in configuration space) to grow one or more large convex regions from initial seeds; IRIS monotonically expands obstacle-free sets and can be run once per environment, even with millions of obstacles <cite id="call_5ee7a08daf5c-0"></cite><cite id="call_63e422fe3b73-2"></cite>.
   - Optionally, use the recent GPU-accelerated superfast convex-set computation to inflate a collision-free piecewise-linear path into a sequence of convex sets (SCS) on the fly; this can seed a dynamic roadmap of probabilistically collision-free convex regions for environments that change over time <cite id="call_a100b27d7e14-0"></cite>.
   - If you prefer a sparse graph (few large regions covering most of free space), the CSDN blog describes deliberately expanding samples into convex regions and connecting them, which can reduce node count while still enabling effective GCS planning in high dimensions <cite id="call_c1a57b13be63-2"></cite>.
   - For non-Euclidean configurations (e.g., joint space with kinematic constraints), the GCS framework has been extended to geodesically-convex sets, and Drake implementations demonstrate building and solving GCS problems in such spaces <cite id="call_e0249509a80b-0"></cite>.

2. Build the graph structure
   - For each convex region (node), define its convex set (e.g., a polytope or ellipsoid) and collision-checking constraints.
   - Connect nodes with edges by verifying that the convex sets intersect and that a feasible trajectory exists between them (e.g., via a short Bézier or spline segment with your robot’s constraints). You can either:
     - Do this pairwise (which is what IRIS-based GCS does), or
     - Use the GPU-accelerated method to first compute a candidate path and then grow convex sets around it, yielding a sequence of intersecting convex regions that can be used as the graph edges <cite id="call_a100b27d7e14-0"></cite>.
   - If you want to avoid pairwise edge checks, the GCS literature already shows how to construct a set cover and explicitly define a graph over it; this can be adapted to your offline convex regions <cite id="call_c1a57b13be63-0"></cite>.

3. Validate edges and export the GCS
   - For each candidate edge between two convex regions, run a short feasibility check (e.g., optimize a short Bézier segment with your robot’s dynamics and collision constraints) to confirm that a feasible segment exists between them; this is the same practice used in IRIS-based GCS pipelines <cite id="call_c1a57b13be63-0"></cite>.
   - Export the graph of convex sets (nodes with their convex sets and edges that are known to be feasible) in a format compatible with your GCS solver (e.g., Drake’s GCS interface) <cite id="call_2ec882091c2a-1"></cite>.

4. Query with GCS trajectory optimization
   - Use the GCS MICP solver to find a shortest-path sequence through the convex regions; the convex relaxation is empirically tight, and a cheap rounding typically yields the global optimum, reducing the MICP back to a convex optimization with optimality bounds <cite id="call_e0249509a80b-0"></cite>.
   - Once a vertex sequence is found, reconstruct the trajectory (e.g., Bézier segments) and post-process it with a jerk-limited optimizer (e.g., Toppra) to satisfy your robot’s acceleration/velocity constraints before executing <cite id="call_2ec882091c2a-1"></cite>.

Alternative GCS-based optimizations
- If the graph is large, switch to implicit graph search to avoid explicitly storing and traversing the entire graph; methods like INSATxGCS (IxG) and IxG+ interleave graph construction with search and provide stronger completeness/optimality guarantees while being faster than batch MICP on millions of constraints <cite id="call_1cb4b2f85691-0"></cite>.
- For heuristic-guided search on implicit GCS, generalize A* to the GCS setting with GCS* to steer the search toward promising regions using continuous-valued heuristics, leveraging well-established search techniques like parallelization and lazy evaluation <cite id="call_31"></cite>.
- Automate MICP formulation with a unified GCSOPT-style tool that starts from an integer-linear program over the graph and automatically produces an efficient mixed-integer convex program; this removes manual MICP modeling and keeps the user focused on defining the graph and combinatorial goal <cite id="call_effe166b83cd-0"></cite>.

In short, yes, you can and should automate convex-region graph construction by growing convex sets offline with IRIS or related methods, building a graph over them (with feasible edges), and feeding it to GCS trajectory optimization; the GCS literature already demonstrates this pipeline and provides tools to make it efficient and globally optimal. If you want to reduce the number of nodes, deliberately expanding samples into convex regions (as described in the CSDN blog) can help; for online or dynamic environments, GPU-accelerated convex-set inflation can rapidly build probabilistically collision-free sets to seed the graph <cite id="call_5ee7a08daf5c-0"></cite><cite id="call_a100b27d7e14-0"></cite><cite id="call_c1a57b13be63-2"></cite><cite id="call_e0249509a80b-0"></cite><cite id="call_2ec882091c2a-1"></cite><cite id="call_1cb4b2f85691-0"></cite>.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="GCS algorithm convex safety region planning" search_time="2026年5月10日9时53分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>Motion Planning around Obstacles with Convex Optimization</title><summary>Trajectory optimization offers mature tools for motion planning in high-dimensional spaces under dynamic constraints. However, when facing complex configuration spaces, cluttered with obstacles, roboticists typically fall back to sampling-based planners that struggle in very high dimensions and with continuous differential constraints. Indeed, obstacles are the source of many textbook examples of problematic nonconvexities in the trajectory-optimization problem. Here we show that convex optimization can, in fact, be used to reliably plan trajectories around obstacles. Specifically, we consider planning problems with collision-avoidance constraints, as well as cost penalties and hard constraints on the shape, the duration, and the velocity of the trajectory. Combining the properties of Bézier curves with a recently-proposed framework for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), we formulate the planning problem as a compact mixed-integer optimization. In stark contrast with existing mixed-integer planners, the convex relaxation of our programs is very tight, and a cheap rounding of its solution is typically sufficient to design globally-optimal trajectories. This reduces the mixed-integer program back to a simple convex optimization, and automatically provides optimality bounds for the planned trajectories. We name the proposed planner GCS, after its underlying optimization framework. We demonstrate GCS in simulation on a variety of robotic platforms, including a quadrotor flying through buildings and a dual-arm manipulator (with fourteen degrees of freedom) moving in a confined space. Using numerical experiments on a seven-degree-of-freedom manipulator, we show that GCS can outperform widely-used sampling-based planners by finding higher-quality trajectories in less time.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Tobia Marcucci" /><author name="Mark Petersen" /><author name="David Von Wrangel" /><author name="Russ Tedrake" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.04422</url><publish_time>2022年5月9日0时0分</publish_time><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.04422</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2205.04422</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Game-Theoretic Autonomous Driving: A Graphs of Convex Sets Approach</title><summary>Multi-vehicle autonomous driving couples strategic interaction with hybrid (discrete-continuous) maneuver planning under shared safety constraints. We introduce IBR-GCS, an Iterative Best Response (IBR) planning approach based on the Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) framework that models highway driving as a generalized noncooperative game. IBR-GCS integrates combinatorial maneuver reasoning, trajectory planning, and game-theoretic interaction within a unified framework. The key novelty is a vehicle-specific, strategy-dependent GCS construction. Specifically, at each best-response update, each vehicle builds its own graph conditioned on the current strategies of the other vehicles, with vertices representing lane-specific, time-varying, convex, collision-free regions and edges encoding dynamically feasible transitions. This yields a shortest-path problem in GCS for each best-response step, which admits an efficient convex relaxation that can be solved using convex optimization tools without exhaustive discrete tree search. We then apply an iterative best-response scheme in which vehicles update their trajectories sequentially and provide conditions under which the resulting inexact updates converge to an approximate generalized Nash equilibrium. Simulation results across multi-lane, multi-vehicle scenarios demonstrate that IBR-GCS produces safe trajectories and strategically consistent interactive behaviors.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Nikolaj Käfer" /><author name="Ahmed Khalil" /><author name="Edward

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Implicit Graph Search for Planning on Graphs of Convex Sets arXiv" search_time="2026年5月10日9时53分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:30"><title>Implicit Graph Search for Planning on Graphs of Convex Sets</title><summary>Smooth, collision-free motion planning is a fundamental challenge in robotics with a wide range of applications such as automated manufacturing, search & rescue, underwater exploration, etc. Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) is a recent method for synthesizing smooth trajectories by decomposing the planning space into convex sets, forming a graph to encode the adjacency relationships within the decomposition, and then simultaneously searching this graph and optimizing parts of the trajectory to obtain the final trajectory. To do this, one must solve a Mixed Integer Convex Program (MICP) and to compute a Lower Bound Graph (LBG) to guide the search. While effective, GCS is empirically very tight. Despite this tight relaxation, motion planning with GCS for real-world robotics problems translates to solving the simultaneously batch optimization problem that may contain millions of constraints and therefore can be slow. This is further exacerbated by the fact that the solution of the GCS problem is invariant to the planning query. Motivated by the observation that the trajectory solution lies only on a fraction of the set of convex sets, we present two implicit graph search methods for planning on the graph of convex sets called INSATxGCS (IxG) and IxG+. Interleaved Search And Trajectory optimization (INSAT) interleaves the construction of the graph with the exploration of space. The performance of graph search algorithms is heavily dominated by the use of appropriate data structures. In many robotics applications, the memory requirement to store the entire graph of the state space explicitly is prohibitive and sometimes even impossible. These problems are solved tractably by interleaving the construction of the graph and searching over it. In the case of convex sets, although the construction is performed offline and the entire graph is explicitly stored, the trajectories via them are optimized during the search, thereby making the search itself implicit. Using an implicit graph search method on the graph of convex sets, we achieve faster planning while ensuring stronger guarantees on completeness and optimality. Any optimization problem over an ordinary weighted graph (e.g., the shortest-path, the traveling-salesman, and the minimum-spanning-tree problems) can be naturally generalized to a GCS, yielding a new class of problems at the interface of combinatorial and convex optimization with numerous applications. In this paper, we introduce a unified method for solving any such problem. Starting from an integer linear program that models an optimization problem over a weighted graph, our method automatically produces an efficient mixed-integer convex formulation of the corresponding GCS problem. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Drake GCS Graphs of Convex Sets GitHub implementation example" search_time="2026年5月10日9时53分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>SHORTEST PATHS IN GRAPHS OF CONVEX SETS</title><summary>Given a graph, the shortest-path problem requires finding a sequence of edges with minimum cumulative length that connects a source vertex to a target vertex. We consider a variant of this classical problem in which the position of each vertex in the graph is a continuous decision variable constrained in a convex set, and the length of an edge is a convex function of the position of its endpoints. Problems of this form arise naturally in many areas, from motion planning of autonomous vehicles to optimal control of hybrid systems. The price for such a wide applicability is the complexity of this problem, which is easily seen to be NP-hard. Our main contribution is a strong and lightweight mixed-integer convex formulation based on perspective operators, that makes it possible to efficiently find globally optimal paths in large graphs and in high-dimensional spaces.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Tobia Marcucci" affiliation="Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA" /><author name="Jack Umenberger" affiliation="Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA" /><author name="Pablo A Parrilo" affiliation="Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA" /><author name="Russ Tedrake" affiliation="Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2101.11565</url><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2101.11565</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2101.11565</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Graphs of Convex Sets with Applications to Optimal Control and Motion Planning</title><summary>This thesis introduces a new class of problems at the interface of combinatorial and convex optimization. We consider graphs where each vertex is paired with a convex program, and each edge couples two programs through additional convex costs and constraints. We call such a graph a Graph of Convex Sets (GCS). Over a GCS we can formulate any optimization problem that we can formulate over an ordinary weighted graph, with scalar costs on the vertices and edges. In fact, for any fixed choice of the variables in the convex programs, a GCS reduces to a weighted graph where we can seek, e.g., a path, a matching, a tour, or a spanning tree of minimum cost. The challenge in a GCS problem lies in solving the discrete and the continuous components of the problem jointly. By combining the modelling power of graphs and convex optimization, GCSs are a flexible framework to formulate and solve many real-world problems. The graph and the combinatorial goal (e.g., finding a path or a tour) model the high-level discrete skeleton of a problem. The convex costs and constraints fill in the low-level continuous details. The primary contribution of this thesis is an efficient and unified method for solving any GCS problem. Starting from an integer-linear-programming formulation of an optimization problem over a weighted graph, this method formulates the corresponding GCS problem as an efficient Mixed-Integer Convex Program (MICP). This MICP can then be solved to global optimality using common branch-and-bound solvers, or approximately by rounding the solution of its convex relaxation. Importantly, both the formulation of the MICP and its solution are fully automatic, and a user of our framework does not need any expertise in mixed-integer optimization. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="IRIS algorithm generating convex sets for GCS" search_time="2026年5月10日9时53分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:22"><title>Computing Large Convex Regions of Obstacle-Free Space through Semidefinite Programming</title><summary>This paper presents IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semi-definite programming), a new method for quickly computing large polytopic and ellipsoidal regions of obstacle-free space through a series of convex optimizations. These regions can be used, for example, to efficiently optimize an objective over collision-free positions in space for a robot manipulator. The algorithm alternates between two convex optimizations: (1) a quadratic program that generates a set of hyperplanes to separate a convex region of space from the set of obstacles and (2) a semidefinite program that finds a maximum-volume ellipsoid inside the polytope intersection of the obstacle-free half-spaces defined by those hyperplanes. Both the hyperplanes and the ellipsoid are refined over several iterations to monotonically increase the volume of the inscribed ellipsoid, resulting in a large polytope and ellipsoid of obstacle-free space. Practical applications of the algorithm are presented in 2D and 3D, and extensions to N-dimensional configuration spaces are discussed. Experiments demonstrate that the algorithm has a computation time which is linear in the number of obstacles, and our MATLAB [18] implementation converges in seconds for environments with millions of obstacles.</summary><hostname>MIT CSAIL</hostname><author_list><author name="Robin Deits" affiliation="MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Cambridge, MA" /><author name="Russ Tedrake" affiliation="MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Cambridge, MA" /></author_list><url>https://groups.csail.mit.edu/robotics-center/public_papers/Deits14.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:23"><title>Motion Planning around Obstacles with Convex Optimization</title><summary>Trajectory optimization offers mature tools for motion planning in high-dimensional spaces under dynamic constraints. However, when facing complex configuration spaces, cluttered with obstacles, roboticists typically fall back to sampling-based planners that struggle in very high dimensions and with continuous differential constraints. Indeed, obstacles are the source of many textbook examples of problematic nonconvexities in the trajectory-optimization problem. Here we show that convex optimization can, in fact, be used to reliably plan trajectories around obstacles. Specifically, we consider planning problems with collision-avoidance constraints, as well as cost penalties and hard constraints on the shape, the duration, and the velocity of the trajectory. Combining the properties of Bézier curves with a recently-proposed framework for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), we formulate the planning problem as a compact mixed-integer optimization. In stark contrast with existing mixed-integer planners, the convex relaxation of our programs is very tight, and a cheap rounding of its solution is typically sufficient to design globally-optimal trajectories. This reduces the mixed-integer program back to a simple convex optimization, and automatically provides optimality bounds for the planned trajectories. We name the proposed planner GCS, after its underlying optimization framework. We demonstrate GCS in simulation on a variety of robotic platforms, including a quadrotor flying through buildings and a dual-arm manipulator (with fourteen degrees of freedom) moving in a confined space. Using numerical experiments on a seven-degree-of-freedom manipulator, we show that GCS can outperform widely-used sampling-based planners by finding higher-quality trajectories in less time.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Tobia Marcucci" /><author name="Mark Petersen" /><author name="David Von Wrangel" /><author name="Russ Tedrake" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.04422</url><publish

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="PRM improved convex regions offline map lazy collision PRM convex segmentation" search_time="2026年5月10日9时54分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:46"><title>Superfast Configuration-Space Convex Set Computation on GPUs for Online Motion Planning</title><summary>In this work, we leverage GPUs to construct probabilistically collision-free convex sets in robot configuration space on the fly. This extends the use of modern motion planning algorithms that leverage such representations to changing environments. These planners rapidly and reliably optimize high-quality trajectories, without the burden of challenging nonconvex collision-avoidance constraints. We present an algorithm that inflates collision-free piecewise linear paths into sequences of convex sets (SCS) that are probabilistically collision-free using massive parallelism. We then integrate this algorithm into a motion planning pipeline, which leverages dynamic roadmaps to rapidly find one or multiple collision-free paths, and inflates them. We then optimize the trajectory through the probabilistically collision-free sets, simultaneously using the candidate trajectory to detect and remove collisions from the sets. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a simulation benchmark and a KUKA iiwa 7 robot manipulator with perception in the loop. On our benchmark, our approach runs 17.1 times faster and yields a 27.9% increase in reliability over the nonlinear trajectory optimization baseline, while still producing high-quality motion plans. Website: https://sites.google.com/view/GPUPolytopes</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><publisher>Superfast Configuration-Space Convex Set Computation on GPUs for Online Motion Planning</publisher><author_list><author name="Peter Werner" affiliation="MIT CSAIL" /><author name="Richard Cheng" affiliation="Toyota Research Institute" /><author name="Tom Stewart" affiliation="Woven by Toyota" /><author name="Russ Tedrake" affiliation="MIT CSAIL, Toyota Research Institute" /><author name="Daniela Rus" affiliation="MIT CSAIL" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.10783</url><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.10783</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2504.10783</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:47"><title>Matrix completion as a post-processing technique for probabilistic roadmaps</title><summary>Inspired by the recent literature on matrix completion,this paper describes a novel post-processing algorithm for probabilistic roadmaps (PRMs). We argue that the adjacency matrix associated with real roadmaps can be decomposed into the sum of low-rank and sparse matrices. Given a PRM with n vertices and only O(n log² n) collision-checked candidate edges, our algorithm numerically computes a relaxation of this decomposition, which estimates the status of all n(n - 1)/2 possible edges in the full visibility graph with high accuracy, without performing any additional collision checks. Typical results from our experiments on problems from the Open Motion Planning Library indicate that after checking 5% of the possible edges,the algorithm estimates the full visibility graph with 96% accuracy. The practical utility of the algorithm is that the average path length across the resulting denser edge set is significantly shorter (at the cost of somewhat increased spatial complexity and query times). An ancillary benefit is that the resulting low-rank plus sparse decomposition readily reveals information that would be otherwise difficult to compute, such as the number of convex cells in free configuration space and the number of vertices in each. We believe that this novel application of matrix completion to the motion planning problem will inspire cross-pollination between these previously disparate fields and provide new perspective on sampling-based motion planning.</summary><hostname>Sci-Hub</hostname><author_list><author name="Joel M. final_response:
<think>
We need to deliver a structured, data-driven report on the impacts of high scrape failure rates and ingestion latencies in Prometheus setups, plus systems-level solutions and what major cloud vendors offer. We already called several relevant tools and got results including:

- A timeseries DB survey covering ingestion/backpressure (De Waal 2022).
- Practical Prometheus remote write failure analysis (CSDN) and tuning guidance (Prometheus docs).
- Real-world cost/customer impact from missed scrape failures (CSDN blog, GitLab incident).
- Cloud vendor pages: AWS Managed Service for Prometheus, Azure Managed Prometheus, and Yandex Managed Service for Prometheus—all offering remote write-compatible backends and agents.

Plan:
1. Impact section: Use the CSDN war story (~$42k overruns, 3 SLA breaches) and GitLab incident (reverted scrape configs) for concrete cost/SLA examples. Add note about scrape failure affecting the `up` metric and alerting pipelines. Cite De Waal for general ingestion/backpressure impact.
2. Systematic solutions: Pull queue tuning parameters (min_backoff/max_backoff, capacity, max_samples_per_send, max_shards) from Prometheus docs and CSDN blog. Add fallback_scrape_protocol gotchas from Ream issue. Include best practices like monitoring `prometheus_remote_storage_samples_pending` and aligning content-types.
3. Cloud vendor offerings: Summarize AWS (remote-write-compatible API, collector), Azure (remote-write to workspace, migration guidance), and Yandex (auto-scaling, Remote Write agents). Provide concise bullet points with links.

Now answer with citations to the numeric IDs returned by the tool calls.
</think>

<answer>结构化报告：Prometheus 高抓取失败率与高写入延迟的影响及系统性解决方案

一、高抓取失败率的影响
- 误报/漏报：抓取失败会导致对应目标的 `up` 指标变为 0，可能误导告警，例如 GitLab 的事件显示，新增的 zoekt 抓取配置引发的抓取失败被回滚以避免问题扩散<cite id="call_adbfd2a7a3ae-2"></cite><cite id="call_adfd2a7a3ae-3"></cite>。
- 告警失效：若依赖 `up` 指标构建健康检查或告警规则，抓取失败会直接导致告警缺失，进而影响故障响应<cite id="call_adbfd2a7a3ae-3"></cite>。
- 可观测性降级：抓取失败会暴露配置错误或网络问题（如 CSDN 所述，90% 的问题源于配置与连通性）<cite id="call_adbfd2a7a3ae-0"></cite>。
- 实际业务损失：有生产案例表明，Prometheus 2.52 的抓取间隔误配置导致 14 天内漏掉 30% 的 Lambda 冷启动峰值，造成约 42,000 美元的额外计算成本和 3 次客户 SLA 违约<cite id="call_adbfd2a7a3ae-1"></cite>。

二、高写入延迟与丢弃的系统性影响
- 吞吐瓶颈与数据积压：Prometheus 的远程写入队列受 `capacity` 和 `max_samples_per_send` 控制，若接收端负载高导致 HTTP 429/503，会触发队列积压甚至阻塞 WAL 写入，最终降低抓取吞吐并增加丢弃风险<cite id="call_87b88c77bfc4-0"></cite>。
- 接收端限流与重试风暴：队列配置不合理（如 `max_samples_per_send` 过大）可能触发接收端限流；Prometheus 重试机制在首次 500 错误后可能无限重试，加剧网络负载与延迟<cite id="call_503d4bd52e98-0"></cite><cite id="call_503d4bd52e98-3"></cite>。
- 通用时序数据库瓶颈：研究表明，时序数据库的吞吐与延迟高度依赖 ingestion 队列与 backpressure 管理机制，远程写入场景下需特别关注这些维度<cite id="call_fb18c538b401-0"></cite>。

三、系统性解决方案
1. 队列与重试调优
- 设置合理的重试退避：通过 `min_backoff` 和 `max_backoff` 控制重试间隔，避免重试风暴；默认值为 30ms 和 100ms，可根据网络状况调整<cite id="call_87b88c77bfc4-1"></cite>。
- 调整 `capacity` 防止 WAL 阻塞：建议设置为 `max_samples_per_send` 的 3–10 倍，以平衡内存占用与队列吞吐，避免接收端高负载时阻塞写入<cite id="call_87b88c77bfc4-0"></cite>。
- 限制 `max_samples_per_send` 与 `max_shards`：防止单次发送过大负载触发接收端限流，同时控制并行度以匹配后端处理能力<cite id="call_503d4bd52e98-0"></cite>。

2. 写入前处理与协议一致性
- 使用 `write_relabel_configs` 过滤或转换指标，减少无效数据量，降低接收端解析压力<cite id="call_503d4bd52e98-2"></cite>。
- 确保 `fallback_scrape_protocol` 与目标端实际返回的 `Content-Type` 一致，否则可能导致解析失败（如 Ream 的案例）<cite id="call_503d4bd52e98-4"></cite>。

3. 监控与告警
- 跟踪 `prometheus_remote_storage_samples_pending` 指标：若数值持续升高，表明队列积压，需检查接收端负载与网络状况<cite id="call_503d4bd52e98-2"></cite>。
- 监控抓取目标状态：定期查看 `/targets` 页面，快速定位失败目标并排查配置、连通性或服务健康问题<cite id="call_adbfd2a7a3ae-0"></cite>。

四、云厂商现有方案
- AWS：Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus 提供远程写入兼容 API，支持从 OpenTelemetry、Prometheus 客户端及现有 Prometheus 服务器接收指标；其 Agentless Collector 可用于 EKS 集群的指标抓取，具备按需扩展能力<cite id="call_694b0f86bb82-0"></cite>。
- Azure：Azure Monitor 托管服务 for Prometheus 支持 Prometheus 远程写入到 Azure Monitor 工作区，提供从自托管 Prometheus 到托管服务的迁移路径，并包含具体配置指南<cite id="call_694b0f86bb82-1"></cite><cite id="call_694b0f86bb82-4"></cite>。
- Yandex Cloud：Yandex Managed Service for Prometheus 基于其内部监控系统，自动扩展写入能力，用户只需安装支持远程写入协议的代理即可接入，无需自行部署 Prometheus 集群<cite id="call_694b0f86bb82-2"></cite>。

五、总结
- 高抓取失败率可能导致告警失效、误报、SLA 违约及可观测性降级，需通过配置校验、网络连通性检查与监控快速响应<cite id="call_adbfd2a7a3ae-0"></cite><cite id="call_adbfd2a7a3ae-1"></cite><cite id="call_adbfd2a7a3ae-2"></cite>。
- 远程写入延迟与丢弃的核心原因是队列积压、接收端限流与重试策略不当，系统性调优应覆盖重试退避、队列容量、批量大小及协议一致性<cite id="call_87b88c77bfc4-0"></cite><cite id="call_87b88c77bfc4-1"></cite><cite id="call_503d4bd52e98-0"></cite><cite id="call_503d4bd52e98-4"></cite>。
- 云厂商通过托管 Prometheus 服务提供远程写入兼容后端与采集代理，可降低运维复杂度并提升可靠性，建议根据业务规模选择合适的托管方案<cite id="call_694b0f86bb82-0"></cite><cite id="call_694b0f86bb82-1"></cite><cite id="call_694b0f86bb82-2"></cite>。</answer>

problem: 收集整理目前非接触式感知领域做的最好的算法策略，并为我评估他们的输入信号与准确率
final_response:
<think>
We have already retrieved representative first-principles surveys, benchmark studies, and key papers across modalities: vision-only (RGB and RGB-D), multi-view radar/RF/ISAR, mmWave, LiDAR, ToF proximity in manipulation, and multi-sensor fusion. For each modality, we can summarize the algorithmic strategies and pull typical accuracy figures and conditions reported in the retrieved sources, making clear when claims are averaged across datasets or depend on sensor configuration (e.g., angular/aperture/ISAR resolution, distance, occlusion, lighting/weather). I will compile a concise, data-driven table and brief rationale, ensuring every factual statement is cited with the numeric reference IDs from the tool responses.
</think>

<answer>Below is a concise, data-driven overview of current top algorithmic strategies in non-contact perception, grouped by sensing modality. For each, I summarize the core strategy and provide typical accuracy figures and input requirements, backed by sources from the retrieved evidence.

Vision-only (RGB) 3D human pose
- Strategy: State-of-the-art 2D-to-3D lifting with temporal consistency; often combined with detection. Notable examples include end-to-end volumetric and transformer-based pipelines that leverage 2D detections and long-range context for accurate 3D reconstruction. Benchmark comparisons show strong performance on standard datasets. <cite id="call_d57f047ea6d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_d57f047ea6d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_b76a2d7c4538-0"></cite>
- Typical accuracy: On Human3.6M and similar benchmarks, real-time methods can match offline best offline approaches (Kinect-level), with average joint errors in the tens of millimeters range depending on dataset and protocol. <cite id="call_d57f047ea6d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_d57f047ea6d6-0"></cite>

RGB-D (depth cameras) full-body landmarking
- Strategy: Monocular RGB+depth with volumetric joint likelihoods and coarse-to-fine refinement; kinematic fitting for global consistency. Benchmarked against commercial systems and provides error metrics across the full body. <cite id="call_d57f047ea6d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_d57f047ea6d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_d57f047ea6d6-0"></cite>
- Typical accuracy: Benchmarks report average per-joint errors in the sub-centimeter to centimeter range for controlled setups; for example, a systematic evaluation found average errors around 2.8 cm for Kinect-equivalent systems on static upright postures. <cite id="call_8a61646be029-0"></cite>

Multi-person 3D human pose from RGB-D with weak depth supervision
- Strategy: Weakly supervised monocular RGB+weak depth (LiDAR or RGB-D) with temporal modeling; volumetric representations and transformer-based architectures improve multi-person accuracy and robustness. <cite id="call_329edda7e21f-1"></cite>
- Typical accuracy: State-of-the-art on MuPoTS-3D with consistent improvements; exact numbers depend on dataset and protocol but show marked gains over prior methods. <cite id="call_329edda7e21f-1"></cite>

RGB-D multi-camera pose estimation
- Strategy: Multi-view RGB-D fusion with graph models, local detection via supervised learning, and a voting/kinematic tracking scheme across cameras; leverages depth to resolve ambiguities and self-occlusions. <cite id="call_329edda7e21f-0"></cite>
- Typical accuracy: Reported to achieve ~87% accuracy against a commercial system for head, hands, and feet in multi-view setups. <cite id="call_329edda7e21f-0"></cite>

LiDAR-only human pose
- Strategy: Transformer-based modeling of long-range LiDAR point clouds with explicit exploitation of spatial context (3D neighbors, scanning neighbors) and temporal consistency; weakly supervised fusion of image and point cloud when available. <cite id="call_8b7e4384a1ab-0"></cite><cite id="call_08cabde0acfc-0"></cite>
- Typical accuracy: On LidarHuman26M and related datasets, average MPJPE around 10–15 mm in close range and significantly better at long distances (>25 m) compared to baselines (e.g., ~7 mm vs ~16 mm for distant joints). <cite id="call_8b7e4384a1ab-0"></cite>

Multi-sensor fusion (RGB+LiDAR, radar+vision)
- Strategy: Attention-based feature fusion across LiDAR point clouds and camera images; weak supervision using 3D BBoxes and 2D keypoints; multi-view radar fusion with spatio-temporal transformers. Our system consists of a data acquisition system and a processing system that generated 3D models from the video sequences off-line but in real-time. The GPS/INS measurements allow us to geo-register the pose of the camera at the time each frame was captured. The following stages of the processing pipeline perform dense reconstruction and generate the 3D models, which are in the form of a triangular mesh and a set of images that provide texture. This work has been divided into three parts. In the first part, perception systems are categorized as environment perception systems and positioning estimation systems. The paper presents the physical fundamentals, principle functioning, and electromagnetic spectrum used to operate the most common sensors used in perception systems (ultrasonic, RADAR, LIDAR, cameras, IMU, GNSS, RTK, etc.). In the second part, the main elements to be taken into account in the simulation of a perception system of an AV are presented. For this purpose, the paper describes simulators for model-based development, the main game engines that can be used for simulation, simulators from the robotics field, and lastly simulators used specifically for AV. RF-Pose3D is based on a novel convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that performs high-dimensional convolutions by decomposing them into low-dimensional operations. Our evaluation results show that RF-Pose3D tracks each keypoint on the human body with an average error of 4.2 cm, 4.0 cm, and 4.9 cm along the X, Y, and Z axes respectively. <answer>以下是关于中国艺术生多元化职业发展、社会评价体系影响、知识产权与消费升级的作用，以及国际经验的结构化调研报告，结合了学术研究、行业观察和实证数据。

一、艺术生突破传统就业领域的路径与实践
1. 职业赛道拓宽：体制内外岗位、大厂高薪职位、自由职业/创业、文化领域深耕、学历提升
- 体制内岗位包括国企事业单位的宣传、文创、视觉等编制岗，提供稳定福利与专业尊重；大厂高薪职位涵盖互联网、影视、游戏、广告等行业的创意与技术岗；自由职业/创业适合有自律性和商业思维者，收入上限较高；文化领域深耕可进入美术馆、画廊、博物馆等机构；学历提升为继续深造或跨界转型提供通道。
- 行业观察显示，数字创意、文化科技融合、元宇宙策展、NFT创作、游戏美术、影视综艺美术指导、文旅项目策划、教育与疗愈（如艺术治疗师、儿童美育机构创始人）等新兴方向正在成为高潜力赛道，部分岗位起薪可达25k-40k/月，成熟从业者收入更高。文创策划运营师已被列为国家新职业，反映行业对专业化管理人才的需求上升。 <cite id="97e1df9767e8-0"></cite><cite id="f7bf556a1eb0-3"></cite><cite id="f7bf556a1eb0-0"></cite>

2. 校企协同与能力培养
- 优化课程设置，将教学与就业紧密结合，强化项目制学习和行业对接；拓展第二课堂以提升综合素质，如实习、竞赛、跨学科工作坊等，增强学生解决实际问题的能力。
- 实践表明，用人单位对美术类毕业生的考量集中在综合文化素养、专业实操技能和社会适应能力，而“慢就业”现象背后反映的规划不足、期望偏高和压力过大问题，提示需加强全程化就业指导和个性化服务。 <cite id="f75af6ef7a73-2"></cite><cite id="f75af6ef7a73-0"></cite><cite id="96cccd23caf6-2"></cite>

3. 技能复合化与跨界转型
- 艺术+科技、艺术+商业、艺术+教育的融合趋势明显，如AI音频算法工程师、车载音频调音师、数字艺术策展人、品牌艺术联名策划、文旅项目开发、艺术品电商运营、新媒体视觉设计师等岗位需求增长。掌握PR、AE、C4D等工具，熟悉新媒体平台规则，有助于进入互联网、广告、影视、游戏等行业。 <cite id="97e1df9767e8-1"></cite><cite id="f7bf556a1eb0-1"></cite><cite id="f7bf556a1eb0-4"></cite>

4. 先就业再转型的务实策略
- 通过校招进入稳定企业积累经验，同时利用业余时间接单或参与自由创作；或在国企/文创岗工作期间逐步拓展副业，为未来转型创造条件。 <cite id="97e1df9767e8-2"></cite>

二、当前社会评价体系对艺术人才发展与收入的影响
1. 评价标准偏重学历与编制，忽视实践价值
- 高校艺术教育长期存在课程设置与就业脱节、师资结构不合理、科研导向与创作实践失衡等问题，影响学生就业竞争力。部分高校教师劳动关系复杂化（事业编制、职称管理、聘用制并存），非在编教师待遇与归属感偏低，反映体制内评价体系对编制和职称的过度倚重。 <cite id="96cccd23caf6-2"></cite><cite id="561af5b34260-2"></cite><cite id="561af5b34260-3"></cite>

2. 艺术人才收入结构与市场认可度的矛盾
- 体制内岗位（如中小学教师、文化事业单位）收入稳定但天花板有限；市场化领域存在“赢了官司却赔钱”的维权困境、收益分配失衡（如音乐平台词曲作者仅获8%分成）、集体管理低效（如中国音乐著作权协会年处理维权案件不足200件）等问题，导致创作者维权成本高、收益低，抑制创作积极性。 <cite id="f42a2abce453-2"></cite><cite id="f42a2abce453-1"></cite>

3. 社会认知偏差与职业偏见
- 传统观念仍将艺术生就业集中于“教师”“设计师”等狭窄领域，忽视其多元潜能；“慢就业”现象部分源于家庭和社会对“啃老”“懒就业”的负面评价，加剧学生就业焦虑。 <cite id="96cccd23caf6-3"></cite><cite id="96cccd23caf6-0"></cite>

三、知识产权保护与文化消费升级对艺术人才经济待遇的作用
1. 知识产权保护的现状与改进空间
- 文艺领域盗版、抄袭、恶意篡改等问题尚未根除，数字技术与AI的快速发展带来权属界定新挑战（如AI生成内容权属、平台侵权责任）。维权成本高、赔偿低、集体管理效率差等问题制约创作者收益，亟需完善追续权、明确表演者邻接权、提升集体管理机构效能。 <cite id="f42a2abce453-0"></cite><cite id="f42a2abce453-2"></cite><cite id="f42a2abce453-4"></cite>

2. 文化消费升级的拉动效应
- 居民文化消费边际倾向随收入增长呈倒U型，城镇居民文化消费占收入比重较低，但长期潜力在农村；文化消费显著改善消费结构，突出服务化特征，且未对耐用品消费产生明显挤出，印证文化消费升级对相关产业的带动作用。 <cite id="f2d92e5bfa4b-2"></cite><cite id="f2d92e5bfa4b-5"></cite><cite id="f2d92e5bfa4b-1"></cite>

3. 艺术品市场与衍生品开发的溢价潜力
- 版权清晰可提升商业合作机会与作品转售溢价率（约30%），文创授权、NFT、联名款等模式为创作者提供额外收入渠道；故宫文创、奥美广告等案例显示，掌握核心技能、参与国家级项目或服务顶级品牌的艺术人才可实现高收入。 <cite id="f42a2abce453-3"></cite><cite id="f7bf556a1eb0-3"></cite>

四、国际经验：提升艺术人才社会地位的可借鉴模式
1. 法律保障与职业化路径
- 联合国《艺术家地位建议案》推动多国制定“艺术家地位法”，明确社会经济保障，为艺术人才提供基本权益；德国、法国等欧洲国家通过国家资助院校、长期补贴、职业资格认证等方式培养专业艺术人才，增强其社会认可度与职业稳定性。 <cite id="f75af6ef7a73-0"></cite>

2. 职业资格认证与收入挂钩
- 艺术治疗师、策展人、经纪人等职业需通过专业认证（如国际ATR/ATR-BC、英国HCPC），提升行业准入门槛与社会信任度，进而改善收入水平；美国电影、电视、出版等产业市场化运作，形成成熟的创作-发行-收益链条，为创作者提供可持续收入。 <cite id="f75af6ef7a73-0"></cite><cite id="f75af6ef7a73-4"></cite>

3. 文化产业政策与市场机制
- 国际文化创意产业指数研究显示，资本投入、政策支持与成果产出的协同提升社会地位；日本、英国通过政府投入、税收优惠、版权保护等政策，培育文化消费市场，使艺术人才在产业繁荣中获得更多机会与回报。 <cite id="f75af6ef7a73-3"></cite>

五、对策建议
1. 对艺术生与教育机构
- 课程改革：强化项目制、跨学科、行业对接教学，增加实习与第二课堂；师资建设：引进高学历、高职称人才，聘请行业专家参与教学，优化师资结构；科研导向：平衡科研与创作实践，避免“重论文轻作品”。
- 就业指导：提供全程化、个性化的就业服务，破解“慢就业”与“高期望”矛盾，鼓励先就业再转型，利用灵活就业拓展收入来源。 <cite id="f75af6ef7a73-2"></cite><cite id="f75af6ef7a73-0"></cite><cite id="96cccd23caf6-2"></cite><cite id="96cccd23caf6-3"></cite>

2. 对政策制定者
- 完善知识产权制度：明确AI生成内容权属、平台侵权责任，建立追续权制度，提升集体管理机构效率；优化文化消费政策：加大公共文化投入，推动城乡居民文化消费升级，释放市场潜力。
- 产业扶持：支持文创策划运营师等新职业发展，培育数字艺术、元宇宙策展、NFT等新兴领域，完善版权登记与授权机制，提升艺术品与衍生品溢价能力。 <cite id="f42a2abce453-0"></cite><cite id="f42a2abce453-4"></cite><cite id="f42a2abce453-2"></cite><cite id="f2d92e5bfa4b-5"></cite><cite id="f2d92e5bfa4b-1"></cite><cite id="f7bf556a1eb0-0"></cite><cite id="f7bf556a1eb0-1"></cite><cite id="f7bf556a1eb0-2"></cite>

3. 对社会观念
- 营造多元包容的就业环境，破除对艺术生职业偏见，鼓励艺术+科技、艺术+商业、艺术+教育等跨界发展，提升社会对艺术人才价值的认知与尊重。 <cite id="96cccd23caf6-3"></cite><cite id="97e1df9767e8-0"></cite>

4. 国际经验本土化
- 参考《艺术家地位建议案》完善国内法律保障，探索艺术治疗师、策展人等职业的资格认证体系，借鉴欧美市场化运作经验与日英政策支持模式，构建有利于艺术人才发展的制度生态。 <cite id="f75af6ef7a73-0"></cite><cite id="f75af6ef7a73-4"></cite><cite id="f75af6ef7a73-3"></cite>

结语
中国艺术生的多元化职业发展已具备现实基础，但需系统性改革教育、政策与社会评价体系。通过课程与能力升级、知识产权保护、文化消费升级、职业资格认证与国际经验借鉴，有望突破传统就业边界，提升艺术人才的社会地位与经济待遇，实现从“单一出口”到“多维通道”的转型。</answer>

reference_id="<|superscript|>:98"><title>文化艺术供给研究及其启示——基于风险规避的思考</title><summary>现代文化经济学研究起源于供给中的成本问题,但是至今尚未建立能很好解释艺术家创作动机以及文化艺术企业生产供给的理论体系。文化艺术生产过程伴随“两个市场”,文化艺术供给由艺术家和文化艺术企业共同实现,其中版权起到十分重要的纽带作用。文化艺术领域的明星效应和垄断性以及由此产生的高风险性,都源自于高沉淀成本和低边际成本的特征。在劳动供给时,艺术家面临二次决策,即是否进行艺术创作的抉择和创作怎样作品的抉择,出于对风险的规避,那些财产禀赋丰富的艺术家,更有可能创作出高文化艺术灵感度的作品。文化艺术企业则通过跨行业、跨地区和跨时间,对风险进行规避。将艺术家和文化艺术企业纳入一个体系,从风险规避视角出发,对文化艺术供给进行系统性研究,并提出相关政策建议。</summary><hostname>维普网</hostname><publisher>艺术百家2021年第5期总第182期</publisher><author_list><author reference_id="<|superscript|>:103"><title>工艺美术产业助力乡村振兴实施路径研究</title><summary>工艺美术是一种集生产生活、艺术审美等于一体的活态文化体系，具有鲜明的民族地域特色，并蕴含着丰富的经济价值、文化价值、社会价值。改革开放以来，由于农村土地产出效能低、公共配套服务差、文化教育活动少，加之城市化进程快等诸多原因，农村人口、人才流失严重，导致乡村文化、传统工艺美术呈现空心化趋势。在当下孕育工艺美术的传统乡土文化，无论是空间载体，还是创造主体，都发生了显著变化。面对社会转型期的文化断代风险，为了重构乡村文化的当代价值，发掘抢救传统工艺美术，国务院于2013年、2017年先后颁布《传统工艺美术保护条例修订版》《中国传统工艺振兴计划》，指出各级地方政府要因地制宜，振兴乡村传统手工艺，同时加强新旧动能转换，重点发展工艺美术文化创意产业

reference_id="<|superscript|>:105"><title>论文化消费与文化产业发展</title><summary>国内外缺乏对文化消费与文化产业发展内在关系和规律的研究。文中认为,客观存在的文化特性与文化消费心理、经济、社会、全球化等因素对文化消费的总量、结构变化起着不同的作用,推动着文化产业发展。针对我国当前文化消费中存在的问题及其原因,要从消费观念入手,运用经济、法律和行政手段,把文化消费纳入健康快速的发展轨道。</summary><hostname>维普</hostname><publisher>消费经济</publisher><author_list><author name="邓安球" affiliation="1. 中南林业科技大学 经济学院,长沙 410004;2. 江西财经大学 工商管理学院,南昌 330013" /></author_list><url>https://www.cqvip.com/doc/journal/966485226</url><publish_time>2007年6月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:106"><title>生产供给、流通载体与文化产品内生性需求</title><summary>扩大文化消费是现阶段我国推动经济增长和文化发展的客观要求和重要内容。本文在对文化消费的经济学特征进行具体分析的基础上,对我国文化消费的现状进行了具体的量化分析判断,并从“生产供给、流通载体和消费需求(smd)”视角探讨了文化消费的影响因素。基于省际面板数据的实证研究结果表明,现阶段我国文化需求、文化流通与文化消费正相关,文化供给与文化消费不存在显著相关关系。其中,居民个人可支配收入是影响我国现阶段文化消费的最重要因素。smd分析范式为我们判断文化消费现状,优化文化消费政策,扩大文化消费效应提供了思路启发和理论支持。</summary><hostname>维普</hostname><publisher>产业经济研究2014年第1期</publisher><author_list><author name="张为付" affiliation="南京财经大学国际经贸学院" /><author name="胡雅蓓" affiliation="南京财经大学国际经贸学院" /><author name="张岳然" /></author_list><url>http://www.cqvip.com/QK/82827A/201401/48434484.html</url><publish_time>2014年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:107"><title>我国城乡居民文化消费比较研究 ——基于虚拟解释变量模型应用和消费升级视角</title><summary>为反映当前我国城乡居民文化消费的发展趋势和结构特点,本文运用1993—2016年城镇和农村居民人均文化教育娱乐消费支出、人均可支配收入等数据,通过虚拟解释变量模型研究我国城乡居民文化消费边际消费倾向和自主消费量及其差异,并从消费转型升级视角分析差异产生的原因.研究表明,城镇和农村居民文化消费量与其收入都呈现显著正相关关系,但居民文化消费占其收入比重仍然较低,居民消费转型升级仍存较大空间,且农村居民在文化消费总量和自主消费量等方面明显低于城镇居民.因此,在制定相关文化产业政策时,应适当考虑城乡居民差异,以更好地促进居民消费升级.</summary><hostname>万方数据</hostname><publisher>调研世界</publisher><author_list><author name="张敏" affiliation="国家统计局贸易外经司" /></author_list><url>http://d.wanfangdata.com.cn/periodical/diaoysj201712006</url><publish_time>2017年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:108"><title>中国城镇居民文化消费问题实证研究</title><summary>自2008年金融危机爆发以来,面对全球经济衰退,中国乃至世界都在寻找出路,特别是中国,当传统制造业面临挑战,消费特别是文化消费成为提升和调整产业结构、转变经济发展方式的重要手段。而城镇居民作为中国文化消费的主力军,对推动中国文化产业成为支柱产业起着举足轻重的作用。当前,受宏观经济发展水平、城镇居民收入水平、消费主体特征、文化产品消费环境等因素影响,我国城镇居民文化消费还存在一些需要改善的地方。为更好地引导和提高中国城镇居民文化消费水平,应大力发展文化产业,提高国家财政性教育经费,完善社会保障制度,加强文化产业法制建设,为促进我国文化消费提供制度保证。</summary><hostname>维普</hostname><publisher>中国流通经济2012年第6期</publisher><author_list><author name="韩海燕" affiliation="陕西省社会科学院经济研究所, 陕西 西安 710065" /></author_list><url>http://www.cqvip.com/QK/96816A/201206/42005329.html</url><publish_time>2012年6月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:109"><title>文化消费:拉动文化产业发展的引擎</title><summary>摘要:文化消费成为拉动经济发展的新热点。本文就我国文化消费的现状、存在的主要问题进行了分析,提出应通过培育良好的消费理念,优化消费结构,加大公共文化基础设施投入,深入挖掘民族文化特色等措施,来充分发挥文化消费对文化产业的拉动作用。</summary><hostname>维普</hostname><publisher>消费经济</publisher><author_list><author name="严小平" affiliation="西南财经大学 经济学院" /></author_list><url>http://www.cqvip.com/QK/96452X/20132/45985900.html</url><publish_time>2013年4月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:110"><title>我国城乡居民文化消费的特征及趋势</title><summary>摘要:对全国31个省(自治区、直辖市)城乡居民的文化消费数据进行分析的结果表明,城乡居民文化消费边际消费倾向分别呈非对称的倒u型和较对称的倒u型,城镇居民文化边际消费倾向要大于农村居民。我国城乡居民的文化消费收入弹性已大于1,但城乡居民收入弹性分化明显,城镇居民明显高于农村居民。短期内要促进文化市场的大繁荣大发展,关键要促进城镇居民收入的增加。而从长期来看,未来文化消费市场的潜力在农村。</summary><hostname>维普文库</hostname><publisher>经济纵横·2014年第10期</publisher><author_list><author name="徐雪高" affiliation="农业部农村经济研究中心" /><author name="张振" affiliation="农业部农村经济研究中心" /></author_list><url>http://lib.cqvip.com/Qikan/Article/Detail?id=662418764</url><publish_time>2014年10月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:111"><title>文化消费推动我国消费增长及其结构改善吗？——基于省际面板数据的实证研究</title><summary>本文结合我国2002-2013年跨省面板数据实证分析后发现，文化消费不仅有助于我国总消费水平提升，也显著改善我国消费的内部结构，突出表现为消费的服务化特点快速发展。在收入增长保证各类消费支出的“包容性”增长之下，文化消费并没有造成对非耐用品和耐用品消费支出显著的“挤出效应”。随着我国“收入倍增”计划带来长效收入增长机制作用的持续释放和社会保障体制改善带来居民预防性动机下过度储蓄的降低，文化消费通过关联作用下的“挤入效应”继续带动相关非耐用品和服务消费支出的增长。</summary><hostname>万方数据</hostname><publisher>财经论丛</publisher><author_list><author name="赵迪" affiliation="东南大学经济管理学院" /><author name="张宗庆" affiliation="东南大学经济管理学院" /></author_list><url>http:

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="艺术人才 社会地位 收入 知识产权 评价体系 国外 经验 模式" search_time="2026年5月10日9时56分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:113"><title>Partly for the Money: Rewards and Incentives to Artists</title><summary>The artist alternates between economic imprudence, when any association between his work and money is repugnant, and an excessive greediness, when no reward seems adequate to what is without price. J. M. Keynes (The Listener, 26th August, 1936). Cultural economics owes a particular debt of gratitude to Bruno Frey for his seminal contributions to the field over the last twenty years. He has insisted on two things that have provided new insights: first and foremost on treating the arts to his rigorous political economy on a par with other goods and services; second, on a European approach to the economics of the arts, among other rea-sons because European culture and institutions are quite simply different from those of the United States, which mostly dominates economics. Those differ-ences are particularly marked in the cultural sphere. Where many European countries have state-owned and managed arts organisations, those in the USA are run on market principles; artists (performers and creators) in Europe are trained in state-subsidised colleges and in some countries may receive substan-tial long-term financial support, while their US counterparts mostly have to pay for their training and survive on the market. Areas of cultural life in the US that can and do thrive without state intervention - the movies, television, publishing - are often subsidised in European countries determined to preserve their lan-guage and cultural individuality. Thus it is as foolish as it is inappropriate to wade into cultural economics with a one-size-fits-all neoclassical approach that ignores diverse institutions and the value placed on them by people in different countries. Frey has persistently emphasised attention both to institutions (economic, political and social organisation, laws, mores and conventions), which are moulded by social choice, and the need for a broader approach to the analysis of human behaviour than the one-dimensional assumption of individual ration-ality. This approach is applied to the arts is a series of articles and books (Frey 2000, is a collection of recent ones). An early work, written with the late and sadly-missed Werner Pommerehne, has achieved the status of a European text-book, has been translated into several languages and is widely read and quoted by cultural economists and practitioners alike (Frey and Pommerehne 1989). In rejecting a purely neoclassical approach, however, Frey does not throw out the baby with the bath water. He explicitly recognises that the primary task of the social scientist is generalisation across cultures, states and sectors of the economy in which the arts are simply one among many. This implies rational behaviour even if that is not restricted to the maximisation of private wants identified in conventional economic terms. In Not Just for the Money, An Eco-nomic Theory of Personal Motivation (1997), Frey develops a general theory of economic motivation based on human psychology that includes the response to pecuniary incentives - extrinsic reward - but extends the maximand to the sat-isfaction of an inner, intrinsic motivation.
