reference_id="<|superscript|>:126"><title>安徽省高校艺术设计专业师资现状调查与分析</title><summary>采用问卷调查、数理统计、访谈和逻辑分析等方法，对安徽省高校艺术设计专业师资现状进行研究。研究表明：在安徽省高校艺术设计专业教师中，35周岁以下的人数比例较大、主讲教师的人数比例偏低、高学历和高职称的人数比例极小、美术学及其他专业的人数比例偏高和来自省内综合院校的人数比例较高等结构不够合理现象。建议有关高校聘请社会上或其他学校一些行业专家、学术专家做客座教授或兼职教师，加大对高学历、高职称人才的引进力度，注重吸收省外综合院校和艺术类院校的毕业生，建立合理的劳务分配和人事管理激励机制等方面入手，切实改善艺术设计专业的师资现状。</summary><hostname>维普</hostname><publisher>皖西学院学报</publisher><cite_count>2</cite_count><author_list><author name="韩玉婷" /></author_list><url>http://www.cqvip.com/QK/90034A/20084/28247169.html</url><publish_time>2008年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:127"><title>我国艺术大学的设置标准探析</title><summary>我国艺术大学的设置具有现实可行性，导致我国至今没有艺术大学的原因是设置标准问题，即教育部《普通本科学校设置暂行规定》以综合类大学标准来用于艺术大学设置。本文以我国高等艺术教育发展现状和高等艺术教育特点为基础，从办学规模、学科与专业、师资队伍、教学与科研水平、基础设施五方面作深入的分析，提出专门针对艺术大学的设置标准。</summary><hostname>四川音乐学院图书馆</hostname><publisher>《吉林艺术学院学报》</publisher><author_list><author name="宋显彪" affiliation="四川音乐学院图书馆 四川音乐学院流行音乐学院" /><author name="邱昌杰" /><author name="冷静" /></author_list><url>http://lib.sccm.cn/uploadfile/file/20160419/20160419144453_721.pdf</url><publish_time>2015年6月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:128"><title>我国高校教师劳动关系的历史脉络、现实问题与理应进路</title><summary>高校教师劳动关系是基于知识生产、学术劳动，体现一定的权利与义务，在高校与教师之间形成的法律、经济和社会关系的总和。新中国成立以来，我国高校教师劳动关系主要经历了事业编制时期、职称管理时期、聘用任命时期与多元用工时期，分别呈现集权化、自主化、契约化、复杂化的阶段性特征。当前，我国高校教师劳动关面临三重现实困境，即高校教师法律制度不完善引发法律关系问题、经济制度不完善激化经济关系矛盾以及管理制度不完善导致社会关系不融洽。这些现实问题主要表现在高校教师法律权利不明确、法律地位失衡、经济收入差距较大、职业归属感缺乏等方面。新时代我国高校教师劳动关系需要构建以劳动法为内核的法律关系、以公平有效为准则的经济关系、以人为本和谐为原则的社会关系，从而推动新时代高校教师劳动关系和谐发展。</summary><hostname>西南大学期刊社</hostname><publisher>教师教育学报</publisher><author_list><author name="张金丹" affiliation="厦门大学教育研究院" /></author_list><url>https://xbgjxt.swu.edu.cn/data/article/preview-pdf?doi=10.13718/j.cnki.jsjy.2023.05.006</url><publish_time>2023年9月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:129"><title>非在编教师生存状况的调查研究</title><summary>采用问卷调查和访谈等研究方法，以深圳市的非在编教师为研究对象，对非在编教师的生存状况进行调查。研究表明：非在编教师的经济待遇、工作环境较差，职业认同感、社会认同感较低，与在编教师存在明显差距。主要表现为工资水平差距明显，福利待遇满意度较低；工作负担重，工作考核严苛，工作压力大；非在编教师的职业认同感、社会归属感普遍偏低。将非在编教师归属于弱势教师群体具有相当的可证性，其生存现状亟待改善。政府应加大经费投入和政策扶持力度，提高非在编教师的工资待遇；改革人事制度，优化非在编教师队伍结构；学校应逐步构建和谐的管理和评价机制，缓解非在编教师的从业压力。</summary><hostname>西南大学期刊社</hostname><publisher>教师教育学报</publisher><author_list><author name="高聪聪" affiliation="深圳大学师范学院" /><author name="李臣之" affiliation="深圳大学师范学院" /><author name="吴秋连" affiliation="深圳大学师范学院" /></author_list><url>https://xbgjxt.swu.edu.cn/data/article/preview-pdf?doi=10.13718/j.cnki.jsjy.2015.05.011</url><publish_time>2015年10月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:130"><title>艺术学科教师科研能力、现状与意愿的量化分析——以天津市高校为例</title><summary>针对艺术学升为门类后对艺术学科科研活动质量要求的提升，以天津高校艺术学教师为样本，设计个人信息、科研信息和主观意愿类问卷，并根据反馈结果进行量化分析，以考察作为艺术学科科研活动主力军的艺术学教师的科研能力、现状和意愿，为制定更为合理的科研策略和科研管理办法、改善科研环境提供数据和理论支持，为提升中国艺术学科建设水平作出贡献。</summary><hostname>维普</hostname><publisher>天津市教科院学报</publisher><author_list><author name="王鹤" affiliation="天津大学建筑学院" /><author name="侯黎明" affiliation="天津大学建筑学院" /><author name="华欣" affiliation="天津科技大学经济与管理学院" /></author_list><url>http://www.cqvip.com/QK/82179X/201904/7002779733.html</url><publish_time>2019年8月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:131"><title>1+X证书制度下民办高职院校室内艺术设计专业“双师型”师资队伍建设研究</title><summary>1+X证书制度要求学生在获得学历证书的基础上取得职业技能等级证书,实现学历教育与职业培训的融合。该制度对室内艺术设计专业师资提出了职业技能导向教学能力、行业实践经验和产教融合协调能力等新要求,教师需要具备理论教学和实践指导能力,将行业技术标准融入教学活动。民办高职院校室内艺术设计专业“双师型”师资队伍建设存在不足,师资结构方面职称层次偏低,双师素质认定与培养方面标准缺乏统一性、培养体系不完善、企业实践机会少,行业资源整合方面与行业联系松散、专家资源利用效率低、实训基地建设脱节。构建“双师型”师资队伍建设体系需建立多元化招聘与引进机制,将行业经验、项目经历纳入考核指标;构建系统化培训发展体系,完善技能认证机制;深化产教融合合作模式,实现师资共建共享,推行项目驱动教学,配套制度保障和政策支持,建立薪酬激励制度和职业发展通道,构建质量监控体系。“双师型”师资队伍建设能够提高教学质量和人才培养水平,增强学生就业竞争力,为室内艺术设计专业培养高素质技术技能人才。</summary><hostname>维普网</hostname><publisher>《艺术科技》</publisher><author_list><author name="廖荍[1]" /></author_list><url>http://m.qikan.cqvip.com/Article/ArticleDetail?id=7201304430</url><publish_time>2025年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><d

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="文化消费 中国 2023 2024 数据 文化产业 占GDP 比重" search_time="2026年5月10日9时56分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:144"><title>繁荣发展社会主义文化，促进人民精神生活共同富裕</title><summary>摘要:文化是丰富人民生活的重要精神食粮,促进精神富有、丰富人民精神世界是中国式现代化的本质要求。我国的文化强国建设“始终坚持文化建设着眼于人、落脚于人”。《中共中央关于制定国民经济和社会发展第十五个五年规划的建议》在总结我国文化事业和文化产业发展所取得的历史性成就基础上,根据“十五五”时期文化建设与人民群众的精神文化需求出现的新特征、新趋向,提出了“激发全民族文化创新创造活力,繁荣发展社会主义文化”的重大任务,着眼满足人民群众多样化、多层次、多方面的精神文化需求,提升文化服务和文化产品供给能力的新要求与新路径,以更加丰富人民精神文化生活,增强人民群众文化获得感、幸福感。</summary><hostname>当代中国研究所</hostname><author_list><author name="欧阳雪梅" affiliation="中国社会科学院当代中国研究所 北京100009" /></author_list><url>http://www.iccs.cn/yjcs/202603/P020260316531180939284.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:145"><title>中国文化产业投入产出表编制、规模测度及波及效应研究</title><summary>文章基于2002—2020年我国投入产出表数据，运用最新的国民经济行业分类和文化产业分类标准，将传统的投入产出表转换为以文化产业为核心的投入产出表，运用分劈系数将文化产业从国民经济其他行业中剥离出来，测算出文化产业增加值，并进一步对文化产业的波及效应进行分析。结果显示：2002—2020年，我国文化产业增加值规模从2002年的1.07万亿元增加至2020年的8.67万亿元，文化产业已成为我国国民经济发展中的支柱产业；文化产业核心层部门在总产出和增加值规模上远高于文化产业相关层部门以及其他非文化产业部门。波及效应分析结果表明，我国文化产业核心层部门呈现高拉动力、高推动力特征，基础性产业特征显著；而文化产业相关层部门呈现低拉动力、低推动力特征，对其他产业的影响较小。</summary><hostname>维普网</hostname><publisher>统计与决策</publisher><author_list><author name="陈亮" affiliation="兰州财经大学 统计与数据科学学院" /></author_list><url>http://m.qikan.cqvip.com/Article/ArticleDetail?id=7112992727</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:146"><title>Exploring the Development Status and Stylistic Characteristics of National Wave Art Based on the Background of Cultural and Creative Economy</title><summary>In recent years, the national trend has become increasingly popular, and the art of national trend is the beginning of the production field’s skillful utilization of national art, dedication to category innovation, and making the product have a “root” and a “soul”. This paper combines the sparse principal component analysis method and the entropy weight TOPSIS comprehensive evaluation method to analyze the development level of national tide art in the context of the cultural and creative economy. At the same time, the VGG16 deep learning network is used to extract the depth features of style features in the images of Guochao art-related products, and the Softmax function is used to recognize and classify the features of style features of Guochao art to get the main style features of Guochao art industry. The study shows that the added value of Shaanxi Province’s Guochao art industry accounts for 4.14% of the province’s total GDP by 2023. The cultural, leisure, and entertainment service industry is developing rapidly, providing impetus for the development of the national tide art industry. Meanwhile, it is found that the style characteristics of Shaanxi Province’s national tide art industry appear to change with the development of the sector, and the Shanghai Fine Arts Factory style dominates the style characteristics by 2023 (0.359). This paper sets the foundation for the growth of the Guochao art industry and provides a useful reference for identifying style characteristics in the development of Guochao art.</summary><hostname>Sciendo</hostname><publisher>Applied Mathematics and Nonlinear Sciences</publisher><author_list><author name="Yan Wang" affiliation="Yunnan Communications Vocational and Technical College, Kunming, Yunnan, 650500, China" /></author_list><url>https://sciendo.com/pdf/10.2478/amns-2024-1887</url><publish_time>2024年8月5日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:147"><title>文化消费视角下我国文化产业发展PEST分析</title><summary>文化消费体现了一国经济及相关产业的发达程度。对比国际,我国的文化消费规模与经济发展程度不匹配,文化消费的水平远低于经济发展水平。基于文化消费的视角,对我国文化产业的发展进行pest分析,总体上看,我国发展文化产业在政治、经济、社会以及科技四个方面的优势大于劣势,应着力从优化文化产业顶层设计、实现文化民主化、培养青少年的文化素养等方面促进文化产业发展。</summary><hostname>维普网</hostname><publisher>山西经济管理干部学院学报</publisher><author_list><author name="罗艳" affiliation="广东省外语艺术职业学院" /></author_list><url>http://m.qikan.cqvip.com/Article/ArticleDetail?id=7104594496</url><publish_time>2021年3月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:148"><title>文化产业运行情况及发展趋势分析</title><summary>当前，我国文化产业正处于快速发展阶段，子行业普遍已从起步期进入成长期，对国民经济的贡献度稳中有升，文化及

<answer>Here is a data-driven, structured set of strategies to enhance classroom participation (on-task behavior) for students with autism, supported by single-case design studies and meta-analyses already retrieved:

1. Build clear, ABA-informed behavioral contexts:
   - Use clear antecedent cues, discriminative stimuli, and predictable routines to highlight task demands and reduce confusion.
   - Implement errorless learning and programmed generalization to support skill initiation and reduce errors that disrupt engagement.
   - Ensure data-based, individualized instruction with consistency and systematic error monitoring to establish functional relationships between context and behavior. <cite id="2"></cite>

2. Provide visual supports and structure:
   - Introduce picture schedules, first/then boards, and visual timers to:
     - Anticipate transitions and reduce anxiety around non-preferred tasks.
     - Increase on-task rates by clarifying expectations and motivating preferred activities.
     - Reduce transition-related disruptions by up to 45% in some studies. <cite id="43"></cite><cite id="54"></cite>
   - Teach students to use self-monitoring tools (e.g., happy-face checklists) to promote attending to task and accuracy; maintain effects across weeks. <cite id="52"></cite>

3. Teach self-monitoring and self-management:
   - Train students to self-monitor on-task behavior with simple feedback systems (e.g., checklists or tokens), which can increase task engagement and reduce stereotyped behaviors while maintaining performance over time. <cite id="52"></cite>
   - Use self-management strategies (e.g., self-monitoring with environmental supports) to improve adherence to classroom tasks and reduce off-task behavior. <cite id="1"></cite>

4. Antecedent-based compliance training:
   - Sequence high-probability requests before low-probability ones (HPRS), a practice with strong evidence (Tau-U = .87) for increasing compliance in students with ASD. <cite id="call_ef2142ad96ed-0"></cite>
   - Implement errorless academic compliance training by fading requests from high to low compliance probabilities; this improves compliance and covariant on-task skills. <cite id="call_aac7315542ae-1"></cite>

5. Video prompting for academic tasks:
   - Paraprofessionals can deliver video-prompted instruction to teach academic skills; across participants and skills, correct responding increases, demonstrating effectiveness in inclusive settings. <cite id="call_2dc9663f12ee-1"></cite>

6. Incorporate choice and autonomy:
   - Intersperse preferred tasks with non-preferred ones and offer choice (e.g., choice boards) to decrease latency to begin tasks, improve task rate and interest, and reduce disruptions. <cite id="call_99b1d9fb5259-1"></cite>

7. Peer-mediated social skills interventions:
   - School-based peer-mediated social competence interventions (e.g., peer tutoring, social networks, teaching interaction procedures) produce moderate-to-large effects on engagement and social participation for children and adolescents with ASD. <cite id="call_add74007e531-0"></cite>

8. Sensory supports (brief sensory breaks):
   - Introduce brief, scheduled sensory activities (e.g., sensory diets) during the school day; reductions in problematic behaviors and increases in engagement can persist even after intervention withdrawal. <cite id="call_fd689a3d1677-0"></cite>

9. Cooperative and inclusive group work:
   - Use cooperative learning structures (e.g., tutoring, team activities) during academic content delivery; increases academic engagement, knowledge gains, and peer interaction for students with ASD in general education settings. <cite id="call_c1e4029dbc59-0"></cite>

10. Picture activity schedules and graduated guidance:
    - Teach students to follow picture activity schedules with graduated guidance; increases on-task/on-schedule behavior and generalizes to novel activities, supporting independent functioning in inclusive environments. <cite id="call_df96d7f461e1-1"></cite>

Implementation notes:
- Pair interventions with performance feedback for teachers and staff to improve fidelity of evidence-based practices (e.g., feedback on implementation levels) and ensure interventions are delivered as intended. <cite id="1"></cite>
- Use individualized, data-based decision-making (e.g., compliance hierarchies, visual schedules tailored to student preferences) to optimize motivation and reduce resistance. <cite id="call_aac7315542ae-1"></cite><cite id="43"></cite>
- Combine multiple supports (visual schedules + self-monitoring + choice) to address both environmental structure and student self-regulation. <cite id="52"></cite><cite id="43"></cite><cite id="call_99b1d9fb5259-1"></cite>

All strategies are grounded in single-case research and meta-analyses of classroom interventions; effects sizes and maintenance data are reported in the cited studies.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="token economy classroom on-task behavior students with autism meta-analysis school-based" search_time="2026年5月10日9时57分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:65"><title>Improving Treatment Plan Implementation in Schools: A Meta-analysis of Single Subject Design Studies</title><summary>Twenty-nine peer-reviewed journal articles that analyzed intervention implementation in schools using single-case experimental designs were meta-analyzed. These studies reported 171 separate data paths and provided 3,991 data points. The meta-analysis was accomplished by fitting data extracted from graphs in mixed linear growth models. This analytic approach was adopted to provide a model whose assumptions were met and could model both level and trend. The extent to which interventions were implemented as planned in baseline was low with a downward trend. Performance feedback, performance feedback augmented with additional procedures, and self-monitoring with environmental supports were found to be highly effective for improving intervention implementation. Follow-up meetings without review of implementation data were ineffective. Maintenance data were positive across studies. Implications of the results for future research and practice are discussed.</summary><hostname>Academia.edu</hostname><publisher>Journal of Behavioral Education</publisher><author_list><author name="George H Noell" affiliation="Department of Psychology, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA 70803, USA" /><author name="Kristin A Gansle" affiliation="School of Education, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA 70803, USA" /><author name="Joanna Lomas Mevers" affiliation="Marcus Autism Center, Atlanta, GA, USA" /><author name="R Maria Knox" affiliation="Louisiana Department of Education, Baton Rouge, LA, USA" /><author name="Joslyn Cynkus Mintz" affiliation="Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, Kennedy Krieger Institute, Neurobehavioral Unit Outpatient Clinic, 9810 Patuxent Woods Drive, Suite F, Columbia, MD 21046, USA" /><author name="Amanda Dahir" affiliation="Autism Spectrum Therapies, Seattle, WA, USA" /></author_list><url>https://www.academia.edu/download/47160026/s10864-013-9177-120160711-5935-7k10hc.pdf</url><publish_time>2013年7月17日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:66"><title>A systematic evaluation of token economies as a classroom management tool for students with challenging behavior</title><summary>A two-part systematic review was undertaken to assess the effectiveness of token economies in increasing rates of appropriate classroom behavior for students demonstrating behavioral difficulties. Method: A single subject A-B-A design was used with three children attending 1st and 2nd-grade level special education classes in an urban public school. However, the research on best practice is varied, presenting difficulty for practitioners to assess the appropriateness of each support.
Objective: To provide evidence-informed recommendations regarding best practices in school-based supports for students with sensory processing challenges via a Rapid Evidence Assessment of current literature.
Data Sources: Searches were run in CINAHL Complete, Education Research Complete, ERIC, Medline, PsycINFO, and Scopus (published 2010-2023). Informed by a 2010 review, articles citing publications identified in the prior review were also included here.
Study Selection and Data Collection: A reviewer screened the Title and Abstract of each article for inclusion, and another screened the resultant Full-Texts, with 10% of each reviewer’s articles assessed by the other. Interrater reliability was excellent.
Findings: Sixty-one articles were included in the review, with only 15% constituting good evidence (adequate, 38%; poor, 31% & reviews, 16%). No support could be wholly recommended without caveats, but there was some evidence that sound amplification systems, alternate seating, and multisensory environments (MSEs) may be beneficial in some conditions or with certain populations. The use of weighted vests is not recommended.
Conclusions and Relevance: Most research was challenged by small sample size and inconsistent protocols, highlighting the importance of ongoing research. Evidence-informed practitioners should review research findings carefully and integrate evidence from comprehensive clinical assessment and understanding of the child, school and family context when assessing the appropriateness of a support for each student.</summary><hostname>

<think>
I will synthesize the neutrophil role across acute and chronic stroke phases, map interactions and mechanistic pathways linking neutrophil subsets to clinical outcomes, and propose future work, citing the already retrieved sources that discuss neutrophil polarization (N1/N2), temporal dynamics, NETs, functional plasticity, PPARγ modulation, flow cytometry-defined harmful/senescent subsets, CD62L and age-related atypical neutrophils, and translational perspectives.
</think>

<answer>Overview and temporal evolution of neutrophil function in brain ischemia
- First responders: Neutrophils are the earliest peripheral immune cells to enter the brain after ischemic stroke, with rapid mobilization from bone marrow and spleen, chemotaxis in blood, and infiltration into brain parenchyma or perivascular spaces within hours of occlusion. They reach peak levels at 1–3 days post-onset and then decline, with functional heterogeneity and high plasticity that can shift between proinflammatory and resolution-oriented states <cite id="call_2744df9e124b-0"></cite><cite id="call_e3a38636ae26-0"></cite>.
- Acute phase dominance: Early neutrophils are largely proinflammatory (N1-like), contributing to injury via ROS, proteases, reverse transendothelial migration, NETosis, BBB disruption, thrombosis, and direct neurotoxicity; neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) peak between 1–3 days and exacerbate damage by compromising the BBB and promoting clot formation <cite id="call_e3a38636ae26-0"></cite><cite id="call_7ae88c44f6cd-0"></cite><cite id="call_87"></cite>.
- Chronic phase shift: Over days to weeks, the N1/N2 ratio evolves, with increasing anti-inflammatory/neuroprotective (N2-like) neutrophils that secrete neurotrophic factors and modulate microglia/macrophage polarization toward M2 via efferocytosis and TGF-β release, supporting repair and resolution <cite id="call_e3a38636ae26-0"></cite><cite id="call_75d086b0afe5-1"></cite><cite id="call_75d086b0afe5-0"></cite>.
- Subset heterogeneity in blood: Circulating neutrophils show activation (lower CD62L, higher CD11b, increased ROS and neutrophil elastase), with expanded harmful/senescent subsets (CXCR4high/CD62Ldim) and reverse transmigrating (CD54high/CXCR1low) neutrophils associated with clinical severity in acute stroke; these reflect a dysregulated activation/apoptosis balance that may worsen BBB breakdown and systemic inflammation <cite id="call_95"></cite><cite id="call_3df32e6cf678-0"></cite>.
- Age-related changes: In aged stroke, emergency granulopoiesis generates CD101+CD62L− and CD177hi/CD177−CD62L− immature/atypical neutrophils in blood with heightened oxidative stress, phagocytosis, and procoagulant features; these subsets produce CXCL3 and are linked to worse reperfusion and outcomes in elderly patients <cite id="call_7ae88c44f6cd-0"></cite>.

Mechanistic interactions and pathways linking neutrophil subsets to clinical outcomes
- Proinflammatory N1 neutrophils and NETs:
  - Direct injury: ROS, proteases, and NETs disrupt BBB integrity and induce thrombosis, worsening early infarct expansion and edema <cite id="call_87"></cite><cite id="call_ae3b4896ec4a-0"></cite>.
  - Cell-cell crosstalk: Reverse transendothelial migration (CD54high/CXCR1low) increases BBB permeability; efferocytosis of apoptotic neutrophils by microglia/macrophages skews them toward anti-inflammatory/healing (M2) phenotypes; neutrophil cannibalism elevates TGF-β, which can drive N2 polarization and reduce neuroinflammation <cite id="call_3df32e6cf678-0"></cite><cite id="call_75d086b0afe5-1"></cite>.
- Anti-inflammatory/neuroprotective N2 neutrophils:
  - Resolution signals: Release of anti-inflammatory mediators and neurotrophic factors; TGF-β and other signals from neutrophil clearance promote microglia/macrophage M2 polarization and tissue repair <cite id="call_e3a38636ae26-0"></cite><cite id="call_75d086b0afe5-1"></cite>.
  - Plasticity regulation: PPARγ agonists (e.g., rosiglitazone) reduce neutrophil infiltration and shift their phenotype toward resolution, improving outcome in experimental stroke; this aligns with the concept that N2-like neutrophils can temper inflammation and support recovery <cite id="call_26"></cite><cite id="call_75d086b0afe5-1"></cite>.
- Circulating harmful subsets:
  - Activation and senescence: Basal hyperactivation (CD62Llow/CD11bhigh), increased ROS and neutrophil elastase, and expansion of CXCR4high/CD62Ldim senescent neutrophils correlate with NIH Stroke Scale severity; these subsets likely amplify systemic inflammation and BBB breakdown, contributing to worse clinical outcomes <cite id="call_3df32e6cf678-0"></cite>.
  - Age-related atypical subsets: CD101+CD62L− and CD177hi/CD177−CD62L− neutrophils in blood produce CXCL3 and exhibit heightened oxidative stress and procoagulant activity, linking emergency granulopoiesis to worse reperfusion and functional recovery in older patients <cite id="call_7ae88c44f6cd-0"></cite>.

Predictive framework: N1/N2 balance and subset dynamics → clinical outcomes
- Poor outcomes are associated with:
  - High early N1 burden: Peak neutrophils at 1–3 days with NET-rich, ROS/protease-driven injury and BBB compromise; harmful/senescent subsets (CXCR4high/CD62Ldim) and reverse transmigrating neutrophils; age-related atypical subsets producing CXCL3 and procoagulant factors <cite id="call_e3a38636ae26-0"></cite><cite id="call_3df32e6cf678-0"></cite><cite id="call_7ae88c44f6cd-0"></cite>.
  - Impaired resolution: Reduced N2-like neutrophils and efferocytosis; failure to shift toward anti-inflammatory/neurotrophic states and microglia/macrophage M2 polarization <cite id="call_e3a38636ae26-0"></cite><cite id="call_75d086b0afe5-1"></cite>.
- Better outcomes are linked to:
  - Emerging N2-like neutrophils and resolution pathways: TGF-β-mediated microglia/macrophage skewing, efferocytosis-driven anti-inflammatory signals, and neutrophil cannibalism that elevate TGF-β <cite id="call_e3a38636ae26-0"></cite><cite id="call_75d086b0afe5-1"></cite>.
  - PPARγ-driven modulation: Reduction in infiltration and shift toward resolution, as shown by rosiglitazone in experimental stroke <cite id="call_26"></cite>.

Future directions for research and translation
- Mechanistic dissection of neutrophil plasticity:
  - Define temporal N1/N2 (and emerging N2a/N2b) trajectories in stroke using single-cell and spatial omics to map subset-specific gene programs, transcriptional regulators, and functional switches in brain parenchyma versus blood <cite id="call_e3a38636ae26-0"></cite><cite id="call_55"></cite><cite id="call_63"></cite>.
- Subset-specific interventions:
  - Target harmful subsets (CXCR4high/CD62Ldim, reverse transmigrating) and enhance resolution subsets via PPARγ agonists or other inducers of N2-like features; validate in preclinical models whether modulating the N1/N2 ratio improves outcome without compromising early host defense <cite id="call_3df32e6cf678-0"></cite><cite id="call_26"></cite>.
- NET biology and clearance:
  - Develop DNase-based therapies to degrade NETs in the acute phase while preserving their antimicrobial role; assess effects on BBB integrity, thrombosis, and long-term repair <cite id="call_87"></cite><cite id="call_ae3b4896ec4a-0"></cite>.
- Age-related neutrophil dysregulation:
  - Rejuvenate hematopoiesis to suppress production of atypical CD101+CD62L− and CD177hi/CD177− neutrophils; translate findings from aged mouse models to elderly patients to improve reperfusion and functional recovery <cite id="call_7ae88c44f6cd-0"></cite>.
- Biomarker-guided stratification:
  - Monitor neutrophil activation (CD62L, CD11b), senescent subsets (CXCR4/CD62L), reverse transmigration (CD54/CXCR1), and age-related atypical markers to identify patients at risk of poor outcomes and guide timely immunomodulatory interventions <cite id="call_3df32e6cf678-0"></cite><cite id="call_7ae88c44f6cd-0"></cite>.
- Crosstalk mapping:
  - Use spatial single-cell transcriptomics to define interactions between neutrophils, microglia/macrophages, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes across acute and chronic phases; identify druggable nodes for shifting harmful subclusters toward beneficial ones <cite id="call_63"></cite><cite id="call_55"></cite>. <cite id="call_75d086b0afe5-1"></cite></answer>

Immune cell infiltration can mediate neuronal apoptosis and aggravate ischemic injury, but it can also promote neuronal repair, differentiation and regeneration. The central nervous system (CNS), which is one of the most important immune privileged parts of the human body, is separated from the peripheral immune system by the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Under physiological conditions, the infiltration of peripheral immune cells into the CNS is controlled by the BBB and regulated by the interaction between immune cells and vascular endothelial cells. As the immune response plays a key role in regulating the development of ischemic injury, neutrophils have been proven to be involved in many inflammatory diseases, especially acute ischemic stroke (AIS). However, neutrophils may play a dual role in the CNS. Neutrophils are the first group of immune cells to enter the brain from the periphery after ischemic stroke, and their exact role in cerebral ischemia remains to be further explored. Elucidating the characteristics of immune cells and their role in the regulation of the inflammatory response may lead to the identification of new potential therapeutic strategies. This process involves the mobilization and activation of neutrophils from peripheral immune organs (including the bone marrow and spleen), their chemotaxis in the peripheral blood, and their infiltration into the brain parenchyma (including disruption of the blood-brain barrier, inflammatory effects on brain tissue, and interactions with other immune cell types). As neutrophils can be divided into N1 and N2 phenotypes in tumors, neutrophils have also been found to have similar phenotypes after ischemic stroke, and play different roles in the development and prognosis of ischemic stroke. N1 neutrophils are dominant during the acute phase of stroke (within three days) and are responsible for the damage to neural structures via the aforementioned mechanisms. However, the proportion of N2 neutrophils gradually increases in later phases, and this has a beneficial effect through the release of anti-inflammatory factors and other neuroprotective mediators. Moreover, the N1 and N2 phenotypes are highly plastic and can be transformed into each other under certain conditions. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="neutrophil subsets N1 N2 neutrophil plasticity brain stroke PPAR alpha 2019 2020 2021 2022" search_time="2026年5月10日9时57分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:78"><title>Neutrophils, the Felons of the Brain</title><summary>See related articles, p e40, e44 Polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) are short-lived but powerful immune cells, providing an early and robust inflammatory response after tissue damage. While the defensive role of PMNs in antimicrobial immunity has long been studied, recent attention has focused on the role of these cells in sterile inflammation after tissue injury. After stroke, PMNs are rapidly recruited to the injured brain. PMNs have been hypothesized to worsen stroke pathology via several mechanisms, including (1) physical blockade within the microvascular network, further reducing cerebral blood flow and (2) direct entry into the brain parenchyma, followed by the release of granules containing antimicrobial enzymes and chemical species that could further injury brain tissue. Based on these assumptions, the prevention of PMN entry into the brain after stroke has been extensively studied as a therapeutic target. Although PMN suppressing therapies showed benefit in numerous preclinical studies, subsequent clinical trials in stroke patients showed no overall benefit. Recently, a growing body of evidence has suggested that PMNs, like other immune cells, may exhibit some level of functional plasticity, analogous to Th1/Th2 (for T cells), M1/ M2 (for macrophages/microglia; Mφ). The N1 PMN phenotype refers to PMNs with stronger proinflammatory/oxidative properties, which possess effective antitumor and antimicrobial actions and may cause greater detrimental effects in the stroke-affected brain. Assuming that the majority of circulating neutrophils are normally in the N1 state, to maximize their ability to effectively engage in antimicrobial activities, the PMNs entering the brain early after stroke may be primarily detrimental. Conversely, the N2 PMN phenotype is characterized by reduced proinflammatory properties and a higher content of beneficial molecules. As such, it is possible that the effect of PNMs on stroke outcome could depend on N1/N2 ratio, which may change with time after stroke, reducing the detrimental effects of infiltrating PMNs—or potentially even conferring benefit to the damaged tissue. Potential mechanisms of PMN-mediated benefit in stroke may involve (1) modification of other cells like macrophages (Mφ) and microglia to an anti-inflammatory healing phenotype, (2) PMN self-limitation of proinflammatory factors, or (3) direct secretion of beneficial factors. Some recent examples of these PMN behaviors after stroke are outlined below. <answer>Title: Integrating AI Psycho-Support with Human-Centered Mental Healthcare: A Data-Driven Strategy

Executive Summary
Available evidence suggests that AI-based conversational agents can meaningfully reduce symptoms of depression and distress when used appropriately, while also highlighting the need for human oversight, cultural sensitivity, and rigorous evaluation to maximize benefits and minimize risks. The most promising integration pathways emphasize complementary roles—screening, engagement, and skill-based augmentation—paired with clinician supervision, human-in-the-loop design, and robust governance. This report outlines a structured, evidence-based approach to integration, with practical guardrails and policy considerations. <cite id="call_5f39c5f8d056-0"></cite><cite id="call_3f59c5f8d056-0"></cite><cite id="call_06f76d018436-0"></cite><cite id="call_06f76d018436-1"></cite><cite id="call_092115cd354c-0"></cite>

Core Integration Strategy: Complementary Roles
1. Screening and triage
- Deploy AI chatbots and symptom checkers as first-contact tools to identify distress, suicide risk, and urgent needs, flagging cases requiring clinician intervention.
- Evidence: Meta-analyses show chatbots can reduce depression and distress; user experience is shaped by perceived safety and therapeutic communication. <cite id="call_5f39c5f8d056-0"></cite><cite id="call_3f59c5f8d056-0"></cite>
- Caution: Avoid overreliance on generative AI for clinical triage; current models can cause harm without safeguards and lack regulatory pathways in mental health. <cite id="call_64e38cc91a88-1"></cite><cite id="call_64e38cc91a88-0"></cite>

2. Engagement and task-sharing in care gaps
- Use AI chatbots to deliver evidence-based psycho-education, coping skills, and low-intensity CBT in non-clinical or under-resourced settings, under clinician supervision or supervision-ready design.
- Evidence: Rule-based and early ML chatbots have shown modest efficacy; human-centered design that surfaces AI predictions to clinicians improves uptake and safety. <cite id="call_5f39c5f8d056-0"></cite><cite id="call_ac058bc31504-0"></cite>
- Task-sharing pilots: Digital tools combined with non-specialist supervision can improve outcomes in low/middle-income contexts, underscoring the value of supervision and training. <cite id="call_bc9f19d78e2a-0"></cite>

3. Human-in-the-loop augmentation
- Embed AI as a real-time support tool within human sessions (e.g., feedback agents for peer supporters) to enhance empathy, self-efficacy, and information exchange without diminishing clinician agency.
- Evidence: AI-in-the-loop peer support increased empathy by 19.6% in a large RCT; decision aids for depression treatment improve decisional conflict, knowledge, and information exchange. <cite id="call_179dcf253520-0"></cite><cite id="call_c360731d3d81-0"></cite>

Implementation Guardrails
- Supervision and escalation
  - Ensure clinician oversight for triage, complex cases, and safety-sensitive decisions; use supervision-ready AI interfaces that surface predictions and recommendations transparently.
  - Evidence: Human-centered design that makes AI outputs explicit supports clinicians and preserves a focus on individualized care. <cite id="call_ac058bc31504-0"></cite>
  - Caution: Avoid unassisted AI triage; models can misread mental states and lack clinician judgment. <cite id="call_64e38cc91a88-0"></cite>

- Human-AI team models
  - Co-design tools that support rather than replace clinicians (e.g., outcome prediction, session summarization) and test them in practice with clinician feedback.
  - Evidence: Human-AI collaboration can empower open-ended tasks like empathic conversations; telepresence coupled with assistive robots is perceived as useful for telerehabilitation. <cite id="call_179dcf253520-0"></cite><cite id="call_b93237b557ee-0"></cite>

- Evaluation and learning
  - Follow a tiered evaluation framework: foundational bench testing, pilot feasibility testing, and clinical efficacy testing; prioritize long-term outcomes and safety monitoring.
  - Evidence: Only a minority of LLM chatbots undergo clinical efficacy testing; robust evidence is needed to compare effectiveness and adverse effects. <cite id="call_5f39c5f8d056-0"></cite><cite id="call_bc9f19d78e2a-0"></cite>

- Cultural safety and accessibility
  - Co-design with end users and clinicians to reflect local norms, languages, and needs; prioritize accessibility and inclusivity.
  - Evidence: User experience and acceptability depend on perceived safety, therapeutic communication, and cultural relevance; task-sharing success hinges on supervision and training adapted to local contexts. <cite id="call_3f59c5f8d056-0"></cite><cite id="call_bc9f19d78e2a-0"></cite>

- Content safety and ethics
  - Implement strong content moderation, trigger-word detection, and safety guardrails; avoid unregulated “wellness” apps that may cross into medical territory.
  - Evidence: Generative AI wellness apps pose health risks when responses increase harm potential; clinician-led evaluations of LLMs reveal inadequate handling of psychosis, mania, and suicide/homicidal content. <cite id="call_64e38cc91a88-1"></cite><cite id="call_64e38cc91a88-0"></cite>

- Equity and deployment
  - Prioritize low/middle-income contexts where workforce shortages and access barriers are acute; integrate AI into primary care and community models.
  - Evidence: Telepsychiatry and assistive robotics can improve access; task-sharing with frontline providers (e.g., Lady Health Workers) has delivered effective, scalable perinatal depression care. <cite id="call_06f76d018436-1"></cite><cite id="call_89"></cite>

Policy and Governance Recommendations
- Regulatory pathways
  - Advocate for clear regulatory frameworks for AI mental health tools, including safety, efficacy, and transparency requirements; align with WHO guidance on large multi-modal models in health.
  - Evidence: WHO guidance outlines over 40 recommendations for governments, companies, and providers to ensure ethical, safe, and equitable deployment of generative AI in health. <cite id="call_092115cd354c-0"></cite>

- Standards and oversight
  - Establish standards for human-AI collaboration, content safety, and supervision; support clinician training on AI tools and their limitations.
  - Evidence: WPA telepsychiatry guidelines and ethics codes emphasize clinician responsibility; human-centered design studies show the importance of balancing AI utility with clinician agency. <cite id="call_06f76d018436-1"></cite><cite id="call_ac058bc31504-0"></cite>

- Research priorities
  - Invest in long-term, comparative trials of AI-human models; assess adverse effects, clinician workload, and clinician-AI team dynamics; improve model robustness for mental health.
  - Evidence: Most trials report low-certainty evidence; LLM chatbots are largely untested clinically; clinician evaluations find current models insufficient for complex mental states. <cite id="call_c360731d3d81-0"></cite><cite id="call_5f39c5f8d056-0"></cite><cite id="call_64e38cc91a88-0"></cite>

- Global collaboration
  - Participate in international governance initiatives (e.g., Shanghai Declaration, WHO guidance) to align on norms, safety, and equity; share evidence and best practices.
  - Evidence: Global governance frameworks emphasize transparency, safety, and equity; WHO guidance provides actionable recommendations for multi-modal health AI. <cite id="call_092115cd354c-3"></cite><cite id="call_092115cd354c-0"></cite>

Conclusion
AI psycho-support can complement human care when deployed with clear roles, clinician oversight, human-in-the-loop design, and rigorous evaluation. The evidence supports screening and triage, engagement in care gaps, and augmentation within sessions, paired with supervision and safety guardrails. Governance must keep pace with innovation to ensure equity, safety, and clinician-centered care. <cite id="call_3f59c5f8d056-0"></cite><cite id="call_5f39c5f8d056-0"></cite><cite id="call_179dcf253520-0"></cite><cite id="call_06f76d018436-1"></cite><cite id="call_092115cd354c-0"></cite></answer>

This systematic review examined different combinations of non-specialists and digital technologies in mental health interventions and their effectiveness in reducing the mental healthcare gap in low-and middle-income countries.
Methods Literature searches were conducted in four databases (September 2023), three trial registries (January–February 2022), and using forward and backward citation searches (May–June 2022). The review included primary studies on mental health interventions combining non-specialists and digital technologies in low-and middle-income countries. The outcomes were: (1) the mental health of intervention receivers and (2) the competencies of non-specialists to deliver mental health interventions. Data were expressed as standardised effect sizes (Cohen’s d) and narratively synthesised. Risk of bias assessment was conducted using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tools for individual and cluster randomised and non-randomised controlled trials.
Results Of the 28 included studies (n = 32 interventions), digital technology was mainly used in non-specialist primary-delivery treatment models for common mental disorders or subthreshold symptoms. The competencies of non-specialists were improved with digital training (d ≤ 0.8 in 4/7 outcomes, n = 4 studies, 398 participants). The mental health of receivers improved through non-specialist-delivered interventions, in which digital technologies were used to support the delivery of the intervention (d > 0.8 in 24/40 outcomes, n = 11, 2469) or to supervise the non-specialists’ work (d = 0.2–0.8 in 10/17 outcomes, n = 3, 3096). Additionally, the mental health of service receivers improved through digitally delivered mental health services with non-specialist involvement (d = 0.2–0.8 in 12/27 outcomes, n = 8, 2335). However, the overall certainty of the evidence was poor.
Conclusion Incorporating digital technologies into non-specialist mental health interventions tended to enhance non-specialists’ competencies and knowledge in intervention delivery, and had a positive influence on the severity of mental health problems, mental healthcare utilization, and psychosocial functioning outcomes of service recipients, primarily within primary-deliverer care models. More robust evidence is needed to compare the magnitude of effectiveness and identify the clinical relevance of specific digital functions. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="AI in mental health ethics suicide risk deep learning 2023 2024 incident report" search_time="2026年5月10日9时58分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:33"><title>Chatbots and mental health: Insights into the safety of generative AI</title><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>Journal of Consumer Psychology</publisher><author_list><author name="Julian De Freitas" affiliation="Marketing Unit, Harvard Business School" /><author name="Ahmet K Uuralp" affiliation="Department of Computer Science, Bilkent University, Turkey" /><author name="Zeliha O Uuralp" affiliation="Department of Psychology, Bilkent University, Turkey" /><author name="Stefano Puntoni" affiliation="Department of Marketing, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Stefano-Puntoni/publication/375008370_Chatbots_and_Mental_Health_Insights_into_the_Safety_of_Generative_AI/links/6571e96bcbd2c535ea0485cb/Chatbots-and-Mental-Health-Insights-into-the-Safety-of-Generative-AI.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年12月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:34"><title>Automatically extracting social determinants of health for suicide: a narrative literature review</title><summary>Suicide is a complex phenomenon that is often not preceded by a diagnosed mental health condition, therefore making it difficult to study and mitigate. Artificial Intelligence has increasingly been used to better understand Social Determinants of Health factors that influence suicide outcomes. In this review we find that many studies use limited SDoH information and minority groups are often underrepresented, thereby omitting important factors that could influence risk of suicide. There has been an increased use of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML), sub-disciplines in AI, in understanding and identifying suicidal ideation, behavior, risk and attempts in both public and clinical contexts. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death for people aged 15-29; over 700,000 people die every year as of 2019¹. For every person who has died by suicide, there are many more who attempt suicide, which increases their risk of dying by suicide in the future². The onset and progression of mental health issues have been linked to a person’s social, economic, political, and physical circumstances³. These circumstances have been summarized in a framework of social factors referred to as Social Determinants of Health (SDoH)⁴ where each factor is considered a driving force behind adverse health outcomes and inequalities (e.g.: hospitalization, increased mortality and lack of access to treatment)⁵. SDoH also affects people living with mental health conditions⁶, where addressing these inequalities across all stages of a person’s life at an indi vidual, local and national level are vital to reduce the number of suicide attempts and deaths by suicide overall⁷. Here, we focus on peer-to-peer mental health support, a setting in which empathy is critical for success, and examine how AI can collaborate with humans to facilitate peer empathy during textual, online supportive conversations. We develop Hailey, an AI-in-the-loop agent that provides just-in-time feedback to help participants who provide support (peer supporters) respond more empathically to those seeking help (support seekers). We evaluate Hailey in a non-clinical randomized controlled trial with real-world peer supporters on TalkLife (N=300), a large online peer-to-peer support platform. Furthermore, we find a larger 38.88% increase in empathy within the subsample of peer supporters who self-identify as experiencing difficulty providing support. We systematically analyze the Human-AI collaboration patterns and find that peer supporters are able to use the AI feedback both directly and indirectly without becoming overly reliant on AI while reporting improved self-efficacy post-feedback. Chatbots for mental health and particularly 'wellness' applications currently exist in a regulatory 'gray area'. Indeed, most generative AI-powered wellness apps will not be reviewed by health regulators. However, recent findings suggest that users of these apps sometimes use them to share mental health problems and even to seek support during crises, and that the apps sometimes respond in a manner that increases the risk of harm to the user, a challenge that the current US regulatory structure is not well equipped to address. In this Perspective, we discuss the regulatory landscape and potential health risks of AI-enabled wellness apps. Although we focus on the United States, there are similar challenges for regulators across the globe. Affective computing is the branch of computer science focused on detecting, interpreting, processing, and simulating human emotion. It has the potential to overcome the limitations of contemporary approaches to digital therapy. Advances in affective computing and adjacent technologies can enhance our understanding and delivery of psychotherapy, though several practical and ethical barriers remain. Effective partnerships between system developers and mental health clinicians and consumers will be crucial to widespread clinical adoption. Psychotherapy, colloquially called the talking cure, is an approach to mental health treatment that traditionally used the relationship between a therapist and a client to impart skills or insight to relieve suffering. Psychotherapeutic approaches differ on several dimensions, including by (individual, family, or group), intended aim (personal insight vs direct behavioral change), the centrality of relational elements, duration, and more. Common themes, however, include attention to emotion, thoughts, and behavior. Although formative concepts of psychotherapy trace their roots much further in human history, the psychoanalytic approach pioneered by Freud in the early twentieth century is commonly accepted as the birth of modern psychotherapy [1]. Contemporary approaches represent an evolution or reaction to analysis. Despite this divergence in foci and content, for most of its history, psychotherapy has primarily been carried out as a face-to-face interaction between a client and a professional mental health care provider. Increasingly, however, the talking cure has evolved into a communication cure, representing a broadening of the definition of therapist interaction and the notion of the "therapeutic space." The modality of communication has become increasingly diverse, ranging from face-to-face to telehealth and even text messaging or live chat. The COVID-19 pandemic also has resulted in a global surge in tele-health and other psychotherapy innovations by both increasing demand and breaking prior service models in the interest of infection control [2]. Emerging technology-first providers such as Ginger.io, which recently merged with Headspace, use a stepped-care model, whereby a spectrum of modalities is offered based on the need. These evolving modalities have also made it possible for therapy to occur asynchronously. In this approach, the interaction with the therapist can occur asynchronously. The client may communicate their thoughts to a clinician via text, email, or video at any hour, and the therapist would respond when available. Although much less widely used than synchronous telehealth, adoption is growing [3]. Although these approaches bring new advantages to the treatment process, they have been principally motivated by a shortage of qualified therapists. For instance, in the United States, in March 2021, 37% of the population lived in an area experiencing mental health professional shortages. This rises to over 94% in more sparsely populated states [4]. These new modalities increase flexibility and, therefore, access to psychotherapy but have limitations. One aspect of traditional psychotherapy and mental health clinical practice more broadly is the mental state examination (MSE), which is used alongside other clinical assessments and therapeutic modalities during psychotherapy. Central to this notion is the recognition that mental health problems can be addressed effectively with resources that every community possesses: people who care for others in their communities. Mental health conditions are not only among the leading causes of the burden of health-related suffering globally, but their contribution to the burden of disease has been rising inexorably in all world regions over the past two decades. This increase is fueled in part by the relative success in the reduction of other burdensome conditions (such as childhood infections and cardiovascular diseases), as well as the absence of effective mental health prevention and care programs. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Artificial Intelligence in Education: Overview of the Field 2020 Baker Greer}" search_time="2026年5月10日9时54分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>Artificial intelligence innovation in education: A twenty-year data-driven historical analysis</title><summary>Reflecting on twenty years of educational research, we retrieved over 400 research article on the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning (DL) techniques in teaching and learning. A computerised content analysis was conducted to examine how AI and DL research themes have evolved in major educational journals. By doing so, we seek to uncover the prominent keywords associated with AI-enabled pedagogical adaptation research in each decade, due to the discipline's dynamism. By examining the major research themes and historical trends from 2000 to 2019, we demonstrate that, as advanced technologies in education evolve over time, some areas of research topics seem have stood the test of time, while some others have experienced peaks and valleys. More importantly, our analysis highlights the paradigm shifts and emergent trends that are gaining prominence in the field of educational research. For instance, the results suggest the decline in conventional tech-enabled instructional design research and the flourishing of student profiling models and learning analytics. Furthermore, this paper serves to raise awareness on the opportunities and challenges behind AI and DL for pedagogical adap-tation and initiate a dialogue.</summary><hostname>ScienceDirect</hostname><publisher>International Journal of Innovation Studies</publisher><author_list><author name="Chong Guan" affiliation="a School of Business, Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS), Singapore; b School of Business, Pusan National University, Busan, 46241, South Korea" /><author name="Jian Mou" affiliation="b School of Business, Pusan National University, Busan, 46241, South Korea" /><author name="Zhiying Jiang" affiliation="a School of Business, Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS), Singapore" /></author_list><url>https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2096248720300369</url><publish_time>2020年9月29日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Application and theory gaps during the rise of Artificial Intelligence in Education</title><summary>Considering the increasing importance of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) and the absence of a comprehensive review on it, this research aims to conduct a comprehensive and systematic review of influential AIEd studies. We also evaluated definitions of AIEd from broad and narrow perspectives and clarified the relationship among AIEd, Educational Data Mining, Computer-Based Education, and Learning Analytics. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Lo et al. 2021 A systematic review of artificial intelligence applications in education" search_time="2026年5月10日9时54分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:15"><title>Application and theory gaps during the rise of Artificial Intelligence in Education</title><summary>Considering the increasing importance of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) and the absence of a comprehensive review on it, this research aims to conduct a comprehensive and systematic review of influential AIEd studies. We analyzed 45 articles in terms of annual distribution, leading journals, institutions, countries/regions, the most frequently used terms, as well as theories and technologies adopted. We also evaluated definitions of AIEd from broad and narrow perspectives and clarified the relationship among AIEd, Educational Data Mining, Computer-Based Education, and Learning Analytics. Results indicated that: 1) there was a continuingly increasing interest in and impact of AIEd research; 2) little work had been conducted to bring deep learning technologies into educational contexts; 3) traditional AI technologies, such as natural language processing were commonly adopted in educational contexts, while more advanced techniques were rarely adopted, 4) there was a lack of studies that both employ AI technologies and engage deeply with educational theories. Findings suggested scholars to 1) seek the potential of applying AI in physical classroom settings; 2) spare efforts to recognize detailed entailment relationships between learners' answers and the desired conceptual understanding within intelligent tutoring systems; 3) pay more attention to the adoption of advanced deep learning algorithms such as generative adversarial network and deep neural network; 4) seek the potential of NLP in promoting precision or personalized education; 5) combine biomedical detection and imaging technologies such as electroencephalogram, and target at issues regarding learners' during the learning process; and 6) closely incorporate the application of AI technologies with educational theories.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><author_list><author name="Xieling Chen" /><author name="Haoran Xie" /><author name="Di Zou" /><author name="Gwojen Hwang" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/publication/344646326_Application_and_theory_gaps_during_the_rise_of_Artificial_Intelligence_in_Education/fulltext/5f86b6df92851c14bcc6ae07/Application-and-theory-gaps-during-the-rise-of-Artificial-Intelligence-in-Education.pdf</url><publish_time>2020年8月5日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:16"><title>A Review of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Education from 2010 to 2020</title><summary>This study provided a content analysis of studies aiming to disclose how artificial intelligence (AI) has been applied to the education sector and explore the potential research trends and challenges of AI in education. A total of 100 papers including 63 empirical papers (74 studies) and 37 analytic papers were selected from the education and educational research category of Social Sciences Citation Index database from 2010 to 2020. The content analysis showed that the research questions could be classified into development layer (classification, matching, recommendation, and deep learning), application layer (feedback, reasoning, and adaptive learning), and integration layer (affection computing, role-playing, immersive learning, and gamification). Moreover, four research trends, including Internet of Things, swarm intelligence, deep learning, and neuroscience, as well as an assessment of AI in education, were suggested for further investigation. However, we also proposed the challenges in education may be caused by AI with regard to inappropriate use of AI techniques, changing roles of teachers and students, as well as social and ethical issues. Furthermore, LA opens the door to opportunities for self-regulated learning in higher education, a circular process in which learners activate and sustain behaviours that are oriented toward their personal learning goals. The potentials of LA and self-regulated learning are huge; however, they are not yet widely applied in higher education institutions. Slovenian higher education institutions have lagged behind other European countries in LA adoption. Our research aims to fill this gap by using a qualitatively and quantitatively led workflow for building a requirement-oriented LA solution, consisting of empirically gathering the students' expectations of LA and presenting a dashboard solution. The interface includes early grade prediction, peer comparison, and historical data overview. Grade prediction is based on a machine learning model built on users' interaction in the virtual learning environment, demographic data and lab grades. First, classification is used to determine students at risk of failing - its precision reaches 98% after the first month of the course. Second, the exact grade is predicted with the Decision Tree Regressor, reaching a mean absolute error of 11.2grade points (on a 100 points scale) after the first month. The proposed system's main benefit is the support for self-regulation of the learning process during the semester, possibly motivating students to adjust their learning strategies to prevent failing the course. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers substantial potential to drive economic progress, foster social development, and enhance human safety and general well-being. Despite these benefits, challenges such as limited Explainability, Data Biases, Privacy Concerns, Security Risks, and Ethical Dilemmas present considerable threats to users, developers, and societies at large. As AI continues to evolve, addressing its ethical and moral principles implications becomes increasingly crucial. Although the idea of "Machine Ethics" emerged around 2006, AI ethics remains a developing discipline. This paper focuses on studying ethical and principles concerns in AI implementation, with frameworks often designed by standards organizations, technology companies, research analysts, and governmental bodies. A critical educational challenge involves figuring out how to support young generations to develop the capabilities that they will need to adapt to, and innovate in, a world with AI. This article argues that both educators and learners should be involved not only in learning but also in co-designing for learning in an AI world. Further, they together should explore the knowledge, goals and actions that could help people shape future AI scenarios, and learn to deal with high degrees of uncertainty. A key contribution of the paper is a re-conceptualization of design for learning in an AI world, which explores a problem space of educational design, and illustrates how educators and learners can work together to re-imagine education futures in an AI world. It then proposes a design framework (ACAD) to support educators and learners’ discussions about design for learning in an AI world. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="AI education policy challenges implementation teacher resistance training 2021 2023 K-12 higher education" search_time="2026年5月10日9时55分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:59"><title>Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning</title><hostname>U.S. Department of Education</hostname><author_list><author name="Miguel A Cardona Edd" /><author name="Roberto J Rodrguez" /><author name="Kristina Ishmael" /></author_list><url>https://www2.ed.gov/documents/ai-report/ai-report.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年5月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:60"><title>AI is Evolving, but Teacher Prep is Lagging: A First Look at Teacher Preparation Program Responses to AI</title><summary>Both the pitfalls and promises of integrating AI into education are now more apparent as we start a third school year in the era of ChatGPT. While AI may provide students with personalized learning opportunities, it might also reduce their ability to socialize or think critically. Generative AI could broaden access to high-quality education and jobs—or worsen existing inequalities. The next generation of educators must be prepared to navigate a shifting AI landscape so they can harness the technology’s advantages while minimizing its harms. But are teacher preparation programs adapting to these new demands, or are they falling behind? To address this question, the Center on Reinventing Public Education (CRPE) reached out to over 500 U.S. education school leaders to understand how they currently integrate AI into their teacher training programs. Through surveys and interviews, we sought to learn how their faculty and preservice teachers engage with AI, their perceptions of the technology’s long-term impact on education, and their institution’s efforts to embed AI into curricula and coursework. While the response rate was moderate (14%), the institutions surveyed educate hundreds of soon-to-be teachers each year and have given us our first insights into the landscape of teacher preparation in the age of generative AI. The data indicate that few institutions are keeping pace with the technological advancements reshaping classrooms nationwide. Our study suggests that schools of education are not likely to move quickly or at a large enough scale to train America’s future teachers in AI without a significant shift in faculty interest and capacity building. We learned that, with few exceptions, schools of education are just now beginning to put new training, curriculum, and coursework into place. They are more focused on supporting faculty than training future teachers in AI, and they are more focused on dealing with student plagiarism than on a broader vision of how AI could transform teaching and learning. While education school leaders are generally optimistic about the positive potential of AI in education, they expressed concern that faculty indifference or resistance could impede their ability to adapt, making it harder to prepare future K-12 teachers for the realities of AI. These data should concern those who believe students and teachers need support to engage safely and effectively with this fast-emerging set of tools. At the end of this brief, we offer recommendations for how schools of education, policymakers, philanthropies, and researchers can help accelerate this process and better prepare America’s future teachers to effectively adapt and instruct in the ever-changing AI landscape.</summary><hostname>U.S. Department of Education</hostname><author_list><author name="Steven Weiner" affiliation="Center on Reinventing Public Education (CRPE)" /><author name="Robin Lake" affiliation="ASU Mary Lou Fulton Teachers College, Arizona State University" /><author name="Jessica Rosner" affiliation="ASU Mary Lou Fulton Teachers College, Arizona State University" /></author_list><url>https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED661791.pdf</url><publish_time>2024年10月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:61"><title>AI Mastery May Not Be For Everyone, But AI Literacy S

The education and training offer's content is dominated by Machine Learning, especially in the case of short courses, with notable attention to AI ethics, while generative AI remains marginal. Most programmes that feature AI topics are offered in the ICT field, but relevant provision also exists in Engineering, Business, administration and law, and other disciplines, albeit with low penetration. Together, these four profiles account for 98% of all job descriptions referring to AI roles. The workshop was premised on two guiding ideas: (1) since the University of Toronto maintains flexible guidelines regarding generative AI policies across courses, undergraduate students benefit from participation in candid discussions of the contextual nature of shifting technological values and (2) first-year university students are in the unique position of also needing to contextualize the shift from high school to university learning contexts, so they are in particular need of opportunities to discuss the diversity of perspectives surrounding the permissibility of genAI use in higher education. However, a Statistics Analysis Software (SAS) survey of businesses reported that 63% of respondents had a skills shortage in AI [15]. final_response:
<think>
Plan: Provide a structured assessment of whether large models can simulate a drug’s systemic impact and enable whole-organism-like evaluation. Cover: (1) Evidence that LLMs/foundation models can reason about biology and drug effects; (2) Emerging “digital twin”/programmable virtual human frameworks integrating multi-scale physiology and omics for end-to-end prediction; (3) Complementary physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) integration; (4) Digital-patient-twin pipelines for virtual trials and synthetic control arms; (5) Case studies using deep databases (e.g., aiHumanoid) to predict toxicity and efficacy at small scale; (6) Limitations: data quality, standardization, interpretability, and validation; (7) Outlook: multi-modal LLMs, hybrid pipelines, and near-term applications in trial design. Insert citations using IDs from prior tool responses.
</think>

<answer><bold>Can large models simulate a drug’s impact across the whole organism and enable systematic, individualized assessment of efficacy and safety? Yes, in emerging ways, but with important caveats.</bold>

- <italic>LLMs and foundation models can act as knowledge-driven biomedical simulators.</italic> Structured prompting of large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 can perform text-based simulations of biological systems and has shown favorable expert ratings in qualitative tasks (e.g., treatment decision support in sepsis) and improved quantitative performance in gene essentiality prediction and progression-free survival regression compared to direct LLM inference, suggesting feasibility of reasoning about drug effects at multiple levels <cite id="call_da2e3ddc8a83-0"></cite><cite id="call_b33eccb72915-0"></cite>. A separate study demonstrated a virtual Phase 1 trial platform (aiHumanoid) using a deep, literature‑validated ontology database to predict toxicity and efficacy for a pancreatic cancer combination regimen across 30 virtual patients, estimating treatment effects with paired t‑tests and Cohen’s d and reporting no individual organoid toxicity exceeding one standard deviation above predicted values at maximal dose <cite id="call_77f2f671fc03-0"></cite>.

- <italic>Programmable virtual humans and multi‑scale physiological integration aim to predict drug behavior end‑to‑end from molecule to phenotype.</italic> A 2025 Drug Discovery Today perspective proposed a programmable virtual human (PVH) framework that unifies multi‑scale physiological models, single‑cell and spatial omics, and AI to simulate a new molecule’s entire pharmacological trajectory in the human body—moving from target‑based to physiology‑based drug discovery and outlining opportunities, challenges, and a roadmap for realization <cite id="call_1af1d10a7b27-1"></cite><cite id="call_1af1d10a7b27-2"></cite>. Reviews of digital twins in drug discovery describe virtual humans that combine real‑time patient data, computational modeling, and multi‑scale physiological data to forecast toxicity, efficacy, and personalized dosing in silico, and to enable virtual clinical trials (e.g., synthetic control arms, optimized trial design), while highlighting standardization, data interoperability, and ethical issues as major barriers <cite id="call_1944c41fee1c-0"></cite><cite id="call_1944c41fee1c-0"></cite><cite id="call_c19bc790adf9-3"></cite>.

- <italic>Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) integration anchors drug distribution and exposure in human physiology.</italic> Industry‑relevant QSP/PBPK models have long predicted drug actions mechanistically, and recent work embeds PBPK within molecular‑generation pipelines to capture the mapping from molecules to therapeutic outcomes by first using a fine‑tuned molecular language model to predict properties fed into PBPK <cite id="call_368137c8d614-0"></cite>. A high‑impact Scientific Reports study used a QSP model integrated with PBPK to simulate clinical trials of anti‑tau and anti‑aSyn antibodies, quantitatively identifying key PK/PD parameters and design improvements (e.g., gradients of decreasing target engagement from CSF to synaptic cleft) and emphasizing the need for QSP modeling to guide antibody development <cite id="call_184"></cite>.

- <italic>Multi‑omics‑enabled digital‑patient‑twin pipelines prioritize individual heterogeneity and systems‑level responses.</italic> Digital‑patient‑twin platforms can encode individual variation (organ function, metabolism pathways, genetics, comorbidities) and simulate multiple doses to predict efficacy, adverse reactions, pharmacokinetics, and disease progression; running these simulations at scale avoids trial‑and‑error treatment and supports real‑time adjustment as the patient’s condition evolves <cite id="call_c19bc790adf9-1"></cite>. Industry‑oriented reports describe using thousands of virtual patients with realistic demographic and biological variation to optimize trial design, predict enrollment requirements, and create synthetic control arms, further reducing reliance on placebo‑controlled cohorts <cite id="call_c19bc790adf9-3"></cite>.

- <italic>Foundation‑model ecosystems span genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and single‑cell/spatial omics to support systems pharmacology.</italic> Reviews of bioinformatics foundation models detail how language, vision, graph, and multimodal models have become central to managing large unlabeled datasets and achieving high accuracy across genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, drug discovery, and single‑cell analysis, providing the representation power needed to link molecular perturbations to whole‑body outcomes <cite id="call_da2e3ddc8a83-0"></cite>.

- <italic>Domain‑specific LLMs and multi‑modal agents are advancing mechanism understanding and modular task execution.</italic> A multi‑modal LLM agent for modular task execution in drug discovery illustrates reasoning about kinase‑inhibitor mechanisms (e.g., BCL‑2, FLT3, MEK), while datasets and evaluations show progress in assessing factual knowledge of drug mechanisms and the ability to reason under novel situations (counterfactuals), pointing to maturing capabilities for mechanism‑based predictions <cite id="call_56d4b85bbaa5-2"></cite><cite id="call_56d4b85bbaa5-1"></cite>.

- <italic>Multi‑omics databases and integrative methods support the training of predictive models of drug impact.</italic> Resources such as scCancerExplorer (single‑cell multi‑omics across cancers), DiabetesOmic (human/mouse multi‑omics in diabetes), and national centers (e.g., CNCB–NGDC) provide the integrated transcriptional, epigenomic, and regulatory data needed to train models that link molecular perturbations to cellular and systemic responses, addressing a key limitation of traditional multi‑omic approaches <cite id="call_79f7899dd38a-2"></cite><cite id="call_79f7899dd38a-3"></cite><cite id="call_79f7899dd38a-1"></cite>.

<bold>Limitations and open challenges</bold>
- <italic>Data quality, standardization, and interoperability remain major bottlenecks.</italic> Reviews and case studies repeatedly cite the scarcity of high‑quality clinical data and the need for standardization and data interoperability as critical barriers to translating digital‑twin models into practice; current platforms rely on curated ontologies and matched multi‑omics/clinical assay data from individuals, with initial applications in oncology <cite id="call_1944c41fee1c-0"></cite><cite id="call_79f7899dd38a-0"></cite>.
- <italic>Interpretability, reproducibility, and validation are still works in progress.</italic> While SimulateGPT improved quantitative predictions compared to direct LLM inference, further development is needed—including web‑search retrieval, integrated mathematical modeling, and fine‑tuning on experimental data—to strengthen reproducibility and trustworthiness in high‑stakes pharmaceutical settings <cite id="call_b33eccb72915-0"></cite>. Similarly, multi‑omics integrative methods are still evolving, with systematic reviews highlighting methodological diversity and the need for rigorous benchmarking <cite id="call_79f7899dd38a-4"></cite>.
- <italic>Scalability and regulatory acceptance are not yet fully realized.</italic> Digital‑twin platforms are beginning to show value in trial design and synthetic control arms, but broader regulatory adoption and validation pathways for in silico trials and predictive agents remain under development <cite id="call_1944c41fee1c-0"></cite><cite id="call_c19bc790adf9-3"></cite>.

<bold>Future outlook and development paths</bold>
- <italic>Hybrid pipelines combining LLM reasoning with mechanistic models and PBPK will be the near‑term norm.</italic> Integrating LLMs for mechanism understanding and property prediction with QSP/PBPK models to anchor distribution and exposure in human physiology is already being explored and is likely to scale as molecular‑level models become more accurate and PBPK libraries mature <cite id="call_368137c8d614-0"></cite><cite id="call_184"></cite>.
- <italic>Multi‑modal LLMs and domain‑specific agents will improve modular task execution and mechanism‑based predictions.</italic> Multi‑modal LLMs that ingest molecules, proteins, and literature and agents that execute modular tasks (e.g., mechanism lookup, property prediction, trial simulation) are emerging tools that can streamline the evaluation of drug impact across scales <cite id="call_56d4b85bbaa5-2"></cite><cite id="call_56d4b85bbaa5-0"></cite>.
- <italic>Multi‑omics‑enabled digital‑patient twins will increasingly support individualized assessment and virtual trials.</italic> Platforms trained on matched multi‑omics and clinical assay data can predict molecular‑level changes and assay outcomes to prioritize compounds, identify biomarkers, and stratify patients; when scaled to thousands of virtual patients, they can optimize trial design and reduce reliance on placebo‑controlled cohorts <cite id="call_79f7899dd38a-0"></cite><cite id="call_c19bc790adf9-3"></cite>.
- <italic>Physiology‑based digital twins and programmable virtual humans aim to deliver whole‑body, phenotypic predictions.</italic> The PVH framework and reviews of digital‑human twins indicate a clear trajectory toward systems‑level prediction (from molecule to phenotype), with multi‑scale physiology and AI as the backbone; near‑term progress will depend on ontology completeness, data sharing, and validation against clinical endpoints <cite id="call_1af1d10a7b27-2"></cite><cite id="call_1af1d10a7b27-1"></cite><cite id="call_1944c41fee1c-0"></cite>.
- <italic>Generative AI and digital twins together promise to accelerate discovery and reduce risk.</italic> Reviews consistently highlight the synergies between generative AI for molecule design and digital twins for preclinical testing, suggesting a future in which new compounds are optimized in parallel across targets, efficacy, toxicity, and dosing before wet lab synthesis <cite id="call_1944c41fee1c-0"></cite><cite id="call_1af1d10a7b27-1"></cite>.

<bold>Conclusion</bold>
Large models—including LLMs, foundation models, and multi‑modal agents—are beginning to enable systematic, macro‑level assessment of a drug’s impact by reasoning about mechanisms, predicting properties, and simulating responses across scales. When integrated with physiologically grounded models (PBPK/QSP), multi‑omics databases, and digital‑patient‑twin pipelines, they move toward whole‑organism evaluation and individualized safety/efficacy assessment. Case studies in virtual Phase 1 trials and oncology simulations already demonstrate proof‑of‑concept for toxicity and efficacy prediction, and programmable virtual‑human frameworks outline a path to end‑to‑end pharmacological prediction. Near‑term progress will hinge on improving data quality and standardization, strengthening interpretability and reproducibility, and establishing regulatory pathways for in silico trials; long‑term, hybrid pipelines and physiology‑based digital twins promise to transform drug evaluation by anchoring molecular perturbations in human physiology and personal variation <cite id="call_b33eccb72915-0"></cite><cite id="call_368137c8d614-0"></cite><cite id="call_184"></cite><cite id="call_1af1d10a7b27-2"></cite><cite id="call_1944c41fee1c-0"></cite><cite id="call_79f7899dd38a-0"></cite>.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="drug impact simulation whole-body model digital twin physiology 2023 2024 review" search_time="2026年5月10日9时58分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:121"><title>FROM MULTISCALE BIOPHYSICS TO DIGITAL TWINS OF TISSUES AND ORGANS: FUTURE OPPORTUNITIES FOR in silico PHARMACOLOGY *</title><summary>With many advancements in in silico biology in recent years, the paramount challenge is to translate the accumulated knowledge into exciting industry partnerships and clinical applications. Achieving models that characterize the link of molecular interactions to the activity and structure of a whole organ are termed multiscale biophysics. Historically, the pharmaceutical industry has worked well with in silico models by leveraging their prediction capabilities for drug testing. However, the needed higher fidelity and higher resolution of models for efficient prediction of pharmacological phenomenon dictates that in silico approaches must account for the verifiable multiscale biophysical phenomena, as a spatial and temporal dimension variation for different processes and models.
