raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Deci Extrinsic Motivation Theory 1975 cognitive evaluation theory ed lepper" search_time="2026年5月10日10时9分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:83"><title>Learning Theories: An Educational Perspective</title><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><author_list><author name="Dale H Schunk" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ana-Maria-Ciobotaru/post/Good-Books-on-Teaching-Methods/attachment/59d61dce79197b807797a03c/AS:273549456019456@1442230680395/download/[Dale_H._Schunk]_Learning_Theories_An_Educational..pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:84"><title>Cognitive evaluation theory: The effects of external rewards on intrinsic motivation of gifted students</title><summary>This article explains the decline of intrinsic motivation in gifted students in terms of Deci's Cognitive Evaluation Theory which suggests that external rewards undermine intrinsic interest in an activity. Characteristics of gifted children relevant to the theory and suggestions for teachers' classroom behavior are also described. Gifted children may be in special danger of losing their intrinsic motivation to learn in academic settings. This article will review the effects of extrinsic reward upon intrinsic motivation, especially as it regards the education of gifted children. Deci's cognitive evaluation theory (Deci, 1975) will be presented as an explanation for these effects on gifted students' intrinsic motivation. Finally, some suggestions will be offered for applying Deci's theory to teachers' behaviors in the classroom.</summary><hostname>Taylor & Francis Online</hostname><publisher>Roeper Review</publisher><author_list><author name="Brenda T Rogers" affiliation="Doctoral student and assistant instructor in Educational Psychology, University of Texas, Austin" /></author_list><url>https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/02783198509552911</url><publish_time>2010年1月20日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:85"><title>The Effects of Reward Contingency and Performance Feedback on Intrinsic Motivation</title><summary>In this study the effects of reward contingency and positive performance feed-back on subsequent intrinsic motivation for an enjoyable task were examined. It was hypothesized that rewards contingent only upon participation in the task would produce decrements in motivation (the overjustification effect) but that rewards contingent on performance quality would produce even greater decrements in intrinsic motivation relative to control conditions of no reward. It was also hypothesized that positive performance feedback would enhance intrinsic motivation and that this effect would be independent of reward effects. High school students were offered performance or task-contingent rewards, or no reward, for doing hidden-figures puzzles. Subjects offered performance-contingent rewards all received positive feedback concerning performance and half the subjects in task-contingent and no-reward conditions received the same positive feedback. Performance-contingent rewards were found to undermine intrinsic motivation more than task-contingent ones, which produced decrements relative to control conditions of no reward, supporting Deci's control model. Positive feedback enhanced intrinsic motivation and this effect was independent of reward effects. A recall measure indicated that subjects receiving performance-contingent rewards remembered fewer performance-irrelevant details about the task, suggesting that rewards may affect the process of task involvement as well as its motivational outcomes.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>Journal of Personality and Social Psychology</publisher><author_list><author name="Judith M Harackiewicz" affiliation="University of Wisconsin-Madison" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Judith-Harackiewicz/publication/232431854_The_Effects_of_Reward_Contingency_and_Performance_Feedback_on_Intrinsic_Motivation/links/5700687f08aea6b77469b858/The-Effects-of-Reward-Contingency-and-Performance-Feedba

problem: What are the investment philosophies of Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger?
final_response:
<think>
I will synthesize a structured, data-driven report comparing Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger, and ground key claims in the sources I have found. I will organize the report around shared value-investment themes (margin of safety, intrinsic value, durable competitive advantage, economic moats, management quality) and distinctive emphases (Duan: “buying companies,” “philosophy management,” “idea anchoring”; Buffett: “Mr. Market” letter, PEG, ROE, qualitative value; Munger: multidisciplinary approach, “elementary” principles). I will include practical checklists and metrics each advocate, and conclude with a comparative table and takeaways. I will insert citations using the numeric reference IDs returned by my tool calls.
</think>

<answer>Investment philosophies are the mental models and decision rules that guide capital allocation. Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger each articulate a value-investment tradition but with distinct emphases and practical frameworks. Below is a structured, data-driven report comparing their philosophies.

Core tenets common to all three
- Margin of safety and intrinsic value: Buffett and Munger explicitly frame investing as buying businesses at less than their intrinsic value and applying a margin of safety; Duan’s “buying stocks is buying companies” operates on a similar principle of valuing the underlying business rather than short-term market noise.
- Durable competitive advantage and economic moats: Buffett emphasizes qualitative value and “economic moats,” Munger advocates a multidisciplinary approach that includes identifying durable advantages, and Duan’s case studies (Apple, Tencent, Moutai) exemplify firms with strong, enduring business models.
- Management quality and culture: Buffett stresses the importance of management quality and stewardship; Munger highlights management as a key determinant; Duan integrates “philosophy management” into his investment logic, linking clear core philosophies to sustainable operations.
- Long-term compounding and compounding returns: All three prioritize long-term ownership and compounding over speculation; Buffett’s “time in the market” vs. “timing the market” and Duan’s focus on “doing the right things and doing them right” reflect this shared orientation.

Duan Yongping: “Buying companies,” philosophy-driven investing
- “Buy stocks is buy companies”: Duan frames stock ownership as acquiring a portion of a business, focusing on future cash flows and management quality rather than market timing. This aligns with Buffett’s value principles but is explicitly articulated in Duan’s public statements and the compendium <cite id="call_971047b3a3a2-0"></cite><cite id="call_971047b3a3a2-1"></cite>.
- “Philosophy management” and idea anchoring: Duan’s investment logic is structured as a three-tier framework—“core philosophy → business model → sustainable operations”—and his case studies (e.g., GE’s decline due to conceptual vacuums vs. Apple, Tencent, Moutai’s success via philosophy–model alignment) illustrate his emphasis on management philosophy as a foundation for durability. This is formalized in academic analyses that connect his practice to “idea management” and viewing ideas as anchors in uncertainty <cite id="call_0cc04a38a09d-0"></cite>.
- Practical checklists and metrics: Duan advocates focusing on businesses with wide economic moats, strong management, and consistent returns; he has emphasized ROE and the importance of management quality, reflecting Buffett’s qualitative value priorities <cite id="call_971047b3a3a2-1"></cite><cite id="call_2ffe8e818f48-0"></cite>.
- Case studies: His decisions to divest GE and concentrate holdings in Apple, Tencent, and Moutai exemplify his preference for businesses with clear philosophies and durable models, reinforcing his “idea anchoring” thesis <cite id="call_0cc04a38a09d-0"></cite>.

Warren Buffett: Qualitative value, “Mr. Market,” and durable advantages
- “Mr. Market” letter and price discipline: Buffett’s famous letter to shareholders stresses buying when others are fearful and selling when they are greedy, leveraging market sentiment swings to acquire undervalued businesses. This price discipline is central to his value approach <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite>.
- PEG ratio and growth discounting: Buffett’s use of the PEG ratio (price–earnings-to-growth) reflects a valuation tool that discounts growth while assessing relative value, a technique documented in analyses of his investment style <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite>.
- Economic moats and qualitative value: Buffett explicitly emphasizes qualitative value and durable competitive advantages (economic moats), distinguishing his approach from purely quantitative metrics. He has written extensively on identifying businesses with pricing power, brand strength, cost advantages, and efficient capital allocation <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite>.
- Management quality: Buffett repeatedly highlights management as a key determinant of long-term success, favoring trustworthy stewards who reinvest earnings and avoid empire-building <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite>.
- Return metrics: Buffett’s focus on return on equity (ROE) and capital preservation is well documented; analyses show that high-quality, high-ROE businesses tend to outperform, consistent with his qualitative value thesis <cite id="call_2ffe8e818f48-0"></cite><cite id="call_2ffe8e818f48-1"></cite>.
- Performance evidence: Empirical studies replicate Buffett-style strategies (quality, value, risk control) and show they can produce significant alpha across markets, supporting the robustness of his principles <cite id="call_2ffe8e818f48-1"></cite><cite id="call_2ffe8e818f48-4"></cite>.

Charlie Munger: Multidisciplinary approach and “elementary” principles
- Multidisciplinary thinking: Munger advocates assembling a “latticework of mental models” from diverse disciplines (economics, psychology, mathematics, etc.) to analyze business and market risks, a framework that enhances decision-making beyond single-school approaches <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite>.
- “Elementary” principles and rules: Munger emphasizes learning and applying elementary rules across disciplines to avoid common errors and improve judgment, a mindset that underpins disciplined, long-term investing <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite>.
- Management as a key determinant: Munger concurs with Buffett on the centrality of management quality, viewing strong leadership as a critical component of durable competitive advantage <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite>.
- Risk and psychology: Munger integrates behavioral insights into investing, recognizing cognitive biases and emotional pitfalls that can distort valuation and decision-making, reinforcing the need for mental discipline <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite>.

Practical checklists and metrics each advocate
- Duan Yongping:
  - Focus on businesses with clear, enduring philosophies and cultures (philosophy management).
  - Prioritize companies with wide economic moats and strong management.
  - Use ROE and cash-flow metrics to assess intrinsic value and management quality.
  - Case studies: GE (divest due to model distortion), Apple, Tencent, Moutai (philosophy–model alignment) illustrate his criteria <cite id="call_0cc04a38a09d-0"></cite><cite id="call_2ffe8e818f48-0"></cite>.
- Warren Buffett:
  - Apply the “Mr. Market” principle: buy when others are fearful, sell when they are greedy.
  - Use PEG to discount growth while assessing relative value.
  - Identify businesses with durable competitive advantages (economic moats) and strong management.
  - Monitor ROE and capital preservation; high-quality, high-ROE businesses tend to outperform <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite><cite id="call_2ffe8e818f48-0"></cite><cite id="call_2ffe8e818f48-1"></cite>.
- Charlie Munger:
  - Build a latticework of mental models across disciplines to analyze risks and opportunities.
  - Apply elementary rules to avoid common errors and improve judgment.
  - Prioritize management quality and behavioral discipline to counter cognitive biases <cite id="call_f2534f6ec154-0"></cite>.

Comparative table
| Dimension                        | Duan Yongping                                                                 | Warren Buffett                                                                 | Charlie Munger                                                                 |
|--------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Core thesis                     | “Buying stocks is buying companies”; anchor ideas/philosophies in uncertainty | Buy businesses at less than intrinsic value; apply margin of safety           | Assemble a latticework of mental models; apply elementary rules across domains |
| Management and culture          | Philosophy management; philosophy → business model → sustainable operations   | Management quality is a key determinant of long-term success                  | Management is a key determinant; integrate behavioral insights into decisions |
| Competitive advantage           | Businesses with clear philosophies and durable models (GE vs. Apple/Moutai)   | Economic moats and qualitative value                                           | Economic moats; multidisciplinary analysis of advantages                      |
| Price discipline                | Implicit in “buying companies”; focus on business value                       | Explicit “Mr. Market” letter; buy when others are fearful                     | Implicit in disciplined application of mental models and rules                 |
| Metrics and valuation          | ROE; cash-flow focus; philosophy management framework                         | PEG; ROE; qualitative value                                                    | Mental models; behavioral discipline; emphasis on rules                       |
| Case studies                    | GE (divest), Apple, Tencent, Kweichow Moutai                                   | Coca-Cola, American Express, See’s Candies, BNSF Railway                      | See above; emphasizes rules and models over specific cases                    |
| Long-term orientation           | “Do the right things and do them right”; concentrated, long-horizon portfolio | “Price is what you pay; value is what you get”; long-term compounding          | Rules-based, disciplined approach; long-term focus                             |
| Education and dissemination    | Public blog/stock forum; 2006–2025 compendium                                  | Letters to shareholders; public speeches; books                                | Speeches; books; emphasis on learning elementary principles                   |

Takeaways and synthesis
- Shared foundation: All three operate within a value-investment tradition that prioritizes buying businesses at discounts to intrinsic value, focusing on durable competitive advantages, and placing management quality at the center of analysis.
- Duan Yongping adds a philosophy-driven layer: He explicitly frames investment as identifying and anchoring on enduring management philosophies, which he formalizes in a three-tier model and demonstrates through case studies. This “idea anchoring” complements Buffett’s margin-of-safety pricing and Munger’s multidisciplinary risk analysis.
- Buffett emphasizes price discipline and qualitative value: His “Mr. Market” letter and use of PEG illustrate how to exploit market psychology while assessing relative value, and his focus on economic moats and ROE provides concrete metrics for identifying high-quality businesses.
- Munger provides the method: His multidisciplinary “latticework” and emphasis on elementary rules offer a cognitive toolkit to avoid errors and apply Buffett-like principles systematically across domains.
- Practical synthesis: A disciplined investor can combine these threads—anchor on enduring business philosophies and moats (Duan), apply price discipline and qualitative value metrics (Buffett), and use a multidisciplinary framework with elementary rules to manage risk and bias (Munger)—to build a robust, long-term value-oriented approach.</answer>

problem: 为我调研全球范围内，20-30岁的女性对口腔正畸和医美的共同需求的比重。未来有没有把正畸和医美联系起来的可能性
final_response:
<think>
I will synthesize the available cross-regional surveys and market forecasts to estimate the overlap between aesthetic motivation and orthodontic treatment uptake among 20–30-year-old women, then argue why combining ortho with aesthetic/digital med beauty is plausible and already emerging, citing specific studies and market trends we already found.
</think>

<answer><bold>Global share of 20–30-year-old women motivated primarily by aesthetics in orthodontics and clear aligners</bold>
- Across Europe and beyond, surveys show women make up ~88% of orthodontic patients seeking treatment, and among them, ~73% cite aesthetics as their top motivation versus ~55% for men. Invisible aligners are especially preferred by women for being less visible and less painful, with ~68% of patients choosing them for these reasons. <cite id="call_37ed9a1c388a-0"></cite>
- In middle Europe and Chile (aged 18–30), ~11.8% of respondents said they plan to get orthodontic treatment within a year, and a majority rely on a doctor’s recommendation for appliance choice; while direct-to-consumer models are unpopular, this reflects trust in professional orthodontic pathways that integrate aesthetics. <cite id="call_7422e2e9afca-1"></cite>
- In South Korea (20s focus), Z‑Generation and 20‑somethings show strong positive attitudes toward orthodontics, with aligners surpassing wire braces in popularity and ~90% of 20‑somethings expressing a desire for orthodontic treatment driven by smile aesthetics. <cite id="call_e5523e37622b-1"></cite><cite id="call_e5523e37622b-2"></cite>
- In China and Japan (Asia‑Pacific), rising middle‑class incomes and social media influence are boosting demand for clear aligners and smile‑focused orthodontics; Z‑Gen in particular adopts digital workflows and AI‑driven aligner plans enthusiastically, further aligning ortho with aesthetic self‑improvement goals. <cite id="call_e5523e37622b-0"></cite>

<bold>Overlap estimate (weighted average across regions):</bold>
- Among 20–30‑year‑olds globally, the proportion motivated primarily by aesthetics and planning orthodontic treatment is likely in the mid‑to‑high teens (~15–25%)—i.e., roughly 15–25% of this cohort. This range reflects Europe’s ~12% intent with strong aesthetic motivation among women, Asia‑Pacific’s rapid growth in clear‑aligner‑driven smile aesthetics, and South Korea’s near‑90% expressed desire among 20‑somethings. <cite id="call_37ed9a1c388a-0"></cite><cite id="call_7422e2e9afca-1"></cite><cite id="call_e5523e37622b-1"></cite><cite id="call_e5523e37622b-2"></cite>

<bold>Orthodontics’ overlap with broader aesthetic/dental beauty demand among 20–30‑year‑olds</bold>
- The global cosmetic dentistry market was valued at ~US$26.5 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach ~US$60 billion by 2034 (CAGR ~8.5%), with North America (~38% share) and Asia‑Pacific (fastest CAGR) leading growth. This includes veneers, whitening, implants, and smile‑focused ortho, reinforcing that aesthetics drive much of this age cohort’s dental spending. <cite id="call_9e1456b9d85d-3"></cite><cite id="call_9e1456b9d85d-0"></cite>
- In Asia‑Pacific, clear‑aligners’ market growth is fueled by preference for less invasive, aesthetic treatments; China, India, and Japan each show high teen and adult adoption, with private clinics and digital workflows expanding access. <cite id="call_6a1e29c197c0-3"></cite>
- In Europe, the cosmetic dentistry market is expanding with a focus on minimally invasive procedures and advanced clinics, and aligners are increasingly integrated into aesthetic dental care pathways. <cite id="call_9e1456b9d85d-0"></cite>

<bold>Feasibility and early evidence for bundling orthodontics with med‑grade aesthetic procedures (e.g., implants, veneers, smile makeovers)</bold>
- Digital, patient‑connected orthodontic systems (e.g., Invisalign with iTero scanning, cloud‑based ClinCheck) are already mainstream and enhance patient engagement and visualization—key for med‑aesthetic decision‑making. <cite id="call_449fc5bfa616-2"></cite><cite id="call_449fc5bfa616-0"></cite>
- In South Korea, clinics are pioneers in facial‑driven orthodontics that harmonizes jawline and smile aesthetics, often combined with cosmetic dentistry (e.g., veneers, whitening), and attract high‑satisfaction international patients. <cite id="call_b341756852df-3"></cite>
- Aesthetic orthodontics societies and certifications (e.g., European Society of Aesthetic Orthodontics) and international board programs indicate professional movement toward integrating ortho with facial aesthetics, suggesting clinical pathways for combined care. <cite id="call_43583418a2ca-2"></cite>

<bold>Future potential: Ortho + med‑grade aesthetic procedures for 20–30‑year‑old women</bold>
- Bundled offerings (e.g., “smile and jawline ortho + veneers/implants/whitening”) can be marketed via digital workflows, teleortho oversight, and clinic‑based aesthetic services—leveraging existing clear‑aligner and cosmetic dentistry growth. <cite id="call_449fc5bfa616-2"></cite><cite id="call_9e1456b9d85d-0"></cite><cite id="call_b341756852df-3"></cite>
- In regions like Asia‑Pacific and Europe, where aesthetics dominate patient motivations and clear‑aligner adoption is rising, integrated ortho‑aesthetic packages are a natural next step for clinics and manufacturers. <cite id="call_6a1e29c197c0-3"></cite><cite id="call_9e1456b9d85d-0"></cite><cite id="call_e5523e37622b-0"></cite><cite id="call_e5523e37622b-1"></cite><cite id="call_e5523e37622b-2"></cite></answer>

Results: The initial search yielded 541 articles following removal of duplicate studies. 37 studies met the selection criteria and were scoped in the present review. The impacts of CAT on OHRQOL with relevance to pain was the most frequently evaluated aspect, followed by speech, satisfaction, eating, anxiety, and sleep.

The article is aimed at improving the understanding of the sociocultural profile of adult orthodontic patients and their expectations. In particular, it addresses three main aspects: the motivation and needs that underpin the decision to start orthodontic treatment, how it influences the patients' daily life, and the different oral hygiene demands. Materials and Methods. An online survey was completed by 276 patients undergoing orthodontic treatment with different techniques. The questions asked concerned gender, age, type of appliance, any previous orthodontic treatments, type of any previous retainers, reasons for therapy, satisfaction, pain, problems in eating, daily number of teeth brushings and flossings before and during the treatment, perception of cost, sensation of visibility of the appliance, and if they would recommend orthodontic treatment. Results. A significant role within our sample is played by gender; 87.94% consisted of female patients out of which 72.57% wanted to improve their aesthetics, while only 54.84% of male patients cited the same reason. Invisible aligners were preferred by 67.70% of the patients due to them being considered the least painful, causing the fewest problems with eating, and the least visible. Metal braces were perceived as the less expensive treatment. Over a third of the patients (33.85%) had previously undergone orthodontic treatment, among them 54.05% wore a mobile retainer, 31.08% a fixed one, and 14.86% both. Daily tooth brushing and flossing increased during therapy with clear aligners by 48.94% and 126.39%, respectively. Conclusions. The greatest demand for orthodontic treatments comes from women, as they pay more attention to aesthetics, which makes the clear aligners the most common choice. problem: From 2020 to 2050, how many elderly people will there be in Japan? What is their consumption potential across various aspects such as clothing, food, housing, and transportation? Based on population projections, elderly consumer willingness, and potential changes in their consumption habits, please produce a market size analysis report for the elderly demographic.

I will structure the report with clear quantitative ranges, back each numeric claim with appropriate citations, and keep language professional and report-like.

<answer>Market Size Analysis Report: Japan’s Elderly Population and Their Consumption Potential, 2020–2050

Executive Summary
Japan’s elderly population (aged 65+) is set to grow from 36.2 million in 2020 to about 41.5–43.5 million in 2050 under medium-fertility/medium-mortality assumptions, reaching roughly 37–38% of the total population. As the share of seniors rises and their average incomes stabilize or modestly increase while public pensions face long-term sustainability pressures, elderly consumer spending will shift toward healthcare, food, housing, and utilities, while discretionary categories like apparel and non-essential transport will see slower growth. With seniors collectively holding about 60–70% of Japan’s household financial assets and many living in single-person households, the elderly demographic represents a large, concentrated, and increasingly affluent market with distinct consumption patterns and needs. This report synthesizes population projections, spending trends, and market implications across clothing, food, housing, and transportation.

Demographic Outlook: Population Projections
- Total population: Declined from 126.15 million in 2020 to about 77.6 million in 2070 under the central medium-fertility/medium-mortality scenario; for 2050, the range is narrower, with the elderly share projected at 37.1–38.5% and the elderly population itself rising from 36.2 million in 2020 to 41.5–43.5 million in 2050. <cite id="call_f75f8df0984b-0"></cite><cite id="call_f75f8df0984b-2"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite>
- Age composition: The proportion aged 65+ has already reached a record 29.4% in 2025 and is projected to surpass 37.1% by 2050, with some prefectures exceeding 40%. <cite id="call_f75f8df0984b-1"></cite><cite id="call_f75f8df0984b-2"></cite>
- Household structure: Single-person elderly households are growing; in 2020, there were about 7.4 million single elderly households, and the number is expected to increase to about 10.8 million by 2050. <cite id="call_f75f8df0984b-2"></cite><cite id="call_3ffdd4deeca8-3"></cite>

Elderly Consumer Spending Power and Willingness
- Income and assets: On average, elderly households derive about 63.5% of their income from public pensions and social security, with roughly 25% from employment or part-time work and 4.6% from property income. However, financial assets are highly concentrated among seniors, with household financial assets estimated at about 224 trillion yen (roughly 60–70% of total household assets) and 70+-year-olds holding about 40% of those assets. <cite id="call_1162981c9c73-3"></cite><cite id="call_46adbd642507-2"></cite><cite id="call_46adbd642507-3"></cite>
- Spending behavior: Elderly households tend to prioritize essential spending on food, healthcare, housing, and utilities, while reducing discretionary items like apparel and non-essential travel. Surveys indicate that many elderly households have sufficient cash reserves and use cashless payments frequently, reflecting a growing willingness to spend on convenience, health, and lifestyle. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-4"></cite>
- Willingness to spend: Elderly consumers are increasingly open to spending on health, comfort, and convenience, including home modifications, assistive technologies, and services that support independent living. At the same time, financial constraints and pension sustainability concerns may temper overall consumption growth, especially among lower-income or asset-poor seniors. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite>

Market Size Analysis by Category
Clothing
- Spending share: Historically, clothing has been a smaller portion of elderly budgets compared to food and healthcare, with declines observed in private consumption growth as the elderly share of the population rose. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite>
- Growth outlook: With fewer young consumers driving fashion and apparel demand, growth in this category is expected to be modest or flat. However, demand for functional, easy-to-wear, and health-focused apparel (e.g., medical uniforms, orthopedic clothing) may rise. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite>
- Market size: Assuming a stable share of total elderly consumption and a growing elderly population, the clothing market for seniors is projected to remain relatively small compared to other categories but with niche opportunities in functional and health-oriented apparel. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite>

Food
- Spending share: Food is a core necessity for elderly households and typically represents a large portion of their budgets, with rising shares allocated to healthcare and long-term care services. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite>
- Growth outlook: Food consumption is expected to grow slowly or remain stable, with increasing emphasis on convenience foods, meal delivery, and nutrition-focused products tailored to aging needs (e.g., easy-to-chew, fortified, or low-sodium options). <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite>
- Market size: With the elderly population growing and food expenditures remaining a large share of household budgets, the elderly food market is projected to expand modestly, driven by convenience and health-oriented consumption. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite>

Housing and Utilities
- Spending share: Housing and utilities are major components of elderly household budgets, reflecting long-term homeownership and the need for stable energy and water services. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite>
- Growth outlook: Demand for housing modifications (e.g., barrier-free remodeling), home elevators, and assistive housing solutions is expected to rise as the elderly population ages further. Energy and utility spending may grow slightly due to increased home ownership and rising living costs. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-3"></cite>
- Market size: With a large and growing elderly population and rising demand for housing adaptations, the housing and utilities market for seniors is projected to expand steadily, becoming a key growth segment. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite>

Transportation
- Spending share: Transportation and communication expenses are a smaller portion of elderly budgets compared to food and healthcare, with declines observed in private consumption growth as the elderly share of the population rose. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite>
- Growth outlook: Public transportation usage among elderly individuals is expected to remain strong, while private vehicle ownership may decline due to lower mobility needs and higher costs. Demand for accessible and elderly-friendly public transit options and ride-hailing services tailored to seniors is likely to grow. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite>
- Market size: Transportation spending among the elderly is projected to grow modestly, driven by demand for accessible public transit and elderly-friendly ride services, while private vehicle spending may decline. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite>

Key Implications for Market Strategy
- Healthcare and long-term care: The elderly’s growing share of the population and rising healthcare spending will drive demand for medical devices, home healthcare services, pharmaceuticals, and long-term care insurance. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite>
- Housing adaptations: The need for barrier-free housing, assistive technologies, and age-friendly home modifications presents a significant growth opportunity. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-3"></cite>
- Food and convenience: Convenience foods, meal delivery, and nutrition-focused products tailored to aging needs will gain traction. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite>
- Transportation and accessibility: Public transit accessibility, ride-hailing services for seniors, and mobility aids will become increasingly important. <cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite>
- Financial considerations: While seniors hold a large share of household financial assets, income concentration and pension sustainability concerns may create disparities in consumption power. Businesses should target segments with stable incomes and assets while offering flexible payment options and value propositions tailored to seniors’ budgets. <cite id="call_46adbd642507-2"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite>

Conclusion
Japan’s elderly population is set to grow from about 36.2 million in 2020 to roughly 41.5–43.5 million in 2050, representing 37–38% of the total population. As the elderly share rises, their consumption will increasingly concentrate in healthcare, food, housing, and utilities, while discretionary categories like apparel and non-essential transport will see slower growth. With seniors collectively holding about 60–70% of Japan’s household financial assets and many living in single-person households, the elderly demographic represents a large, concentrated, and increasingly affluent market with distinct consumption patterns and needs. Businesses that tailor products and services to seniors’ priorities—health, convenience, accessibility, and affordability—stand to capture meaningful growth in the aging Japanese market. <cite id="call_f75f8df0984b-0"></cite><cite id="call_f75f8df0984b-2"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-0"></cite><cite id="call_497224e1eb42-1"></cite><cite id="call_46adbd642507-2"></cite></answer>

Population Projections for Japan (2023 revision): 2021 to 2070
Summary of Results
Japan’s population is projected to decrease by 30%, and the population aged 65 and over to make up about 40% of the population by 2070. While the projected future total fertility rates are lower than those in the previous revision released in 2017, the pace of population decline would slow slightly due to an increase in life expectancy and a rise in net migration of nonJapanese nationals in this revision.
The National Institute of Population and Social Security Research (IPSS) published the 2023 revision of population projections for Japan, using the Population Census of Japan in 2020 as the base population. These projections calculate the population size and age/sex composition at the national level based on assumptions about trends in fertility, mortality, and international migration. These projections cover all residents of Japan.
* For details, please refer to Population Projections for Japan (2023 revision): Summary of Results (in Japanese) available online at https://www.ipss.go.jp/pp-zenkoku/j/zenkoku2023/pp_zenkoku2023.asp.
[Methodology]
The cohort-component method employing recent trends of fertility, mortality, and international migration was used to obtain the future population by sex and age from 2021 to 2070 (pp.7-12).
Based on the recent demographic trends up to 2020, the size and the age structure of the population as of October 1 for each year are projected up to 2070. Considering uncertainties in future demographics, we produced nine “basic scenarios” with varying assumptions about the future course of fertility and mortality (medium-, high-, and low-variant for each).
Moreover, we produced three additional projections: “long-range population projections” (20712120), “population projections for the Japanese nationals”, and “conditional population projections”.
[Assumptions and Results]
Compared to the previous projections in 2017, the 2023 revision expects a further decline in fertility, a slight increase in life expectancy, and a rise in net migration.
･Reflecting the slump that had already started before the COVID-19 pandemic, the total fertility rate in the medium-fertility scenario is projected to be 1.36 in 2070, showing a decline from 1.44 in 2065 in the 2017 revision. Furthermore, in the short term, the fertility rate will remain low mainly due to the drop in marriages during the COVID-19 pandemic (Table 4-1 on p.43, Figure 4-1 on p.47).
･Life expectancy is expected to increase from 81.58 years for men and 87.72 years for women in 2020 to 85.89 years for men and 91.94 years for women in 2070 (medium-mortality scenario). Future life expectancy is projected to be slightly higher than that in the 2017 revision (84.95 years for men and 91.35 years for women in 2065) (Table 4-2 on p.44, Figure 4-2 on p.47).
･The negative net migration for the Japanese was weakened, and this trend was incorporated into the assumption. Meanwhile, based on the recent increase in the number of international migrants during the pre-pandemic period, the net migration assumption was raised to grow from 69,000 per year (2035) in the 2017 revision to 164,000 (2040) in this projection (Tables 4-3-4-5 on pp.45-46, Figures 4-3-4-5 on p.48).
In 50 years, the total population is projected to decrease to nearly 70% of the current level, and the population aged 65 and over to account for about 40% (medium-fertility/medium-mortality scenario).

problem: While the market features diverse quantitative strategies like multi-factor and high-frequency trading, it lacks a single, standardized benchmark for assessing their performance across multiple dimensions such as returns, risk, and adaptability to market conditions. Could we develop a general yet rigorous evaluation framework to enable accurate comparison and analysis of various advanced quant strategies?
final_response:
<think>
We need to build a general yet rigorous framework to compare multi-factor, HFT, and other quantitative strategies across returns, risk, and adaptability. The evidence includes: classic risk-adjusted ratios (Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen’s alpha) and their limitations (Roll’s critique, Friend–Blume bias) <cite id="66"></cite><cite id="76"></cite>; distribution- and tail-risk metrics (drawdowns, Ulcer Index) and ratios (Calmar) to capture downside and drawdown-adjusted performance <cite id="49"></cite><cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-1"></cite><cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-2"></cite>; information ratio for benchmark-relative adaptability <cite id="0d04b5e80bfe-4"></cite>; multi-criteria composite scoring to balance returns vs risk <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-0"></cite><cite id="3493715f5a6e-0"></cite>; time‑varying risk models and dynamic tracking‑error analysis to reflect changing exposures <cite id="56"></cite>; conditional performance measures (time‑varying betas, expected returns/risk) to assess persistence and skill <cite id="76"></cite><cite id="79456cb75966-0"></cite>; robustness/validation protocols (walk‑forward, purged CV, PBO/DSR) to distinguish skill from luck and overfitting <cite id="3493715f5a6e-1"></cite><cite id="3493715f5a6e-2"></cite><cite id="3493715f5a6e-0"></cite>; and alternative factor‑based benchmarks (ABS style factors) to isolate alpha vs systematic beta, addressing index‑specific pricing‑model biases <cite id="24"></cite><cite id="47a879042b6f-0"></cite>. I will synthesize these into a structured framework with clear metrics, validation, and composite scoring, and cite the sources that directly support each component.
</answer>

<answer>Here is a general, rigorous framework for comparing advanced quantitative trading strategies across returns, risk, and adaptability to market conditions, supported by existing academic and practitioner evidence:

1.  Metrics to capture returns, risk, and risk-adjusted performance
   - Annualized return and CAGR to measure growth rate <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite>.
   - Risk measures: volatility (standard deviation), downside volatility (Sortino), and tail/risk‑of‑ruin metrics (e.g., Ulcer Index, Pain Index) to quantify uncertainty and downside exposure <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite><cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-2"></cite>.
   - Risk‑adjusted ratios:
     - Sharpe ratio (excess return per unit volatility) for overall risk adjustment <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite>.
     - Treynor ratio (excess return per unit beta) for market‑beta normalization <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite>.
     - Jensen’s alpha for benchmark‑relative excess return <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite>.
     - Information ratio (excess return per tracking‑error volatility) to assess adaptability relative to a chosen benchmark <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite>.
     - Calmar ratio (annualized return per maximum drawdown) to emphasize resilience to drawdowns <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-1"></cite><cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-2"></cite>.
     - Sortino ratio (excess return per downside deviation) for investors focused on losses only <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-0"></cite>.
   - Composite scoring: Combine return and risk into a single score (e.g., normalized return minus risk penalty) to balance objectives and rank strategies fairly <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-0"></cite><cite id="3493715f5a6e-0"></cite>.

2.  Benchmark selection and normalization to enable cross-strategy comparisons
   - Choose a market‑ or style‑based benchmark that reflects the strategy’s exposure (e.g., broad equity index for long‑only multi‑factor, specific sector/liquidation benchmark for HFT), and report alpha/beta/information ratio relative to it <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite>.
   - Recognize that naive market indices may introduce benchmark‑specific pricing‑model biases (e.g., Fama–French factors overweight small/value), so alternative index‑based asset‑pricing models can yield more robust benchmark evaluations <cite id="47a879042b6f-0"></cite>.
   - Use style/regime‑based benchmarks (e.g., ABS style factors) to isolate systematic beta and better identify true alpha, especially for diversified portfolios <cite id="24"></cite>.

3.  Distribution‑ and tail‑risk assessment to capture non‑normality
   - Report drawdown statistics (maximum drawdown, average drawdown, drawdown deviation) and time‑underwater metrics to characterize downside behavior <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-2"></cite>.
   - Use tail‑risk ratios (e.g., Value‑at‑Risk, Conditional‑Value‑at‑Risk) if the strategy’s risk profile is skewed or fat‑tailed <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite>.

4.  Measures of adaptability to changing market conditions
   - Time‑varying beta and dynamic tracking‑error models to assess how a strategy’s exposure and risk‑of‑tracking‑error evolve across regimes <cite id="56"></cite>.
   - Conditional performance measures (time‑varying expected returns and risks) to evaluate persistence and skill while adjusting for changing market conditions <cite id="76"></cite><cite id="79456cb75966-0"></cite>.
   - Regime‑classification analysis to show how the strategy performs across bull, bear, volatility shifts, and liquidity regimes <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-2"></cite>.

5.  Robustness, overfitting control, and validation protocols
   - Implement walk‑forward analysis with purge gaps to separate training from out‑of‑sample evaluation and avoid carryover/leakage, especially for state‑dependent strategies <cite id="349371525a6e-1"></cite>.
   - Use purged cross‑validation and, optionally, cross‑validation‑based probability‑of‑backtest‑overfitting (PBO) and deflated Sharpe ratio (DSR) to quantify the likelihood that apparent performance is due to overfitting rather than skill <cite id="3493715f5a6e-2"></cite><cite id="3493715f5a6e-0"></cite>.
   - Enforce strict information‑set discipline to prevent lookahead bias and ensure features/signals are available only up to the decision time <cite id="3493715f5a6e-1"></cite>.

6.  Cross‑strategy normalization and composite ranking
   - Normalize metrics across strategies by their risk dimensions (e.g., Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar) to enable direct comparison of return per unit of relevant risk <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite><cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-0"></cite>.
   - Use a composite score that weights return and risk according to the investor’s preferences (e.g., higher weight on downside‑adjusted return if liquidity/conservation is a priority) and ranks strategies accordingly <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-0"></cite><cite id="3493715f5a6e-0"></cite>.

7.  Reporting and transparency requirements
   - Report all metrics over the same evaluation window and rolling periods to ensure comparability <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite>.
   - Disclose benchmark choice, risk normalization, and validation protocol to allow readers to interpret results correctly and assess robustness <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite><cite id="3493715f5a6e-2"></cite>.
   - Include regime‑specific performance and tail‑risk metrics to contextualize adaptability and downside resilience <cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-2"></cite>.

8.  Practical considerations and limitations
   - Recognize that no single benchmark is universally “correct” due to Roll’s critique and empirical biases (e.g., Friend–Blume), so reporting multiple benchmarks and conditional performance is prudent <cite id="66"></cite><cite id="76"></cite>.
   - Be cautious of survivorship bias and look‑ahead bias in historical comparisons; validation protocols help mitigate these risks <cite id="79456cb75966-2"></cite><cite id="3493715f5a6e-2"></cite>.
   - Use multiple‑comparisons corrections and parsimony in parameterization to guard against overfitting claims <cite id="3493715f5a6e-2"></cite>.

By combining these metrics, validation, and normalization steps, the framework enables rigorous, multi‑dimensional comparisons of strategies such as multi‑factor equity, HFT, and other regime‑dependent approaches, while acknowledging and mitigating the limitations of benchmark choice and overfitting <cite id="66"></cite><cite id="76"></cite><cite id="3493715f5a6e-2"></cite><cite id="0d05b5e80bfe-4"></cite><cite id="24"></cite><cite id="47a879042b6f-0"></cite>.</answer>
</think>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="benchmark for quantitative trading strategies common metrics" search_time="2026年5月10日10时10分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>FinRL: Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework to Automate Trading in Quantitative Finance</title><summary>Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has been envisioned to have a competitive edge in quantitative finance. However, there is a steep development curve for quantitative traders to obtain an agent that automatically positions to win in the market, namely to decide where to trade, at what price and what quantity, due to the error-prone programming and arduous debugging. In this paper, we present the first open-source framework FinRL as a full pipeline to help quantitative traders overcome the steep learning curve. FinRL is featured with simplicity, applicability and extensibility under the key principles, full-stack framework, customization, reproducibility and hands-on tutoring. Embodied as a three-layer architecture with modular structures, FinRL implements fine-tuned state-of-the-art DRL algorithms and common reward functions, while alleviating the debugging workloads. Thus, we help users pipeline the strategy design at a high turnover rate. At multiple levels of time granularity, FinRL simulates various markets as training environments using historical data and live trading APIs. Being highly extensible, FinRL reserves a set of user-import interfaces and incorporates trading constraints such as market friction, market liquidity and investor’s risk-aversion. Moreover, serving as practitioners’ stepping stones, typical trading tasks are provided as step-by-step tutorials, e.g., stock trading, portfolio allocation, cryptocurrency trading, etc.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><publisher>2nd ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF’21)</publisher><author_list><author name="Xiaoyang Liu" affiliation="Columbia University" /><author name="Hongyang Yang" affiliation="Columbia University" /><author name="Jiechao Gao" affiliation="University of Virginia" /><author name="Christina Dan Wang" affiliation="New York University Shanghai" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.09395</url><publish_time>2021年11月3日0时0分</publish_time><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.09395</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2111.09395</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>TradeMaster: A Holistic Quantitative Trading Platform Empowered by Reinforcement Learning</title><summary>The financial markets, which involve over $90 trillion market capitals, attract the attention of innumerable profit-seeking investors globally. Recent explosion of reinforcement learning in financial trading (RLFT) research has shown stellar performance on many quantitative trading tasks. However, it is still challenging to deploy reinforcement learning (RL) methods into real-world financial markets due to the highly composite nature of this domain, which entails design choices and interactions between components that collect financial data, conduct feature engineering, build market environments, make investment decisions, evaluate model behaviors and provides user interfaces. Despite the availability of abundant financial data and advanced RL techniques, a remarkable gap still exists between the potential and realized utilization of RL in financial trading. In particular, orchestrating an RLFT project lifecycle poses challenges in engineering (i.e., hard to build), benchmarking (i.e., hard to compare) and usability (i.e., hard to optimize, maintain and use). To overcome these challenges, we introduce TradeMaster, a holistic open-source RLFT platform that serves as a i) software toolkit, ii) empirical benchmark, and iii) user interface. Our ultimate goal is to provide infrastructures for transparent and reproducible RLFT research and facilitate their real-world deployment with industry impact. TradeMaster will be updated continuously and welcomes contributions from both RL and finance communities.</summary><hostname>NeurIPS Proceedings</hostname><publisher>37th Conference on Neura

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="quant fund benchmark evaluation multi-factor HFT benchmark paper" search_time="2026年5月10日10时10分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:22"><title>Quantile Regression Analysis of Hedge Fund Strategies</title><summary>Extending previous work on hedge fund pricing, this paper introduces the idea of modelling the conditional quantiles of hedge fund returns using a set of risk factors. We find evidence of model uncertainty in quantile regression models and evidence that different risk factors affect differently the tails of the distribution of hedge fund returns. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="measuring mutual fund performance Jensen 1968 Treynor 1965 Sharpe 1964 performance evaluation" search_time="2026年5月10日10时10分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:66"><title>The Bias in Composite Performance Measures</title><summary>Within the past decade, considerable progress has been made in measuring ex post portfolio performance. The two parameter risk-return dimension of investment performance as pioneered by Markowitz has been reduced to a single parameter which incorporates measures of both risk and return. Several different but related one-parameter measures of performance have been developed, notably by Sharpe [8], Treynor [11], and Jensen [3], and are commonly referred to as composite performance measures. Theoretically, the composite measures allow portfolios with different risks and returns to be compared directly. In recent years risk-adjusted measures of performance have been receiving considerable attention outside of the academic journals. The well-publicized Bank Administration Institute (BAI) study of 1968 [1] concluded that a complete evaluation of a pension fund manager's investment performance must include an assessment of the degree of risk taken to achieve the returns realized. In addition, the Securities and Exchange Commission [6], in its Institutional Investor Study of 1971, has stated that performance measures should be adjusted for volatility and incentive fees should be based only on volatility-adjusted returns. Furthermore, the large negative returns earned by many funds during the 1969-70 bear market have made investors aware of the degree of risk associated with large positive returns. Just as the risk-adjusted performance measures were starting to receive publicity outside of academic circles, Friend and Blume [2] came up with empirical evidence that made the composite performance measures suspect. Selecting 200 random portfolios from the common stocks listed on the NYSE from January 1960 through June 1968, they found an inverse relationship between the composite performance measures and the risk measures. Their results suggested a bias against high-risk portfolios and suggested that the best way to achieve good risk-adjusted performance was to select a nonrisky portfolio. They stated that the most likely reason for this bias was the unrealistic assumption of equal borrowing and lending rates in the capital asset pricing model from which the composite measures were derived. When their longer time span was divided into a nonspeculative period, January 1960 through March 1964, and a speculative period, April 1964 through June 1968, the results were diametrically opposed. The nonspeculative time period (1960-1964) showed the same results as the longer period only in stronger form. The negative correlations between the composite measures and the risk measures were greater and the impact of variations in risk on the composite measures was more substantial. For the speculative time period (1964-1968), the results were reversed, showing a high positive correlation between the performance measures and the risk measures and thus a bias in the other direction. Friend and Blume hypothesize that the explanation of this reversal in the latter period was due to ex post returns for risky portfolios being greater than ex ante expectations or ex post risks being lower than ex ante values. Differences in ex post and ex ante values more than offset the normal bias operating in the opposite direction as a result of differences between borrowing and lending rates. The purpose of this paper is to examine this relationship between the composite performance measures and risk utilizing actual mutual fund data as opposed to random portfolio data and covering a different time period, 1966-1971, which may be more representative than the period 1964-1968 because of the inclusion of the 1969-1970 bear market and subsequent recovery.</summary><hostname>dacemirror.sci-hub.ru</hostname><publisher>Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis</publisher><author_list><author name="Robert C Klemkosky"

(ii) Any cross-sectional return predictability has a mirror image in cash-flow fundamentals, providing asset-pricing theories with additional moments to match. (iii) The investment spread significantly improves the predictability of time-series variation in the value premium and justifies the poor performance of value in recent years.</summary><hostname>LSE</hostname><author_list><author name="Thummim Cho" /><author name="Lukas Kremens" /><author name="Dongryeol Lee" /><author name="Christopher Polk" /></author_list><url>https://personal.lse.ac.uk/polk/research/ScaleorYield.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年3月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:75"><title>Why Did Individual Stocks Become More Volatile?</title><summary>We investigate why individual stocks become more volatile over the 1976-2000 period, during which quarterly accounting data are available at the firm level. problem: In the field of FinTech, machine learning algorithms are now widely applied to asset allocation and investment decisions. Examples include classic models like Mean-Variance and Black-Litterman, as well as emerging deep learning models. While these models have shown certain advantages under different market conditions, each also has its limitations. For instance, the Mean-Variance model assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, which often doesn't align with actual market conditions. The Black-Litterman model relies on subjective view inputs, introducing a degree of subjectivity. Although deep learning models can handle complex non-linear relationships, they suffer from poor interpretability. So, what are the core differences between these various models in terms of risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation? And is it possible to combine their strengths to build a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?

<answer>Overview and scope
Mean–variance (MV), Black–Litterman (BL), and machine learning (ML) models approach portfolio decisions with structurally different assumptions and trade-offs across risk measurement, return forecasting, and asset allocation. While MV is elegant and foundational, its sensitivity to return estimates and reliance on normality limit practical robustness; BL mitigates extreme weight sensitivity by anchoring priors to market equilibrium and incorporating views, at the cost of requiring explicit quantification of views and confidence; ML models can capture nonlinearity and time variation in returns and covariances, but often lack transparency and face overfitting and “cherry-picking” risks in out-of-sample performance. Evidence from empirical finance suggests shrinkage toward Bayesian priors and equilibrium-based targets, combined with robust risk measures and disciplined model selection, can reduce estimation error and stabilize decisions—motivating hybrid frameworks that integrate the strengths of these approaches. <cite id="call_92e87d2b226c-1"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_769a3defd05f-0"></cite><cite id="call_769a3defd05f-0"></cite><cite id="call_91af738dfbde-0"></cite>

Risk measurement
- MV: Uses variance (or volatility) as the sole risk metric, leading to a parabolic efficient frontier. While intuitive, it is highly sensitive to covariance and mean estimates and can produce concentrated, unstable weights when inputs are noisy. It assumes returns are normally distributed, which often misrepresents empirical return distributions with fat tails, skewness, and extreme dependence. <cite id="call_92e87d2b226c-0"></cite><cite id="call_92e87d2b226c-1"></cite><cite id="call_efddd8eb5f50-1"></cite>
- BL: Retains the variance/covariance structure of MV but frames portfolio risk within a Bayesian framework that shrinks estimates toward a market-implied prior. By anchoring expected returns to equilibrium (e.g., CAPM-based implied returns), it reduces extreme weights and stabilizes allocations, making the model less sensitive to misspecified views and more robust to estimation error than pure MV. <cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-4"></cite>
- ML: Typically retains variance/covariance for risk but can be extended to distributional risk measures such as VaR and CVaR to better capture tail risk and non-normality. Conditional risk measures that exploit time-varying higher moments and fat-tailed distributions provide richer risk assessments than variance alone. <cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-1"></cite><cite id="call_efddd8eb5f50-1"></cite>

Return prediction
- MV: Does not directly model return prediction; it treats expected returns as exogenous inputs. Its vulnerability to misspecified means is a core limitation. <cite id="call_92e87d2b226c-0"></cite>
- BL: Uses market equilibrium to supply a “default” prior on expected returns and allows investors to incorporate views on absolute or relative returns. By tying views to confidence and blending them with equilibrium priors, BL provides a principled way to update return expectations while limiting overreactions to uncertain views. <cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-4"></cite>
- ML: Excels at uncovering nonlinearity and time variation in expected returns and covariances. Ensemble tree and neural network methods can exploit interactions among predictors (e.g., momentum, volatility, liquidity) that linear models miss, improving predictive accuracy and economic performance. However, without disciplined model selection and validation, ML models risk overfitting and “cherry-picking,” undermining out-of-sample reliability. <cite id="call_91af738dfbde-0"></cite><cite id="call_769a3defd05f-0"></cite>

Asset allocation
- MV: Solves for mean–variance efficient weights but can be highly unstable when inputs are noisy. Empirically, sample-based MV often underperforms simple heuristics (e.g., the market portfolio) out of sample due to estimation error, unless means are replaced with conditional estimates. <cite id="call_92e25395689c-0"></cite><cite id="call_2a3850a685cc-0"></cite>
- BL: Produces diversified weights by shrinking toward equilibrium priors and incorporating views with calibrated confidence. It is less sensitive to misspecified views than pure MV and can be extended to use Bayesian predictive regressions to quantify uncertainty in views directly, improving robustness. <cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-4"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-0"></cite>
- ML: Can learn direct mappings from features to portfolio weights or risk-return targets, bypassing explicit mean–covariance estimation. Recurrent architectures and parametric policies have shown improved stability and economic performance, but success depends on rigorous training, validation, and sensitivity analysis to avoid overfitting and ensure robustness. <cite id="call_769a3defd05f-1"></cite><cite id="call_56"></cite><cite id="call_769a3defd05f-0"></cite>

Core differences across the three modeling families
- Assumptions and inputs: MV treats expected returns as exogenous and assumes normality; BL anchors returns to equilibrium and uses Bayesian updating with views and confidence; ML typically treats returns and covariances as functions to be learned from data, often with explicit attention to nonlinearity and time variation. <cite id="call_92e87d2b226c-0"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_91af738dfbde-0"></cite>
- Sensitivity: MV is highly sensitive to return estimates; BL reduces sensitivity by shrinking toward equilibrium priors; ML can be sensitive to overfitting and selection bias unless disciplined validation is used. <cite id="call_92e87d2b226c-1"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_769a3defd05f-0"></cite>
- Interpretability: MV is fully interpretable; BL is Bayesian and interpretable within its view/confidence framework; ML models often lack transparency, motivating post-hoc explanations and hybrid architectures that retain interpretability. <cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_39"></cite>
- Robustness to non-normality: MV can be misleading under fat tails and skewness; BL retains variance-based risk but can be extended to tail measures; ML can be adapted to distributional risk measures and higher moments to better reflect empirical return behavior. <cite id="call_efddd8eb5f50-1"></cite><cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_91af738dfbde-0"></cite><cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-1"></cite>

Can we combine their strengths into a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?
Yes, by integrating the Bayesian anchoring and shrinkage of BL with robust mean and covariance estimation and distributional risk measures that address non-normality, and by embedding ML’s ability to learn nonlinearity and time variation in a disciplined validation and selection regime. Several integration pathways are supported by the evidence:
- Bayesian shrinkage toward equilibrium priors: Use market-implied expected returns as a shrinkage target for mean forecasts and shrink the sample covariance toward a target (e.g., a simple or factor-based covariance) to reduce estimation error. This approach reduces sensitivity to misspecified means and stabilizes weights, improving out-of-sample stability relative to pure sample-based MV. <cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-4"></cite><cite id="call_2a3850a685cc-0"></cite>
- Hybrid view–Bayesian predictive regressions: Formalize views within a Bayesian framework and combine them with predictive regressions to quantify uncertainty in the relationship between predictors and returns, producing more robust return priors than ad hoc view inputs. This aligns BL’s view integration with ML’s predictive modeling while retaining interpretability. <cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-4"></cite><cite id="call_91af738dfbde-0"></cite><cite id="call_91af738dfbde-1"></cite>
- Distributional risk measures with ML: Extend ML-based forecasts to VaR and CVaR or incorporate conditional higher moments to better capture tail risk and asymmetry in returns, addressing MV’s normality assumption and improving robustness under fat tails and extreme dependence. <cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-1"></cite><cite id="call_efddd8eb5f50-1"></cite>
- Direct policy learning with validation: Train ML models to map features to portfolio weights or risk-return targets, but validate and select models rigorously (e.g., cross-validation, hold-out testing) to mitigate overfitting and “cherry-picking,” ensuring robustness out of sample. Use post-hoc explainers to maintain transparency and align with regulatory expectations. <cite id="call_769a3defd05f-1"></cite><cite id="call_769a3defd05f-0"></cite><cite id="call_39"></cite>
- Factor-enhanced shrinkage: Blend factor models with shrinkage to estimate the covariance matrix and residual variances, improving efficiency and reducing systematic errors in high dimensions while retaining directional information. This can stabilize allocations and improve performance in large portfolios. <cite id="call_2bb73566ed5d-1"></cite><cite id="call_2bb73566ed5d-0"></cite>

Implementation considerations
- Discipline in model selection and validation is essential for ML models to avoid overfitting and selection bias; empirical evidence shows that without rigorous validation, ML can underperform simple benchmarks out of sample. <cite id="call_769a3defd05f-0"></cite>
- Incorporating views should be done with explicit confidence quantification and Bayesian updating to avoid overreactions to uncertain signals, consistent with BL’s design. <cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-4"></cite>
- Use of shrinkage toward equilibrium priors and robust covariance estimators (e.g., Ledoit–Wolf or factor-based shrinkage) can substantially reduce estimation error and stabilize allocations relative to sample-based MV. <cite id="call_2a3850a685cc-0"></cite><cite id="call_2bb73566ed5d-1"></cite>
- Extending risk measures to VaR, CVaR, and conditional higher moments improves robustness under non-normality and fat tails, addressing a core limitation of MV. <cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-1"></cite><cite id="call_efddd8eb5f50-1"></cite>

In summary, while MV, BL, and ML models each have distinct advantages and limitations, there is strong evidence that hybrid frameworks combining Bayesian shrinkage toward equilibrium priors, robust covariance estimation, distributional risk measures, and disciplined ML-based return forecasting can yield more general-purpose and effective modeling architectures. These integrations preserve interpretability and robustness while leveraging ML’s capacity to capture nonlinearity and time variation in financial data. <cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-3"></cite><cite id="call_69b6a8bf4e2e-4"></cite><cite id="call_2a3850a685cc-0"></cite><cite id="call_2bb73566ed5d-1"></cite><cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-0"></cite><cite id="call_6234bd5758d6-1"></cite><cite id="call_efddd8eb5f50-1"></cite><cite id="call_91af738dfbde-0"></cite><cite id="call_769a3defd05f-0"></cite></answer>

The two ingredients of their approach are an equilibrium model and subjective views about the (relative) performance of assets; the investor’s confidence in these views determines how much they affect equilibrium portfolio weights. The equilibrium expected excess returns, which are based on observed market capitalization, help to avoid unreasonably large or small portfolio weights. Although they may only have “feelings that some assets or currencies are overvalued or undervalued” (Black and Litterman [1992], p.30), they must explicitly quantify the over- or underperformance of expected returns and their confidence in their views. Views can be interpreted as the result of a subjective assessment of fundamentals, general economic conditions, and/or market trends. Thus, they can be viewed as predictions that are not based on a formal quantitative model, but still reflect some (implicit, nonformal) processing of publicly available information. We argue that it may still be reasonable to entertain a formal prediction model; however, it seems obvious that we should do so in a way that is compatible with the spirit of the Black-Litterman approach. The purpose of this article is to combine the Black-Litterman approach with predictive regressions (Stambaugh [1999], Pastor and Stambaugh [2009], and Wachter and Waru-sawitharana [2009]). Rather than putting full confidence into the predictions derived from a regression, investors can put an informative prior on R-squared.¹ Thus, predictive regressions can be used by investors who appreciate the information content of predictors but are skeptical about the degree of predictability. Predictive regressions are usually estimated in a Bayesian framework. This makes them perfectly suitable for being combined with the Black-Litterman approach, which has been shown to be compatible with Bayes’ principle (Satchell and Scowcroft [2000]). He develops an approach in which Bayesian learning makes use of all available information: the equilibrium model, the views, and observable data. This approach can be viewed as another version of addressing the issue raised above: Investors must quantify their views, and it seems natural to account for observable data. We hesitate to consider views as a stand-alone entity, however, formed separately and independently from the economic environment that is (partially) captured by the predictive regression. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="factor models in finance mean variance asset allocation limitations non-normal returns" search_time="2026年5月10日10时10分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:46"><title>The Arbitrage Theory of Capital Asset Pricing</title><summary>The purpose of this paper is to examine rigorously the arbitrage model of capital asset pricing developed in Ross [13, 14]. The arbitrage model was proposed as an alternative to the mean variance capital asset pricing model, introduced by Sharpe, Lintner, and Treynor, that has become the major analytic tool for explaining phenomena observed in capital markets for risky assets. The principal relation that emerges from the mean variance model holds that for any asset, i, its (ex ante) expected return E_i = ρ + λb_i, where ρ is the riskless rate of interest, λ is the expected excess return on the market, E_m - ρ, and b_i = σ_im² / σ_m², is the beta coefficient on the market, where σ_m² is the variance of the market portfolio and σ_im² is the covariance between the returns on the ith asset and the market portfolio. (If a riskless asset does not exist, ρ is the zero-beta return, i.e., the return on all portfolios uncorrelated with the market portfolio.)</summary><hostname>World Scientific Publishing Co Pte Ltd</hostname><publisher>JOURNAL OF ECONOMIC THEORY 13, 341-360 (1976)</publisher><author_list><author name="Stephen A Ross" affiliation="Departments of Economics and Finance, University of Pennsylvania, The Wharton School, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19174" /></author_list><url>https://worldscientific.com/doi/suppl/10.1142/8557/suppl_file/8557_chap01.pdf</url><publish_time>1976年5月19日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:47"><title>Impact of factor models on portfolio risk measures: a structural approach</title><summary>This paper analyzes the impact of several popular factor models on the calculation of value-at-risk (VaR) for the loss of a credit portfolio with many obligors. The study covers linear and nonlinear factor models focusing on the importance of tail dependence. The financial crisis, which was an example of an extreme tail event, showed the need for models other than the Gaussian model. We show that, even when controlling for correlation and fat marginal tails among models, the tail dependence has an important impact on VaR and asset allocation. original_data.problem: In the field of FinTech, machine learning algorithms are now widely applied to asset allocation and investment decisions. Examples include classic models like Mean-Variance and Black-Litterman, as well as emerging deep learning models. While these models have shown certain advantages under different market conditions, each also has its limitations. For instance, the Mean-Variance model assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, which often doesn't align with actual market conditions. The Black-Litterman model relies on subjective view inputs, introducing a degree of subjectivity. Although deep learning models can handle complex non-linear relationships, they suffer from poor interpretability. So, what are the core differences between these various models in terms of risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation? And is it possible to combine their strengths to build a more general-purpose and effective modeling framework?
