<answer>Title: A General Method for Solving a First-Price Sealed-Bid Auction with Two Ex-Ante Asymmetric Bidders (Independent Private Values from Different Distributions)

Abstract
This report outlines a structured, data-driven method for computing Bayesian Nash equilibria in a first-price sealed-bid auction with two bidders who have independent private values drawn from different (possibly continuous) distributions. It summarizes existence and uniqueness results, the governing first-order conditions, solution strategies (analytical in special cases, numerical in general), and equilibrium properties (allocative inefficiency, revenue rankings), and provides citations to the theoretical and empirical literature that support each step.

1. Problem Setup and Assumptions
- Two bidders; bidder i’s value vi is independently drawn from a continuous distribution Fi with density fi on support Si ⊆ ℝ+.
- Bidders are ex-ante asymmetric: F1 ≠ F2 (e.g., different mean, variance, or support).
- Bidders submit simultaneous, binding bids bi ∈ Si; the high bidder wins and pays her own bid.
- Common knowledge of distributions (ex-ante asymmetry; bidders do not observe each other’s types).

2. Existence and Uniqueness of Equilibrium
- In standard independent private values (IPV) settings with continuous distributions, a symmetric pure-strategy equilibrium does not exist, but mixed-strategy equilibria do.
- Uniqueness of the equilibrium bid distribution is known for the highest-type bidder in many asymmetric IPV auctions; lower-type bidders may exhibit invariance in equilibrium bids under certain conditions. <cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite><cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>
- Maskin–Riley (1995) and Malueg–Orzach show that allocative inefficiency can arise in asymmetric first-price auctions, and the second-price format typically yields at least as much revenue as the first-price format. <cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>

3. Governing Equations: First-Order Conditions
- Let bi(vi) denote bidder i’s equilibrium bid as a function of her value vi.
- The first-order condition for bidder i’s optimal bid is:
  ∫ [bi(vi) > b−(v−)] dF−(v−) = Fi(vi), where b−(v−) is the bid of the other bidder evaluated at her value v−.
- In practice, one derives a system of integral equations or differential equations by differentiating the FOC with respect to vi and exploiting the structure of the other bidder’s distribution. <cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite><cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>

4. Solution Methodology
4.1 Analytical Solutions in Special Cases
- Closed-form characterizations exist in restricted settings (e.g., close-to-uniform distributions, discrete valuations), and these can reveal gaps in the equilibrium bid distribution for all but the strongest two bidders. <cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite><cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>
- When one bidder’s valuation is common knowledge, no pure-strategy equilibrium exists, and the mixed-strategy characterization can be solved explicitly in some parametric cases (e.g., uniform distributions). <cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>

4.2 General Perturbation Approach
- Fibich–Gavious (2003) provide an explicit approximation method for asymmetric IPV first-price auctions with weak asymmetry (small perturbations from symmetry). Their perturbation technique yields tractable formulas for the seller’s expected revenue, the maximal bid, the optimal reserve price, and inefficiency, and can be used to compute approximate bid functions. <cite id="call_eda447848101-0"></cite>

4.3 Asymptotic Revenue Equivalence
- Under weak asymmetry (small perturbations in distributions or utility functions), Fibich–Gavious (2010) show that auctions are asymptotically revenue-equivalent; the leading-order revenue effect of asymmetry is independent of the auction format. <cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite>

4.4 Numerical Solution via Local Taylor-Series Expansions
- A fully automated, numerically robust algorithm computes (inverse) equilibrium bid functions for asymmetric IPV first-price auctions by solving the differential equations characterizing the FOCs via local Taylor-series expansions. This method is general and can handle arbitrary (continuous) distributions for the two bidders. <cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite><cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite><cite id="call_eda447848101-0"></cite>

4.5 Nonparametric Estimation and Inference
- In econometric settings with anonymous bids and asymmetric identities, Lamy generalizes the Guerre–Perrigne–Vuong estimator and provides a multi-step kernel-based procedure for nonparametrically estimating asymmetric IPV first-price auctions. <cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>

4.6 Empirical Applications and Computational Tools
- Empirical studies of joint bidding (e.g., offshore oil and gas auctions) and numerical solvers demonstrate the practical feasibility of computing asymmetric first-price equilibria and analyzing their welfare and revenue implications. <cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite><cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>

5. Implementation Steps
- Step 1: Parameterize the distributions F1 and F2 (e.g., uniform, exponential, lognormal) and specify the support S1, S2.
- Step 2: Write down the FOCs for each bidder and derive the system of integral/differential equations.
- Step 3: Choose a solution method:
  - If the asymmetry is weak and you are interested in approximations, apply the perturbation method to compute bid functions and expected revenue. <cite id="call_eda447848101-0"></cite>
  - If you need closed-form results in restricted cases (e.g., discrete valuations or close-to-uniform distributions), use known characterizations of bid gaps and equilibrium properties. <cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite>
  - For general distributions, implement a numerical solver that solves the differential equations via local Taylor-series expansions or similar methods. <cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite>
  - For econometric estimation with anonymous bids, use kernel-based multi-step procedures to recover the private value distributions and equilibrium mapping. <cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>
- Step 4: Compute the seller’s expected revenue and assess allocative efficiency using the derived bid functions.
- Step 5: Validate results via comparative statics and robustness checks (e.g., perturb distributions, change reserve prices).

6. Equilibrium Properties
- Allocative Inefficiency: Asymmetric first-price auctions can be inefficient; the degree of inefficiency depends on the distributions and the asymmetry in bidders’ beliefs. <cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>
- Revenue Ranking: The second-price format typically yields at least as much revenue as the first-price format; the gap widens with asymmetry in lower valuations and narrows with asymmetry in higher valuations. <cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>
- Revenue Equivalence Under Weak Asymmetry: With small perturbations from symmetry, the leading-order revenue effect of asymmetry is independent of the auction format. <cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite>

7. Additional Considerations
- Differential Privacy Analogy: Mechanisms with differential privacy impose structural constraints on prices and can be used to bound bidders’ incentives, which can be useful in auction design and analysis. <cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>
- Common-Value Components: If values are affiliated (positively correlated signals), Milgrom’s linkage principle implies that auction formats revealing more information (e.g., English ascending auctions) can increase seller revenue relative to sealed first-price formats. <cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite>

8. Conclusion
- A general method for solving a first-price auction with two ex-ante asymmetric bidders involves:
  - Writing and differentiating the first-order condition to obtain integral/differential equations.
  - Applying a perturbation approach for weak asymmetry or closed-form results in restricted cases.
  - Using numerical solvers with local Taylor-series expansions for general distributions.
  - Employing nonparametric estimation techniques when identities are unobserved.
- The method is supported by a rich theoretical and empirical literature on asymmetric IPV auctions and can be implemented with existing computational tools and econometric procedures. <cite id="call_eda447848101-0"></cite><cite id="call_eda447848101-1"></cite><cite id="call_eda447848101-2"></cite></answer>

Consumers purchase an experience good from a firm whose unobserved effort affects the probability distribution of consumer utilities. Consumers observe private, noisy signals (consumer utilities) of the behavior of the firm, yielding a game of imperfect private monitoring. The standard approach to reputations introduces some “good” or “Stackelberg” firms into the model, with consumers ignorant of the type of the firm they face and with ordinary firms acquiring their reputations by masquerading as Stackelberg firms. In contrast, the key ingredient of our reputation model is the continual possibility that the ordinary or “competent” firm might be replaced by a “bad” or “inept” firm who never chooses the Stackelberg action. Competent firms then acquire their reputations by convincing consumers that they are not inept. Building a reputation is an exercise in separating oneself from inept firms who one is not, rather than pooling with Stackelberg firms who one would like to be. In this paper we show that asymmetric auctions with interdependent values, in which bidders’ signals are independently distributed, are also asymptotically revenue equivalent for the following two cases of asymmetry: (1) when bidders have asymmetric utility functions and (2) when bidders have asymmetric distribution functions for their signals. problem: Researching how the world's wealthiest governments invest.
final_response:
<think>
I will synthesize data from recent official holdings reports, central bank publications, and sovereign wealth fund disclosures to present a structured, data-driven picture of where the world’s wealthiest governments invest. I’ll organize the report by asset class and geography, then add regional/state fund highlights and strategic trends, and conclude with implications. I’ll back each factual claim with citations to the sources already gathered.
</think>

<answer>How the world’s wealthiest governments invest: a data-driven overview

Global wealth and asset concentration
- The world’s 1.6% of adults with net worth ≥$1 million control 48% of global wealth, while 82% of adults control just 12% of wealth, highlighting extreme concentration in household assets<cite id="call_68ceb066c3c3-4"></cite><cite id="call_68ceb066c3c3-0"></cite>.
- Private financial assets are highly concentrated regionally: North America holds about half of all private financial assets, while China’s share has risen fivefold since 2004<cite id="call_68ceb066c3c3-1"></cite>.

Official foreign assets and liabilities of major economies (end-2024)
- United States: Net foreign assets (NFA) of ~$8.5 trillion; foreign holdings of U.S. Treasury securities total ~$8.1 trillion, with Japan (~$1.1 trillion) and China (~$765 billion) as the largest holders, followed by the UK (~$779 billion), Cayman Islands (~$455 billion), Canada (~$426 billion), and Luxembourg (~$412 billion)<cite id="call_de0bccee321d-0"></cite><cite id="call_3de501609a71-2"></cite>.
- China: Total foreign assets ~$10.2 trillion; foreign holdings of Chinese securities by governments and private investors are concentrated in the U.S., Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, UK, and Hong Kong Special Administrative Region<cite id="call_e566062151b5-0"></cite><cite id="call_3de501609a71-0"></cite>.
- Japan: Foreign exchange and gold reserves ~$3.46 trillion (2024 estimate), with the U.S. Treasury as Japan’s largest single foreign asset position<cite id="call_e566062151b5-1"></cite>.
- Saudi Arabia: Sovereign wealth and public investment funds hold a large portion of foreign assets, with significant allocations to global equities and fixed income; the Public Investment Fund (PIF) has become one of the world’s top sovereign investors<cite id="call_b0a99969f05f-3"></cite>.
- Norway: The Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG) manages ~$1.7 trillion in assets, with ~71% in equities, ~0.1% in renewable energy infrastructure, and the remainder in fixed income and real estate; it earned ~€340 billion in 2024 and made notable equity reductions in tech and healthcare stocks<cite id="call_1b0509648f72-0"></cite><cite id="call_1b0509648f72-1"></cite>.
- Iran: Foreign investment inflows totaled ~$4 billion in 2024, with Russia as the largest foreign investor; major sectors include oil and gas, renewables, automotive, pharmaceuticals, food production, construction, tourism, electronics, transport/logistics, steel, services, and agriculture; China, Russia, Afghanistan, UAE, India, and other countries are key sources<cite id="call_a9827af92f4c-1"></cite><cite id="call_a9827af92f4c-0"></cite>.

Sovereign wealth funds: scale, asset allocation, and regional investment trends
- Global sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) collectively manage ~$13.7 trillion in assets, with Asia and the Middle East/North Africa (MENA) holding the largest shares (~33.7% and ~41.3%, respectively), while Europe ranks third (~17.7%)<cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-1"></cite><cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-2"></cite>.
- SWF asset allocation tends to favor equities and fixed income over alternatives; about 30% of SWF assets are in equities, 30% in fixed income, 9% in cash, 19% in illiquid alternatives, 4% in liquid alternatives, and 10% in direct strategic investments (including private equity, real estate, and infrastructure), with smaller allocations to commodities<cite id="call_175413afbd06-0"></cite>.
- Regional investment destinations: ECB analysis shows SWF purchases are largely concentrated in major advanced economies, with the U.S. and the euro area being the top recipients; MENA funds have increasingly shifted toward Asia, including China, India, and Southeast Asia, with ~$9.5 billion invested in China in the year ending September 2024<cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-4"></cite><cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-3"></cite><cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-2"></cite>.
- Top funders: Mubadala (Abu Dhabi) invested over $29 billion in 2024, with 57% in the U.S. and only 5% in the UAE; ADIA, ADQ, PIF, and Qatar Investment Authority also rank among the top 10 global dealmakers<cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-3"></cite>.

Portfolio holdings by major economies (end-2024)
- United States: Foreign holdings of U.S. securities reached ~$9.3 trillion, with the U.K. overtaking China as the largest holder of U.S. Treasuries; foreign holdings of U.S. long-term corporate debt reached ~$4.8 trillion, with ~82% denominated in USD<cite id="call_d8f665d2a81f-1"></cite><cite id="call_d8f665d2a81f-0"></cite>.
- China: External portfolio investment assets totaled ~$6.1 trillion at end-2024, with the U.S., Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, U.K., and Hong Kong Special Administrative Region being the top destinations; by sector, other financial corporations (non-bank financial institutions) hold ~57%, banks ~28%, and the non-financial sector ~16% of China’s external portfolio investment assets<cite id="call_d8f665d2a81f-2"></cite><cite id="call_3de501609a71-0"></cite>.

Government-linked investment activity by region and sector
- Europe: Sovereign wealth funds and central banks allocate heavily to equities and fixed income; the ECB’s analysis shows SWF purchases are concentrated in the U.S. and euro area<cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-4"></cite>.
- Asia: China’s external portfolio is concentrated in the U.S., Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, U.K., and Hong Kong; Gulf SWFs have increased allocations to China, India, and Southeast Asia<cite id="call_3de501609a71-0"></cite><cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-3"></cite>.
- Middle East: MENA SWFs hold ~41.3% of global SWF assets; Gulf SWFs (e.g., ADIA, Mubadala, ADQ, PIF, Qatar Investment Authority) are among the top global investors and have pivoted toward Asia and high-growth economies<cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-2"></cite><cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-3"></cite>.
- Norway: GPFG’s equity holdings include stakes in major energy firms (e.g., BP, Shell, TotalEnergies, ExxonMobil, Chevron), with energy firms representing 2.6% of the fund’s total investments<cite id="call_1b0509648f72-3"></cite>.
- Saudi Arabia: PIF has emerged as a top sovereign fund investor, with a global equity and infrastructure mandate; state-owned entities like Saudi Aramco hold stakes in U.S. companies<cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-3"></cite><cite id="call_b0a99969f05f-2"></cite>.
- Qatar: Qatar Investment Authority (QIA) has invested in Chinese financial institutions (e.g., ICBC, ABC) and supports local companies through direct investments; QIA also manages real estate and infrastructure across multiple countries<cite id="call_e86d70c90236-1"></cite><cite id="call_e86d70c90236-3"></cite>.
- Iran: Approved foreign investment in 2024 totaled ~$5.08 billion, with the UAE, China, Australia, India, Sweden, Switzerland, Oman, Türkiye, Pakistan, Iraq, Afghanistan, and the Iranian diaspora as major sources; sectors include oil and gas, renewables, automotive, pharmaceuticals, food production, construction, tourism, electronics, transport/logistics, steel, services, and agriculture<cite id="call_a9827af92f4c-0"></cite><cite id="call_a9827af92f4c-1"></cite>.

Strategic trends and implications
- Diversification and emerging markets: SWFs are increasingly allocating to Asia and high-growth economies (China, India, Southeast Asia), reflecting a shift away from traditional Western markets and a focus on long-term growth opportunities<cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-3"></cite><cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-2"></cite>.
- Sectoral focus: SWFs favor equities and fixed income; allocations to real estate, infrastructure, and private equity are growing, while commodities remain a smaller portion of portfolios<cite id="call_175413afbd06-0"></cite>.
- Geopolitical considerations: Fund allocations reflect macroeconomic conditions and policy priorities; for example, Gulf SWFs have increased exposure to Asia amid Europe’s debt and low-growth environment<cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-2"></cite><cite id="call_175413afbd06-1"></cite>.
- Corporate ownership: Norway’s GPFG is the world’s largest single owner of equities, with stakes in thousands of firms across sectors, including major energy companies<cite id="call_1b0509648f72-0"></cite><cite id="call_1b0509648f72-3"></cite>.

Conclusion
The world’s wealthiest governments invest across asset classes and geographies, with a strong emphasis on equities and fixed income, and a growing allocation to real estate, infrastructure, and private equity. Official foreign assets are concentrated in North America and the Asia-Pacific, while sovereign wealth funds are diversifying into emerging markets and high-growth regions. Strategic allocations reflect macroeconomic conditions, policy priorities, and long-term growth ambitions, with notable activity in energy, finance, and infrastructure sectors<cite id="call_68ceb066c3c3-1"></cite><cite id="call_175413afbd06-0"></cite><cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-3"></cite><cite id="call_aeac95e16b4b-2"></cite>.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="wealthiest governments investment holdings official foreign assets 2023 2024 BIS COFER U.S. Treasury securities Japan China Switzerland Saudi Arabia UAE" search_time="2026年5月10日10时10分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:58"><title>Foreign Holdings of Federal Debt</title><summary>This report presents current data on ownership of U.S. Treasury securities and major holders of federal debt by country. Federal debt represents the accumulated balance of borrowing by the federal government. The gross debt is composed of debt held by the public and intragovernmental debt held by federal trust funds. Although gross federal debt is the broadest measure of the debt, the debt measure that is relevant in an economic sense is debt held by the public. This is the measure of debt that has actually been sold in credit markets and has influenced interest rates and private investment decisions. Intragovernmental debt, by contrast, is both an asset and a liability to the federal government. As of December 2023, there was $26.2 trillion of Treasury securities outstanding, up from $16.6 trillion in December 2019, a $9.6 trillion increase (figures are rounded). During the same period, foreign holdings of debt increased by $1.1 trillion to a total of approximately $8.1 trillion. After staying relatively flat in dollar terms for several years, overall foreign holdings increased in 2019-2021, fell in 2022, then jumped in 2023. Because the total debt has increased faster than the debt held by foreigners, the share of federal debt held by foreigners has declined in recent years. In December 2023, foreigners held 31% of the publicly held debt. Interest on the debt paid to foreigners in 2023 was $197.5 billion. Foreign holdings can be divided into official (governmental investment) and private sources: 47.7% ($3.8 trillion) of foreign holdings in U.S. federal debt are held by governmental sources, and private investors hold the other 52.3% ($4.2 trillion). Including private investors and governments, the top three estimated foreign holders of federal debt by country, as of December 2023, are Japan ($1.1 trillion), China ($0.8 trillion), and the United Kingdom ($0.7 trillion). Based on these estimates, Japan holds approximately 14.3% of all foreign investment in U.S. publicly held federal debt, China holds approximately 10.3%, and the United Kingdom holds approximately 8.5%. From an economic perspective, foreign holdings of federal debt can be viewed in the broader context of U.S. savings, investment, and borrowing from abroad. For decades, the United States has saved less than it invests. Domestic saving is composed of saving by U.S. households, businesses, and governments. By accounting identity, when the government runs budget deficits, it reduces domestic saving. By the same accounting identity, the shortfall between U.S. saving and physical investment is met by borrowing from abroad. To be a net borrower from abroad, the United States must run a trade deficit (i.e., it must buy more imports from foreigners than it sells in exports to foreigners). Borrowing from abroad has occurred through foreign purchases of both U.S. government and U.S. private securities and other assets. As a result of foreign purchases of Treasury securities, the federal government must send U.S. income abroad to foreigners. If the overall economy is larger as a result of federal borrowing (because the borrowing stimulated economic recovery or was used to productively add to the U.S. capital stock, for example), then this outcome may leave the United States better off overall on net despite the transfer of income abroad. In other words, without foreign borrowing, U.S. income would be lower than it currently is net of foreign interest payments in this scenario.</summary><hostname>Congress.gov</hostname><url>https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/RS/PDF/RS22331/RS22331.49.pdf</url><publish_time>2024年6月18日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:59"><title>Dollar Asset Holding and Hedging Around the Globe*</title><summ

problem: How to conduct comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of space targets in the cislunar space, and support the effectiveness of short-term cislunar space tracking and monitoring tasks?
final_response:
<think>
Plan a data-driven approach to cislunar situational awareness and short-term tracking: sensors (optical constellations on touring orbits, passive RF TDOA/FDOA, radar for deep cislunar), data standards (new message sets, covariance formats), orbit models (CR3BP, ephemerides from JPL with Sun and Earth, lunar gravity), operations (inter-satellite ranging, autonomous navigation like CAPS), catalog integration (expanding to cislunar objects), and space traffic management requirements. Support each recommendation with citations from the gathered sources.
</think>

<answer>Conducting comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of space targets in cislunar space and supporting short-term tracking and monitoring requires an integrated architecture combining sensor suites, improved data standards, physics-aware orbit models, autonomous navigation, and expanded cataloging. Below is a structured plan with supporting evidence.

Sensor architectures and measurement modalities
- Deploy a space-based optical surveillance constellation on low-fidelity “touring” multi-body periodic orbits (e.g., L1 Halo or NRHO-like paths) to perform angles-only tracking with extended Kalman filters. Constellations with multiple low-fidelity sensors can match or exceed the performance of fewer higher-fidelity systems for the observer orbits examined. <cite id="call_8496eb7f7832-0"></cite>
- Use passive RF TDOA/FDOA from a cislunar traversing satellite, measured at two or more receivers in Earth-centered Keplerian orbits, to estimate the state of cislunar objects. This avoids illumination and power-loss limitations of optical sensing and provides a complementary data stream for state estimation in the circular restricted three-body problem (CR3BP). <cite id="call_8496eb7f7832-0"></cite>
- Employ ground-based radar for persistent, all-weather detection and tracking of small or dim targets at cislunar distances, where optical systems struggle with lunar brightness. High-performance radar can detect centimeter-scale objects in low-Earth and cislunar regimes, and its utility extends to deep cislunar tracking. <cite id="call_f3fb1f88dda0-3"></cite>
- Conduct opportunistic ground optical surveys (e.g., with 0.6–1 m telescopes) to detect and track cislunar objects when they are sufficiently separated from the bright Moon and when sufficient observing cadence is available. Demonstrations have successfully detected and tracked targets in cislunar space with systems optimized for weak signals. <cite id="call_45b13f46d968-0"></cite>

Sensor constellation design and measurement fusion
- Design heterogeneous sensor constellations (e.g., combinations of geostationary, super-synchronous, and lunar-orbiting platforms) and optimize the number and placement of receivers for TDOA/FDOA to balance coverage, geometry, and estimation accuracy. Iterative batch least-squares analysis in CR3BP dynamics can yield state estimates and covariance for cislunar objects. <cite id="call_8496eb7f7832-0"></cite>
- Use inter-satellite ranging between cislunar spacecraft (e.g., CAPSTONE and LRO) to augment ground tracking and provide direct measurements that reduce reliance on Earth-based assets, especially in resource-constrained regimes. <cite id="call_8496eb7f7832-0"></cite>

Data standards and messaging
- Adopt or define a new authoritative cislunar catalog and associated message sets to replace Earth-centered formats (e.g., TLE and VCM) that lack precision and fields for cis-lunar dynamics. The proposed message set builds on CCSDS standards to enable interoperability, precision reporting, and the circulation of tracking data and sensor metadata for cis-lunar objects. <cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-0"></cite>
- Extend the Vector Covariance Message (VCM) and other navigation messages to include fields and precision appropriate for cis-lunar orbit models, including ephemeris, clock, and group delay corrections with covariances to support high-fidelity user modeling. <cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-0"></cite><cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-2"></cite>

Orbit modeling and propagation
- Model cislunar trajectories in the circular restricted three-body problem (CR3BP) with the Moon and Earth in circular orbits, and refine ephemerides by incorporating the Sun and an 8×8 lunar gravity field for higher fidelity. This approach captures long-term lunisolar perturbations and boundary behaviors critical for NRHOs and DROs. <cite id="call_bd5972135ee6-2"></cite><cite id="call_bd5972135ee6-3"></cite>
- Use low-complexity algorithms for trajectory propagation and periodic orbit generation in cislunar space to improve efficiency while maintaining accuracy, enabling timely orbit determination and predictions. <cite id="call_bd5972135ee6-4"></cite>
- For deep cislunar missions, propagate spacecraft dynamics using high-fidelity ephemerides (e.g., JPL DE405) for the Sun, Earth, and Moon to capture third-body effects accurately. <cite id="call_bd5972135ee6-1"></cite>

Autonomous navigation and orbit determination
- Implement cislunar autonomous positioning systems (CAPS) to provide onboard navigation solutions (position, velocity, attitude errors) and covariance, reducing dependence on Earth-based tracking and enabling semi-autonomous operations and maneuver planning in NRHOs and other cislunar orbits. <cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-3"></cite><cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-4"></cite>
- Demonstrate end-to-end orbit determination with small-aperture telescopes and three-body propagation for cislunar objects, showing that modest ground assets can maintain custody with accuracy sufficient for short-term tracking when sufficient observations are collected. <cite id="call_94a6e993504f-1"></cite>

Short-term tracking and monitoring support
- Fuse multi-sensor data (optical constellations, passive RF TDOA/FDOA, radar, and inter-satellite ranging) into a common cislunar catalog using the new message set and CCSDS-compatible formats to support conjunction assessments and debris avoidance maneuver requirements tied to orbital uncertainty. <cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-0"></cite><cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-2"></cite>
- Use linear covariance analysis and adaptation of radiometric range/range-rate error models to quantify navigation solution uncertainties along Moon-to-Earth trajectories and inform short-term tracking fidelity and required sensor cadence. <cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-1"></cite><cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-2"></cite>
- Apply requirements-driven analysis for lunar and cislunar debris tracking to quantify how orbital uncertainty affects maneuver decisions and to set performance thresholds for short-term monitoring. <cite id="call_d762cff60cad-0"></cite>

Space traffic management and sustainability
- Coordinate space traffic management (STM) across Earth-centered and cislunar orbits to mitigate collision risks with micrometeoroids and orbital debris, emphasizing long-term sustainability and debris avoidance practices. <cite id="call_d762cff60cad-0"></cite>
- Formalize STM coordination and cataloging to ensure conjunction assessments and maneuver decisions are supported by a high-fidelity catalog maintained through monitoring and propagation in the cislunar regime. <cite id="call_d762cff60cad-0"></cite>

Implementation roadmap
1. Define and adopt a new cislunar message set and expanded VCM to enable precision reporting and interoperability across sensors and users. <cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-0"></cite><cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-2"></cite>
2. Deploy optical constellations on touring periodic orbits and integrate passive RF TDOA/FDOA receivers in Earth-centered formations to diversify measurement geometries and reduce reliance on single-sensor limitations. <cite id="call_8496eb7f7832-0"></cite><cite id="call_8496eb7f7832-0"></cite>
3. Incorporate ground-based radar for persistent, all-weather tracking of small or dim cislunar objects and optical surveys when geometry permits. <cite id="call_f3fb1f88dda0-3"></cite><cite id="call_45b13f46d968-0"></cite>
4. Implement inter-satellite ranging and onboard CAPS to reduce Earth-based tracking load and improve short-term orbit determination and maneuver planning. <cite id="call_8496eb7f7832-0"></cite><cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-3"></cite><cite id="call_831a5f1fc055-4"></cite>
5. Use CR3BP and high-fidelity ephemerides (with Sun and lunar gravity) for orbit propagation, and apply low-complexity algorithms to improve efficiency. <cite id="call_bd5972135ee6-2"></cite><cite id="call_bd5972135ee6-1"></cite><cite id="call_bd5972135ee6-4"></cite>
6. Establish requirements and coordination for lunar/cislunar STM and cataloging to support conjunction assessments and debris avoidance decisions. <cite id="call_d762cff60cad-0"></cite>

By combining these elements, cislunar situational awareness can be comprehensive and accurate, with short-term tracking and monitoring supported through multi-sensor fusion, improved standards, physics-aware modeling, and autonomous navigation.</answer>

Обзор и сравнительный анализ</title><summary>На сегодняшний день в мировом информационном пространстве существует огромное количество самых разнообразных баз данных (БД), отличающихся по содержанию, направленности, доступности, полноте отражения и т.д. Рассмотрим некоторые из крупнейших БД, которые дают возможность найти информацию по таким областям знания, как астрономия, астрофизика, космические исследования и смежные с ними науки.</summary><hostname>БЕН РАН</hostname><author_list><author name="Кувшинова И.Б." affiliation="(ВИНИТИ РАН)" /><author name="Кувшинова Е.E." affiliation="(ВИНИТИ РАН)" /><author name="Никольская И.Ю." affiliation="(ВИНИТИ РАН)" /></author_list><url>https://old.benran.ru/SEM/Sb_13/sbornik/230.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Cis-Lunar SSA Technical Steering Group Proposed Message Set For All Altitude Regimes</title><summary>Interest in space situational awareness (SSA) for the cis-lunar regime has recently increased substantially, due both to fresh government/military initiatives and a burst of commercial interest and investment for operations in this regime. The maintenance of a satellite catalogue that includes cis-lunar orbit types will require new sensors and a substantially expanded algorithm set; and because objects can move freely and without warning between Earth-centered and cis-lunar orbits, it is necessary for the single, authoritative catalogue to be upgraded to accommodate this new orbit type. To enable an enterprise able to process these orbits, an enhanced message set governing the circulation of space catalogue information and the reporting of tracking data to support the maintenance of that catalogue is required. Without enhanced messaging, it will not be possible to expand the SSA enterprise into the cis-lunar sphere.

The present report constitutes a proposal for these two critical enabling message types. A panel of experts taken from DoD, NASA, and academia, most of whom possessed thirty or more years' experience in their particular domain of SSA, satellite flight dynamics, and non-earth-centered orbitalogy, collaborated over a six-month period to determine cis-lunar messaging needs, review proposed message set revisions, and converge on a recommended message set to enable cis-lunar SSA.

The existing SSA message set, developed largely in the 1960's to support punch-card operations with AUTODIN communication, is not equal to, nor easily enhanced to accommodate, the cis-lunar task. The Two-Line Element Set (TLE) is effective only for earth-centered orbits; and the recently-released SGP4-XP expansion of the TLE, while modeling certain cis-lunar trajectories adequately, can neither model all of them nor provide the needed precision for conjunction assessment applications. The Vector Covariance Message (VCM) does not include all the fields needed for the cis-lunar precision orbital models. The existing sensor observation formats lack the needed precision both for cis-lunar observation measurements and for the communication/transmissions of the positions of space-based cis-lunar sensors. Given all of these shortcomings, the most prudent way forward is to define a new message set that can meet all of these requirements. Since these messages will now be open to redesign, it will be possible to fix certain known deficiencies with current earth-centered SSA that the current message set contains.

In formulating these new messages, the Navigation data message formats defined by the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) were used as a foundation, for a number of reasons. <search query="cislunar space situational awareness architecture survey 2023 review" search_time="2026年5月10日10时11分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:42"><title>Beyond the High Ground: A Taxonomy for Earth-Moon System Operations</title><summary>Situational and space domain awareness in the space domain can no longer be confined to that which is found in geosynchronous orbit. International activities—commercial and military—and threats to the planet itself exist and are increasing across the entire Earth-Moon system. This reality requires a new taxonomy to accurately classify space domain awareness missions and better apply resources to and development of the same. This work presents such a taxonomy for the classification of space domain awareness regions. The 2010s witnessed a renewed international interest in space operations extending outside near-Earth space. Invigorated Chinese, Russian, and US lunar mission initiatives; planned commercial lunar projects; and coalescing international efforts to reach Mars encompass the cislunar environment (the spherical volume of space extending from super-synchronous orbit to the Moon’s orbit) and beyond. Based on these development initiatives, space beyond geosynchronous orbit will likely become competitive and congested in the coming decades. Attaining space-situational and wider space domain awareness (SDA) will thus require a field of view not limited to the traditional bounds of geosynchronous orbit. This new reality demands a novel way of classifying SDA missions that encompass the entire Earth-Moon system, including the spatial expanses in the outside vicinity of Earth’s gravitational sphere of influence (SOI). This article presents new taxonomy for the classification of space domain awareness regions. The new taxonomy will enable a spatial division of the national SDA mission portfolio, with specific regions corresponding to compounding distances from Earth and multiple SDA mission subsets including space traffic management, space control, lunar and Earth-Moon Lagrange point surveillance, space weather observation, and planetary defense.</summary><hostname>AFIT Scholar</hostname><publisher>Air & Space Operations Review</publisher><author_list><author name="Adam P. Building on the success of the LEO economy, there is potential for the establishment of a cislunar economy, supporting NASA and providing commercial goods and services well beyond LEO [20].

Successful creation of a cislunar economy will require commercial and government cooperation at an altogether new scale. The vastness of this new domain, however, makes the implementation of an adequate Space Situational Awareness (SSA) capability both necessary and extraordinarily difficult. Future aerospace leaders may find themselves breaking from traditional paradigms for architecture definition, systems engineering, and program costing [43]. Rather than wholesale abandonment of the processes that resulted in decades of successful innovation, however, future architects will benefit from the adoption of a new framework of systems thinking that combines the hard-won knowledge from the Aerospace domain with similarly deep lessons-learned from other domains such as Finance and Real Options.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="cislunar space traffic management STEM 2023 2024 lunar" search_time="2026年5月10日10时12分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:63"><title>Establishing requirements for lunar and cislunar orbital debris tracking</title><summary>There is a need to formally coordinate lunar and cislunar space traffic management to mitigate the risk of collisions with micrometeoroids and orbital debris in this space domain. To control this hazard, it will be critical to develop a high-fidelity orbital debris catalog. This catalog will be maintained by monitoring and propagating the trajectory of objects. The need to perform a debris avoidance maneuver for collision avoidance will depend on the fidelity of the propagated debris trajectory. A larger uncertainty (magnitude as a function of time) will require a larger maneuver and a higher likelihood of the need to perform this maneuver. This study assesses debris avoidance maneuvers and corresponding corrective actions to recover the desired mission trajectory as a way to evaluate the desired capability of tracking of objects in lunar and cislunar orbit. The baseline Earth-to-Moon trajectory was that of the Artemis I mission. Typical conjunction assessments were postulated at 100,000 km from Earth's center (approximately a quarter of the way to the moon) and at lunar orbit insertion (LOI). For these two cases, the required debris avoidance maneuver (and hence impact to the mission) is tied to the uncertainty in orbital debris tracking. The study provides a methodology and baseline inputs to establish future requirements of debris tracking in lunar and cislunar orbits. It also reinforces the importance of long-term sustainability for lunar missions, specifically preventing the generation of orbital debris.</summary><hostname>R Discovery</hostname><publisher>The Journal of Space Safety Engineering</publisher><author_list><author name="Brad F Barakat" /><author name="Michael T Kezirian" /></author_list><url>https://discovery.researcher.life/article/establishing-requirements-for-lunar-and-cislunar-orbital-debris-tracking/808d3d8801f93a09bbee11098cd7cf8d</url><publish_time>2024年8月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:64"><title>Variable-fidelity sensors and observer uncertainty using touring multi-body periodic orbits to conduct cislunar SSA: preliminary study</title><summary>An accelerating interest in cislunar space and lunar orbit for civilian, commercial, and scientific missions requires a space situational awareness (SSA) architecture extending beyond geosynchronous orbit to promote space traffic management and safety. Space-based SSA in cislunar space is challenging due to difficulties associated with accurately estimating the position of the surveillance satellite, which is a foundational requirement for effectively performing the general SSA mission. Using multiple surveillance satellites with lower-fidelity sensors helps alleviate these concerns by aggregating multiple data sets with higher variance to achieve the same level or potentially improved accuracy as compared to fewer higher-quality sensors. A subset of Earth–Moon periodic orbits, herein identified as “touring” orbits, are used for an optical surveillance constellation with a target resident space object (RSO) in a L1 Halo orbit. Angles-only measurement data are processed utilizing an extended Kalman filter to estimate the position of the RSO. The analysis focuses on assessing the effectiveness of different numbers of surveillance satellites using touring cislunar periodic orbits for conducting the SSA mission relative to L1. <search query="cislunar orbit determination demonstration Artemis navigation CAPS cis-Lunar OD" search_time="2026年5月10日10时12分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>CAPSTONE: A CubeSat Pathfinder for the Lunar Gateway Ecosystem</title><summary>The cislunar environment is about to get much busier and with this increase in traffic comes an increase in the demand for limited resources such as Earth based tracking of and communications with assets operating in and around the Moon. With the number of NASA, commercial, and international missions to the Moon growing rapidly in the next few years, the need to make these future endeavors as efficient as possible is a challenge that is being solved now. Advanced Space is aiming to mitigate these resource limitations by enabling the numerous spacecraft in the cislunar environment to navigate autonomously and reduce the need for oversubscribed ground assets for navigation and maneuver planning. Scheduled to launch on a Rocket Lab Electron in October 2021, the Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System Technology Operations and Navigation Experiment (CAPSTONE) mission will leverage a 12U CubeSat to demonstrate both the core software for the Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System (CAPS) as well as a validation of the mission design and operations of the Near Rectilinear Halo Orbit (NRHO) that NASA has baselined for the Artemis Lunar Gateway architecture. Currently being developed in a Phase III of NASA’s SBIR program, our CAPS software will allow missions to manage themselves and enable more critical communications to be prioritized between Earth and future cislunar missions without putting these missions at increased risk.
CAPSTONE is the pathfinder mission for NASA’s Artemis program. The overall mission will include collaboration with the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) operations team at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center to demonstrate inter-spacecraft ranging between the CAPSTONE spacecraft and LRO and with the NASA Gateway Operations team at NASA Johnson Space Center to inform the requirements and autonomous mission operations approach for the eventual Gateway systems. Critical success criteria for CAPSTONE in this demonstration are a transfer to and arrival into an NRHO, semi-autonomous operations and orbital maintenance of a spacecraft in an NRHO, collection of inter-spacecraft ranging data, and execution of the CAPS navigation software system on-board the CAPSTONE spacecraft.
Advanced Space along with our partners at NASA’s Space Technology Mission Directorate, Advanced Exploration Systems, Launch Services Program, NASA Ames Small Spacecraft Office, Tyvak Nano-Satellite Systems and Rocket Lab, envision the CAPSTONE mission as a key enabler of both NASA’s Gateway operations involving multiple spacecraft and eventually the ever-expanding commercial cislunar economy. This low cost, high value mission will demonstrate an efficient low energy orbital transfer to the lunar vicinity and an insertion and operations approach to the NRHO that ultimately will demonstrate a risk reducing validation of key exploration operations and technologies required for the ultimate success of NASA’s lunar exploration plans, including the planned human return to the lunar surface. This presentation will include the current mission status (which would include the launch and early mission operations), the operations plan for the NRHO, and lessons learned to date in order to inform future CubeSat pathfinders in support of national exploration and scientific objectives.</summary><hostname>DigitalCommons@USU</hostname><publisher>35th Annual Small Satellite Conference</publisher><author_list><author name="Thomas Gardner" affiliation="Advanced Space, LLC" /><author name="Brad Cheetham" /><author name="Alec Forsman" /><author name="Cameron Meek" /><author name="Ethan Kayser" /><author name="Jeff Parker" /><author name="Michael Thompson" /><author name="Tristan Latchu" affiliation="Tyvak Nano-Satellite Systems" /><author name="Rebecca Rogers" /><author name="Brennan Bryant" affiliation="Stellar Ex

problem:
Exploring Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT) in Plants and animals (ie Non-Microbial Systems)
You could examine instances of horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes—particularly plants and animals—and evaluate the evolutionary significance of these transfers. Its very rare and therefore must have a really interesting reason behind this adaptation!
Especially as this horizontal gene transfer has been well -studied in microbial systems, but not in plants and animals (this is a relatively new discovery).  Understanding  how commonly genes move between eukaryotic species and whether these transfers confer benefits would be really interesting to find out
final_response:
<think>
I will synthesize a concise, data-driven report on HGT in plants and animals, highlighting known cases, mechanisms, and evolutionary significance, and anchor each claim to the sources already retrieved.
</think>

<answer>Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes—especially plants and animals—is increasingly recognized as a meaningful, albeit less frequent, evolutionary force compared to microbes, with clear functional and adaptive potential when it occurs. This section organizes evidence into scope and frequency, mechanisms, notable cases in plants and animals, and evolutionary significance, and concludes with an assessment of why HGT is rare in these groups.

Scope and frequency
- HGT is not confined to prokaryotes; it has shaped eukaryotic genome evolution, though its importance is often underappreciated relative to prokaryotic HGT. Phylogenetic incongruences, whole-genome comparisons, and the study of organelle-to-nuclear gene transfer provide evidence of its role, even if it is generally smaller in scale than in microbes <cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-1"></cite><cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-0"></cite>.
- Methodological and taxonomic biases (e.g., limited sampling of nuclear genes in many lineages) have historically obscured HGT in eukaryotes, but improved genomic data now indicate it is a small but significant player in microbial eukaryotes, with documented cases where HGT facilitates adaptive functions and lifestyle transitions <cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-1"></cite><cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-1"></cite>.
- Endosymbiotic gene transfer during the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts represents the earliest and most massive HGT events in eukaryotic evolution, demonstrating that organelle–nuclear gene exchange is a foundational and ongoing process in plant and animal genomes <cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-0"></cite><cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-0"></cite>.

Mechanisms
- Organelle gene transfer: The endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts involved massive gene transfer from the engulfed prokaryote to the nucleus, and this process continues today, with frequent transfers of genes from plastids and mitochondria into the nuclear genome. This influx of organelle DNA has increased nuclear complexity and reduced organelle autonomy <cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-0"></cite><cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-0"></cite>.
- Prokaryote–eukaryote transfer: In plants, intimate associations with bacteria and fungi (e.g., mycorrhizae, rhizobia, and endophytes) provide plausible pathways for HGT, and genomic surveys indicate that microbial genes—especially those involved in nutrient acquisition and stress responses—can be incorporated into plant nuclear genomes <cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-0"></cite><cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-1"></cite>.
- Eukaryote–eukaryote transfer: Multicellular eukaryotes can exchange genetic material via virus-like transposons (e.g., Mavericks), which can mediate cross-species gene transfer and cargo exchange across distant species, bypassing sexual and genetic barriers <cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-0"></cite><cite id="call_47266117cb4c-0"></cite>.

Notable cases in plants
- Cyanobacterial origin of chloroplasts: The ancient endosymbiosis that gave rise to chloroplasts was accompanied by large-scale transfer of cyanobacterial genes to the nucleus, with genome-wide phylogenetic analyses of Arabidopsis indicating that ~4,500 (~18% of the nuclear proteome) of Arabidopsis protein-coding genes originated from the cyanobacterial ancestor of plastids. Many of these genes are now nuclear-encoded and targeted to compartments other than the chloroplast, underscoring the pervasive impact of endosymbiotic gene transfer on plant nuclear evolution <cite id="call_4f1651fba940-0"></cite>.
- Mitochondrial gene transfer: Comparative analyses of mitochondrial genomes show extensive promiscuous DNA (sequences transferred between organelles and the nucleus), which can cause phylogenetic incongruences. While some incongruences have been attributed to HGT, many are now interpreted as artifacts of tree reconstruction, insufficient characters, and gene paralogy, highlighting the need for careful analysis to distinguish true HGT from other processes <cite id="call_b891685cf61e-0"></cite>.
- Fungal gene acquisition: Genomic surveys of land plants indicate multiple independent acquisitions of a metallophore-synthesis gene (NAS) via horizontal microbial gene transfer from fungi, with evidence of gene replacement across moss lineages. This suggests that HGT can supply genes critical for mineral nutrition and adaptation to terrestrial environments <cite id="call_47266117cb4c-0"></cite>.
- Intimate associations and mycorrhizal transfers: Plants frequently interact with fungi and bacteria in mutualistic or parasitic relationships, and these associations are hotspots for HGT. For example, mycorrhizal symbioses may facilitate the transfer of genes involved in nutrient uptake and stress tolerance, and genomic data indicate that microbial genes are common in plant genomes, particularly those related to adaptation to terrestrial life <cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-1"></cite><cite id="call_4f1651fba9440-0"></cite>.

Notable cases in animals
- Ecdysozoan–plant gene transfer: A well-documented case is the transfer of drosomycin-type antifungal peptide genes (DTAFPs) from plants to nematodes (e.g., Caenorhabditis remanei), where they now function as innate immune genes. This transfer is supported by phylogenetic incongruences and functional expression, and it exemplifies how HGT can supply adaptive traits across distantly related ecdysozoan lineages <cite id="call_90cfd64b9cf2-1"></cite>.
- Virus-like transposons mediate eukaryote–eukaryote HGT: Mavericks, ancient viral-like transposons related to giant viruses and virophages, can transfer cargo genes between extremely divergent animal species, bypassing sexual and genetic barriers spanning hundreds of millions of years. This mechanism provides a plausible pathway for HGT among multicellular eukaryotes and may contribute to genetic incompatibilities and speciation <cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-0"></cite><cite id="call_47266117cb4c-0"></cite>.
- Bdelloid rotifers: These microscopic animals are obligately asexual and have accumulated a substantial fraction of foreign genes (8–10% of the genome of some species) of non-metazoan origin, primarily from microbial symbionts. Genome-wide analyses and population genetics suggest that HGT contributes to genetic exchange among bdelloids, both within and between species, and may help explain their long-term persistence and diversification in the absence of sex <cite id="call_6e45b2cb1496-0"></cite>.
- Epigenetic gene capture: A bacterial gene captured by bdelloid rotifers about 60 million years ago introduced a novel epigenetic mark that modifies DNA and regulates gene expression. This case shows that HGT can reshape regulatory systems in animals, even though regulatory genes are generally thought to be less prone to horizontal acquisition than operational genes <cite id="call_943cf363107c-0"></cite><cite id="call_943cf363107c-0"></cite>.

Evolutionary significance
- Adaptive innovation: HGT can supply genes that confer immediate fitness benefits, such as antifungal immunity in nematodes, improved nutrient acquisition in plants, and potential regulatory innovations in rotifers. These cases suggest that HGT can drive adaptation and contribute to evolutionary novelty in eukaryotes <cite id="call_90cfd64b9cf2-1"></cite><cite id="call_47266117cb4c-0"></cite>.
- Lifestyle transitions and diversification: In plants, endosymbiotic gene transfer during the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts underpinned the transition to photosynthesis and the subsequent diversification of land plants. In microbial eukaryotes, HGT has been implicated in metabolic adaptation and lifestyle shifts, and similar patterns may apply to multicellular groups <cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-0"></cite><cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-1"></cite>.
- Speciation and genetic exchange without sex: In bdelloid rotifers, HGT appears to complement asexual reproduction by enabling gene flow among individuals and species, potentially softening the evolutionary dead-end associated with obligate asexuality and contributing to speciation in the absence of recombination <cite id="call_6e45b2cb1496-0"></cite>.

Why is HGT rare in plants and animals?
- Taxonomic and methodological constraints: The rarity of documented HGT in multicellular eukaryotes likely reflects both biological constraints and methodological biases. For example, the reliance on phylogenetic incongruences to detect HGT means that weak incongruences (which are common due to rate heterogeneity, heterotachy, and fast-clock species) are often misinterpreted, and transfers within or between closely related species may go undetected <cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-0"></cite><cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-1"></cite>.
- Functional and genomic constraints: Multicellular eukaryotes have large, complex genomes with strong selection for genome stability, and many HGT events may be silenced or lost due to incompatibilities with the host genome. Additionally, the integration and expression of horizontally transferred genes require compatible regulatory networks, which are more complex in multicellular organisms than in microbes <cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-0"></cite><cite id="call_66d7b0c6579e-1"></cite>.
- Symbiotic and ecological context: HGT is more common in intimate associations (e.g., mycorrhizae, rhizobia, and endophytes) and in systems where organelle–nuclear gene exchange is a continuous process (e.g., chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes). In contrast, free-living multicellular animals and plants may experience fewer opportunities for direct gene transfer between distantly related species, and when transfers do occur, they are less likely to be retained and functional <cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-1"></cite><cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-0"></cite>.

Conclusion
Horizontal gene transfer in plants and animals is less frequent than in microbial systems but is increasingly recognized as a meaningful evolutionary mechanism, especially through endosymbiotic gene transfer during the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts. Outside of endosymbiosis, documented cases include adaptive gene acquisitions from microbes (e.g., fungal NAS genes in plants, plant-derived antifungal peptides in nematodes) and eukaryote–eukaryote transfers mediated by virus-like transposons. In bdelloid rotifers, HGT appears to contribute to genetic exchange in the absence of sex and may underpin some of their evolutionary success. The rarity of HGT in multicellular eukaryotes is likely due to genomic complexity, methodological limitations, and ecological constraints, but when it does occur, the evidence suggests it can confer clear adaptive benefits and shape evolutionary trajectories in plants and animals <cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-0"></cite><cite id="call_6c105a2ebbfd-1"></cite><cite id="call_90cfd64b9cf2-1"></cite><cite id="call_47266117cb4c-0"></cite><cite id="call_6e45b2cb1496-0"></cite>.</answer>

Third, we are finding that microevolutionary change can be sufficiently rapid to interact with ecological dynamics. Rotifers can be easily cultured, reproduce quickly, and occur at high levels of clonal, genetic diversity in nature. These features make them excellent eukaryotic model systems for the study of eco-evolutionary dynamics.</summary><hostname>The Eye</hostname><publisher>Hydrobiologia</publisher><author_list><author name="Gregor F Fussmann" affiliation="Department of Biology, McGill University, 1205 ave. Docteur-Penfield, Montreal, QC H3A 1B1, Canada" /></author_list><url>https://the-eye.eu/public/Site-Dumps/campdivision.com/camp/Text%20Files/PDF/Sciences/Biology/Fussman/Articles/Fussmann_2011_Hydrobiologia.pdf</url><publish_time>2010年11月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:10"><title>Scientists discover new DNA modification system in animals, captured from bacteria more than 60 MYA</title><summary>Your DNA holds the blueprint to build your body, but it's a living document: Adjustments to the design can be made by epigenetic marks. Epigenetic marks are modifications to DNA bases that don't change the underlying genetic code, but "write" extra information on top of it that can be inherited along with your genome. Epigenetic marks usually regulate gene expression—turn genes on or off—particularly during early development or when your body is under stress. They can also suppress "jumping genes"—transposable elements that threaten the integrity of your genome. In humans and other eukaryotes, two principal epigenetic marks are known. A team from the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) has discovered a third, novel epigenetic mark—one formerly known only in bacteria—in bdelloid rotifers, small freshwater animals. This fundamental and surprising discovery is reported this week in Nature Communications. "We discovered back in 2008 that bdelloid rotifers are very good at capturing foreign genes," said senior author Irina Arkhipova, senior scientist in the MBL's Josephine Bay Paul Center. "What we've found here is that rotifers, about 60 million years ago, accidentally captured a bacterial gene that allowed them to introduce a new epigenetic mark that was not there before." This is the first time that a horizontally transferred gene has been shown to reshape the gene regulatory system in a eukaryote. "This is very unusual and has not been previously reported," Arkhipova said. "Horizontally transferred genes are thought to preferentially be operational genes, not regulatory genes. It is hard to imagine how a single, horizontally transferred gene would form a new regulatory system, because the existing regulatory systems are already very complicated."</summary><hostname>Phys.org</hostname><publisher>Nature Communications</publisher><url>https://phys.org/news/2022-02-scie

By expanding the gene pool beyond species boundaries, HGT events can drive genomic and phenotypic changes that increase fitness substantially. Accumulating evidence suggests that HGT is particularly prevalent between organisms that are either intimately associated or establish at least occasionally cell-cell contacts (e.g. in mutualistic or parasitic relationships). Here, I summarize current knowledge about HGT in plants, discuss possible molecular mechanisms and adaptive values of HGT events and highlight recent progress made in reconstructing HGT processes in laboratory experiments. Horizontal gene transfer (HGT), often also referred to as lateral gene transfer (LGT), is any process in which a recipient organism acquires genetic material from a donor organism by asexual means. By contrast, the transmission of genetic material from parent to offspring via reproduction is called vertical gene transfer. Given that HGT occurs by asexual processes, it is not restricted by species boundaries; therefore, organisms as diverse as prokaryotes and eukaryotes can engage in the horizontal exchange of genetic information. HGT events are usually detected as incongruences in molecular phylogenetic trees. If the phylogenetic tree based on sequences of gene A is in disagreement with the tree obtained with sequences of gene B, then HGT could be a possible explanation. However, a major limitation of this phylogenetic approach is that it largely restricts HGT discovery to unrelated (i.e. sexually incompatible) species and misses HGT events within or between closely related species. The tempo of evolution can vary across different genes and taxa, which can lead to tree-construction artefacts. Common problems include among-site rate heterogeneity (i.e. variation in substitution rates among different sites in a sequence), heterotachy (i.e. shifts in site-specific evolutionary rates over time) and inclusion of 'fast-clock' species (i.e. species with abnormally high rates of nucleotide substitution). Therefore, only strong incongruences between phylogenetic trees are usually accepted as solid evidence of HGT. Also, HGT can be difficult to tell apart from ancestral gene duplication followed by differential gene loss [1,2]. Finally, the presence of promiscuous DNA (i.e. DNA sequences transferred between different compartments of the eukaryotic cell, such as from plastidial or mitochondrial genomes into the nuclear genome; reviewed in Refs [3,4]) in conjunction with the different tempos of evolution in the three genomes of the plant cell [5] can cause artefactual trees, if the location of a gene in a particular genome (i.e. nuclear, plastidial or mitochondrial) was not verified. The endosymbioses that gave rise to mitochondria and chloroplasts might represent the evolutionarily earliest examples of massive HGT [9,10]. Treatment of tumor DNA with DNAase abolished the acceleration. Renaturation rates for DNA from bands 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 12 and 14 were not affected by tumor DNA. DNA from band 3 showed a slight rate increase in the presence of tumor DNA, indicating 21-27 copies of 14-18% of the DNA sequences in this (doublet) band. The band 3 doublet was separated by electrophoresis into bands 3a and 3b. Tumor DNA had little effect on the rate of reassociation of labeled band 3a DNA. Band 3b DNA renatured rapidly in the presence of tumor DNA, and its rate increase indicated that approximately 18 copies of 40% of band 3b DNA sequences are present per diploid tumor cell. This amounts to 3.7 × 10⁶ daltons of foreign genetic information and represents a contribution of 0.0011% to the DNA content of the tumor cell. The relationship between this plant tumor and virally induced animal tumor systems is discussed. DNA homology studies have demonstrated that in some instances, the large virulence plasmids of different A. tumefaciens strains are only distantly related to one another (Currier and Nester, 1976a). Fingerprinting of plasmid restriction endonuclease digests confirms this conclusion (Sciaky, 1977). If all virulence genes are closely related, they must therefore constitute only a minor fraction of the plasmid genome. Only a few genetic markers have thus far been found to reside on virulence plasmids. First, tumor tissue stably exhibits altered growth requirements in the absence of the inciting bacterium. The tumor cells grow in vitro in the absence of viable bacteria on agar lacking auxin and cytokinin hormones, a medium on which normal plant tissue is unable to grow. Hormone independence persists indefinitely in cultured tumor tissue. Acquisition of new genetic information from the bacterium could explain this heritable alteration. Second, crown gall tumor cells produce unusual amino acid derivatives. <answer>Title: Scaling Ion Trap Quantum Computing: Strategies, Feasibility, and Pathways to Real-World Problem Solving

Executive Summary
Trapped-ion quantum computing is uniquely positioned to scale toward large-scale, fault-tolerant systems due to high-coherence qubits, near-unitary measurements, and flexible connectivity via Coulomb interactions or photonic interconnects. The most promising scaling pathways are (1) microfabricated 2D surface-electrode arrays with shuttling and local-mode gates, (2) dense microchip arrays coupled with integrated photonics for programmable localized phonon modes and Rydberg-like parallelism, and (3) modular architectures that link microchip “QCCD modules” via quantum matter links and photonic entanglement. These routes are complementary: arrays provide dense qubit connectivity and reconfigurable gates; modules enable distributed, fault-tolerant architectures; and integrated control (e.g., WISE) and materials advances address the wiring and integration challenges that limit I/O and noise. Current demonstrations show these approaches are within reach for hundreds to thousands of physical qubits, with error rates and transport/coherence that are compatible with error mitigation and surface-code thresholds, though full fault tolerance requires further work on crosstalk, control latency, and materials. The most likely path to solving real-world problems is a hybrid system combining dense microchip arrays with modular linking and integrated control.

1. Microfabricated 2D Surface-Electrode Arrays and Shuttling-Based QCCD
A scalable route to dense, reconfigurable ion arrays is the grid-based surface-electrode Paul trap, which supports multi-species crystals and conditional transport operations across the grid. By combining cowired control electrodes with site-specific voltage gates, this architecture enables sorting, reordering, and conditional exchange of ion crystals across multiple sites, consistent with the QCCD vision of a reconfigurable qubit register on a chip. Transport operations in two separate systems (¹⁷¹Yb⁺–¹³⁸Ba⁺ and ¹³⁷Ba⁺–⁸⁸Sr⁺) show subquantum motional excitation at exchange rates of ~2.5 kHz, with logic controlled in software and hardware-compatible crossover switches planned. These results demonstrate the feasibility of dynamically reconfigurable arrays at scale, a core requirement for scaling gate-model quantum processors. <cite id="15"></cite>

Surface-electrode microchip traps have also achieved high-fidelity gates and readout in linear arrays, and modular linking via photon-mediated entanglement has been demonstrated at rates approaching the decoherence times of remote qubits, validating the modular approach as a pathway to utility-scale systems. <cite id="26"></cite>

2. Integrated Optics and Photonics for Dense Arrays
Integrated photonic chips deliver multiple wavelengths to Sr⁺ ion qubits on surface-electrode traps, improving stability against platform vibrations and enabling robust packaging. This integration is a key advance toward portable, scalable trapped-ion sensors and processors, and it paves the way for on-chip photonic routing and detection that reduces the burden of free-space optics as arrays grow larger. <cite id="17"></cite>

Complementary to integrated optics, programmable optical tweezer arrays can be used to pin ions in a linear trap and engineer localized phonon modes, enabling scalable and parallel entangling gates across long ion strings. Because the gate time depends only on the localized mode splitting and not the total number of ions, this approach promises high parallelism and resilience to crosstalk when combined with optimal control of pulse amplitudes. Demonstrations of optical segmentation and Rydberg-like gates illustrate the practicality of this strategy for dense arrays. <cite id="38"></cite>

3. Modular Architectures: Matter Links and Photonic Networking
A practical mechanism for linking microchip modules is the quantum matter link—repeated, high-rate ion transport between adjacent modules with an ion-loss infidelity below 7×10⁻⁸ and minimal phase-coherence degradation. With transport rates of ~2.4 kHz per ion and negligible phase disturbance, this link supports the QCCD vision of moving qubits between modules while preserving coherence, enabling modular, fault-tolerant architectures. <cite id="30"></cite>

Commercial and lab efforts have also demonstrated photonic interconnects that entangle remote trapped-ion modules, validating the generation, transmission, and detection of photons used to link commercial systems. IonQ’s roadmap projects interconnected two-chip modules with ~20,000 physical qubits and photonic networking, projecting ~1,600 error-corrected logical qubits by 2028—crossing the threshold for some cryptographically relevant applications. Theoretical progress has improved photonic entanglement rates by ~6 orders of magnitude, with recent rates approaching 250 Hz, reinforcing the viability of photonic linking for modular scaling. <cite id="33"></cite><cite id="34"></cite><cite id="35"></cite>

4. Integrated Control and Materials Integration
The “wiring challenge” of scaling control I/O is addressed by Integrated Switching Electronics (WISE), which integrates simple switching on the ion-trap chip while retaining complex electronics externally. This reduces the I/O footprint from ~N per qubit to ~200 sources for a 1000-qubit system and enables gate-layer rates of ~40–2600 per second, demonstrating that dense arrays can be operated with practical control infrastructure. <cite id="62"></cite>

Materials integration is another critical enabler: reducing electric-field noise from trap-electrode surfaces, improving compatibility between optics/electronics and ion-trap chips, and exploring unconventional materials (e.g., graphene, indium tin oxide) for hybrid systems. These efforts aim to minimize crosstalk and decoherence while enabling the coexistence of integrated photonic, fiber, and mirror components on trapped-ion platforms. <cite id="70"></cite><cite id="61"></cite>

5. Readout, Control, and Crosstalk Mitigation in Dense Arrays
Individual addressing of ions in microfabricated traps using on-chip magnetic field gradients has been demonstrated, yielding ~2.2% crosstalk and no measurable degradation of spin-echo coherence times. This shows that optical qubit transitions can be selectively addressed in dense arrays without compromising coherence, a prerequisite for scalable error mitigation and measurement-based protocols. <cite id="9"></cite>

For collective addressing and readout via Coulomb-crystal buses, recent work outlines technologies for integrating fibers, mirrors, and hybrid materials to refine how ions are confined and controlled, with a focus on reducing undesired coupling between components. These advances are essential for scaling collective bus architectures while maintaining gate and measurement fidelities. <cite id="61"></cite>

6. Feasibility and Practical Implementation Challenges
- Error rates and coherence: Gates in dense arrays have reached fidelities above 99% (e.g., 99.3% Bell-state fidelity with integrated optics), and transport links have loss infidelities below 7×10⁻⁸, with minimal phase disturbance. Photonic entanglement rates are approaching the decoherence rates of remote qubits, supporting modular entanglement at the module level. These results indicate that current error rates and coherence times are compatible with error mitigation and surface-code thresholds for hundreds to thousands of physical qubits. <cite id="2"></cite><cite id="30"></cite><cite id="34"></cite>
- Crosstalk and control latency: Programmable tweezer-engineered phonon modes and optimized pulse sequences can minimize crosstalk in parallel gates, while WISE reduces I/O and control latency for dense arrays. Individual addressing and magnetic gradients further suppress crosstalk during single-qubit operations. <cite id="38"></cite><cite id="62"></cite><cite id="9"></cite>
- Integration and materials: Integrated photonics, hybrid materials, and on-chip switching are advancing the integration of optics and electronics on ion-trap chips, but long-term fault tolerance requires continued materials research to suppress electric-field noise and enable robust packaging and routing. <cite id="17"></cite><cite id="70"></cite><cite id="61"></cite>

7. Pathways to Solving Real-World Problems
To deliver quantum advantage on real-world problems (e.g., quantum chemistry, materials simulation, and cryptography), the most likely route is a hybrid system:
- Dense microchip arrays with programmable tweezer or segmented potentials for localized phonon modes, enabling parallel, high-fidelity gates and reconfigurable connectivity. <cite id="38"></cite>
- Integrated optics and WISE to manage control I/O and improve stability, facilitating operation at hundreds to thousands of qubits. <cite id="17"></cite><cite id="62"></cite>
- Modular linking via quantum matter links and photonic entanglement to build distributed, fault-tolerant architectures once error rates and coherence meet surface-code thresholds. <cite id="30"></cite><cite id="34"></cite>

8. Conclusion
The most effective approaches to scaling trapped-ion quantum computing are:
- Microfabricated 2D surface-electrode arrays with shuttling and local-mode gates (QCCD), supported by grid-based transport and reconfiguration. <cite id="15"></cite>
- Dense microchip arrays coupled with integrated photonics for programmable localized phonon modes and Rydberg-like parallelism. <cite id="38"></cite><cite id="17"></cite>
- Modular architectures that link microchip modules via quantum matter links and photonic entanglement, validated by high-rate transport and inter-module entanglement demonstrations. <cite id="30"></cite><cite id="34"></cite>

These strategies are complementary and increasingly within reach, with current error rates, coherence, and control capabilities compatible with error mitigation and surface-code thresholds. Continued advances in materials integration, on-chip switching, and programmable coupling will determine the speed and reliability of scaling to large-scale systems capable of solving real-world problems. <cite id="70"></cite><cite id="62"></cite><cite id="38"></cite><cite id="34"></cite></answer>
