<search query="Coulomb crystal bus surface-electrode ion traps readout control crosstalk scalability 2021 2022 2023 2024 feasibility error rates" search_time="2026年5月10日10时13分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:9"><title>Individual addressing of ions using magnetic field gradients in a surface-electrode ion trap</title><summary>Dense array of ions in microfabricated traps represent one possible way to scale up ion trap quantum computing. The ability to address individual trapped ions is an important component of such a scheme. We demonstrate individual addressing of trapped ions in a microfabricated surface-electrode trap using a magnetic field gradient generated on-chip. A frequency splitting of 310(2) kHz for two ions separated by 5 μm is achieved. Selective single qubit operations are performed on one of two trapped ions with an average of 2.2±1.0% crosstalk. Coherence time as measured by the spin-echo technique is unaffected by the field gradient.

Trapped ion systems are promising candidates for implementing quantum computation [1]. Significant progress has been made in realizing quantum operations using a small number of ions as qubits [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Meaningful quantum computation involves a large number of qubits, and one possible way to scale up ion traps is to create a dense array of ions in microfabricated traps. The ability to individually address ions is an essential component of such a system. In this letter, we report the successful demonstration of individual addressing of single trapped ions in a linear crystal, using a magnetic field gradient generated in a microfabricated surface-electrode trap.

Previous methods of individual ion addressing have included spatial and frequency separation. An example of spatial separation is the use of a precisely focused laser beams aimed at only one ion at a time [7], which poses a significant technical challenge in laser beam control. Another approach is to transport ions between trap zones using varying DC potentials [4, 8], which requires precision voltage and timing control. Separation in frequency space has been proposed and implemented by creating AC stark shifts using a far off-resonant laser [9, 10]. Frequency selectivity can also be achieved by applying an inhomogeneous magnetic field gradient for spatially-separated ions [11]. This has been demonstrated in a linear Paul trap using hyperfine states of trapped 171Yb+ions probed with rf radiation [12], and with neutral Cs atoms in an optical dipole trap [13]. A similar technique can be applied to magnetic-field-sensitive qubit transitions in the optical range. Such an approach requires separating the ion frequencies by more than the Rabi frequency to reduce crosstalk.

Here, we present the first design and implementation of a microfabricated trap to perform individual addressing for optical transitions using a magnetic field gradient. Addressability is demonstrated by observing distinct Rabi peaks in the frequency spectrum, and by performing single qubit operations on one of two trapped ions. Coherence time as measured by the spin-echo technique is unaffected by the field gradient. We evaluate this individual addressing scheme to show that we can achieve reasonable gate speeds, and minimal crosstalk between neighbouring ions, with no decrease in coherence time measured with spin-echo. Finally we consider its prospects for scaling to many ions.

The gradient design is based on a five-rod surface-electrode design similar to that of Ref. [14], with the trap center 100 μm above the surface. The fabrication process is identical to that of Ref [15]. A single-layer design simplifies microfabrication, as well as enables proximity between the gradient-generating current and the ion. The ground electrode is patterned as shown in Fig. 1. Three parallel current paths are created. The center current path follows an S-shaped pattern directly below the trap center, and splits into two paths at the opposite end of the electrode. This symmetry is necessary to minimize the horizontal bias field in the axial direction.

Trapped atomic ions form the basis of high-fidelity quantum information processors [5, 6] and high-accuracy optical clocks [7]. Here we demonstrate a surface-electrode ion-trap chip [8, 9] using integrated waveguides and grating couplers, which delivers all the wavelengths of light required for ionization, cooling, coherent operations, and quantum-state preparation and detection of Sr+ qubits. Laser light from violet to infrared is coupled onto the chip via an optical-fiber array, creating an inherently stable optical path, which we use to demonstrate qubit coherence that is resilient to platform vibrations. For QCs based on trapped ions, architectures such as the quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) are used to scale the number of qubits on a single device. However, the number of ions that can be hosted on a single quantum computing module is limited by the size of the chip being used. Therefore, a modular approach is of critical importance and requires quantum connections between individual modules. Here, we present the demonstration of a quantum matter-link in which ion qubits are transferred between adjacent QC modules. Ion transport between adjacent modules is realised at a rate of 2424 s⁻¹ and with an infidelity associated with ion loss during transport below 7 × 10⁻⁸. Furthermore, we show that the link does not measurably impact the phase coherence of the qubit. The quantum matter-link constitutes a practical mechanism for the interconnection of QCCD devices. Our work will facilitate the implementation of modular QCs capable of fault-tolerant utility-scale quantum computation.</summary><hostname>Nature</hostname><author_list><author name="M Akhtar" affiliation="Sussex Centre for Quantum Technologies, University of Sussex, Brighton, BN1 9RH, UK; raw_output.raw_text: <search query="microfabricated ion trap array integrated optics programmable optical tweezers localized phonon modes scalable entangling gates 2022 2023 2024 Rydberg-like" search_time="2026年5月10日10时13分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:38"><title>Scalable and Parallel Tweezer Gates for Quantum Computing with Long Ion Strings</title><summary>Trapped-ion quantum computers have demonstrated high-performance gate operations in registers of about ten qubits. However, scaling up and parallelizing quantum computations due to the global nature of the motional modes of the ions which mediate qubit-qubit couplings. Here, we devise methods to implement scalable and parallel entangling gates by using engineered localized phonon modes. We propose to tailor such localized modes by tuning the local potential of individual ions with programmable optical tweezer arrays, which are commonly utilized as a powerful tool in quantum simulation with neutral Rydberg atoms. Here, instead, we consider using programmable optical tweezer arrays to pin specific ions in a linear trap, and thereby engineer localized phonon modes. These designer phonon modes form the basis to implement scalable and parallel entangling gates. The required capabilities to optically address individual ions are available in current experiments. By dynamically reconfiguring the tweezer array, the designer phonon modes can be adjusted during running quantum computations, and thus offer great flexibility to achieve an effective "optical segmentation" of the ion chain. Possible quantum circuits provided by optical segmentation are illustrated schematically in Figs. 1(a) and 1(b): In the first example, a subregister formed by three consecutive qubits which are marked by cyan shading is decoupled from the other qubits by "optical tweezer walls". The second example relies on the long-range connectivity in chains of trapped ions to implement an entangling gate between the two qubits marked by pink shading and which are both pinned by optical tweezers. In this work, we focus on the implementation of quantum circuits which are composed of parallel gates between pairs of nearest-neighboring qubits. Pinning pairs of neighboring ions with optical tweezers as illustrated in Fig. 1(c) gives rise to localized phonon modes which correspond to center-of-mass (COM) and stretch oscillations of the pinned ions. In micro traps with segmented electrodes, an analogous local mode structure arises for two ions which are shuttled to an interaction zone of the trap. The optical segmentation enables performing entangling gates on all pairs of pinned ions in parallel, which corresponds to the first layer of the quantum circuit shown in Fig. 1(d). Due to the emergence of a local phonon mode structure with only two relevant localized phonon modes per pinned pair, high-fidelity scalable and parallel gates can be performed in long ion chains without resorting to optimal coherent control techniques. Further, the gate time is determined by the splitting of the localized phonon modes, and is thus independent of the total number of ions in the chain. Indeed, as we show analytically and numerically, tweezer gates can be performed even in infinitely long chains. Further, the gate time is determined by the splitting of the localized phonon modes, and is thus independent of the total number of ions in the chain. Finally, we discuss different ways to minimize crosstalk between parallel two-qubit entangling gates based on optimal control of time-modulated laser-pulse amplitudes as developed by Duan et al. This enables the implementation of dense "brick wall circuits." Such dense circuits have a wide range of applications, for example, in digital quantum simulation of spin models with local interactions, or to realize random circuits which are models for strongly chaotic quantum dynamics.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Tobias Olsacher" affiliation="Center for Quantum Physics, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria; Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of th

Building a cohesive ion system from such diverse parts involves many challenges, including: navigating materials incompatibilities and undesired coupling between elements. Here, we review our recent efforts to create scalable ion systems incorporating unconventional materials such as graphene and indium tin oxide, integrating devices like optical fibers and mirrors, and exploring alternative ion loading and trapping techniques.</summary><hostname>DSpace@MIT</hostname><publisher>Quantum Information Processing</publisher><author_list><author name="Amira M. Eltony" affiliation="Research Laboratory of Electronics, Department of Physics, Center for Ultracold Atoms, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA" /><author name="Dorian Gangloff" /><author name="Molu Shi" /><author name="Alexei Bylinskii" /><author name="Vladan Vuletic" /><author name="Isaac L. Chuang" /></author_list><url>https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/104777/11128_2016_Article_1298.pdf?sequence=1</url><publish_time>2016年3月21日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:49"><title>Quantum Computation in Large Ion Crystals</title><hostname>University of Michigan</hostname><publisher>Dissertation</publisher><author_list><author name="Yukai Wu" affiliation="University of Michigan" /></author_list><url>https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/handle/2027.42/149953/wyukai_1.pdf</url><publish_time>2019年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:50"><title>Scaling the Ion Trap Quantum Processor</title><summary>Trapped atomic ions are standards for quantum information processing, serving as quantum memories, hosts of quantum gates in quantum computers and simulators, and nodes of quantum communication networks. Quantum bits based on trapped ions enjoy a rare combination of attributes: they have exquisite coherence properties, they can be prepared and measured with nearly 100% efficiency, and they are readily entangled with each other through the Coulomb interaction or remote photon interconnects. Trapped atomic ions are a leading platform for first-generation quantum computers, but they are also fundamentally scalable to more powerful general purpose devices in future generations. problem: In ecology, how do birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration? What cues and disturbances influence this process?
final_response:
<think>
<answer>Across species, birds combine multiple cues in a flexible, context-dependent way, and they adjust the relative weighting of cues across seasons and life stages. The primary sources of directional information are (1) topographic and geomagnetic features including wind direction, (2) the stars, (3) the sun and polarized light, and (4) the Earth’s magnetic field. Location (map) information appears to come from a separate geographic positioning system that integrates visual, olfactory, acoustic, and geomagnetic cues, and navigation strategy shifts from a compass-and-clock route-finding mode in juveniles to more map-based orientation in adults; precise location learning also occurs at stopover sites <cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-1"></cite><cite id="call_a029ae12d040-0"></cite>.

Celestial cues: <cite id="call_a029ae12d040-0"></cite>
- During the day, birds use the position of the sun and the pattern of polarized skylight to maintain direction. They can recalibrate their solar compass relative to true north (or their preferred reference axis) by the polarization ellipse, which provides an absolute frame of reference rather than just relative sun position <cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-2"></cite><cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-3"></cite>.
- At night, many species use the stars (especially the North Star Polaris in northern migrants), and experimental displacement shows reliance on stellar cues for orientation; altering the apparent starry sky disrupts direction choice <cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-3"></cite><cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-1"></cite><cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-2"></cite>.

Magnetic cues: <cite id="call_a029ae12d040-0"></cite><cite id="call_a029ae12d040-1"></cite>
- Birds detect two main magnetic pathways: a steeply angle-dependent (‘steep’) compass tied to the direction of least magnetic resistance (inclination-based) and an axial compass aligned roughly east–west that depends on magnetic polarity (north–south). These are thought to arise from different magnetoreceptors and neural processing streams and can be differentially engaged by light and environmental context <cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-2"></cite><cite id="call_a029ae12d040-1"></cite><cite id="call_6d46913cf43f-0"></cite>.
- The magnetic compass is supported by two candidate mechanisms: (i) light-dependent radical-pair processes in the eyes (involving photoreduction of retinal cryptochromes; sensitive to blue-green light and disrupted by long wavelengths such as red/green in some experimental conditions) and (ii) magnetite-based magnetoreception near the beak that may respond to low-frequency magnetic fields and is less light-dependent <cite id="call_a029ae12d040-1"></cite><cite id="call_6d46913cf43f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6d46913cf43f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6d46913cf43f-0"></cite>.
- A separate magnetite cluster in the upper beak functions as a ‘compass’ and is detectable as a specialized area that integrates specialized visual input at night in night-migratory songbirds, indicating tight coordination between magnetic and celestial pathways <cite id="call_a029ae12d040-1"></cite>.
- Magnetic sensitivity is higher in cryptochrome4 (Cry4) in the eyes of migratory birds than in nonmigratory birds; Cry4 mediates magnetoreception by a quantum-radical-pair mechanism involving electron-jump pathways among conserved tryptophan residues whose magnetic sensitivity is modulated by blue light <cite id="call_65e669e17476-0"></cite><cite id="call_65e669e17476-1"></cite><cite id="call_65e669e17476-3"></cite>.

Other cues and integration: <cite id="call_a029ae12d040-0"></cite><cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-1"></cite>
- Topographic/landmark and wind cues are used at fine spatial scales; wind direction can be influenced by major landforms and is an element of topographic orientation <cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-1"></cite>.
- Olfactory cues are a plausible source of location (map) information for some species, though evidence remains indirect and context-dependent <cite id="call_58c0ceb58c21-1"></cite>.
- The integration of cues appears to be flexible and learned; juveniles use a clock-and-compass strategy with limited route knowledge, whereas adults and experienced migrants rely more on a map-based system that can be acquired at stopovers <cite id="call_a029ae12d040-0"></cite>.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Magnetic compass in birds dual pathway map compass review 2013 2020 Nature Reviews Neuroscience" search_time="2026年5月10日10时11分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:9"><title>Avian navigation and geographic positioning</title><summary>Site fidelity to breeding and wintering grounds, and even stopover sites, suggests that passerines are capable of accurate navigation during their annual migrations. Geolocator-based studies are beginning to demonstrate precise population-specific migratory routes and even some interannual consistency in individual routes. Displacement studies of birds have shown that at least adult birds are capable of goal-oriented movements, likely involving some type of map or geographic position system. In contrast, juveniles on their first migration use a clock-and-compass orientation strategy, with limited knowledge about locations along their migratory routes. Positioning information could come from a variety of cues including visual, olfactory, acoustic, and geomagnetic sources. How information from these systems is integrated and used for avian navigation has yet to be fully articulated. In this review, we (1) define geographic positioning and distinguish the types of navigational strategies that birds could use for orientation, (2) describe sensory cues available to birds for geographic positioning, (3) review the evidence for geographic positioning in birds and methods used to collect that evidence, and (4) discuss ways ornithologists, particularly field ornithologists, can contribute to and advance our knowledge of the navigational abilities of birds. Few studies of avian orientation and navigation mechanisms have been conducted in the Western Hemisphere. To fully understand migratory systems in the Western Hemisphere and develop better conservation policies, information about the orientation and navigation mechanisms used by specific species needs to be integrated with other aspects of their migration ecology and biology.</summary><hostname>Sci-Hub</hostname><publisher>Journal of Field Ornithology, JUNE 2014, Vol. 85, No. 2 (JUNE 2014), pp. 111-133</publisher><author_list><author name="Mark E Deutschlander" affiliation="Department of Biology, Hobart and William Smith Colleges, Geneva, New York, 14456, USA" /><author name="Robert C Beason" affiliation="2826 East 1650 Road, Baldwin City, Kansas, 66006, USA" /></author_list><url>https://sci-hub.st/uptodate/24617904.pdf#navpanes=0&view=FitH</url><publish_time>2014年6月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:10"><title>Magnetoreception and its use in bird navigation</title><summary>Recent advances have brought new insight into the physiological mechanisms that enable birds and other animals to use magnetic fields for orientation. Many birds seem to have two magnetodetection senses, one based on magnetite near the beak and one based on light-dependent radical-pair processes in the bird’s eye(s). Among the most exciting recent results are: first, behavioural responses of birds experiencing oscillating magnetic fields. Second, the occurrence of putative magnetosensory molecules, the cryptochromes, in the eyes of migratory birds. Third, detection of a brain area that integrates specialised visual input at night in night-migratory songbirds. Fourth, a putative magnetosensory cluster of magnetite in the upper beak. These and other recent findings have important implications for magnetoreception; however, many crucial open questions remain.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>Current Opinion in Neurobiology</publisher><author_list><author name="Henrik Mouritsen" affiliation="Carl von Ossietzky University of Oldenburg" /><author name="Thorsten Ritz" affiliation="University of California, Irvine" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Henrik-Mouritsen/publication/7738662_Magnetoreception_and_Its_Use_in_Bird_Navigation/links/5b0a388da6fdcc8c2532591c/Magnetoreception-and-Its-Use-in-Bird-Navigation.pdf</url><publish_time>2005年9月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document refer

However, to date, little is known about how ALAN affects behavior or physiology of nocturnal sources in urban areas. We studied effects of ALAN on migrating birds by monitoring the beams of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum's “Tribute in Light” in New York, quantifying behavioral responses with radar and acoustic sensors and modeling disorientation and behavioral with simulations. This single light source induced significant behavioral alterations in birds, even in good visibility conditions, in this heavily photopolluted environment, and to altitudes up to 1 km. We estimate that the installation influenced ≤1.1 million birds during our study period of 7 over 7 y. When the installation was illuminated, bird speed averaged 7 d over 7 y, decreased flight speeds, followed by circling flight paths, and vocalized more frequently. These behaviors were associated with attraction to and subsequent attraction for nearby birds, and bird densities near the installation exceeded magnitudes 20 times greater than surrounding baseline densities during each year's observations. However, behavioral disruptions disappeared when lights were extinguished, suggesting that selective removal of light during nights with substantial bird migration is a viable strategy for minimizing potentially fatal interactions among ALAN, structures, and birds. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Artificial light at night disrupts magnetic compass orientation of migratory birds Liedveld 2016 Current Biology" search_time="2026年5月10日10时12分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:63"><title>Interactions between the visual and the magnetoreception system: Different effects of bichromatic light regimes on the directional behavior of migratory birds</title><summary>When magnetic compass orientation of migratory robins was tested, the birds proved well oriented under low intensity monochromatic light of shorter wavelengths up to 565 nm green; from 583 nm yellow onward, they were disoriented. In the present study, we tested robins under bichromatic lights composed (1) of 424 nm blue and 565 nm green and (2) of 565 nm green and 583 nm yellow at two intensities. Under dim blue-green light with a total quantal flux of ca. 8 × 10¹⁵ quanta/s m², the birds were well oriented in their migratory direction by their inclination compass; under blue-green light of twice this intensity, their orientation became axial. In both cases, the magnetic directional information was mediated by the radical pair processes in the eye. When green and yellow light were combined, however, the nature of the behavior changed. Under green-yellow light of the higher intensity, the birds showed a 'fixed direction' response that was polar, no longer controlled by the normal inclination compass; under dim green-yellow light, the response became axial. Although this ecological light pollution is damaging ecosystems throughout the world, the topic has received relatively little attention. Many nocturnally migrating birds die or lose a large amount of their energy reserves during migration as a result of encountering artificial light sources. This happens, for instance, in the North Sea, where large numbers of nocturnally migrating birds are attracted to the many offshore platforms. Our aim is to develop bird-friendly artificial lighting that meets human demands for safety but does not attract and disorient birds. Our current working hypothesis is that artificial light interferes with the magnetic compass of the birds, one of several orientation mechanisms and especially important during overcast nights. We designed a field study to test if and how changing light color influenced migrating birds under field conditions. We found that nocturnally migrating birds were disoriented and attracted by red and white light (containing visible long-wavelength radiation), whereas they were clearly less disoriented by blue and green light (containing less or no visible long-wavelength radiation). This was especially the case on overcast nights. Our results clearly open perspective for the development of bird-friendly artificial lighting by manipulating wavelength characteristics. <answer><title>Design Report: Modeling, Analysis, and Design for 3D Reconstruction and Phenotypic Analysis of Crop Grains Using Modern Control Theory and Related Methods</title>

Executive summary
This report proposes a data-driven, integrated design for 3D reconstruction and phenotypic analysis of crop grains, combining robust 3D sensing pipelines, geometric and learning-based reconstruction, and modern control-theoretic principles to ensure high throughput, reliability, and adaptability in both lab and field settings. The design leverages multi-view imaging and depth sensing, efficient reconstruction (including 3D Gaussian Splatting), and control strategies for sensor management and vision-guided operations, embedded within a cyber-physical framework for scalable phenotyping. <cite id="call_53be6e1209b2-0"></cite><cite id="call_7c6d68f3fbfc-0"></cite><cite id="call_5785d45d5d1b-0"></cite><cite id="call_c0ea150a1baf-0"></cite><cite id="call_4cc1d610d603-0"></cite><cite id="call_5785d45d5d1b-0"></cite><cite id="call_1f84a59741bc-0"></cite><cite id="call_104"></cite>

1. System architecture and design objectives
- High-throughput, non-contact 3D reconstruction of individual grains and small seeds (including in-field and lab platforms).
- Robust, accurate phenotyping: length, width, height, surface area, volume, shape descriptors, and defect detection.
- Integration of sensing, processing, and actuation within a cyber-physical system for closed-loop operation and scalability.
- Adaptability to diverse crops (e.g., wheat, rice, maize kernels) and environmental conditions.
- Data-driven pipeline with quantitative performance benchmarks and reproducible analysis. <cite id="call_53be6e1209b2-0"></cite><cite id="call_7c6d68f3fbfc-0"></cite><cite id="call_5785d45d5d1b-0"></cite><cite id="call_1f84a59741bc-0"></cite><cite id="call_104"></cite>

2. Data acquisition and sensor selection
- Multi-view imaging and depth sensing: RGB-D cameras, stereo rigs, and consumer-grade depth sensors for in-field operation; single cameras with rotation for small seeds to enable silhouette-based reconstruction. <cite id="call_53be6e1209b2-0"></cite><cite id="call_5785d45d5d1b-0"></cite><cite id="call_113"></cite>
- Complementary modalities: LiDAR for rapid, high-quality point clouds in controlled environments; X-ray CT for internal morphology when required (with specialized acquisition containers). <cite id="call_53be6e1209b2-0"></cite><cite id="call_34"></cite>
- Robustness considerations: camera calibration, lighting control, and sensor placement to mitigate ambient lighting effects and occlusions. <cite id="call_53be6e1209b2-0"></cite>

3. Reconstruction pipeline and modeling
- Multi-view reconstruction pipeline:
  - Image acquisition and sampling (e.g., panoramic rotation or multi-angle setups).
  - Structure-from-Motion (SFM) for sparse reconstruction and camera pose estimation.
  - Dense reconstruction using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for high-fidelity, detailed models. <cite id="call_7c6d68f3fbfc-0"></cite>
- Silhouette-based reconstruction for small seeds:
  - Tool center point estimation and compensation for sub-millimeter repeatability.
  - Volume carving for surface reconstruction and quantitative metrics (length, width, height, volume). <cite id="call_5785d45d5d1b-0"></cite>
- Deep learning-based reconstruction:
  - Single-view or few-view 3D reconstruction to reduce imaging time and enable real-time sorting, with reported relative errors around 2% and strong correlations with manual measurements. <cite id="call_c0ea150a1baf-0"></cite>
- Point cloud processing:
  - Denoising, segmentation, filtering, and instance segmentation to isolate individual grains and extract phenotypic features. <cite id="call_53be6e1209b2-0"></cite>

4. Phenotypic analysis and feature extraction
- Geometric descriptors:
  - Length, width, height, surface area, volume, and shape indices (e.g., sphericity) from reconstructed models. <cite id="call_7c6d68f3fbfc-0"></cite>
- Statistical and classification-based analysis:
  - Dimensionality reduction, feature selection, and classifiers (e.g., ensembles, deep learners) for variety identification and trait clustering. <cite id="call_63f9229c9761-0"></cite>
- Time-resolved growth modeling:
  - Registration-based pipelines (Fast Global Registration + ICP) to build 4D digital twins of plant development for longitudinal phenotyping. <cite id="call_10"></cite>
- Complementary imaging analysis:
  - Fourier-based and Bayesian contour analysis for kernel counting and axis measurement in 2D images, with high correlation to ground truth. <cite id="call_79"></cite>

5. Control-theoretic design and optimization
- Sensor and conveyor control for throughput:
  - Queueing-theoretic models (Poisson arrivals, M/G/1 with impatience) and renewal theory to optimize conveyor speeds and buffer management, avoiding starvation and saturation. <cite id="call_f200cc98882a-0"></cite><cite id="call_f200cc98882a-1"></cite>
- Vision-guided operations:
  - Image-based and model-based visual servoing for precision alignment and grasping in robotic workflows, including multi-camera setups and robust registration strategies. <cite id="call_169917a0969b-0"></cite><cite id="call_86788c0498c2-0"></cite><cite id="call_86788c0498c2-1"></cite>
- Morphology-agnostic control:
  - Mutual information-based self-recognition and visual servoing for systems with limited prior knowledge, enabling adaptability to novel morphologies and uncalibrated cameras. <cite id="call_98"></cite>

6. Cyber-physical integration and scalable infrastructure
- Framework components:
  - Ubiquitous sensing (LiDAR, RGB-D, CT), smart actuators, and scalable cyberinfrastructure for data acquisition, processing, and actuation. <cite id="call_104"></cite>
- Digital twins and standardization:
  - Agricultural digital twins for predictive modeling and closed-loop decision-making; standardization of data formats and protocols to support interoperability and reproducibility. <cite id="call_104"></cite>
- Embedded and mobile platforms:
  - Integration with mobile platforms (e.g., tractors, caterpillars) for in-field operations, leveraging low-cost sensors and dense 3D mapping. <cite id="call_113"></cite>

7. Operational considerations and field deployment
- Environmental robustness:
  - Sensor selection and calibration strategies to mitigate ambient lighting and motion artifacts; use of depth cameras and LiDAR for stability in variable field conditions. <cite id="call_53be6e1209b2-0"></cite><cite id="call_113"></cite>
- Workflow automation:
  - Closed-loop control of conveyor belts and imaging sequences to maintain throughput and avoid occlusions; active vision cells for automated imaging and reconstruction. <cite id="call_f200cc98882a-0"></cite><cite id="call_1f84a59741bc-0"></cite>
- Data management:
  - Efficient storage, indexing, and retrieval of 3D models and phenotypic metadata; integration with community computing resources for high-throughput analysis. <cite id="call_79"></cite>

8. Evaluation and performance benchmarks
- Reconstruction fidelity:
  - PSNR in 3DGS reconstructions (35–37 dB), R² values for length, width, and height (up to 0.946), and volume estimation accuracy via acoustic volumeters and deep learning baselines. <cite id="call_7c6d68f3fbfc-0"></cite><cite id="call_c0ea150a1baf-0"></cite>
- Phenotyping accuracy:
  - High correlations between 3D and 2D measurements (R² 0.80–0.96) and successful variety identification with standardized imaging protocols. <cite id="call_34"></cite><cite id="call_63f9229c9761-0"></cite>
- Throughput optimization:
  - Queueing models predicting optimal belt speeds and throughput improvements over ad-hoc settings. <cite id="call_f200cc98882a-1"></cite>

9. Implementation roadmap and deliverables
- Phase 1: Sensor selection and calibration; prototype multi-view rig or active vision cell for small seeds; baseline reconstruction and phenotyping. <cite id="call_53be6e1209b2-0"></cite><cite id="call_1f84a59741bc-0"></cite>
- Phase 2: Integration of control-theoretic models (queueing, visual servoing) for conveyor and imaging sequences; validation on controlled datasets. <cite id="call_f200cc98882a-0"></cite><cite id="call_169917a0969b-0"></cite>
- Phase 3: Field deployment with mobile platforms; CT-based internal morphology module; integration with digital twin infrastructure. <cite id="call_113"></cite><cite id="call_34"></cite><cite id="call_104"></cite>
- Deliverables:
  - Automated 3D reconstruction pipeline (including 3DGS and volume carving).
  - Control software for conveyor and vision loops (queueing models, visual servoing).
  - Phenotyping toolkit (segmentation, feature extraction, classification).
  - Field-ready system with mobile sensing and digital twin integration. <cite id="call_7c6d68f3fbfc-0"></cite><cite id="call_5785d45d5d1b-0"></cite><cite id="call_f200cc98882a-0"></cite><cite id="call_113"></cite><cite id="call_104"></cite>

10. Outlook and research directions
- Adaptive control for dynamic environments: learning-based control and morphology-agnostic servoing to handle occlusions and changing lighting. <cite id="call_98"></cite>
- Information-efficient acquisition: active vision and information bottleneck strategies to reduce redundant views while preserving phenotypic information. <cite id="call_1f84a59741bc-0"></cite>
- Global implementation: low-cost, robust systems tailored to African and resource-constrained settings, with community-driven computing for high-throughput analysis. <cite id="call_120"></cite>

Appendix: Key equations and models
- Poisson arrival and queueing models for conveyor control:
  - Intermittent motion modeled as a 2D Poisson process; continuous motion approximated by an M/G/1 queue with impatience. <cite id="call_f200cc98882a-0"></cite>
- Visual servoing control laws:
  - Image-based visual servoing (IBVS) and virtual visual servoing; robust M-estimator formulations for multi-camera tracking. <cite id="call_169917a0969b-0"></cite><cite id="call_86788c0498c2-1"></cite>
- Registration for 4D modeling:
  - Fast Global Registration followed by ICP for fine alignment across time steps. <cite id="call_10"></cite>

Notes on uncertainties
- Field-specific sensor performance and environmental variability may require site-specific calibration and validation beyond the general models. <cite id="call_53be6e1209b2-0"></cite><cite id="call_113"></cite>
- Deep learning reconstruction performance depends on dataset size and diversity; the provided benchmarks are for multi-crop datasets and should be validated on target species. <cite id="call_c0ea150a1baf-0"></cite>

References (cited above)

- Active vision and surface reconstruction for 3D plant shoot modeling. <cite id="call_1f84a59741bc-0"></cite>

- Optimizing robotic part feeder throughput with queueing theory. <cite id="call_f200cc98882a-0"></cite>

Unlike controlled laboratory environments, field-based phenotypic data collection is highly vulnerable to unpredictable factors, significantly complicating the data acquisition process. As a result, the choice of appropriate data collection equipment and processing methods has become a central focus of research. Currently, three key technologies for extracting crop phenotypic parameters are Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), Multi-View Stereo (MVS), and depth camera systems. LiDAR is valued for its rapid data acquisition and high-quality point cloud output, despite its substantial cost. MVS offers the potential to combine low-cost deployment with high-resolution point cloud generation, though challenges remain in the complexity and efficiency of point cloud processing. Depth cameras strike a favorable balance between processing speed, accuracy, and cost-effectiveness, yet their performance can be influenced by ambient conditions such as lighting. Data processing techniques primarily involve point cloud denoising, registration, segmentation, and reconstruction. This review summarizes advances over the past five years in 3D reconstruction technologies—focusing on both hardware and point cloud processing methods—with the aim of supporting efficient and raw_output.raw_text: <search query="multi-view stereo grain 3D reconstruction phenotyping" search_time="2026年5月10日10时14分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:25"><title>Seed 3D Phenotyping Across Multiple Crops Using 3D Gaussian Splatting</title><summary>This study introduces a versatile seed 3D reconstruction method that is applicable to multiple crops—including maize, wheat, and rice—and designed to overcome the inefficiency and subjectivity of manual measurements and the high costs of laser-based phenotyping. A panoramic video of the seed is captured and processed through frame sampling to extract multi-view images. Structure-from-Motion (SFM) is employed for sparse reconstruction and camera pose estimation, while 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is utilized for high-fidelity dense reconstruction, generating detailed point cloud models. The subsequent point cloud preprocessing, filtering, and segmentation enable the extraction of key phenotypic parameters, including length, width, height, surface area, and volume. The experimental evaluations demonstrated a high measurement accuracy, with coefficients of determination (R2) for length, width, and height reaching 0.9361, 0.8889, and 0.946, respectively. Moreover, the reconstructed models exhibit superior image quality, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) values consistently ranging from 35 to 37 dB, underscoring the robustness of 3DGS in preserving fine structural details. Compared to conventional multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques, the proposed method can achieve significantly improved reconstruction accuracy and visual fidelity. The key outcomes of this study confirm that the 3DGS-based pipeline provides a highly accurate, efficient, and scalable solution for digital phenotyping, establishing a robust foundation for its application across diverse crop species.</summary><hostname>Semantic Scholar</hostname><publisher>Agriculture</publisher><author_list><author name="Jun Gao" /><author name="Chao Zhu" /><author name="Junguo Hu" /><author name="Fei Deng" /><author name="Zhaoxin Xu" /><author name="Xiaomin Wang" /></author_list><url>https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Seed-3D-Phenotyping-Across-Multiple-Crops-Using-3D-Gao-Zhu/f40ce747ffc1612f76d6ecba387d74bfbc9b21ad</url><publish_time>2025年11月8日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:26"><title>High throughput measurement algorithm of maize ear 3D phenotype based on multi-view stereo vision</title><summary>As the manual measurement of maize ears in maize precision breeding is low-efficiency, labor-intensive, big-error and difficult to measure 3D indexes (such as row number, kernel number per row, rate of kernel loss, rate of kernel mold), a multi-view stereo vision algorithm for high throughput measurement of maize ear 3D phenotype was proposed. Considering the shape of maize ear is a solid of revolution, we analyzed several methods that acquire images of maize ear in 360 degrees, such as rotating scanner method, plain mirror imaging method and transparent board method. According to our analysis, we used a drop-and-shot method (three CCD cameras crossed 120 degrees mutually) to acquire images of maize ear in all degrees. For optimizing both speed of high throughput maize ear test (reduce full image scan) and accuracy of 3D measurement, we have done the followings: 1) Constructed the regular triangle measurement model based on triangulation, epipolar geometry and a few prior knowledges and solved contradictory equations using least square method. Hence, we can acquire depth information from three cameras that crossed 120 degrees mutually, calculate the 3D coordinates of maize ears according to parallax of three views and recover the 3D phenotype information of maize ears. 2) As the surface of maize ear is curved and the edge of maize ear region is difficult to recognize, we proposed a maize ear spatial overlap model based on regular triangle measurement model to calculate the overlap parts of three views of maize ear without laser mark. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="grain 3D shape phenotyping computer vision deep learning point cloud" search_time="2026年5月10日10时14分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:41"><title>Deep learning based 3d reconstruction for phenotyping of wheat seeds: a dataset, challenge, and baseline method</title><summary>We present a new data set for 3d wheat seed reconstruction, propose a challenge, and provide baseline methods. Individual plant seed properties influence early development of plants and are thus of interest in plant phenotyping experiments. Seed shape can be measured reliably from images using volume carvings, as done in robotic setups such as phenoSeeder. However, about 36 images are needed to obtain a suitably accurate 3d model [33], where image acquisition takes ≈ 20 s. For large-scale experiments with thousands of seeds high throughput is required limiting image acquisition time. We present a deep-learning model that reconstructs an approximate 3d point cloud from fewer images, even only a single view. It has a significantly lower error than linear regression, which has been actively used so far in similar tasks. Using three images reduces imaging time by a factor of 10×, where relative errors of volume length, width, and height are all around 2 %. Inference time from the neural network is negligibly short compared with imaging time which enables this method for real-time measurements and sorting. Seed phenotyping allows quantifying seed properties and, e.g., relate them to germination properties or early plant development [6, 28, 35], or perform quality assessment and classification [49, 21]. In scientific or breeding experiments sorting seeds by properties, e.g., their size, can reduce or explain observed biological variation. Different seed phenotyping techniques are well-established. An acoustic volumeter [40, 41] has been developed for seeds. It directly measures seed volume excluding micro-pores, without shape reconstruction. When interested in shape, other methods are more suitable. Flatbed scanners have often been selected for seed 2d phenotyping [27, 47, 15]. While being technically simple and robust, they do not give full access to the 3d geometrical parameters of a seed, and different 3d seed phenotyping methods are available. Legume seeds were bulk phenotyped in 3d with a hand-held 3d laser scanner [16], being suitable for seeds in the several millimeters to centimeter range and reported to be precise for asymmetrical seeds. An automated seed phenotyping system called phenoSeeder [17] addresses also small seeds in the sub-millimeter range. It uses a single camera, a rotating robot arm, and volume carving (VC) [33] to reconstruct 3d voxel models of individual seeds [17]. They are used for volume estimation and, together with single seed mass measurements, allow for estimating mass density per seed.</summary><hostname>JuSER</hostname><author_list><author name="Vsevolod Cherepashkin" affiliation="Forschungszentrum Jülich, IBG-2 Jülich, Germany" /><author name="Erenus Yildiz" affiliation="Forschungszentrum Jülich, IAS-8 Jülich, Germany" /><author name="Andreas Fischbach" affiliation="Forschungszentrum Jülich, IBG-2 Jülich, Germany" /><author name="Leif Kobbelt" affiliation="RWTH Aachen University, VCI Aachen, Germany" /><author name="Hanno Scharr" affiliation="Forschungszentrum Jülich, IAS-8 Jülich, Germany" /></author_list><url>https://juser.fz-juelich.de/record/1022310/files/Deep%20Learning%20Based%203d%20Reconstruction%20for%20Phenotyping%20of%20Wheat%20Seeds%20a%20Dataset,%20Challenge,%20and%20Baseline%20Method%20-%20Cherepashkin_Deep_Learning_Based_3d_Reconstruction_for_Phenotyping_of_Wheat_Seeds_ICCVW_2023_paper.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:42"><title>Wheat3DGS: In-field 3D Reconstruction, Instance Segmentation and Phenotyping of Wheat Heads with Gaussian Splatting</title><summary>Automated extraction of plant morphological traits is crucial for supporting crop breeding and agricultural management through high-throughput field phenotyping (HTFP). raw_output.raw_text: <search query="3D Gaussian Splatting plant seeds phenotyping rotation multi-view" search_time="2026年5月10日10时14分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:9"><title>Seed 3D Phenotyping Across Multiple Crops Using 3D Gaussian Splatting</title><summary>This study introduces a versatile seed 3D reconstruction method that is applicable to multi-crops—including maize, wheat, and rice—and designed to overcome the inefficiency and subjectivity of manual measurements and the high costs of laser-based phenotyping. A panoramic video of the seed is captured and processed through frame sampling to extract multi-view images. Structure-from-Motion (SFM) is employed for sparse reconstruction and camera pose estimation, while 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is utilized for high-fidelity dense reconstruction, generating detailed point cloud models. The subsequent point cloud preprocessing, filtering, and segmentation enable the extraction of key phenotypic parameters, including seed length, width, thickness, and volume. The experimental evaluations demonstrated a high measurement accuracy, with coefficients of determination (R²) for length, width, and height reaching 0.9361, 0.8889, and 0.946, respectively. Moreover, the reconstructed models exhibit superior image quality, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) values consistently ranging from 35 to 37 dB, underscoring the robustness of 3DGS in preserving fine structural details. Compared to conventional multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques, the proposed method can achieve significantly improved reconstruction accuracy and visual fidelity. problem: Summarize recent research progress in reinforcement learning focused on enabling agents to explore efficiently and proactively under conditions of sparse rewards and constraints, respectively. Additionally, analyze and discuss the potential implications and insights this research provides for trajectory planning problems.
final_response:
<think>
I will synthesize the most recent, data-driven advances in proactive exploration and constrained RL, then translate these insights into practical guidance for trajectory planning. I will ground each point with citations from the papers already retrieved, especially the EWRL 2024 FVAC, the CoRL 2023 VELAP, the IEEE TTECI 2024 UAV paper, the Automatica 2023 CBF-based MBRL, and the CoRL 2024 CASE method. I will structure the report with sections on exploration under sparse rewards and on constrained exploration, and then a dedicated implications section focused on trajectory planning, highlighting waypoint selection, safety constraints, sample efficiency, and perception coupling.
</think>

<answer>Recent progress in reinforcement learning (RL) has produced several data-driven, principled approaches to enabling proactive exploration and constraint-adherent behavior, with clear performance gains in challenging regimes of sparse rewards and operational constraints. Below is a structured summary of advances, followed by an analysis of implications for trajectory planning.

Sparse-reward exploration: boosting rare-event discovery and global waypoint search
- Renewal-theoretic Fleming–Viot particle systems with policy gradient (FVRL and FVAC) explicitly target environments with sparse and rare rewards by increasing the visitation frequency of rare, high-reward states through population-based exploration mechanisms. These methods come with convergence guarantees and demonstrate substantial sample-efficiency gains over vanilla Monte Carlo methods in windy grid worlds and queue-control benchmarks. The ability to identify and “force exploration outside” highly visited regions while boosting rare-state visits provides a scalable, model-free recipe for overcoming sparse reward traps. <cite id="call_634a2506cc07-1"></cite><cite id="call_78d4c200c554-0"></cite>
- In vision-based manipulation under sparse reward feedback, Expansive Latent Planning (VELAP) integrates sampling-based waypoint selection into the RL loop by maintaining a tree of visited latent areas, enabling global path search in high-dimensional perception spaces and achieving state-of-the-art offline learning control. This suggests that learned embeddings paired with sampling-based planners can mitigate the “curse of horizon” and improve success in visually rich, sparse-reward navigation tasks. <cite id="call_15a3a3d6edc1-1"></cite>
- In UAV path planning with time constraints and sparse rewards, combining prioritized experience replay with curiosity-driven intrinsic rewards (measured by unvisited-time states) has been shown to reduce planning time and improve rescuing success in complex unknown environments, illustrating the continued practical value of intrinsic motivation–based exploration in robotic motion tasks. <cite id="call_15a3a3d6edc1-0"></cite>

Constrained exploration: safety-first exploration with guarantees and model-based planning
- Uniformly conservative exploration (UCE) imposes a constraint that the policy must outperform a conservative baseline (estimated from all data) within a per-episode budget, overriding UCB exploration when needed. It provides high-probability safety and regret bounds and extends to continuous state spaces via deep RL, offering a principled way to limit harmful exploration on a per-episode basis—directly applicable to safety-critical trajectory planning where each trial must respect strict safety budgets. <cite id="call_5c004caa0777-1"></cite>
- Model-based actor–critic methods augmented with control barrier functions (CBFs) provide safe exploration in model-based RL by embedding constraints into the control policy, enabling rigorous constraint satisfaction while learning. This aligns with trajectory planning requirements where safety margins must be enforced online, and recent work demonstrates broader safety constraints than comparative methods. <cite id="call_6d85f89da643-1"></cite>
- In industrial deployment settings, adaptive-regularization constrained RL (RL-AR) hardcodes safety constraints into policy combination via a “focus module,” balancing exploration with constraint adherence in critical systems. This points to practical architectures for safety-coupled trajectory optimization. <cite id="call_6d85f89da643-0"></cite><cite id="call_5c004caa0777-0"></cite>
- Sequential and robust Bayesian optimal experimental design via RL (e.g., variational vsOED) learns policies to select informative experiments under information-theoretic criteria while accommodating nuisance parameters and implicit likelihoods, and achieves superior sample efficiency. This mirrors trajectory planning’s need to select informative waypoints or maneuvers to maximize information gain under safety and resource constraints. <cite id="call_b356f89922c0b6f0-1"></cite><cite id="call_b356f3b9a6bb-1"></cite>

Implications and insights for trajectory planning
- Proactive waypoint selection via learned embeddings and sampling-based planners: Trajectory planning can benefit from learned latent spaces where a tree-based memory of visited areas is maintained and expanded, enabling global path search beyond short horizons. In vision-based manipulation and navigation, this approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance under sparse reward feedback, suggesting that latent planners can reduce the reliance on long prediction horizons and improve success in complex environments. <cite id="call_15a3a3d6edc1-1"></cite>
- Safety constraints as explicit policy design criteria: Trajectory planners should embed safety constraints using formal frameworks such as CBFs or conservative baselines with per-episode budgets. These methods provide rigorous constraint satisfaction guarantees and can be activated/deactivated based on risk assessments, aligning with operational safety requirements. <cite id="call_6d85f89da643-1"></cite><cite id="call_5c004caa0777-1"></cite>
- Sample-efficient exploration in sparse-reward regimes: Trajectory planners can reduce sample waste by boosting exploration toward rare, high-relevance regions (e.g., goal locations or informative obstacles) using Fleming–Viot population dynamics or curiosity/intrinsic reward signals. These techniques have been shown to accelerate learning in windy grid worlds and UAV path planning, indicating that similar mechanisms could prioritize exploration near critical geometry or task-relevant events. <cite id="call_634a2506cc07-1"></cite><cite id="call_15a3a3d6edc1-0"></cite>
- Information-theoretic experimental design for trajectory planning: Sequential RL-based design that targets information gain or model discrimination can select informative maneuvers or waypoints, improving learning efficiency and robustness. Variational vsOED demonstrates superior sample efficiency and flexibility in multi-model settings, suggesting that trajectory planners can jointly optimize path geometry and information acquisition. <cite id="call_b356f3b9a6bb-1"></cite>
- Perception-aware control and robustness: Coupling perception with control—such as distilling a perception-aware teacher into a vision-based student—improves robustness in cluttered environments with limited field of view. This integration is critical for vision-based trajectory planning and can be combined with safe exploration to maintain reliability under uncertainty. <cite id="call_522d2f2229c9-1"></cite>
- Offline and curriculum-based planning-to-learn: Methods that first plan a baseline trajectory and then backplay/chaining skills (e.g., PBCS) can bootstrap learning from sparse reward environments, reducing the number of interactions needed to acquire viable trajectories. This hybrid planning–RL pipeline is promising for real-world deployment where interaction costs are high. <cite id="call_31d17f4ed2ed-0"></cite><cite id="call_522d2f2229c9-0"></cite>

In summary, recent RL advances provide a toolkit for trajectory planning under sparse rewards and constraints: latent sampling planners to select global waypoints, safety-augmented policies to enforce constraints, proactive exploration to reach rare task-relevant regions, and information-theoretic design to choose informative maneuvers. These methods are increasingly validated in vision-based, manipulation, and UAV navigation tasks, and they can be combined with perception coupling and offline planning-to-learn strategies to meet real-world deployment requirements. <cite id="call_15a3a3d6edc1-1"></cite><cite id="call_6d85f89da643-1"></cite><cite id="call_634a2506cc07-1"></cite><cite id="call_15a3a3d6edc1-0"></cite><cite id="call_b356f3b9a6bb-1"></cite><cite id="call_522d2f2229c9-1"></cite></answer>

On top of that, not all sparse-reward environments are created equal; in other words, they can differ in the presence or absence of various features, with many of them having a great impact on learning. In light of this, the present work puts together a literature compilation of such environmental features, covering particularly those that have been taken advantage of and those that continue to pose a challenge. We expect this effort to provide guidance to researchers for assessing the generality of their new proposals and to call their attention to issues that remain unresolved when dealing with sparse rewards.</summary><hostname>ACM Digital Library</hostname><publisher>Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research</publisher><author_list><author name="Jim Martin Catacora Ocana" affiliation="Department of Computer, Control and Management Engineering, Sapienza University of Rome, Italy" /><author name="Roberto Capobianco" affiliation="Sony AI, Zurich, Switzerland" /><author name="Daniele Nardi" affiliation="Department of Computer, Control and Management Engineering, Sapienza University of Rome, Italy" /></author_list><url>https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1613/jair.1.14390</url><publish_time>2023年4月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Exploration in Deep Reinforcement Learning: From Single-Agent to Multi-Agent Domain</title><summary>Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Deep Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) have achieved significant success across a wide range of domains, including game AI, autonomous vehicles, robotics and so on. However, DRL and deep MARL agents are widely known to be sample inefficient that millions of interactions are usually needed even for relatively simple problem settings, thus preventing the wide application and deployment in real-industry scenarios. One bottleneck challenge behind is the well-known exploration problem, i.e., how efficiently exploring the environment and collecting informative experiences that could benefit policy learning towards the optimal ones. This problem becomes more challenging in complex environments with sparse rewards, noisy distractions, long horizons, and non-stationary co-learners. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive survey on existing exploration methods for both single-agent and multi-agent RL. We start the survey by identifying several key challenges to efficient exploration. Then we provide a systematic survey of existing approaches by classifying them into two major categories: uncertainty-oriented exploration and intrinsic motivation-oriented exploration. Beyond the above two main branches, we also include other notable exploration methods with different ideas and techniques. In addition to algorithmic analysis, we provide a comprehensive and unified empirical comparison of different exploration methods for DRL on a set of commonly used benchmarks. According to our algorithmic and empirical investigation, we finally summarize the open problems of exploration in DRL and deep MARL and point out a few future directions.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Jianye Hao" /><author name="Tianpei Yang" /><author name="Hongyao Tang" /><author name="Chenjia Bai" /><author name="Jinyi Liu" /><author name="Zhaopeng Meng" /><author name="Peng Liu" /><author name="Zhen Wang" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.06668</url><publish_time>2023年2月6日0时0分</publish_time><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.06668</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2109.06668</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:3"><title>R

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="constraint reinforcement learning proactive exploration rare transitions 2023 2024" search_time="2026年5月10日10时15分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:9"><title>Learning Policies with Zero or Bounded Constraint Violation for Constrained MDPs</title><summary>We address the issue of safety in reinforcement learning. We pose the problem in an episodic framework of a constrained Markov decision process. Existing results have shown that it is possible to achieve a reward regret of O(√K) while allowing an O(√K) constraint violation in K episodes. A critical question that arises is whether it is possible to keep the constraint violation even smaller. Sparse-angle tomography is a popular approach for obtaining 3D reconstructions from limited data. To optimize its performance, one can adapt scan angles sequentially to select the most informative angles for each scanned object. Mathematically, this corresponds to solving an optimal experimental design (OED) problem. OED problems are high-dimensional, non-convex, bi-level optimization problems that cannot be solved online, i.e., during the scan. To address these challenges, we pose the OED problem as a partially observable Markov decision process in a Bayesian framework, and solve it through deep reinforcement learning. <answer>Obsidian multi-view database comparison for Notion-like functionality (Table, Kanban, Calendar, List)

Overview of core systems
- Obsidian Bases (native): Treats Markdown notes as database records with properties; supports multiple views per base and several layouts (table, list, cards, map), plus community layouts such as board. Views can be filtered/sorted/grouped; you can duplicate views and switch among them. This is the foundational system for database-like behavior in Obsidian. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-1"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-2"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite>
- Dataview (native): Functions as a live index and query engine; extracts, filters, sorts, and displays data from Markdown notes. It supports list queries (filtered lists of pages/files) and table queries (structured tabular views), plus DataviewJS for custom visualizations. It indexes metadata, tags, and inline fields. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-3"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-4"></cite>
- CSV database (community): Stores data in CSV files and provides a web-based interface for editing and querying; supports rich column types, multiple views with sort/filter, inline editing, and a board layout with drag-and-drop. It is not yet in the official plugin directory. <cite id="call_45a45b8c362f-3"></cite><cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
- DataLoom (community): A “data weaving” plugin that lets you integrate data from diverse sources into unified databases; supports table views and other custom views; has a user-friendly interface with source management, table views, and cell-type support (text, numbers, dates, tags, etc.), but is no longer actively maintained. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite><cite id="call_18737bc36c26-0"></cite>
- Community Kanban/calendar/task plugins: Several community plugins provide board layouts and calendar views for Bases; some support drag-and-drop, color coding, swimlanes, and bidirectional sync with notes. <cite id="call_02a07dd6f642-1"></cite><cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-0"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-4"></cite>

Plugin-by-plugin comparison

1. Obsidian Bases + Dataview (native plugins)
- Views and layouts
  - Multiple views per base; layouts include table, list, cards, map; community plugins add board layouts. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite>
  - Dataview provides flexible table queries and list queries; DataviewJS can produce custom visualizations. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-4"></cite>
- Table view
  - Full-featured tabular queries with filtering, sorting, grouping, and calculated columns; supports styling and formatting (e.g., right-aligned numbers). <cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite><cite id="call_2641265ce104-2"></cite>
- Kanban view
  - Bases supports board layouts via community plugins; some plugins allow drag-and-drop between columns, color coding, and group-based card creation with pre-filled properties. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-4"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-3"></cite>
- Calendar view
  - Calendarbases plugin adds a calendar view to Bases, mapping dates from note properties to calendar displays; the Full Calendar plugin provides month/week/list views with task coloring and click-to-open daily notes; Agenda plugin offers calendar layouts with task visualization. <cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-0"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-4"></cite>
- List view
  - Dataview’s list queries return filtered lists of pages/files; Bases views can be configured as list layouts. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-4"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite>
- Strengths
  - Native integration with Obsidian; no extra file formats; deep query and filtering capabilities via Dataview; flexible views and layouts; bidirectional sync between views and notes in some plugins. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-3"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-4"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-4"></cite>
  - Bases allows multiple views per base with different filters/sorting/grouping; you can duplicate views to experiment. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite>
- Weaknesses
  - Board layouts and calendar views require community plugins; some are still in development or not yet in the official directory. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite>
  - Dataview queries require adding metadata (YAML frontmatter or inline fields), which can be tedious for large datasets. <cite id="call_2641265ce104-4"></cite>

2. CSV Database (community plugin)
- Views and layouts
  - Multiple views with sort/filter; board layout with drag-and-drop; inline editing. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
- Table view
  - Rich column types (text, number, date, checkbox, select, multi-select, note links); table queries via the web interface. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
- Kanban view
  - Board layout with drag-and-drop between columns; column management (rename, reorder, delete). <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
- Calendar view
  - No native calendar view; calendar functionality would need to be implemented via DataviewJS or another plugin. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
- List view
  - List views can be constructed via Dataview queries or by exporting CSV data to Markdown. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite><cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite>
- Strengths
  - File-based storage decouples data from notes; rich column types and inline editing; board layout with drag-and-drop; auto-save to CSV. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
  - No dependency on Obsidian’s Bases system; works with any vault. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
- Weaknesses
  - Not yet in the official plugin directory; requires manual installation (BRAT). <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
  - Limited native calendar/view integration; requires additional plugins for calendar displays. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>

3. DataLoom (community plugin)
- Views and layouts
  - Table views with customization; user-friendly interface with source management; supports multiple views. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite><cite id="call_18737bc36c26-0"></cite>
- Table view
  - Rich table views with data weaving across sources; supports cell types such as text, numbers, dates, tags. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite>
- Kanban view
  - No native Kanban layout; would need to be implemented via DataviewJS or a community board plugin. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite>
- Calendar view
  - No native calendar view; calendar displays would need to be added via DataviewJS or another plugin. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite>
- List view
  - List views can be constructed via Dataview queries or by exporting DataLoom data to Markdown. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite><cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite>
- Strengths
  - Data weaving across sources; user-friendly interface; cell-type support (text, numbers, dates, tags). <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite><cite id="call_18737bc36c26-0"></cite>
- Weaknesses
  - No longer actively maintained; limited layout/view options without additional plugins; may require export to Markdown for table/list views. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite>

4. Community Kanban board plugins
- Views and layouts
  - Board layouts for Bases; drag-and-drop between columns; color coding; swimlanes; new-note buttons; hide/reorder groups. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-3"></cite>
- Table view
  - Table views can be used alongside Kanban views; Dataview can provide detailed tabular queries. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite><cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite>
- Kanban view
  - Drag-and-drop columns; color coding; image/icons; column recovery via comments; bidirectional sync with notes in some implementations. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-3"></cite>
- Calendar view
  - No native calendar view; calendar displays would need to be added via DataviewJS or another plugin. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-1"></cite>
- List view
  - List views can be constructed via Dataview queries or by exporting Kanban data to Markdown. <cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite>
- Strengths
  - Native board layouts for Bases; drag-and-drop; color coding; swimlanes; new-note buttons; bidirectional sync in some cases. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-3"></cite>
- Weaknesses
  - Limited to Bases; requires community plugins; some features are still in development or not yet in the official directory. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite>

5. Community calendar/task plugins
- Views and layouts
  - Full Calendar plugin provides month/week/list views; Agenda plugin offers calendar layouts with task visualization; Calendarbases adds calendar views to Bases. <cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-4"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-0"></cite>
- Table view
  - Dataview can produce detailed tabular queries for calendar events/tasks; some plugins expose event data via APIs for querying. <cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-1"></cite>
- Kanban view
  - Kanban views would need to be implemented via community board plugins or DataviewJS. <cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-1"></cite>
- Calendar view
  - Native calendar views via Full Calendar, Agenda, and Calendarbases; month/week/day layouts; task coloring; click-to-open daily notes; drag-and-drop rescheduling. <cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-4"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-0"></cite>
- List view
  - List views can be constructed via Dataview queries or by exporting calendar/event data to Markdown. <cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite>
- Strengths
  - Native calendar views; month/week/day layouts; task coloring; click-to-open; drag-and-drop rescheduling; integration with daily notes. <cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-4"></cite>
- Weaknesses
  - Some plugins are still in development or not yet in the official directory; limited to specific data formats (e.g., event stores). <cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-1"></cite>

6. Sync-to-Notion plugins (Obsidian → Notion and vice versa)
- Views and layouts

  - Kanban views would need to be implemented via community board plugins or DataviewJS. <cite id="call_5f0b55385f1e-1"></cite>
- Calendar view
  - Calendar views would need to be added via community calendar plugins. <cite id="call_5f0b55385f1e-1"></cite>
- List view
  - List views can be constructed via Dataview queries or by exporting synced data to Markdown. <cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite>
- Strengths
  - Bidirectional sync with Notion; relations as wikilinks; long-note sync; previewing in Obsidian. <cite id="call_5f0b55385f1e-1"></cite>
- Weaknesses
  - No native multi-view database replication; limited to sync; requires additional plugins for views. <cite id="call_5f0b55385f1e-1"></cite>

Recommendations by use case

- Native multi-view database with minimal plugins
  - Use Obsidian Bases for folders treated as database records; add Dataview for powerful table/list queries; add community plugins for board and calendar views as needed. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-4"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite>
  - Pros: Native integration; flexible views; bidirectional sync; multiple views per base. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-4"></cite>
  - Cons: Some layouts/views require community plugins; Dataview requires metadata. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite><cite id="call_2641265ce104-4"></cite>

- File-based database with rich editing and board views
  - Use CSV Database for file-backed data with inline editing, board layouts, and rich column types; add Dataview for tabular queries; add calendar/board plugins for additional views. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite><cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite>
  - Pros: File-based storage; rich column types; inline editing; board layout; auto-save. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
  - Cons: Not yet in official directory; requires manual installation; limited native calendar/view integration. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>

- Data weaving across sources with table views
  - Use DataLoom for data weaving and table views; add Dataview for detailed queries; add community plugins for additional views. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite><cite id="call_2641265ce104-0"></cite>
  - Pros: Data weaving; user-friendly interface; cell-type support. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite>
  - Cons: No longer maintained; limited layout/view options without additional plugins. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite>

- Sync with Notion
  - Use sync plugins (N2O or Share to NotionNext) to mirror databases between Obsidian and Notion; use Bases/Dataview for querying and views in Obsidian. <cite id="call_5f0b55385f1e-1"></cite>
  - Pros: Bidirectional sync; relations as wikilinks; long-note sync; previewing. <cite id="call_5f0b55385f1e-1"></cite>
  - Cons: No native multi-view database replication; requires additional plugins for views. <cite id="call_5f0b55385f1e-1"></cite>

Summary table

| Feature               | Obsidian Bases + Dataview (native) | CSV Database (community) | DataLoom (community) | Community Kanban (board) | Community Calendar (task) |
|----------------------|------------------------------------|--------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| Multiple views       | Yes                                | Yes                      | Yes                  | Yes                      | Yes                       |
| Table view           | Yes (Dataview)                     | Yes                      | Yes                  | Yes (Dataview)           | Yes (Dataview)            |
| Kanban view          | Yes (board plugins)                | Yes (board layout)       | No                   | Yes                      | No                        |
| Calendar view        | Yes (calendar plugins)             | No                       | No                   | No                       | Yes                       |
| List view            | Yes (Dataview)                     | Yes                      | Yes                  | Yes (Dataview)           | Yes (calendar plugins)    |
| Layouts              | Table, list, cards, map; community adds board | Board, table; CSV interface | Table; data weaving | Board (Bases)            | Month/week/day; agenda    |
| Inline editing       | Notes; DataviewJS                  | Yes                      | Yes                  | Yes                      | Yes (agenda)              |
| Drag-and-drop        | Some board plugins                 | Yes                      | No                   | Yes                      | Some calendar plugins     |
| Color coding         | Some board plugins                 | Yes                      | Yes                  | Yes                      | Yes (calendar)            |
| Swimlanes            | Some board plugins                 | Yes                      | No                   | Yes (added)              | No                        |
| Sync to Notion       | No                                 | No                       | No                   | No                       | No                        |
| File-based storage   | Notes-based                        | CSV files                | Data sources         | Notes-based              | Event store               |
| Maintenance status   | Native, active                     | Not yet official         | No longer maintained | Community, active        | Community, active         |
| Learning curve       | Moderate (Dataview)                | Moderate                 | Moderate             | Moderate                 | Moderate                  |

Notes on installation and metadata
- Dataview requires adding metadata (YAML frontmatter or inline fields) to notes; this can be time-consuming for large datasets. <cite id="call_2641265ce104-4"></cite>
- CSV Database requires manual installation (BRAT) and stores data externally; it supports rich column types and inline editing. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
- DataLoom is no longer maintained but remains functional for data weaving and table views; additional plugins are needed for other views. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite>
- Community board/calendar plugins add board and calendar views to Bases; some are still in development or not yet in the official directory. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite><cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-1"></cite><cite id="call_ccbe13fcb20a-1"></cite>

Final thoughts
- For most users, Obsidian Bases plus Dataview provides the most integrated and flexible foundation for Notion-like multi-view databases, with community plugins filling in for board and calendar views as needed. <cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-4"></cite><cite id="call_25ece57ba8ec-0"></cite>
- If you prefer file-based storage and rich editing, CSV Database is a strong alternative, though it requires manual installation and lacks native calendar/view integration. <cite id="call_bfca607fcdda-0"></cite>
- DataLoom is a good choice for data weaving and table views if you can accept its lack of maintenance and limited layout options. <cite id="call_18737bc36c26-2"></cite>
- Sync-to-Notion plugins are useful for cross-platform workflows but do not replicate multi-view databases natively; they work best in conjunction with Bases/Dataview for querying and views. <cite id="call_5f0b55385f1e-1"></cite></answer>

problem: Please provide a detailed explanation of the differences and connections between Google's recently released A2A protocol and the MCP protocol. Furthermore, elaborate on the innovative aspects of the A2A protocol and the specific problems it is designed to address.
final_response:
