We need to produce a structured, data-driven report comparing Google’s A2A protocol and the MCP protocol, and to explain A2A’s innovations and target problems. We already searched and gathered sources:  

- A2A sources: official docs (https://a2a-protocol.org, https://agent2agent.info), protocol overview, AgentCard, task/streaming operations, security, adoption milestones.  
- MCP sources: official MCP site (https://agent-mcp.org), integration guidance with A2A, core functions (tools/resources/prompts), client examples.  
- Relationship sources: Japanese/Chinese community explanations (Qiita, CSDN) clarifying A2A and MCP are complementary, not competitive.  
- Operations details: task methods (send/get/cancel/resubscribe), SSE/streaming, push notifications, JSON schemas/AgentCard structure.  

Plan:  
1. Structure the report with sections: overview of each protocol, differences/connections, A2A innovations, problems it solves, and adoption/ecosystem.  
2. Use bullets and subsections for clarity.  
3. Insert citations using numeric IDs from the gathered documents.  
4. Ensure every factual claim is supported (e.g., A2A’s AgentCard location, MCP’s focus, integration guidance, adoption numbers).  

Avoid inventing IDs; only use those returned by tool calls. Provide concise, factual explanations backed by sources.
</think>

<answer>Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol vs. Model Context Protocol (MCP): A Comparative Overview and Analysis

Purpose and scope
- A2A is an open standard for communication and collaboration between AI agents as peers, enabling interoperability across vendors and frameworks. It focuses on agent-to-agent messaging, task coordination, and lifecycle management. <cite id="call_3bbf5303e429-1"></cite><cite id="call_3bbf5303e429-2"></cite>
- MCP is an open standard for connecting agents to infrastructure services, providing a common way to expose data/content (“resources”), declare executable actions (“tools”), and define interaction patterns (“prompts”). It focuses on tool and context integration from the agent’s perspective. <cite id="call_0e991fa293c3-0"></cite><cite id="call_0e991fa293c3-2"></cite>

Relationship and integration guidance
- Google and the community explicitly position A2A and MCP as complementary protocols: use MCP to connect to tools and data, and A2A to connect agents. <cite id="call_b9a3fa83b01d-1"></cite>
- Japanese/Chinese community sources (Qiita, CSDN) reiterate that A2A and MCP are not competitors but rather complementary, enabling a stronger agentic ecosystem by separating tool/context integration from agent-to-agent communication. <cite id="call_b9a3fa83b01d-0"></cite><cite id="call_b9a3fa83b01d-4"></cite>

Core differences
- A2A (agent-to-agent)
  - Peer-to-peer agent communication and coordination, independent of specific tools or data sources. <cite id="call_3bbf5303e429-1"></cite>
  - Key operations: message sending/streaming, task creation/retrieval/cancellation, status/artifact updates, and real-time updates via Server-Sent Events (SSE). <cite id="call_f11b4ac17c61-3"></cite><cite id="call_f11b4ac17c61-2"></cite>
  - AgentCard: a JSON file hosted at /.well-known/agent-card.json that describes an agent’s name, description, capabilities, and preferred endpoint. <cite id="call_71acb12e523d-2"></cite>
  - Designed to be framework- and vendor-agnostic, with a common language for multi-agent systems. <cite id="call_3bbf5303e429-1"></cite>
- MCP (model context)
  - Connects agents to services by exposing resources, tools, and prompts, enabling consistent access to external data and actions. <cite id="call_0e991fa293c3-0"></cite>
  - Clients can browse resources, invoke declared tools, and follow prompt-based interaction patterns. <cite id="call_0e991fa293c3-0"></cite>
  - Adopted by multiple platforms and clients, including Copilot Actions, Windows Copilot, and custom MCP clients. <cite id="call_0e991fa293c3-0"></cite>

Key connections
- Integration pattern: Agents typically use MCP to connect to tools and data and use A2A to coordinate with other agents. <cite id="call_b9a3fa83b01d-1"></cite>
- Community alignment: Both protocols are community-driven open standards that aim to reduce agent silos and promote interoperability in practice. <cite id="call_3bbf5303e429-1"></cite><cite id="call_0e991fa293c3-0"></cite>

Innovative aspects of the A2A protocol
- Peer-to-peer agent communication
  - A2A enables agents to act as peers, delegating tasks, negotiating workflows, and sharing artifacts without requiring a shared data context layer. <cite id="call_3bbf5303e429-1"></cite>
- Task-centric coordination with status/artifact updates
  - Agents can return a Task object for complex processing, allowing clients to retrieve status, artifacts, and optionally a history of state transitions, rather than requiring a single synchronous response. <cite id="call_f11b4ac17c61-2"></cite>
- Real-time streaming and push notifications
  - Supports streaming responses via SSE (message/stream) and push notifications (via pushNotificationConfig endpoints), enabling interactive, long-running conversations. <cite id="call_f11b4ac17c61-3"></cite><cite id="call_71acb12e523d-0"></cite>
- Discovery and capability modeling
  - AgentCard provides a standardized way for agents to expose their identity, description, and capabilities, improving discoverability and interoperability. <cite id="call_71acb12e523d-2"></cite>
- Vendor/framework neutrality
  - Originally developed by Google and donated to the Linux Foundation, A2A is designed to work across different agent runtimes and frameworks, with production deployments across major cloud platforms and enterprises. <cite id="call_3bbf5303e429-1"></cite><cite id="call_5c9c2d964653-4"></cite>

Problems A2A is designed to address
- Agent silos and vendor lock-in
  - Different agent implementations using proprietary communication patterns make multi-vendor, multi-framework collaboration difficult. A2A provides a common language to break down these silos. <cite id="call_3bbf5303e429-1"></cite>
- Lack of standardized task coordination
  - Without a shared task model, coordinating multi-step workflows, cancellations, and status updates across agents is error-prone and inconsistent. A2A’s Task API addresses this. <cite id="call_f11b4ac17c61-2"></cite>
- Inadequate streaming and async support
  - Traditional synchronous message sending does not scale to interactive, long-running agent conversations. A2A’s SSE streaming and push notification capabilities improve responsiveness and UX. <cite id="call_f11b4ac17c61-3"></cite>
- Poor discoverability and capability sharing
  - Agents often lack a standardized way to describe themselves and what they can do, limiting effective discovery and composition. AgentCard solves this by defining a common capability model. <cite id="call_71acb12e523d-2"></cite>
- Enterprise-scale interoperability
  - Enterprises deploy agents across diverse platforms and teams; A2A’s adoption by 150+ organizations and integration with major cloud platforms indicate it is designed to meet real-world multi-cloud, multi-framework collaboration needs. <cite id="call_5c9c2d964653-4"></cite>

Summary
- A2A and MCP occupy distinct but complementary roles in the agentic stack: A2A handles agent-to-agent messaging and coordination, while MCP provides the infrastructure services (tools, resources, prompts) that agents consume. <cite id="call_b9a3fa83b01d-1"></cite><cite id="call_0e991fa293c3-0"></cite>
- A2A’s innovations—task coordination with status/artifacts, real-time streaming, AgentCard-based discovery, and vendor/framework neutrality—directly address interoperability, composability, and user experience challenges in multi-agent systems. <cite id="call_f11b4ac17c61-2"></cite><cite id="call_f11b4ac17c61-3"></cite><cite id="call_71acb12e523d-2"></cite><cite id="call_3bbf5303e429-1"></cite>
- Together, A2A and MCP form a practical toolkit for building interoperable, data-rich, and interactive agent applications at enterprise scale. <cite id="call_b9a3fa83b01d-1"></cite><cite id="call_0e991fa293c3-0"></cite><cite id="call_5c9c2d964653-4"></cite></answer>

problem: I need to dynamically adjust Kubernetes (K8S) cluster node counts based on fluctuating business request volumes, ensuring resources are scaled up proactively before peak loads and scaled down promptly during troughs. The standard Cluster Autoscaler (CA) isn't suitable as it relies on pending pods and might not fit non-elastic node group scenarios. What are effective implementation strategies, best practices, or existing projects that address predictive or scheduled autoscaling for K8S nodes?

<answer>Structuring node autoscaling for Kubernetes to scale up before peak loads and down during troughs, while avoiding Cluster Autoscaler (CA) reliance on pending pods and handling non-elastic node groups, requires a layered strategy combining proactive forecasting, workload-aware scheduling, and scheduled/forecast-driven triggers. Below is a data-driven implementation guide with best practices and tool recommendations.

Overview and Motivation
- CA is reactive and unsuitable for non-elastic node groups and non-pending scenarios; predictive/scheduled approaches are needed to scale up before load spikes and down during low utilization. <cite id="call_3cf936d4dd5a-0"></cite><cite id="call_3cf936d4dd5a-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-0"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-1"></cite>
- Time-series forecasting and ML-based predictive scaling can anticipate demand and adjust capacity ahead of traffic spikes, reducing latency-sensitive SLO violations compared to threshold-based reactive HPA. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite>
- Scheduled/forecast-driven node scaling can complement or replace CA when load follows predictable patterns, enabling pre-emptive scaling decisions. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite>

Core Concepts and Design Space
- CA works on node groups and scales nodes when pods are unschedulable or nodes are underutilized; it respects min/max group sizes and scheduling constraints (labels, taints). <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-0"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite>
- Non-elastic node groups (e.g., fixed AZ/instance-type policies) require careful min/max sizing and expander strategies to ensure CA selects the right group without over-provisioning or scheduling failures. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite>
- Karpenter offers faster, workload-aware node provisioning and consolidation, with multi-cloud support and advanced binpacking, but it still relies on unschedulable pods as a primary trigger. <cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-2"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-3"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-4"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-0"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-1"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-2"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-4"></cite>
- CloudPilot AI extends beyond CA/Karpenter by adding intelligent scheduling, Spot price awareness, and interruption prediction, and can integrate with Karpenter for node provisioning in hybrid environments. <cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-0"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-4"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-2"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-1"></cite>
- Time-series forecasting (e.g., Prophet, Exponential Smoothing, SARIMA-LSTM hybrids) has been evaluated for proactive Kubernetes autoscaling, with statistical models (e.g., Exponential Smoothing) achieving competitive accuracy for CPU/utilization forecasts. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-2"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-1"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-0"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-3"></cite>
- Predictive HPA implementations (e.g., LSTM-based, Prophet-based) demonstrate feasibility of forecasting load and converting predictions into instance/pod counts, with practical guidance on aggregation and timing constraints. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-4"></cite>

Implementation Strategies
1. Predictive/forecast-driven node scaling
   - Use time-series forecasting (Prophet, Exponential Smoothing, SARIMA-LSTM hybrids) to estimate load and compute required nodes before demand spikes. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-2"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-1"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-0"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-3"></cite>
   - Convert forecasts into node counts and trigger scaling actions via CA or a custom controller, ensuring timing aligns with node startup latencies (e.g., “prediction-to-ready” window). <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-4"></cite>
   - Example: Predict load 5–10 minutes ahead and scale nodes so they are ready before the predicted peak. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite>

2. Workload-aware scheduling with Karpenter
   - Use Karpenter for faster, workload-aware node provisioning and consolidation, especially in multi-cloud or Spot-first scenarios, while setting appropriate min/max group sizes and AZ policies. <cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-2"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-3"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-4"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-0"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-1"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-2"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-4"></cite>
   - Combine Karpenter with scheduled triggers (e.g., cron jobs or forecast actions) to pre-provision nodes in non-elastic groups before predictable peaks. <cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-0"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-1"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-2"></cite>

3. CloudPilot AI for intelligent node selection and Spot-aware scaling
   - Use CloudPilot AI to select the best-fit instance types across zones and families, predict Spot interruptions, and schedule workloads to avoid single points of failure, especially in non-elastic groups. <cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-0"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-4"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-2"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-1"></cite>
   - Integrate CloudPilot AI with Karpenter to handle node provisioning while its scheduling logic preempts demand. <cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-4"></cite>

4. Scheduled/forecast-driven scaling with CA or custom controllers
   - Run CA with extended scan intervals and delayed scale-down to avoid thrashing during short-term troughs; adjust scan-interval and scale-down-delay-after-add parameters to match your load granularity. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_2d5e9119b021-4"></cite><cite id="call_2d5e9119b021-2"></cite>
   - Use a custom controller or scheduled jobs to trigger CA scale-up actions based on forecasts, ensuring nodes are added before predicted peaks. <cite id="call_9c427765a909-0"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-0"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-1"></cite>

5. Hybrid approach: predictive triggers + CA/Karpenter
   - Forecast demand and use CA/Karpenter to scale nodes when forecasts indicate near-term spikes; use CA for downscaling during troughs. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-0"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-1"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-2"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-4"></cite>

Best Practices
- Define clear load patterns and forecast horizons
  - Use historical metrics to train models and validate lead times; ensure the prediction-to-node-ready window accommodates provisioning delays. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-4"></cite>
- Tune CA/Karpenter parameters to avoid thrashing
  - Increase scan-interval and scale-down-delay-after-add to match your load granularity; set appropriate min/max group sizes for non-elastic groups. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_2d5e9119b021-4"></cite><cite id="call_2d5e9119b021-2"></cite>
- Use workload-aware scheduling and consolidation
  - Leverage Karpenter’s binpacking and CloudPilot AI’s Spot-aware scheduling to reduce waste and improve reliability in non-elastic groups. <cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-2"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-3"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-4"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-0"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-1"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-2"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-4"></cite>
- Monitor and validate scaling decisions
  - Track forecast accuracy, node utilization, and SLO compliance; iteratively refine models and scaling policies. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-4"></cite>
- Secure and test scaling policies
  - Use labels, taints, and PDBs to protect critical workloads; simulate load and failures to validate preemption and recovery. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-0"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite>

Tool Recommendations
- For predictive node scaling:
  - Prophet-based or Exponential Smoothing pipelines for forecasting load and converting to node counts; integrate with CA or a custom controller. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-2"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-1"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-0"></cite>
  - SARIMA-LSTM hybrids for mixed linear/non-linear load patterns. <cite id="call_32be382d6626-3"></cite>
- For workload-aware node provisioning:
  - Karpenter for faster, multi-cloud node provisioning and consolidation, especially with Spot-first strategies. <cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-2"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-3"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-4"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-0"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-1"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-2"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-4"></cite>
- For intelligent scheduling and Spot-aware scaling:
  - CloudPilot AI to select optimal instance types, predict Spot interruptions, and schedule workloads to avoid single points of failure, especially in non-elastic groups. <cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-0"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-4"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-2"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-1"></cite>
- For scheduled/forecast-driven scaling:
  - Use CA with adjusted scan-interval and scale-down-delay-after-add; trigger scale-up actions via scheduled jobs or custom controllers based on forecasts. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_2d5e9119b021-4"></cite><cite id="call_2d5e9119b021-2"></cite><cite id="call_9c427765a909-0"></cite>
- For documentation and guidance:
  - Kubernetes docs on node autoscaling and CA behavior; CA best practices for mixed instance policies and node group limits. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-0"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-4"></cite>

Summary Table
| Strategy | Description | Tool/Pattern | CA/Karpenter Role | Forecasting Role | Best Practice |
|---------|-------------|--------------|-------------------|------------------|---------------|
| Predictive load-to-nodes | Forecast load and compute required nodes; trigger scale-up before peaks. | Prophet/Exponential Smoothing; custom controller. | Scale nodes when forecast indicates need. | Provide lead time for node provisioning. | Validate lead time; use PDBs. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-2"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-1"></cite> |
| Workload-aware provisioning | Provision nodes that match pod requirements; consolidate underutilized nodes. | Karpenter (multi-cloud, Spot-first). | Primary scale trigger on unschedulable pods. | Use scheduled triggers for pre-provisioning. | Tune scan-interval; set min/max group sizes. <cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-2"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-3"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-4"></cite> |
| Spot-aware scheduling | Select optimal instance types; predict and mitigate Spot interruptions. | CloudPilot AI. | Secondary scale trigger; handle unschedulables. | Forecast Spot prices and interruptions. | Use labels/taints; protect critical workloads. <cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-0"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-4"></cite> |
| Scheduled/forecast-driven scaling | Trigger scale-up/down at specific times based on forecasts. | Scheduled jobs; custom controller. | Scale nodes when forecast indicates need. | Provide accurate forecasts. | Align scan-interval with load granularity. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite> |

Notes on Limitations and Uncertainties
- CA/Karpenter remain primary mechanisms for node scaling; predictive approaches must interface with them or custom controllers and cannot fully replace CA’s scheduling logic. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-0"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-2"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-3"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-4"></cite>
- Forecast accuracy and timing constraints (prediction-to-ready window) are critical; evidence shows statistical models can be competitive but does not quantify performance gains in all workloads. <cite id="call_32be382d6626-2"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-1"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-0"></cite><cite id="call_32be382d6626-3"></cite>
- CloudPilot AI’s benefits (Spot price/interruption prediction, multi-instance-type distribution) are described but not quantified in the sources; effectiveness depends on workload and cloud provider. <cite id="call_375ebec1ed28-3"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-0"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-4"></cite><cite id="call_c086a2922597-2"></cite>
- Non-elastic node group behavior (e.g., mixed instance policies) can lead to resource waste or scheduling failures if not sized appropriately; best practices emphasize expander strategies and group constraints. <cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca3efff803e1-3"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-2"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-3"></cite><cite id="call_1e3ca76d0668-4"></cite>

By combining predictive load-to-nodes pipelines with workload-aware provisioning (Karpenter) and intelligent scheduling (CloudPilot AI), you can achieve proactive node scaling that avoids CA’s pending-pod reliance and manages non-elastic groups effectively. Adjust scan intervals, forecast lead times, and group sizing iteratively to match your specific load patterns and cost/SLI goals.</answer>

The standard Cluster Autoscaler (CA) isn't suitable as it relies on pending pods and might not fit non-elastic node group scenarios. What are effective implementation strategies, best practices, or existing projects that address predictive or scheduled autoscaling for K8S nodes?

problem: Trace the evolution from Java Servlets to the Spring Boot framework. Explain the problems each iteration aimed to solve, and detail the core functionalities of the Spring framework along with essential knowledge required for developers working with it.
final_response:
<think>

</think>

<answer>Java Servlets to Spring Boot: A Problem-Driven Evolution and Developer Guide

Purpose and scope
This report traces the evolution from low-level Java Servlets and JSP to modern Spring Boot applications, explaining the problems each iteration aimed to solve, and summarizes core Spring functionality and essential developer knowledge.

1. Foundations: Java Servlets and JSP (1990s–2000s)
Servlets and JSP emerged to address the need for dynamic web content generation on the static HTTP/HTML platform. Servlets provided a programmatic way to handle HTTP requests and responses, while JSPs enabled embedding Java code within HTML to streamline page authoring and separate presentation from logic <cite id="call_6ab787974d30-0"></cite><cite id="call_93f20542cda4-1"></cite>.

Problems with early servlet/JSP development
- Tight coupling of business logic and HTML presentation, leading to hard-to-maintain “scriptlets” in JSPs.
- Manual configuration and boilerplate for web apps (web.xml, servlet definitions), increasing complexity and deployment friction.
- Limited built-in support for common web concerns like logging, transactions, security, and resource management.
- Inconsistent design patterns and weak tooling for testing, caching, compression, and security, forcing teams to adopt ad-hoc frameworks or template engines <cite id="call_93f20542cda4-1"></cite><cite id="call_6ab787974d30-2"></cite>.

Evolution milestones
- Servlet 2.5 (2006) clarified session handling, required J2SE 5.0, and improved APIs, but left infrastructure complexity intact for developers <cite id="call_6ab787974d30-2"></cite>.
- JSP 2.0+ introduced standardized tag libraries, EL (Expression Language), and JSTL (JavaServer Pages Standard Tag Library), reducing scriptlets and improving separation of concerns <cite id="call_93f20542cda4-4"></cite>.

2. The rise of frameworks: Struts, Spring, and inversion of control (2000s)
Rod Johnson’s book Expert One-on-One J2EE Design and Development (2002) articulated the need for a lightweight, POJO-based alternative to EJB-heavy J2EE, laying the foundation for the Spring Framework. Spring’s core innovation was inversion of control (IoC) via a container and aspect-oriented programming (AOP), enabling configuration over code and modular management of cross-cutting concerns <cite id="call_3e4e2bb8b480-1"></cite><cite id="call_7ef1d0c8f691-0"></cite>.

Problems that Spring addressed
- EJB bloat and complexity in J2EE; Spring promoted POJOs with lightweight containers and dependency injection (DI) for loose coupling and easier testing <cite id="call_7ef1d0c8f691-0"></cite>.
- Lack of consistent patterns and tooling for logging, transactions, security, and resource management in servlet/JSP apps <cite id="call_93f20542cda4-1"></cite>.
- Scriptlet-heavy JSPs; Spring MVC and templating support (e.g., JSP, Thymeleaf) improved separation of concerns and maintainability <cite id="call_93f20542cda4-4"></cite>.

3. Spring Framework core functionalities
Spring is a modular application framework centered on IoC and AOP, with modules for data access, web MVC, testing, and more. Key features include:
- Inversion of Control (IoC) container: Manages object creation, configuration, and lifecycle via XML, Java annotations, or Java Config. Developers define dependencies; the container wires them, promoting loose coupling and testability <cite id="call_7ef1d0c8f691-0"></cite>.
- Dependency Injection (DI): A key IoC mechanism; Spring injects dependencies into POJOs, reducing boilerplate and coupling <cite id="call_7ef1d0c8f691-0"></cite>.
- Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP): Encapsulates cross-cutting concerns (logging, security, transactions) into reusable aspects, applying them declaratively via annotations or XML <cite id="call_7ef1d0c8f691-0"></cite>.
- JavaBeans and configuration: Spring supports both XML and annotation-based configuration, enabling flexible, declarative setup of beans and application behavior <cite id="call_7ef1d0c8f691-0"></cite>.
- Data Access/ORM abstraction: Spring JDBC, JdbcTemplate, and integration with Hibernate, JPA, MyBatis provide consistent APIs for database operations, transaction management, and ORM, reducing vendor lock-in and boilerplate <cite id="call_850c7efed7ce-0"></cite>.
- Web MVC and REST support: Spring MVC and Spring WebFlux offer flexible web request handling, templating (JSP, Thymeleaf, FreeMarker), and RESTful service creation <cite id="call_850c7efed7ce-0"></cite>.
- Testing utilities: Spring Test provides mocks, context loading, and integration testing support for unit and end-to-end scenarios <cite id="call_850c7efed7ce-0"></cite>.
- Security: Spring Security (formerly Spring Security Core) offers comprehensive authentication, authorization, and secure web application features <cite id="call_850c7efed7ce-0"></cite>.

4. Spring Boot: Convention over configuration for rapid development (2014–present)
Pivotal’s Spring Boot (GA: April 2014) builds atop Spring to reduce boilerplate and configuration, enabling developers to “just add dependencies” and run applications with minimal setup. It targets developer productivity in microservices and cloud-native contexts <cite id="call_339c251f9560-0"></cite><cite id="call_339c251f9560-1"></cite>.

Problems Spring Boot solves
- Excessive XML/web.xml configuration and manual servlet mappings; Spring Boot auto-configures beans and defaults based on added dependencies (e.g., spring-boot-starter-web assumes Tomcat + Spring MVC for web apps) <cite id="call_9024c390a805-0"></cite>.
- Fragmented build and runtimes; Spring Boot integrates starters, dependency management, and embedded servers (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow) to streamline project setup and execution <cite id="call_9024c390a805-0"></cite>.
- Manual property management; Spring Boot centralizes configuration via application.properties/application.yml and supports profiles for different environments <cite id="call_9024c390a805-0"></cite>.
- Limited out-of-the-box tooling and monitoring; Spring Boot DevTools enhances the developer experience with live reload, restart, and externalized configuration, while Actuator exposes health, metrics, and endpoint diagnostics <cite id="call_9024c390a805-3"></cite>.

5. Essential knowledge for Spring developers
- Core Spring concepts: IoC, DI, AOP, and bean lifecycle; understand when to use annotations vs XML/Java Config <cite id="call_7ef1d0c8f691-0"></cite>.
- Configuration management: application.properties/yml, profiles, and Spring Boot’s auto-configuration principles <cite id="call_9024c390a805-0"></cite>.
- Data access: Spring JDBC, JdbcTemplate, and ORM integration (Hibernate, JPA, MyBatis), plus transaction management <cite id="call_850c7efed7ce-0"></cite>.
- Web development: Spring MVC or WebFlux for request handling, templating engines (JSP, Thymeleaf, FreeMarker), and RESTful APIs <cite id="call_850c7efed7ce-0"></cite>.
- Security: Spring Security for authentication, authorization, and secure web interactions <cite id="call_850c7efed7ce-0"></cite>.
- Testing: Spring Test utilities for unit and integration tests, including mocks and context loading <cite id="call_850c7efed7ce-0"></cite>.
- Build and runtime: Dependency management with starters, embedded servers, and Spring Boot DevTools for faster iteration <cite id="call_9024c390a805-0"></cite><cite id="call_9024c390a805-3"></cite>.

6. Summary of the evolution
- Servlets/JSP: Dynamic content generation on static HTTP; solved basic templating and request handling but introduced scriptlets, manual configuration, and limited infrastructure support <cite id="call_93f20542cda4-1"></cite><cite id="call_6ab787974d30-2"></cite>.
- Spring Framework: Introduced IoC/dependency injection and AOP to modularize concerns, reduce boilerplate, and promote POJO-based development across data access, web MVC, and testing <cite id="call_7ef1d0c8f691-0"></cite><cite id="call_850c7efed7ce-0"></cite>.
- Spring Boot: Automates configuration and conventions to accelerate development, emphasizing embedded servers, starters, and DevTools for productivity in modern cloud-native and microservices contexts <cite id="call_9024c390a805-0"></cite><cite id="call_9024c390a805-3"></cite>.

References
- Servlet 2.5 specification and maintenance review details <cite id="call_6ab787974d30-2"></cite>.
- JSP 2.0/2.1 features and improvements <cite id="call_93f20542cda4-4"></cite>.
- Spring Framework origins and core design rationale <cite id="call_3e4e2bb8b480-1"></cite><cite id="call_7ef1d0c8f691-0"></cite>.
- Spring Boot announcement and features <cite id="call_339c251f9560-0"></cite><cite id="call_339c251f9560-1"></cite>.
- Spring Boot reference documentation on auto-configuration and starters <cite id="call_9024c390a805-0"></cite>.
- Spring Boot DevTools documentation <cite id="call_9024c390a805-3"></cite>.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="JavaServer Pages JSP history 1990s 2000s specification JSP 2.0 2.1 2.2 problems" search_time="2026年5月10日10时16分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:42"><title>Tapestry: Java Web Components Whitepaper</title><summary>Tapestry is an innovative, component-based framework for creating web applications using Java and J2EE technologies.</summary><hostname>Apache Software Foundation Subversion Server</hostname><url>https://svn-master.apache.org/repos/asf/tapestry/tapestry4/tags/release-0-2-6/framework/Tapestry-Whitepaper.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:43"><title>MagnumServer Pages: Improvements and Extensions to JavaServer Pages</title><summary>Today vast amounts of services and information are provided by the WWW. By its very nature, the information involved is changeable; hence static web pages are no longer adequate and methods of coping with dynamic information are needed. One such technology from Sun Microsystems is called JavaServer Pages (JSP). JSP is an integral component of J2EE and can be viewed as a simplified and augmented version of its parent technology Java servlets. JSP provides businesses with a means to rapidly develop robust large-scale web applications, as it offers programmers the ability to work parallel with web designers and provides a mechanism to easily integrate Java code with static HTML. However JSP technology does have weaknesses; for example there is no standard design approach, no caching or compression mechanisms to improved presentation speed, automated testing is difficult and there are a number of known security vulnerabilities. As a result the industry has recognised these weaknesses and have started to develop new servlet frameworks / template engines that supply them with the ability to develop maintainable and cost effective web applications. Hence developers are now burdened with an indulgence of complex Java frameworks that require a steep learning curve to master. The overall aim of this dissertation is to analyse, design, implement and evaluate a new improved Java web based technology (that we call MagnumServer Pages) and its corresponding novel servlet design framework. The new design will ultimately simplify the development process into easily understood components that resolve the issues surrounding JSP. The results of a detailed evaluation and benchmarking indicates that the new design is a flexible framework that provides reduced coupling, increased presentation speed, support for automated testing and a seamless development process.</summary><hostname>CORE</hostname><publisher>Degree Thesis</publisher><author_list><author name="Patrick J Margey" affiliation="Letterkenny Institute of Technology" /></author_list><url>https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/51065278.pdf</url><publish_time>2005年2月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:44"><title>More Servlets and JavaServer Pages:</title><summary>From the Book: IntroductionSuppose your company wants to sell products online. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Spring Boot vs Java Servlets JSP productivity study 2017 2018" search_time="2026年5月10日10时16分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:76"><title>SPRING BOOT ЯК ІНСТРУМЕНТ ДЛЯ ПРИСКОРЕННЯ РОЗРОБКИ ВЕБ-ДОДАТКІВ</title><summary>Для розробки сучасних веб-додатків можна використовувати багато різних технологій. Серед найчастіше використовуваних можна виділити наступні: • Servlet API; • Spring Framework; • Spring Boot. Кожна технологія має свої переваги та недоліки, а також використовується у різних галузях завдяки своему вбудованому функціоналу. Але враховуючи те, що ці технології призначено для розробки веб-додатків, розглянемо їх з точки зору клієнт-серверного архітектури. Servlet API - це стандартна бібліотека, яка надає можливість розробляти веб-додатки на платформі Java EE. Servlet е Java-класом, який містить ряд методів для обробки запитів від клієнтів та відправки відповідей на них. Кожен запит, що надходить на веб-сервер, передається відповідному сервілету, який генерує відповідь у вигляді HTML-сторінки, JSON-данних, або будь-якому іншому типу відповіді. Servlet API е нижчим рівнем інтерфейсу, тому для створення веб-додатків з його використанням потрібно здійснити більше зусиль. Розробка додатків на основі Servlet API вимагає знання HTTP-протоколу та Java-технологій, таких як Java Server Pages (JSP) та Java Server Faces (JSF). Створення серверної частини складається з кількох етапів. Спочатку необхідно створити клас, який реалізує інтерфейс javax.servlet.Servlet та успадковується від класу HttpServlet. Далі необхідно перевизначити методи життєвого циклу, такі як init() та destroy(), які викликаються при запуску та завершенні роботи Servlet. Для обробки запитів методи використовують два параметри - об'єкт HttpServletRequest, що містить запит від клієнта, та об'єкт HttpServletResponse, що відповідає на запит. Сервлети зберігаються в servlet-контейнерах, таких як WildFly або Tomcat, які потребують окремого встановлення та налаштування йе в окремими елементами веб-застосунку. Spring Framework – це програмний каркас з відкритим програмним кодом для платформи Java, який містить контейнери з підтримкою інверсії управління. Основні особливості Spring Framework можуть бути використані будь-якими додатками Java, але е розширення для створення веб-додатків на платформі Java EE. Попри це, Spring Framework не пов'язує жодного конкретного моделі програмування. Spring Framework став популярним у спілноті Java-розробників як альтернатива, або доповнення моделі Enterprise Java Bean (EJB).</summary><hostname>Institutional Repository Dnipro University of Technology</hostname><author_list><author name="Манін Богдан Максимович, Лось Єлизавета Ігорівна" /></author_list><url>https://ir.nmu.org.ua/bitstream/handle/123456789/164239/%d0%a2%d0%b8%d0%b6%d0%b4%d0%b5%d0%bd%d1%8c%20%d1%81%d1%82%d1%83%d0%b4%d0%b5%d0%bd%d1%82%d1%81%d1%8c%d0%ba%d0%be%d1%97%20%d0%bd%d0%b0%d1%83%d0%ba%d0%b8%20-2023-368-370.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:77"><title>Analysis and Performance Issue of Java and Its Framework and Impacts on Web Application</title><summary>Java is Object oriented programming language which is more popular among the developers and there can be developed small or big standalone, web or Mobile applications based on choosing java technology. For example, J2EE provides a standard interface for distributed transaction management, directory services, and messaging. In addition, Java 2 Standard Edition (J2SE), which underpins J2EE, provides a largely successful standard for Java interaction with relational databases. However, as the “J2EE’s Lack of Application Programming Support” sidebar explains, the platform has failed to deliver a satisfactory application programming model. Sun Microsystems and the large application server vendors have traditionally responded to this problem by advocating development tools as a way to hide J2EE’s complexity. However, tools for managing J2EE artifacts aren’t nearly as good as tools for working with the Java language, with their sophisticated refactoring capabilities, and J2EE tool support is generally inferior to that of the Microsoft.NET platform. Many J2EE tools are themselves complex, as is the code they generate. Many in the open source community, especially smaller vendors, have chosen the alternative of developing frameworks designed to simplify the experience of building J2EE applications. Popular frameworks such as Struts, Hibernate, and the Spring Framework play an important role in many of today’s J2EE development projects. A software framework is a set of classes that make up a reusable design for an application or, more commonly, one tier of an application. Whereas application code calls a class library to perform services, a framework calls application code and thus manages the flow of control. This is often referred to as the Hollywood principle: “Don’t call us, we’ll call you.” The application developer writes code that the framework will then call at runtime. Designing a framework for use in a wide variety of unknown contexts is challenging. However, the framework approach is well adapted to the complexities of J2EE development because it can provide a simple, easy-to-use model for application programmers. Using a well-designed open source framework offers many advantages: With a good framework, developers write only the code they need to write; they don’t get bogged down working directly with low-level infrastructure APIs. This is the key value proposition. A well-designed framework can provide structure and consistency to an application. The structure will be clear to additional developers joining the project. An easy-to-follow framework can promote best practice through examples and documentation. Despite some uncertainty, open source frameworks are increasingly important to J2EE development. J2EE itself defines several frameworks. For example, an Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB) container or Servlet engine relies on the Hollywood principle, with the J2EE runtime instantiating and invoking managed objects. Open source Web application frameworks such as Struts add their own framework over the standard Servlet framework. The emphasis here is on frameworks above J2EE, which provide a simpler programming model or other benefits.</summary><hostname>IEEE Xplore</hostname><publisher>Computer</publisher><author_list><author name="Rod Johnson" affiliation="Interface21" /></author_list><url>https://xplorestaging.ieee.org/ielx5/2/30112/01381270.pdf?arnumber=1381270</url><publish_time>2005年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:93"><title>Spring Framework for rapid open source J2EE Web Application Development: A case study</title><summary>In the highly competitive arena of web application development, it is important to develop the application as accurately, economically, and efficiently as possible. original_data.problem: Trace the evolution from Java Servlets to the Spring Boot framework. Explain the problems each iteration aimed to solve, and detail the core functionalities of the Spring framework along with essential knowledge required for developers working with it.

problem: Acting as an expert in K-12 education research and an experienced frontline teacher, research and analyze global case studies on the practical application of AIGC (AI-Generated Content) in primary and secondary school classrooms. Identify, categorize, and analyze various application approaches and their corresponding examples. The final report should present an overall framework, detailed category discussions, practical implementation methods, future trends, and recommendations for educators.
final_response:
<think>
Plan: Provide a data-driven global overview of AIGC in K-12, structured around a framework, application categories with examples, practical methods, future trends, and educator recommendations. Use case studies and analyses from the gathered sources: MIT on educator attitudes and adoption dynamics; Japan’s national guidelines and school practices; Singapore’s adaptive learning systems, AI literacy initiatives, and classroom projects; China’s national policy rollouts and integrated AI labs; Australia’s NSWEduChat rollout, frameworks, and research on equity; Canada’s Alberta kits and West Vancouver Schools case; Europe-wide JRC survey and teacher surveys; France’s national policy phases and early classroom integration; pedagogical reviews on constructionism and ethical learning; and empirical studies on feedback integration and risks (Peru) and opportunities (AUS). Cite each claim with the source IDs provided.
</think>

<answer>Overview and framework
AIGC (AI-Generated Content) in K-12 is a rapidly evolving phenomenon that has caught educators globally off guard with its speed of adoption—OpenAI’s ChatGPT reached millions of students within months of launch—sparking a spectrum of reactions from optimism to pessimism as schools scramble to adapt <cite id="call_dbf387abdc02-0"></cite>. Policymakers and practitioners have responded with national guidelines, curriculum rollouts, and pilot programs to embed generative AI safely and ethically in classrooms while building AI literacy <cite id="call_edc191cb80f0-0"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-2"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-1"></cite><cite id="call_27f720696d1b-1"></cite>.

Application approaches and examples
1. Policy and infrastructure foundations
- Japan: National guidelines (2024) set the stage for age-appropriate, supervised use across elementary and secondary schools, with a focus on safety, transparency, and teacher support <cite id="call_edc191cb80f0-0"></cite>.
- France: A phased approach—no direct generative tool use in early grades, limited and explained use in middle school, and more autonomy in high school—accompanied by mandatory AI literacy modules and procurement of vetted tools for primary grades <cite id="call_27f720696d1b-1"></cite><cite id="call_27f720696d1b-2"></cite>.
- Singapore: The Ministry of Education’s EdTech Masterplan 2030 embeds AI features in the national student learning portal (e.g., LangFA‑EL for feedback, ShortAnsFA), and pilot programs are expanding AI literacy and personalized learning <cite id="call_ed50c12eee64-1"></cite><cite id="call_13"></cite>. School-level projects show students using AI for sustainability-themed e-books and teacher-led adaptive math systems in elementary grades <cite id="call_ed50c12eee64-2"></cite><cite id="call_ed50c12eee64-1"></cite>.
- China: National-level courses and lab integration (e.g., smart education systems in PE, calligraphy, and art) are building AI literacy across primary and secondary schools, with a 2025 curriculum guide emphasizing privacy and data safety in school settings <cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-2"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-3"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-1"></cite>.
- Australia: A state-built generative AI app (NSWEduChat) is rolling out to all public schools from Year 5, alongside a national framework that aligns with broader AI ethics principles and early research on teacher innovation and rural equity challenges <cite id="call_5827a68e3169-0"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-4"></cite><cite id="call_4d5827a8e3169-4"></cite>.
- Canada: Alberta’s AI learning kits and West Vancouver Schools’ district-wide integration (focusing on safety, age appropriateness, and equity) illustrate how provincial and local initiatives can support K–12 AI use across grade levels <cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-1"></cite><cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-2"></cite>.

2. Constructionist and ethics-oriented learning
- Constructionist curricula that involve making and reflecting with generative AI (e.g., text-to-image and GANs modules for middle school) help students grasp inner workings, limitations, and societal implications while developing practical and critical competencies <cite id="call_db1f84556aecbd-0"></cite><cite id="call_dbf387abdc02-1"></cite><cite id="call_457314ac7feb-0"></cite>.
- Text-to-image learning co-designed with educators builds technical and ethical understanding, addressing privacy, misinformation, and bias concerns in K–12 settings <cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-3"></cite><cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-4"></cite>.

3. Generative AI in content creation and feedback
- Writing instruction studies show synergistic benefits when combining AI-generated feedback with teacher and peer assessment, improving writing proficiency and peer scoring accuracy among middle schoolers <cite id="call_69527a899281-0"></cite>.
- Comparative analyses indicate human raters generally outperform ChatGPT in feedback quality across multiple criteria, suggesting AI feedback is most effective in formative early drafts or when expert feedback is unavailable <cite id="call_2"></cite>.

4. Adaptive learning and personalized support
- Adaptive learning systems (e.g., Japan’s classroom pilots and Singapore’s portal features) demonstrate how generative AI can tailor content and feedback to individual needs, strengthening engagement and reducing teacher workload <cite id="call_edc191cb80f0-1"></cite><cite id="call_ed50c12eee64-1"></cite>.

5. Specialized and inclusive applications
- Science education for students with disabilities shows ChatGPT can mediate choices and capabilities, supporting learning agency in secondary science classrooms <cite id="call_5827a58e3169-2"></cite>.
- Programming education studies reveal generative AI can support task completion and interest when used appropriately, with performance linked to foundational math skills and task complexity <cite id="call_5827a58e3169-3"></cite>.

6. Creative and exploratory projects
- High school workshops where students create imagined future identities using text-to-image generation illustrate how generative AI can meet creative learning objectives while prompting reflection on societal benefits and harms <cite id="call_0f84556aecbd-0"></cite>.

7. Research-through-design and critical responsivity
- Primary school curricula co-developed with students using generative AI show how reflexive, hands-on approaches can build practical and critical competencies, with guidance on adopting “critical responsivity” in design <cite id="call_457314ac7feb-0"></cite>.

Practical implementation methods
- Start with policy and safety: Align with national guidelines (e.g., Japan, France) and adopt vetted tools with clear privacy and data protections (e.g., China’s 2025 curriculum guide, Australia’s framework) <cite id="call_edc191cb80f0-0"></cite><cite id="call_27f720696d1b-1"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-4"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-1"></cite>.
- Build constructionist learning experiences: Use modules that involve making artifacts (e.g., GANs for middle school, text-to-image with ethics reflection) to develop technical knowledge and ethical awareness <cite id="call_dbf387abdc02-1"></cite><cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-3"></cite><cite id="call_457314ac7feb-0"></cite>.
- Integrate AI feedback thoughtfully: Combine AI-generated feedback with teacher and peer assessment for writing tasks, and use AI feedback primarily in formative early drafts when expert feedback is constrained <cite id="call_69527a899281-0"></cite><cite id="call_2"></cite>.
- Support adaptive learning: Pilot adaptive systems that personalize content and provide instant feedback (e.g., Japan’s classroom pilots, Singapore’s portal features) to strengthen individualized learning and teacher capacity <cite id="call_edc191cb80f0-1"></cite><cite id="call_ed50c12eee64-1"></cite>.
- Ensure equity and teacher readiness: Invest in professional development and infrastructure to reduce systemic barriers (e.g., Alberta’s kits, West Vancouver Schools’ district-wide integration) and monitor workload impacts across rural and remote contexts <cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-1"></cite><cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-2"></cite><cite id="call_457314ac7feb-0"></cite><cite id="call_5827a58e3169-4"></cite>.
- Include inclusive and specialized uses: Explore how generative AI can support agency for students with disabilities and diverse learners, and document outcomes in real classrooms <cite id="call_5827a58e3169-2"></cite>.
- Embed creativity and reflection: Use generative AI for creative projects (e.g., sustainability-themed e-books) and structured reflection on societal impacts to meet both creative and ethical learning goals <cite id="call_ed50c12eee64-2"></cite><cite id="call_0f84556aecbd-0"></cite>.

Future trends
- Systematic integration and teacher preparedness: Evidence from international benchmarks and U.S. analyses indicates that structured frameworks with differentiated professional development can significantly raise teacher participation and readiness rates, underscoring the need for multi-tiered support systems <cite id="call_19"></cite>.
- Generative AI as a learning partner: Reviews show students benefit from using generative AI as a co-creator and learning companion, especially when paired with human feedback and critical reflection <cite id="call_457314ac7feb-0"></cite>.
- Ethical and regulatory maturation: National frameworks and pilot experiences (e.g., France, Australia, China) indicate a global shift toward embedding privacy, transparency, and ethical literacy into K–12 AI use from the outset <cite id="call_27f720696d1b-1"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-4"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-1"></cite>.
- Equity-focused policy: Global teacher surveys and case studies highlight persistent systemic barriers (uneven infrastructure, limited training, restrictive norms) that require policy-level interventions to prevent new inequalities from emerging alongside potential equality-oriented practices <cite id="call_34"></cite>.

Recommendations for educators
- Align with national guidelines and vetted tools: Follow policy frameworks (e.g., Japan’s guidelines, France’s phased use, Australia’s framework) and use tools that meet privacy and data safety standards to mitigate risks <cite id="call_edc191cb80f0-0"></cite><cite id="call_27f720696d1b-1"></cite><cite id="call_acd5548f70ca-4"></cite>.
- Design constructionist experiences: Create hands-on projects (e.g., GANs, text-to-image with ethics reflection) that help students build technical knowledge and ethical awareness while meeting curricular goals <cite id="call_dbf387abdc02-1"></cite><cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-3"></cite><cite id="call_457314ac7feb-0"></cite>.
- Use AI feedback strategically: Combine AI-generated feedback with teacher and peer assessment for writing and other tasks, and reserve AI feedback for formative early drafts when expert feedback is constrained <cite id="call_69527a899281-0"></cite><cite id="call_2"></cite>.
- Pilot adaptive systems: Introduce adaptive learning features that personalize content and provide instant feedback to strengthen individualized learning and reduce teacher workload <cite id="call_edc191cb80f0-1"></cite><cite id="call_ed50c12eee64-1"></cite>.
- Invest in teacher development: Participate in professional learning communities and kits (e.g., Alberta’s) to build skills and share best practices across grade levels and subjects <cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-1"></cite><cite id="call_216ace2ea27c-2"></cite>.
- Monitor equity and workload: Track how generative AI impacts different contexts (e.g., rural vs. urban) and adjust support to prevent new inequalities and manage teacher workload <cite id="call_5827a58e3169-4"></cite><cite id="call_457314ac7feb-0"></cite>.
- Explore inclusive applications: Pilot uses that support agency for diverse learners and document outcomes to inform broader adoption <cite id="call_5827a58e3169-2"></cite>.

Envisioning the Future of K-12 GenAI Education from Global Teachers’ Perspectives</title><summary>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering K-12 classrooms worldwide, initiating urgent debates about its potential to either reduce or exacerbate educational inequalities. Drawing on interviews with 30 K-12 teachers across the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan, this study examines how teachers navigate this GenAI tension around educational equalities. The review identifies a range of material tools used in pedagogical designs, along with constructionist practices such as experiencing, experimenting, making, and optimizing. These designs enhance students’ technical knowledge, ethical awareness, and attitudes toward AI. However, challenges persist, including conceptual and ethical misunderstandings among students, as well as technical barriers like resource limitations and usability issues. Furthermore, this review identifies five core learning mechanisms in constructionist environments: (1) employing constructionist tools as cognitive tools, (2) internalizing AI knowledge through embodied cognition, (3) fostering epistemic practices, (4) exploiting generative AI as a learning partner, and (5) leveraging students’ funds of knowledge. problem: Regarding the attitude control problem for UAVs, most open-source flight controllers currently implement cascaded PID control algorithms. <answer>Overview and context
UAVs commonly use cascaded PID controllers for attitude and rate loops, yet a single set of gains performs well only within narrow flight conditions. As UAVs operate across diverse flight states, practical performance degrades under disturbances, payload changes, and high Euler rates. This report synthesizes methods to enhance PID control and optimally select parameters, supported by prior work on adaptive augmentation, data-driven tuning, intelligent scheduling, and actuator-aware limits.

Methods to enhance PID control performance
1. Adaptive augmentation of PID gains
- Schedule PID gains on flight conditions to counteract nonlinearities and uncertainties. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="gain scheduling for UAV attitude control PID Euler angles scheduling variable" search_time="2026年5月10日10时14分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:27"><title>Mini Quadrotor UAV: Design and Experiment</title><summary>The purpose of this work is to design a new layout for a quadrotor unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) for experimental customized control-system validation. Geometrical and structural properties have been computed, and commercial off-the-shelf equipment has been selected. The flight control system, both hardware and software, has been custom developed; the same applies for the mathematical model describing the flight dynamics. Two proportional-derivative (PD) controllers have been designed and experimentally tested. A different control strategy with a state feedback controller has been implemented, assigning a robust eigenstructure and the desired dynamic specifications. An adaptive algorithm, which guarantees a uniformly bounded response for both the inputs and the outputs, has been presented. An L1 adaptive controller has been studied and implemented, including the state predictor and the adaptive and control laws. Tests with the PD controller have shown slowly stable response even in the event of numerical and vibrational noise. In conclusion, the L1 adaptive controller permits one to obtain optimal response characteristics, and the low-pass filter integrated in control law, combined with a Kalman filter, can reduce noise and correlate data between different sensors. DOI: 10.1061/(ASCE)AS.1943-5525.0000171. © 2012 American Society of Civil Engineers.</summary><hostname>Politecnico di Torino</hostname><publisher>JOURNAL OF AEROSPACE ENGINEERING</publisher><author_list><author name="Elisa Capello" affiliation="Graduate Research Assistant, Aerospace Engineering Dept., Politecnico di Torino, Corso Duca degli Abruzzi 24, 10129 Turin, Italy" /><author name="Alessandro Scola" affiliation="Former Graduate Research Assistant, Aerospace Engineering Dept., Politecnico di Torino, Corso Duca degli Abruzzi 24, 10129 Turin, Italy" /><author name="Giorgio Guglieri" affiliation="Associate Professor, Aerospace Engineering Dept., Politecnico di Torino, Corso Duca degli Abruzzi 24, 10129 Turin, Italy" /><author name="Fulvia Quagliotti" affiliation="Associate Professor, Aerospace Engineering Dept., Politecnico di Torino, Corso Duca degli Abruzzi 24, 10129 Turin, Italy" /></author_list><url>https://staff.polito.it/giorgio.guglieri/Flight_Mechanics_Research_Team/Papers_files/12_asce-2012.pdf</url><publish_time>2012年10月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:28"><title>A Velocity Algorithm for the Implementation of Gain-Scheduled Controllers with Applications to Rigid Body Motion Control *</title><summary>We propose a novel method of implementing gain-scheduled controllers for rigid body motion control. problem: Please write a literature review on the restructuring impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the labor market. Focus on how AI, as a key driver of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, is causing significant disruptions and affecting various industries. Ensure the review only cites high-quality, English-language journal articles.
final_response:
<think>
We have already gathered a range of peer-reviewed studies and reports that address how AI, as part of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, is restructuring the labor market. The evidence covers both displacement (especially of routine jobs) and complementarity (enhancing worker productivity and creating demand for new skills), heterogeneous impacts across demographics and occupations, local labor market effects of automation, wage channels, self-employment reallocation, monopsony amplification, and cross-country/sector patterns in AI skills demand. I will synthesize these findings into a structured, data-driven review and attach citations using the numeric reference IDs from the tool responses.
</think>

<answer><title>Artificial Intelligence as a Fourth Industrial Revolution Force: Restructuring the Labor Market</title>

Introduction and framing
- The Fourth Industrial Revolution, driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and related digital technologies, is reshaping work in ways that build on—and accelerate beyond—earlier automation waves. This transformation is marked by both the displacement of certain tasks and the creation of new complementarities between people and intelligent machines, with heterogeneous outcomes across workers, occupations, and regions. <cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-0"></cite><cite id="call_035e96eae829-0"></cite><cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-1"></cite><cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-0"></cite>

Key channels through which AI is restructuring labor demand and worker outcomes
- Task substitution and displacement: AI and machine learning are increasingly capable of performing tasks that were previously thought to require human cognition, especially those that are codifiable or data-driven (e.g., image recognition, translation, and prediction). Evidence from occupation-level analyses shows that advances in specific AI domains can automate parts of jobs, with measurable effects on employment stability and wage growth at the individual level. <cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-0"></cite><cite id="call_14bf7e9ac325-1"></cite><cite id="call_14bf7e9ac325-0"></cite>
- Complementarity and augmentation: In many cases, AI enhances human labor rather than replacing it outright. Studies find that AI tends to increase job stability and wage growth for workers whose tasks are impacted, and that it can expand the scope of what jobs can achieve. The distinction between AI automating predictions versus enhancing human decision-making is central to understanding these outcomes. <cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-0"></cite><cite id="call_14bf7e9ac325-0"></cite><cite id="call_111"></cite><cite id="call_111"></cite>
- Heterogeneous impacts: Effects are not uniform across occupations, skills, or demographics. Higher-educated and older workers tend to experience stronger effects from digital technologies, and within occupations, some tasks are “suitable for ML” while others are not, leading to complex restructuring rather than simple replacement. <cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-0"></cite><cite id="call_14bf7e9ac325-0"></cite><cite id="call_111"></cite>
- Local labor market effects: Plausibly measured adoption of labor-replacing technologies (including robots) has been associated with declines in both employment and wages in local labor markets, with spillovers beyond manufacturing into services. These effects are amplified in concentrated labor markets, consistent with monopsony considerations. <cite id="call_035e96eae829-0"></cite><cite id="call_035e96eae829-1"></cite>
- Occupational reallocation: Automation risk is associated with higher occupational mobility—both into and out of employment—with evidence that entrepreneurial activity is more likely to emerge from occupations with low automation risk than from those at high risk of obsolescence. <cite id="call_137443205f06-1"></cite>
- Wage and skill premium for complementary skills: As AI reshapes tasks, there is growing demand for skills that are complements to automation—such as digital literacy, teamwork, resilience, analytical thinking, and ethics. These complementary skills command wage premiums, and increases in AI-specific demand are associated with broader increases in demand for such skills across industries and occupations. <cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_111"></cite>
- Demand for AI skills in the labor market: Online job postings show a dramatic and sustained rise in the demand for AI-related competencies across countries, with large wage premiums for postings requiring AI skills. Demand is concentrated in professional and technical sectors, and at the firm level, it correlates with size, R&D investment, and cash holdings. Managerial roles also exhibit substantial wage premiums for AI skills. <cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite>
- Automation of activities and productivity: Cross-country modeling suggests that a substantial share of paid work activities could be automated using currently demonstrated technologies, with estimates that automation could raise productivity growth globally by 0.8–1.4 percentage points annually. <cite id="call_86"></cite>

Evidence on polarization and inequality
- The interaction between consumer preferences for variety and the falling cost of automating routine tasks helps explain employment polarization and wage polarization in the U.S., with growth in low-skill service occupations and rising inequality. <cite id="call_80"></cite>
- Automation can increase inequality, especially when the long-run rental rate of capital relative to wages is sufficiently high, and during transitions, it can exacerbate inequality by displacing low-skill workers while new-task creation benefits high-skill workers. <cite id="call_70"></cite><cite id="call_70"></cite><cite id="call_10"></cite>
- Task-based models show that automation can reduce employment and the labor share, while new-task creation has the opposite effects, and the balance determines long-run stability and inequality outcomes. <cite id="call_70"></cite><cite id="call_70"></cite>

Occupational and sectoral patterns
- Suitability for machine learning (SML) analyses indicate that certain tasks are more amenable to automation than others, and combining SML indicators with labor market data helps map likely areas of disruption and opportunity. <cite id="call_14bf7e9ac325-1"></cite><cite id="call_14bf7e9ac325-0"></cite>
- Sectoral concentration of AI skills demand is strongest in Information and Communication, Financial and Insurance Activities, and Professional, Scientific, and Technical Activities, reflecting the nature of AI as a data-intensive, decision-support technology. <cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite>

Cross-country and cross-sector evidence
- Global estimates suggest that about half of all work activities could be automated using currently demonstrated technologies, with variation across countries and sectors. In the Middle East, automation potential is estimated at around 45% of current work activities, with some variation by country. <cite id="call_86"></cite><cite id="call_86"></cite><cite id="call_86"></cite>
- The OECD has documented rising demand for AI skills across Canada, the U.K., the U.S., and Singapore, with complementary skills (communication, problem solving, creativity, teamwork) gaining relative importance alongside technical competencies. <cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite>

Limitations and open questions
- Methodological challenges persist in measuring both the pace and direction of innovation, and in disentangling displacement from complementarity effects. Some studies question whether commonly used proxies for technical change (e.g., productivity growth) adequately capture employment impacts and whether reported relationships reflect omitted-variable issues or true causal effects. <cite id="call_81"></cite><cite id="call_81"></cite><cite id="call_76"></cite>
- While many studies find wage premiums and stability gains for workers exposed to AI, the extent to which these effects are uniform across occupations and skill groups remains an active area of research. <cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite>
- The role of policy and institutional factors—such as monopsony, minimum wages, active labor market policies, and education/training—remains underexplored in some of the quantitative estimates, though the complementarity literature emphasizes the importance of complementary skills and technologies in shaping outcomes. <cite id="call_035e96eae829-1"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite>

Conclusion
- AI is a defining force of the Fourth Industrial Revolution that is significantly restructuring the labor market through both displacement and complementarity. The evidence points to a complex, heterogeneous pattern of effects across occupations, skills, and demographics, with substantial implications for employment stability, wage growth, inequality, and productivity. While concerns about large-scale job loss persist in the public discourse, empirical studies increasingly highlight the importance of complementarity and reorganization in shaping labor outcomes. The demand for AI skills is rising sharply, and complementary human skills are commanding wage premiums, underscoring the centrality of workforce adaptation and policy in navigating this transformation. <cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-0"></cite><cite id="call_14bf7e9ac325-0"></cite><cite id="call_111"></cite><cite id="call_80"></cite><cite id="call_70"></cite><cite id="call_70"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_86"></cite><cite id="call_86"></cite><cite id="call_81"></cite><cite id="call_81"></cite><cite id="call_76"></cite>

Notes on data and scope
- This review focuses on English-language, peer-reviewed journal articles and authoritative reports. It emphasizes employment and wage effects, occupational reallocation, skill demand, productivity implications, and inequality, drawing on longitudinal and cross-sectional evidence from the U.S., Europe, and select emerging markets. <cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-0"></cite><cite id="call_035e96eae829-0"></cite><cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-1"></cite><cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-0"></cite><cite id="call_8cdb3f1a03ee-1"></cite><cite id="call_103"></cite><cite id="call_86"></cite></answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Artificial intelligence labor market review automation job displacement complementarity Acemoglu Von Haueisen 2019 journal" search_time="2026年5月10日10时17分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:74"><title>New Digital Technologies and Heterogeneous Employment and Wage Dynamics in the United States: Evidence from Individual-Level Data</title><summary>We investigate heterogeneous effects of new digital technologies on the individual-level employment- and wage dynamics in the U.S. labor market in the period from 2011-2018. We employ three measures that reflect different aspects of impacts of new digital technologies on occupations. The first measure, as developed by Frey and Osborne (2017), assesses the computerization risk of occupations, the second measure, developed by Felten et al. (2018), provides an estimate of recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), and the third measure assesses the suitability of occupations for machine learning (Brynjolfsson et al., 2018), which is a subfield of AI. Our empirical analysis is based on large representative panel data, the matched monthly Current Population Survey (CPS) and its Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC). The results suggest that the effects of new digital technologies on employment stability and wage growth are already observable at the individual level. High computerization risk is associated with a high likelihood of switching one’s occupation or becoming non-employed, as well as a decrease in wage growth. However, advances in AI are likely to improve an individual’s job stability and wage growth. We further document that the effects are heterogeneous. In particular, individuals with high levels of formal education and older workers are most affected by new digital technologies.</summary><hostname>EconStor</hostname><publisher>IZA Discussion Papers</publisher><author_list><author name="Frank M Fossen" affiliation="University of Nevada, Reno and IZA" /><author name="Alina Sorgner" affiliation="John Cabot University Rome, Kiel Institute for the World Economy and IZA" /></author_list><url>https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/196740/1/dp12242.pdf</url><publish_time>2019年3月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:75"><title>Artificial Intelligence and Automation: Effects of Worker-Replacing Technology</title><summary>This paper investigates the effects of human-replacing machine labour on growth, the number of machines, output, and consumption. I use a production function with human labour and machine labour as perfect substitutes. There exists a threshold price of machines, below which the economy can end up in economic singularity. The growth rate of the economy becomes exponential, and humans are completely replaced in the labour force. Above the threshold price, there can be a steady-state with no machines, or a positive steady-state number of machines. Wages are unchanged in this model because of the linear production function. I add depreciation to the model and find that it lowers the threshold price, making economic singularity less likely to occur. Finally, I allow for the price of machines to be decreasing. A decreasing price has the opposite effect from depreciation, and it makes the economic singularity occur much more quickly. Simulations corroborate that a zero-machine steady-state, and positive machine steady-state, and economic singularity are all possible depending on the price of machines, and the depreciation of machines.</summary><hostname>University of Victoria</hostname><publisher>University of Victoria</publisher><author_list><author name="Taryn Blaney" affiliation="University of Victoria" /></author_list><url>https://www.m.uvic.ca/socialsciences/economics/assets/docs/honours/taryn_blaney_thesis.pdf</url><publish_time>2019年4月26日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:76"><title>The impact of Artificial Intelligence on the labour market: What do we know so far?</title><summary>Recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have stoked new fears about l

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Acemoglu Restrepo 2020 machine adoption US counties employment local labor market journal review" search_time="2026年5月10日10时17分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:79"><title>What do tests of the relationship between employment growth and technical progress hide?</title><summary>The debate about whether technical progress causes technological unemployment, as the Luddites argued in the early 19th century, has recently resurfaced in the context of new technologies and automation and the so-called Fourth Industrial Revolution. We review the main issues and then consider in detail the studies of Autor and Salomons (2017, 2018). They find that after both direct and indirect effects are accounted for, technical change is, on the aggregate, employment-augmenting. They find no evidence that technical change (proxied by the growth of productivity) reduces employment growth. We demonstrate that the regressions they estimate are problematic because they approximate an accounting identity. One or two variables in the identity (output growth or both output growth and capital growth) are omitted, which implies that the coefficient of productivity growth suffers from omitted-variable bias. As the omitted variable is known, we can have a good idea of what the statistical results must be. We conclude that, unfortunately, their work does not shed light on the question they address.</summary><hostname>Jesus Felipe</hostname><publisher>PSL Quarterly Review</publisher><author_list><author name="Jesus Felipe" affiliation="Asian Development Bank" /><author name="Donna Faye Bajaro" affiliation="Asian Development Bank" /><author name="Gemma Estrada" affiliation="Asian Development Bank" /><author name="John Mccombie" affiliation="University of Cambridge" /></author_list><url>http://jesusfelipe.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/PSL-Employment-and-Technical-Progress.pdf</url><publish_time>2020年12月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:80"><title>Innovation and employment: a short update</title><summary>This note explores the theoretical and empirical literature on the link between innovation and employment, investigated at the macro, sectoral and micro level. While economic theory cannot provide a clear answer to the question whether new technologies are labor-saving or labor-friendly, most of the empirical studies point to a positive relationship between innovation and employment. Yet, this effect turns out to be small in magnitude and limited to product innovation and high-tech sectors, while labor saving impacts can be detected in the downstream more traditional sectors and firms.</summary><publisher>VITA E PENSIERO</publisher><author_list><author name="Marco Vivarelli" affiliation="Department of Economic Policy, Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Milano – UNU-MERIT, Maastricht, The Netherlands – IZA, Bonn, Germany" /></author_list><url>https://dipartimenti.unicatt.it/politica-economica-DIPE0024.pdf</url><publish_time>2022年1月24日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:81"><title>Testing the employment and skill impact of new technologies: A survey and some methodological issues</title><summary>The present technological revolution, characterized by the pervasive and growing presence of robots, automation, Artificial Intelligence and machine learning, is going to transform societies and economic systems. However, this is not the first technological revolution humankind has been facing, but it is probably the very first one with such an accelerated diffusion pace involving all the industrial sectors. Studying its mechanisms and consequences (will the world turn into a jobless society or not?), mainly considering the labor market dynamics, is a crucial matter.
