raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Acemoglu Orray 2021 AI automation task-level machine learning job tasks content" search_time="2026年5月10日10时17分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:9"><title>The Turing Transformation: Artificial intelligence, intelligence augmentation, and skill premiums</title><summary>We ask whether a technical objective of using human performance of tasks as a benchmark for AI performance will result in the negative outcomes highlighted in prior work in terms of jobs and inequality. Instead, we argue that task automation, especially when driven by AI advances, can enhance job prospects and potentially widen the scope for employment of many workers. The neglected mechanism we highlight is the potential for changes in the skill premium where AI automation of tasks exogenously improves the value of the skills of many workers, expands the pool of available workers to perform other tasks, and, in the process, increases labour income and potentially reduces inequality. We label this possibility the “Turing Transformation.” As such, we argue that AI researchers and policymakers should not focus on the technical aspects of AI applications and whether they are directed at automating human-performed tasks or not and, instead, focus on the outcomes of AI research. In so doing, our goal is not to diminish human-centric AI research as a laudable goal. Instead, we want to note that AI research that uses a human-task template with a goal to automate that task can often augment human performance of other tasks and whole jobs. Furthermore, there are concerns about employee well-being and the broader work environment, linked to the idea that AI may soon become pervasive in the workplace and threaten and undermine humans’ place in it. However, AI also has the potential to complement and augment human capabilities, leading to higher productivity, greater demand for human labour and improved job quality. From a theoretical perspective, the impact of AI on employment and wages is ambiguous, and it may depend strongly on the type of AI being developed and deployed, how it is developed and deployed, and on market conditions and policy. However, the empirical evidence based on AI adopted in the last 10 years does not support the idea of an overall decline in employment and wages in occupations exposed to AI. While AI is capable of performing some non-routine cognitive tasks, some bottlenecks to adoption still remain, and many tasks still require humans to carry them out. Thus, much of the impact of AI on jobs is likely to be experienced through the reorganisation of tasks within an occupation. Certain groups of workers may be more capable or better positioned to take advantage of the benefits that AI brings, use AI in a way that is complementary to their work, and avoid its negative impacts. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Frey Osborne 2017 future of employment automation susceptibility occupations" search_time="2026年5月10日10时17分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:25"><title>THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON WORK: An evidence review prepared for the Royal Society and the British Academy</title><hostname>The Royal Society</hostname><url>https://royalsociety.org/~/media/policy/projects/ai-and-work/frontier-review-the-impact-of-AI-on-work.pdf</url><publish_time>2018年9月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:26"><title>The Automation of Jobs: A Threat for Employment or a Source of New Entrepreneurial Opportunities?</title><summary>New and emerging technologies pose a serious challenge for the future of employment. As machines learn to accomplish increasingly complex production tasks, the concern arises that automation will wipe out a great number of jobs. This paper investigates the relationship between the risk posed by the automation of jobs and individual-level occupational mobility using a representative German household survey. It provides an overview of current trends and developments on the labor markets due to the automation of jobs. It also describes the most recent dynamics of self-employment and relates it to the risk of the automation of jobs. The results suggest that the expected occupational changes such as losing a job, demotion at one's current place of employment, or starting a job in a new field are likely to be driven by the high occupation-specific risk of automation. However, the switch to self-employment, both with and without employees, is more likely to occur from paid employment in occupations with a low risk of automation. Hence, the rising level of entrepreneurial activities is less likely due to jobs becoming obsolete over the course of automation, but rather due to the high number of opportunities offered by the digital age. The issues addressed within the paper provide room for further investigation. Particularly, an important question concerns which additional skills workers in jobs with a high risk of automation should acquire in order to make themselves less susceptible to the negative consequences of such a change. Chemical Engineering, Universidad Iberoamericana; Master of Business Administration, Carnegie Mellon University" /></author_list><url>https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/80667/857767881-MIT.pdf?sequence=2</url><publish_time>2013年6月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:48"><title>A Bibliographic Study on Big Data: Concepts, Trends and Challenges</title><summary>Purpose: The purpose of the current study is twofold. Firstly, it provides a consolidated overview of the existing literature on "Big data". Secondly, it presents the current trends and opens up various future directions for researchers who wish to explore and contribute in this rapidly evolving field. Design/methodology/approach: To achieve the objective of this study, the bibliographic and network techniques of citation and co-citation analysis was adopted. This analysis involved an assessment of 57 articles published over a period of 5 years (2011-2015) in 10 selected journals. Findings: The findings reveal that the number of articles devoted to the study of 'Big data' has increased rapidly in recent years. Moreover, the study identifies some of the most influential articles of this area. Finally, the article highlights the new trends and discusses the challenges associated with Big Data. Research limitations/implications: This study focuses only on big data concepts, trends and challenges and excludes research on its analytics. <answer><title>A New Paradigm of Holistic Empowerment in Elementary English Education and Teaching: A Teacher-Centered, Research-Informed Approach</title>

Abstract
This paper proposes a new paradigm for elementary English education grounded in holistic empowerment: an integrated, student-centered model that nurtures cognitive, socioemotional, and cultural development through inquiry-based teaching, responsive assessment, and collaborative meaning-making. Drawing on classroom-based research and evidence-based practices, the paradigm emphasizes teacher inquiry, interactive reading and writing, comprehension strategy instruction, culturally sustaining pedagogy, and student voice—all designed to build agency and achievement in young English learners. The paper includes practical guidance for novice teachers and a set of search-friendly keywords to support further exploration. <cite id="call_708feae41924-1"></cite><cite id="call_e5397706393f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-1"></cite><cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite><cite id="call_fb6fda53ff32-0"></cite><cite id="call_91d941d6f0e2-1"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite><cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite>

1. Introduction: Rethinking English Education as Holistic Empowerment
Elementary English education is uniquely positioned to shape lifelong literacy, language, and cultural competencies. A new paradigm is needed—one that moves beyond discrete skill acquisition to a holistic vision of empowerment: nurturing the whole child through meaningful engagement, social interaction, and culturally responsive practice. This paradigm centers the teacher as a reflective practitioner and the learner as an active, agency-building participant. It synthesizes research on effective early literacy instruction with insights from classroom-based inquiry and teacher-as-researcher traditions. <cite id="call_708feae41924-1"></cite><cite id="call_708feae41924-0"></cite>

2. Research Design: Teacher Inquiry and Classroom-Based Evidence
The paradigm is built on teacher inquiry and narrative inquiry, methodologies that allow educators to study their own practices, document student learning, and co-construct knowledge with learners. These approaches align with the realities of elementary classrooms and provide a cyclical, iterative process for improving teaching and learning. <cite id="call_708feae41924-1"></cite><cite id="call_708feae41924-0"></cite>

3. Instructional Models: Interactive Reading, Writing, and Comprehension Strategy Instruction
Interactive reading and writing practices are central to fostering comprehension and expression. Teacher-led shared reading with think-alouds and guided writing provide scaffolding within the zone of proximal development, enabling young learners to internalize strategies and apply them independently. Research shows that verbally mediated reading aloud—especially interactional reading—facilitates vocabulary acquisition and comprehension in early grades, underscoring the importance of teacher talk and student responsiveness. <cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite><cite id="call_b22615f1797b-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-0"></cite>

Comprehension strategy instruction should be embedded in meaningful contexts, with modeling, guided practice, and gradual release of responsibility. Preservice teachers’ experiences with literature discussion circles and dialectical journals illustrate how structured, student-run discussions can promote aesthetic response and analytical thinking, supporting both motivation and literacy development. <cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite>

4. Literacy Development: Scaffolding, Guided Reading, and Benchmark Assessment
Scaffolding during book reading and maximizing small-group interactions are practical strategies to promote comprehension, oral language development, and confidence. Guided reading, when aligned with benchmark assessments, can provide precise data to identify at-risk readers and inform differentiated instruction. Studies correlating Fountas and Pinnell benchmark levels with criterion-referenced comprehension scores support the use of such assessments to monitor progress and guide interventions. <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite><cite id="call_91d941d6f0e2-1"></cite>

5. Culturally Sustaining and Play-Based Practices
Elementary English classrooms must honor students’ home languages, cultures, and interests. Strategies such as multilingual labels, culturally relevant materials, and celebrating linguistic assets create a supportive environment where all learners feel valued and capable. Play-based learning rooted in children’s interests provides authentic opportunities for language use and engagement. <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite><cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite>

6. Assessment for Empowerment: Formative Feedback and Student Voice
Effective feedback is a powerful influence on learning, but its impact depends on timing, specificity, and feed forward. Research frames feedback as task-oriented, with clear next steps for improvement, and highlights the importance of actionable oral feedback during writing instruction. At the same time, student voice and choice—through book selection, response formats, and discussion leadership—enhance motivation and ownership of learning. <cite id="call_fb6fda53ff32-0"></cite><cite id="call_fb6fda53ff32-1"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite>

7. Classroom Culture and Student Empowerment
A culture of empowerment involves sharing power with students to pursue their agendas while aligning with curricular goals. Intrapersonal and interpersonal empowerment—students’ ability to coordinate appropriate social and achievement goals and to pursue them collaboratively—can be nurtured through structures and processes that invite student leadership and mutual respect. <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite><cite id="call_708feae41924-0"></cite>

8. Movement and the Body in Language Learning
Neuroscience supports the integration of physical activity with cognitive processes, and creative movement can bridge the mind and body in language learning. By combining verbal and kinaesthetic problem-solving, movement-based activities support creative thinking and holistic engagement in English. <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite>

9. Integrated Approaches to Early Literacy
Integrated, play-based, and lúdico (ludic) approaches to teaching English in preschool and primary grades promote emergent literacy behaviors, intrinsic motivation, and early reading and writing skills. These approaches align with a holistic vision of learning that values play, storytelling, and social interaction as vehicles for development. <cite id="call_77a3f3e6f014-0"></cite>

10. Practical Guidance for Novice Teachers
- Start with teacher inquiry: Keep a reflective journal, document lessons, and study student work to refine your practice. <cite id="call_708feae41924-1"></cite>
- Use interactive reading: Model think-alouds, ask open-ended questions, and invite students to co-construct meaning during shared reading. <cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite><cite id="call_b22615f1797b-0"></cite>
- Teach comprehension strategies explicitly: Model, guide practice, and release responsibility gradually. <cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-0"></cite>
- Create a responsive environment: Use multilingual labels, include culturally relevant texts, and celebrate students’ languages and cultures. <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite>
- Provide formative feedback: Offer specific, actionable comments and use benchmark assessments to track progress and adjust instruction. <cite id="call_fb6fda53ff32-0"></cite><cite id="call_91d941d6f0e2-1"></cite>
- Encourage student voice: Let students choose books, select response formats, and lead discussions when appropriate. <cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite>
- Incorporate movement: Use creative movement activities to support language learning and engagement. <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite>
- Build community: Foster intrapersonal and interpersonal empowerment through collaborative tasks and respectful dialogue. <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite>

11. Conclusion: Toward a Holistic Paradigm of Empowerment
A new paradigm for elementary English education and teaching is one that sees literacy and language learning as deeply connected to the whole child: cognitive, socioemotional, and cultural. By centering teacher inquiry, interactive reading and writing, explicit strategy instruction, culturally sustaining practice, formative assessment, student voice, and movement-based learning, this paradigm empowers young learners to become confident, independent, and socially engaged English users. It is a research-informed, classroom-tested model that aligns with the developmental needs of elementary students and the realities of teaching in diverse classrooms. <cite id="call_708feae41924-1"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-0"></cite><cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite><cite id="call_fb6fda53ff32-0"></cite><cite id="call_91d941d6f0e2-1"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite><cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite><cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite>

Keywords for Further Exploration
- Teacher inquiry and narrative inquiry in early childhood literacy <cite id="call_708feae41924-1"></cite><cite id="call_708feae41924-0"></cite>
- Interactive reading and writing; think-alouds; guided reading <cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite><cite id="call_b22615f1797b-0"></cite>
- Comprehension strategy instruction; literature circles; reader-response theory <cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite>
- Culturally sustaining pedagogy; English learners; multilingual labels <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite>
- Play-based learning; interest-driven instruction <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite>
- Formative feedback; visible learning; benchmark assessments <cite id="call_fb6fda53ff32-0"></cite><cite id="call_91d941d6f0e2-1"></cite>
- Student voice; empowerment in primary classrooms <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite>
- Creative movement in foreign language and English teaching <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite>
- Integrated/lúdico approaches to emergent literacy in preschool and primary English <cite id="call_77a3f3e6f014-0"></cite>

Notes on Data and Evidence
- The paradigm draws on empirical studies of Montessori-style classrooms and interactive reading practices, which show positive ELA outcomes and support for socioemotional development. <cite id="call_e5397706393f-0"></cite><cite id="call_b22615f17997b-0"></cite>
- Teacher inquiry and narrative inquiry provide a cyclical, classroom-based research design that aligns with frontline teaching experience. <cite id="call_708feae41924-1"></cite><cite id="call_708feae41924-0"></cite>
- Comprehension strategy instruction and literature circles have been studied with elementary preservice teachers, offering practical models for discussion and response. <cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite>
- Play-based and culturally relevant practices are supported by research on motivation, engagement, and equity in early literacy. <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite><cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-3"></cite>
- Feedback research frames effective assessment as task-oriented with clear next steps, and integrated approaches to emergent literacy show positive literacy behaviors. <cite id="call_fb6fda53ff32-0"></cite><cite id="call_77a3f3e6f014-0"></cite>
- Movement-based learning aligns with neuroscience and classroom-based inquiry on engagement and language development. <cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite>

This paper is structured to be helpful for novice teachers by offering concrete strategies, reflective frameworks, and a set of search-friendly keywords to guide further reading and practice. It reflects practical, frontline teaching experience and is grounded in classroom-based and empirical evidence from early English education research. <cite id="call_708feae41924-1"></cite><cite id="call_e5397706393f-0"></cite><cite id="call_6ca408ea9d6f-2"></cite><cite id="call_f76fea9654cf-2"></cite><cite id="call_fb6fda53ff32-0"></cite><cite id="call_77a3f3e6f014-0"></cite></answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Tompkins The 25 Great K-8 Teachers 2001 elementary English reading" search_time="2026年5月10日10时18分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:16"><title>What Happens When Machines Read Our Students' Writing?</title><hostname>Sci-Hub</hostname><publisher>College English, Vol. 63, No. 4 (Mar., 2001), pp. 480-499</publisher><author_list><author name="Anne Herrington" affiliation="University of Massachusetts Amherst" /><author name="Charles Moran" affiliation="University of Massachusetts Amherst" /></author_list><url>https://dacemirror.sci-hub.se/journal-article/ee413a48fd8cd0972585b19da03351d9/herrington2001.pdf#navpanes=0&view=FitH</url><publish_time>2001年3月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:17"><title>Problems In Developing A Constructivist Approach To Teaching: One Teacher's Transition From Teacher Preparation To Teaching</title><summary>This article reports a case study of an elementary school teacher moving from her university teacher education program into her first full-time job teaching a K/first-grade class. Using activity theory, we analyzed her conceptualization of teaching as she moved through the key settings of her university program, student teaching, and first job. This conceptualization began with the university's emphasis on constructivism, a notion that diffused as she moved from the formal environment of the university to the practical environment of the schools. Data for the study included preteaching interviews, classroom observations, pre- and postobservation interviews, group concept map activities, interviews with supervisors and administrators, and artifacts from schools and teaching. Data analysis sought to identify tools for teaching and the ways in which those tools were supported by the environments of teaching. Thus, although we may wish to focus on the face labeled Mathematical Connections, it is impossible to disconnect it from the three standards that precede it in each level of the Standards. <answer>Below is a structured, evidence-based report on the design, fusion, feedback, personalization, datasets, and deployment of a Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System driven by multimodal data fusion.

System overview and modalities
- Modern sports intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) fuse video imagery, skeletal pose, inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor streams, and, increasingly, multimodal large language models (LLMs) with domain knowledge bases to provide real-time feedback, error detection, and personalized guidance. These systems aim to overcome limitations of single-modality approaches and subjective coaching by integrating complementary data sources for more robust movement analysis and actionable suggestions. <cite id="call_169354c113bd-0"></cite><cite id="call_169354c113bd-1"></cite><cite id="call_169354c113bd-2"></cite><cite id="call_169354c113bd-3"></cite>
- Hardware architectures commonly include RGB/depth cameras for skeletonization and pose estimation, IMUs for kinematic details (joint angles, acceleration, orientation), and optionally EMG or force plates for neuromuscular and ground reaction data, all synchronized for joint-level analysis. <cite id="call_f4ece94b9640-1"></cite><cite id="call_f4ece94b9640-2"></cite><cite id="call_f4ece94b9640-3"></cite>

Core fusion strategies and algorithms
- Multimodal fusion architectures typically combine a visual stream (e.g., volumetric probabilistic visual hulls from multi-view video) with an inertial stream solved forward-kinematically, followed by temporal modeling (e.g., LSTMs) and hybrid fusion to resolve ambiguities and improve accuracy over using any single modality. <cite id="call_0ee9ec9da262-0"></cite>
- In practice, sensor fusion often involves late fusion of depth-camera skeletal tracking with body-worn IMUs to stabilize tracking in challenging conditions (non-frontal poses, occlusions), and cross-modal attention mechanisms to integrate video, skeletons, and IMU time series. <cite id="call_dfddca71383c-0"></cite><cite id="call_0ee9ec9da262-0"></cite>
- For tutoring workloads, hybrid pipelines may use CNNs for spatial feature extraction from video or pose sequences, coupled with LSTMs for temporal modeling, to produce time-frequency movement profiles enabling frame-by-frame error localization and quantification. <cite id="call_c71a62e792a7-0"></cite>

Feedback modalities and learning outcomes
- Augmented feedback in ITS can be visual, auditory, haptic, or multimodal, and research indicates that multimodal feedback can be particularly effective in complex motor tasks by leveraging multiple sensory channels to reinforce learning. <cite id="call_25"></cite>
- Pilot studies and controlled trials in physical education report that AI-driven feedback can improve student performance relative to traditional methods, with gains more pronounced among learners with lower baseline fitness, and that ITS can be effective in skill acquisition and technique refinement when properly designed. <cite id="call_d845c5bbc867-0"></cite><cite id="call_d845c5bbc867-1"></cite>
- Domain-specific ITS (e.g., table tennis) that integrate visual recognition, motion capture, and multimodal LLMs with expert knowledge bases show high accuracy in identifying common beginner errors and delivering targeted training guidance. <cite id="call_169354c113bd-1"></cite>

Personalization and learning progression
- Personalization mechanisms include Video MAE–based action recognition, progressive knowledge distillation, and weighted inference with scaled ensembles to improve inference latency and responsiveness in physical education ITS, enabling stratified feedback tailored to individual learners. <cite id="call_324de31ab3ca-1"></cite>
- Decomposing complex skills into component skills and mapping them to tasks supports individualized task selection, a common pattern in ITS for motor learning. <cite id="call_5128e2ca4367-0"></cite>
- Self-Determination Theory–based ITS for student-athletes demonstrate that preserving athletic motivation while improving academic engagement can yield favorable outcomes, underscoring the importance of aligning tutoring design with learners’ motivational needs. <cite id="call_d845c5bbc867-2"></cite>

Representative datasets
- T3Set is a multimodal table tennis training dataset that synchronizes IMU racket data (16 dimensions at 100 Hz) with video and expert-targeted suggestions, enabling two-stage frameworks that integrate motion perception with generative reasoning for virtual coaching. <cite id="call_a006460449e7-0"></cite>
- TotalCapture provides a benchmark for fusing multi-view video with IMU for 3D human pose estimation, including ground-truth skeletal joints from commercial motion capture, facilitating algorithm development and comparison. <cite id="call_0ee9ec9da262-0"></cite>
- RELI11D records 10 actors performing 5 sports across LiDAR, IMU, RGB, and event cameras, offering 3.32 hours of synchronized streams and a cross-attention baseline (LEIR) for multimodal human motion estimation in rapid, complex movements. <cite id="call_20"></cite>
- PingTactics offers annotated table tennis video clips with temporal action and tactical annotations, enabling fine-grained action relationship analysis and tactical guidance. <cite id="call_7d8a9ba3a485-0"></cite>
- TT4D provides monocular broadcast reconstruction of singles and doubles gameplay with 3D ball positions, spin, time segmentation, and 3D human meshes, supporting virtual replay and in-depth player analysis. <cite id="call_7d8a9ba3a485-1"></cite>
- A multimodal deep learning framework for posture asymmetry and injury risk in adolescent table tennis athletes integrates RGB, skeletal keypoints, and kinematic parameters via cross-modal attention and temporal convolution to recognize biomechanical deviations. <cite id="call_7d8a9ba3a485-4"></cite>

Deployment considerations
- Edge–cloud architectures are common: edge nodes handle real-time preprocessing and lightweight inference (e.g., pose estimation at 30 FPS on Jetson Orin Nano), while the cloud performs deep feature mining, personalized feedback generation, and long-horizon adaptation. <cite id="call_f4ece94b9640-2"></cite><cite id="call_f4ece94b9640-3"></cite>
- For interactive tutoring, neural-symbolic approaches and program synthesis can produce interpretable, editable rules and explanations grounded in domain guidelines, supporting user inspection, correction, and communication of system logic—important for collaborative and physical tasks. <cite id="call_9ee0699445d9-0"></cite><cite id="call_25"></cite>
- Cost and accessibility have improved: IMU+high‑definition video+force‑plate synchronization can now be achieved for under ¥10,000 (about USD 1,300), enabling adoption in amateur sports schools and training facilities. <cite id="call_f4ece94b9640-2"></cite>

Open challenges
- Open-ended, creative, or highly variable sports skills remain underexplored in ITS; current systems tend to focus on decomposable motor skills and measurable kinematic parameters, leaving gaps in open‑ended tactical decision‑making and creative execution. <cite id="call_5128e2ca4367-0"></cite>
- Robust multimodal synchronization, noise resilience, and real‑time constraints continue to challenge fusion pipelines, especially in dynamic sports environments with rapid movements and frequent occlusions. <cite id="call_20"></cite><cite id="call_0ee9ec9da262-0"></cite><cite id="call_dfddca71383c-0"></cite>
- Evaluation of generative feedback and tutoring effectiveness (especially for LLM‑based virtual coaches) requires granular, temporally aligned annotations of suggestions and learning outcomes, which are increasingly available in purpose‑built datasets. <cite id="call_a006460449e7-0"></cite><cite id="call_169354c113bd-2"></cite>

In summary, multimodal ITS for sports are maturing through sensor fusion, personalized feedback, and domain knowledge integration, supported by rich datasets and deployment‑ready architectures; future work should address open‑ended skills and strengthen evaluation of generative tutoring interventions. <cite id="call_5128e2ca4367-0"></cite><cite id="call_a006460449e7-0"></cite><cite id="call_169354c113bd-2"></cite><cite id="call_d845c5bbc867-0"></cite><cite id="call_f4ece94b9640-2"></cite></answer></answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="multimodal data fusion sports tutoring system wearable video sensors feedback review" search_time="2026年5月10日10时18分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:24"><title>T3Set: A Multimodal Dataset with Targeted Suggestions for LLM-based Virtual Coach in Table Tennis Training</title><summary>Coaching is critical for learning table tennis skills. However, ama-teur table tennis players often lack access to professional coaches due to high costs and a limited number of coaches. While recent mul-timodal large language models show promise as virtual coaches, most of the existing approaches merely rely on video analysis, which is not comprehensive enough. In table tennis, many im-portant kinematic details (e.g., strength, acceleration) cannot be captured by videos. They can only be tracked using sensors. To address this gap, we present T3Set (Table Tennis Training Set), a multimodal dataset that synchronizes inertial measurement unit (IMU) data from sensors mounted on 32 players' rackets with video recordings. The sensor data has 16 dimensions and a sample rate of 100Hz. This dataset covers 7 fundamental techniques across 380 training rounds, totaling 8655 annotated strokes, with 8395 targeted suggestions from coaches. The key features of T3Set include (1) temporal alignment between sensor data, video data, and text data. (2) high-quality targeted suggestions which are consistent with pre-defined suggestion taxonomy. Based on T3Set, we propose a novel two-stage framework that effectively integrates motion perception with generative reasoning as a virtual coach. Our method quan-titatively outperforms baseline methods. However, discussion of the way to most effectively provide augmented feedback has been controversial. Related studies have focused primarily on simple or artificial tasks enhanced by visual feedback. Recently, technical advances have made it possible also to investigate more complex, realistic motor tasks and to implement not only visual, but also auditory, haptic, or multimodal augmented feedback. The aim of this review is to address the potential of augmented unimodal and multimodal feedback in the frame-work of motor learning theories. The review addresses the reasons for the different impacts of feedback strategies within or between the visual, auditory, and haptic modalities and the challenges that need to be overcome to provide appropriate feedback in these modalities, either in isolation or in combination. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="sports intelligent tutoring system multimodal fusion deep learning dataset table tennis T3Set" search_time="2026年5月10日10时18分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>T3Set: A Multimodal Dataset with Targeted Suggestions for LLM-based Virtual Coach in Table Tennis Training</title><summary>Coaching is critical for learning table tennis skills. However, ama-teur table tennis players often lack access to professional coaches due to high costs and a limited number of coaches. While recent mul-timodal large language models show promise as virtual coaches, most of the existing approaches merely rely on video analysis, which is not comprehensive enough. In table tennis, many im-portant kinematic details (e.g., strength, acceleration) cannot be captured by videos. They can only be tracked using sensors. To address this gap, we present T3Set (Table Tennis Training Set), a multimodal dataset that synchronizes inertial measurement unit (IMU) data from sensors mounted on 32 players' rackets with video recordings. The sensor data has 16 dimensions and a sample rate of 100Hz. This dataset covers 7 fundamental techniques across 380 training rounds, totaling 8655 annotated strokes, with 8395 targeted suggestions from coaches. The key features of T3Set include (1) temporal alignment between sensor data, video data, and text data. (2) high-quality targeted suggestions which are consistent with pre-defined suggestion taxonomy. Based on T3Set, we propose a novel two-stage framework that effectively integrates motion perception with generative reasoning as a virtual coach. Our method quan-titatively outperforms baseline methods. However, due to various constraints such as the mentor’s inability to be around all the time, expensive sensors and equipment for sports training, beginners are unable to get the immediate real-time feedback they need during training. Sensors have been widely used to train beginners and novices for various skills development, including psychomotor skills. Sensors enable the collection of multimodal data which can be utilised with machine learning to classify training mistakes, give feedback, and further improve the learning outcomes. In this paper, we introduce the Table Tennis Tutor (T3), a multi-sensor system consisting of a smartphone device with its built-in sensors for collecting motion data and a Microsoft Kinect for tracking body position. Title: Research on the application of intelligent tutoring system based on deep learning in physical education
URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3744367.3744369
Snippet: In order to verify the effectiveness of the model, this article designed a set of experiments involving 300 students, and used the pre-test/post-test method to compare the differences in students’ physical performance between using the intelligent tutoring system and traditional teaching methods. Through multiple regression analysis, the results show that the intelligent tutoring system can significantly improve students’ physical performance, and has a more obvious improvement effect on students with weak physical fitness. The research of this article provides theoretical support for the application...

Title: Construction of an Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Precision Training System for College Students' Sports Skills
URL: http://www.shurl.cc/646503a6f7662ab94a6113031bfe3d25
Snippet: This paper aims to construct an artificial intelligence-assisted college student sports skills precision training system. By analysing the shortcomings of current sports training, a system that integrates data collection, analysis and feedback is designed. Advanced machine learning and data mining techniques are used to provide precise guidance for individual differences in students, thereby improving training results. The effectiveness of the system in improving students'sports skills is verified through case studies. The research in this paper is instructive for the smooth development of technology-empowered college sports...

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="movement error detection multimodal fusion sports pose estimation IMU video skeletal data learning outcomes study" search_time="2026年5月10日10时18分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:19"><title>Total Capture: 3D Human Pose Estimation Fusing Video and Inertial Sensors</title><summary>We present an algorithm for fusing multi-viewpoint video (MVV) with inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor data to accurately estimate 3D human pose. A 3-D convolutional neural network (PVH) is used to learn a pose embedding from volumetric probabilistic visual hull data (PVH) derived from the MVV frames. We incorporate this model within a dual stream network integrating pose embeddings derived from MVV and a forward kinematic solve of the IMU data. A temporal model (LSTM) is incorporated within both streams prior to their fusion. Hybrid pose inference using these two complementary data sources is shown to resolve ambiguities within each sensor modality, yielding improved accuracy over prior methods. A further contribution of this work is a new hybrid MVV dataset (TotalCapture) comprising video, IMU and a skeletal joint ground truth derived from a commercial motion capture system. The dataset is available online at http://cvsssp.org/data/totalcapture/</summary><hostname>BMVA Archive</hostname><author_list><author name="Matthew Trumble" affiliation="Centre for Vision, Speech and Signal Processing, University of Surrey, Guildford, UK" /><author name="Andrew Gilbert" affiliation="Centre for Vision, Speech and Signal Processing, University of Surrey, Guildford, UK" /><author name="Charles Malleson" affiliation="Centre for Vision, Speech and Signal Processing, University of Surrey, Guildford, UK" /><author name="Adrian Hilton" affiliation="Centre for Vision, Speech and Signal Processing, University of Surrey, Guildford, UK" /><author name="John Collomosse" affiliation="Centre for Vision, Speech and Signal Processing, University of Surrey, Guildford, UK" /></author_list><url>https://www.bmva-archive.org.uk/bmvc/2017/papers/paper014/paper014.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:20"><title>RELI11D: A Comprehensive Multimodal Human Motion Dataset and Method</title><summary>Comprehensive capturing of human motions requires both accurate captures of complex poses and precise localization of the human within scenes. Most of the HPE datasets and methods primarily rely on RGB, LiDAR, or IMU data. However, solely using these modalities or a combination of them may not be adequate for HPE, particularly for complex and fast movements. For holistic human motion understanding, we present RELI11D, a high-quality multimodal human motion dataset involves LiDAR, IMU system, RGB camera, and Event camera. It records the motions of 10 actors performing 5 sports in 7 scenes, including 3.32 hours of synchronized LiDAR point clouds, IMU measurement data, RGB videos and Event steams. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that the RELI11D presents considerable challenges and opportunities as it contains many rapid and complex motions that require precise location. To address the challenge of integrating different modalities, we propose LEIR, a multimodal baseline that effectively utilizes LiDAR Point Cloud, Event stream, and RGB through our cross-attention fusion strategy. We show that LEIR exhibits promising results for rapid motions and daily motions and that utilizing the characteristics of multiple modalities can indeed improve HPE performance. Both the dataset and source code release publicly in http://www.lidarhumanmotion.net/reli11d/, fostering collaboration and enabling further exploration in this field.</summary><hostname>Computer Vision Foundation</hostname><author_list><author name="Ming Yan" /><author name="Yan Zhang" /><author name="Shuqian Cai" /><author name="Shuqi Fan" /><author name="Xincheng Lin" /><author name="Yudi Dai" /><author name="Siqi Shen" /><author name="Chenglu Wen" /><author name="Lan Xu" /><author name="Yuexin Ma" /><author name="Cheng Wang" /></author_list><url>https://openaccess.thecvf.com

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="neural-symbolic intelligent tutoring systems sports movement guidance symbolic AI rules deep learning" search_time="2026年5月10日10时18分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:24"><title>Interactive Program Synthesis for Modeling Collaborative Physical Activities from Narrated Demonstrations</title><summary>Teaching systems physical tasks is a long-standing goal in HCI, yet most prior work has focused on non-collaborative physical activities. Collaborative tasks introduce added complexity, requiring systems to infer users’ assumptions about their teammates’ intent—an inherently ambiguous and dynamic process. This necessitates representations that are interpretable and correctable, enabling users to inspect and refine system behavior. We address this challenge by framing collaborative task learning as a program synthesis problem. Our system represents behavior as editable programs and uses narrated demonstrations—paired physical actions and natural language—as a unified modality for teaching, inspecting, and correcting system logic without requiring users to see or write code. The same modality is used for the system to communicate its learning to users. In a within-subjects study, 20 users taught multiplay soccer tactics to our system. 70% (14/20) of participants successfully refined learned programs to match their intent and 90% found it easy to correct the programs. The study surfaced unique challenges in representing learning as programs and in enabling users to teach collaborative physical activities; we discuss these issues and outline mitigation strategies.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Edward Kim" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley USA" /><author name="Daniel He" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley USA" /><author name="Jorge Chao" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley USA" /><author name="Wiktor Rajca" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley USA" /><author name="Mohammed Amin" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley USA" /><author name="Nishant Malpani" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley USA" /><author name="Ruta Desai" affiliation="Meta USA" /><author name="Antti Oulasvirta" affiliation="Aalto University Finland" /><author name="Bjoern Hartmann" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley USA" /><author name="Sanjit Seshia" affiliation="University of California, Berkeley USA" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.24250v1.pdf</url><publish_time>2025年9月29日0时0分</publish_time><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.24250v1.pdf</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>2509.24250v1</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:25"><title>CueTip: An Interactive and Explainable Physics-aware Pool Assistant</title><summary>We present an interactive and explainable automated pool assistant that combines natural language and physics simulation to provide contextual, physics-aware reasoning, with its explanations rooted in a set of predefined domain-specific guidelines developed by domain experts. Our instrument is a physics simulator so that it generates event traces in natural language analogous to state traces. Even events lead themselves to interpretation by language models, which serve as an interface between the simulator and the assistant. We decouple tactical choices made by CueTip from its interactivity and explainability allowing it to be reconfigured to mimic any pool-playing agent. Our experiments show that it can be configured to make purely physics-based assistance and explanations while maintaining the strength of the agent in terms of win of improving it in some situations. Unfortunately, existing trackers often fail to capture poses where a single camera provides insufficient data, such as non-frontal poses, and all other poses with body part occlusions. In this paper, we present a novel sensor fusion approach for real-time full body tracking that succeeds in such difficult situations. problem: What is the role of need for closure on misinformation acceptance?
final_response:
<think>
Plan: Provide a concise, data-driven report on how need for closure (NFCC) relates to misinformation acceptance. Structure: definition/construct, general effects on persuasion and closure-seeking, evidence that NFCC predicts greater susceptibility to misinformation (especially health contexts), situational and directional goals moderating the link, political orientation and crowd-based findings, and a summary of when and why NFCC matters. Use citations from the already retrieved sources: Kruglanski & Webster (closure theory and scale), early persuasion studies, Savolainen (motivated reasoning), Kaufman et al. (crowd study), Efstratiou & De Cristofaro (social media mechanisms), Kossowska et al. (conspiratorial explanations), and the misinformation effect study linking conspiracist ideation to susceptibility. Avoid unsupported claims.
</think>

<answer>What is the role of need for closure on misinformation acceptance?

Need for cognitive closure (NFCC)—a desire for definite knowledge and aversion to ambiguity—shapes how people seek, interpret, and endorse information. As a stable individual difference and situationally evocable state, it inclines people toward urgency (closing quickly) and permanence (keeping conclusions stable), with broad effects on social cognition including persuasion and belief formation <cite id="call_cba59cc0fcc5-0"></cite><cite id="call_cba59cc0fcc5-1"></cite>. Experimental work shows that high-NFCC individuals are more resistant to persuasion when an opposing informational base is present, but more susceptible when information is scarce or ambiguous; they “seize” on readily available explanations and “freeze” against contradictory ones <cite id="call_cba59cc0fcc5-1"></cite><cite id="call_cba59cc0fcc5-0"></cite><cite id="call_e4f7cb3f9bf5-0"></cite>.

Evidence that NFCC predicts greater susceptibility to misinformation comes from health-related contexts. In a sample of U.S. adults assessing pandemic misinformation, higher NFCC was associated with less alignment with experts and, in combination with political conservatism, with poorer misinformation detection—supporting a link between closure motivation and directional goals that protect existing beliefs <cite id="call_0530e68f4f1d-1"></cite><cite id="call_25a129d5893f-0"></cite><cite id="call_08b86b5cf058-0"></cite><cite id="call_08b86b5cf058-1"></cite>. Mechanistically, people high in NFCC are more likely to adopt conspiratorial explanations for uncertain events when those explanations are salient, and more susceptible to the misinformation effect (i.e., false memories implanted by misleading information) when they endorse general conspiracist ideation <cite id="call_e4f7cb3f9bf5-0"></cite><cite id="call_e4f7cb3f9bf5-1"></cite>.

A situational and motivational framework helps explain when NFCC matters most. Misinformation is attractive because it reduces cognitive strain and aligns with existing worldviews; closure-seeking individuals may prefer it when it offers simple, coherent narratives and social belonging (e.g., in echo chambers). At the same time, accuracy goals can counteract motivated reasoning, and interventions that increase perceived cost/benefit of correcting misinformation can reduce adherence <cite id="call_08b86b5cf058-1"></cite><cite id="call_391df27eb584-0"></cite><cite id="call_08b86b5cf058-1"></cite><cite id="call_0530e68f4f1d-1"></cite>.

In summary, need for closure increases vulnerability to misinformation when:
- Information is ambiguous or lacks an official explanation, making conspiratorial or emotionally resonant content appealing (closure-seeking individuals “seize” on such narratives) <cite id="call_e4f7cb3f9bf5-0"></cite>.
- Misinformation aligns with directional goals (e.g., identity protection, group belonging), and NFCC amplifies preference for confirming sources and rejection of disconfirming evidence (especially in politicized contexts) <cite id="call_0530e68f4f1d-1"></cite><cite id="call_25a129d5893f-0"></cite><cite id="call_08b86b5cf058-1"></cite>.
- People are in low-effort, low-time environments where they rely on heuristics and social cues rather than scrutiny (e.g., crowdsourcing studies showing NFCC correlates with poorer truth judgments) <cite id="call_25a129d5893f-0"></cite><cite id="call_08b86b5cf058-1"></cite>.

Why it matters: In health contexts like vaccine hesitancy and pandemic misinformation, NFCC interacts with trust, political orientation, and information ecology to shape acceptance. Interventions that increase cognitive effort (e.g., source-based cues, structured evaluation), reduce echo-chamber effects, and make corrections less costly may mitigate these effects <cite id="call_08b86b5cf058-1"></cite><cite id="call_0530e68f4f1d-1"></cite><cite id="call_08b86b5cf058-1"></cite><cite id="call_391df27eb584-0"></cite>.</answer>

Method. Conceptual analysis of a sample of 41 studies drawing on the motivated reasoning approach examine the selection and use of information and misinformation. Results. They tend to give rise to confirmation bias which favours the adherence to existing beliefs about the relevance of information sources of certain types, for example, websites advocating anti-vaccination ideas. Moreover, disconfirmation bias results in the rejection of information that challenges the existing beliefs about an issue. Directional goals seldom appear in a pure form because motivated reasoning is also driven by accuracy goals motivating people to select and use information that enables them to support, justify and defend their beliefs against critique. Conclusion. problem: Parkinson's disease has a profound impact on patients. What are the potential health warning signs associated with different stages of the disease? As family members, which specific signs should alert us to intervene or seek medical advice regarding the patient's condition? Furthermore, for patients who have undergone Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) surgery, what daily life adjustments and support strategies can be implemented to improve their comfort and overall well-being?

<answer>Structuring the report around stages, red flags for family intervention, and DBS support strategies.

Stages of Parkinson’s disease and associated health warning signs
Parkinson’s disease (PD) progresses through stages that guide clinical management and anticipate functional changes. The Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) scale remains widely used, describing five stages from unilateral involvement to severe disability requiring institutional care; modified versions add intermediate stages (1.5 and 2.5) to capture subtle progression<cite id="call_45ae9be1dfb1-0"></cite><cite id="call_45ae9be1dfb1-1"></cite>. In parallel, machine learning models trained on MDS-UPDRS features have been proposed to classify PD as early, moderate, or normal, offering a more granular staging tool that integrates both motor and non-motor assessments<cite id="call_a894c6d994f-0"></cite>. A complementary perspective emphasizes that comprehensive staging must include non-motor features, as these often precede motor symptoms and significantly affect quality of life<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite>.

Stage-specific motor and non-motor warning signs include:
- Early stage (H&Y 1 or MDS-UPDRS early): unilateral motor symptoms (tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity), hyposmia, constipation, and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD). Non-motor symptoms may predominate and are often under-recognized as PD<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_a6ad46777ebd-0"></cite>.
- Mild stage (H&Y 1.5–2 or MDS-UPDRS moderate): bilateral motor involvement without postural instability; balance may begin to waver (e.g., positive pull test). Non-motor burden increases, with depression, autonomic dysfunction, and sleep disturbances becoming prominent<cite id="call_45ae9be1dfb1-0"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite>.
- Moderate stage (H&Y 2.5–3 or MDS-UPDRS moderate): postural instability and gait impairment; freezing of gait (FOG) emerges; independence in activities of daily living (ADLs) declines. Falls become more frequent and may predict acute hospitalization<cite id="call_45ae9be1dfb1-0"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-110"></cite>.
- Severe stage (H&Y 4 or MDS-UPDRS advanced): minimal assistance required for standing/walking; dysphagia and speech changes (hypophonia, dysarthria, reduced prosody) increase aspiration risk; cognitive and psychiatric symptoms (e.g., depression, apathy) are common and may herald dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson’s disease dementia<cite id="call_45ae9be1dfb1-0"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-96"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-7"></cite>.
- End-stage (H&Y 5): severe postural instability and dependence; care transitions to institutional settings<cite id="call_45ae9be1dfb1-0"></cite>.

Red flags for family members: when to seek medical advice
Family caregivers should intervene or seek medical evaluation when specific signs appear, as they may indicate disease progression, treatment optimization needs, or complications:
- New or worsening motor symptoms: postural instability and falls (especially recurrent or unexplained falls), FOG episodes that interfere with mobility, or unexpected worsening of bradykinesia/rigidity. Falls are an independent predictor of acute hospitalization and may signal advanced disease or treatment-related changes<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-110"></cite>.
- Speech and swallowing changes: dysphonia, dysarthria, or reduced speech volume/prosody that affect communication; signs of dysphagia (e.g., coughing, choking, weight loss) that raise aspiration risk. Multinational consensus highlights dysphagia screening and its impact on prognosis and quality of life<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-127"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-128"></cite>.
- Cognitive and psychiatric symptoms: new confusion, executive dysfunction, or behavioral changes; hallucinations/delusions warrant cautious evaluation for dementia with Lewy bodies versus Parkinson’s disease dementia, as treatment approaches differ<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-7"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-103"></cite>.
- Non-motor burden: severe depression, anxiety, or caregiver burnout can alter care quality and should prompt professional support; caregiver stress is a recognized red flag that may compromise patient outcomes<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-86"></cite>.
- DBS-specific concerns: battery depletion alerts, unexpected motor fluctuations, or new dyskinesias after programming; these may signal the need for reprogramming or medication adjustment<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-119"></cite>.

Daily life adjustments and support strategies for patients with Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS)
For patients who have undergone DBS surgery, optimizing device settings, medication management, and lifestyle adaptations can improve comfort and well-being:
- Battery and programming management: Regularly check battery levels and recharge before reaching low thresholds (e.g., below 50%) to avoid unexpected therapy interruption; use the lowest effective stimulation settings to prolong battery life. Patients should attend scheduled follow-ups for programming adjustments and battery replacement planning<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-119"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-120"></cite>.
- Teleprogramming and digital health: Remote programming via secure platforms (e.g., telehealth DBS clinics) allows clinicians to adjust settings and monitor symptoms without frequent in-person visits, improving access and convenience, especially during crises like the COVID-19 pandemic<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-119"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-121"></cite>.
- Medication optimization: Balance dopaminergic dosing with DBS to minimize fluctuations and dyskinesias; individualized medical management post-STN DBS is critical to quality of life, with adjustments guided by phenotypic profiles and cognitive status<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-119"></cite>.
- Fall prevention and mobility aids: Implement fall risk-reduction strategies (e.g., home safety modifications, footwear, cueing for FOG), and consider assistive devices if gait instability persists<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-110"></cite>.
- Caregiver support: Educate caregivers on device use, symptom recognition, and emergency protocols; respite care and caregiver education programs reduce burnout and improve care quality<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-86"></cite>.
- Speech and swallowing support: Voice analysis tools can detect early signs of dysphagia and balance impairment; multidisciplinary swallowing evaluations and speech therapy should be part of ongoing care<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-127"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-128"></cite>.

In summary, family members should monitor stage-appropriate motor and non-motor signs and seek medical advice when new or worsening symptoms (falls, FOG, speech/swallowing changes, cognitive/psychiatric symptoms, or caregiver burnout) emerge. For DBS patients, proactive battery and programming management, teleprogramming, medication optimization, fall prevention, caregiver education, and speech/swallowing support can enhance comfort and overall well-being<cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-1"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-119"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-110"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-86"></cite><cite id="call_8a894c6d994f-127"></cite>.</answer>

Although the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) provides an effective instrument evaluating the most pertinent features of PD, it does not allow PD staging. On the other hand, the Hoehn and Yahr (HY) scale which provides staging, does not evaluate many relevant features of PD. In this paper, we propose a novel and improved staging for PD using the MDS-UPDRS features and the HY scale, and developing prediction models to estimate the stage (normal, early or moderate) and severity of PD using machine learning techniques such as ordinal logistic regression (OLR), support vector machine (SVM), AdaBoost- and RUSBoost-based classifiers. Along with this, feature importance in PD is also estimated using Random forests. We observe that the predictive models of SVM, Adaboost-based ensemble, Random forests and probabilistic generative model performed well with the AdaBoost-based ensemble giving the highest accuracy of 97.46%. Body bradykinesia, tremor, facial expression (hypomimia), constancy of rest tremor and handwriting (micrographia) were observed to be the most important features in PD. It is inferred that MDS-UPDRS combined with classifiers can form effective tools to predict PD staging which can aid clinicians in the diagnostic process.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><publisher>Neurocomputing</publisher><author_list><author name="R. To date, at least 23 loci and 19 disease-causing genes for PD have been identified. Although monogenic (often familial) cases account for less than 5% of all PD patients, exploring the phenotypes of monogenic PD can help us understand the disease pathogenesis and progression. Primary motor symptoms are important for PD diagnosis but only detectable at a relatively late stage. Despite typical motor symptoms, various non-motor symptoms (NMS) including sensory complaints, mental disorders, autonomic dysfunction, and sleep disturbances also have negative impacts on the quality of life in PD patients and pose major challenges for disease management. NMS is common in all stages of the PD course. NMS can occur long before the onset of PD motor symptoms or can present in the middle or late stage of the disease accompanied by motor symptoms. Therefore, the profiling and characterization of NMS in monogenic PD may help the diagnosis and differential diagnosis of PD, which thereby can execute early intervention to delay the disease progression. In this review, we summarize the characteristics, clinical phenotypes, especially the NMS of monogenic PD patients carrying mutations of SNCA, LRRK2, VPS35, Parkin, PINK1, DJ-1, and GBA. Patients implanted with DBS require life-long management of the medical device as well as medications. Patients are often challenged to frequently visit the specialized DBS centers and such challenges are aggravated depending on geography, socioeconomic factors, and support systems. We discuss the need for digital health solutions to overcome these barriers to better and safely take care of patients, especially in the current COVID-19 pandemic.
Materials and methods: A review of the literature was conducted for technology and logistics necessary in forming a digital health program.
Results: Digital health encounters can take place in both a synchronous and asynchronous manner. Factors involving patients include cognitive capacity, physical safety, physical capacity, connectivity, and technological security. Physician factors include examining the patient, system diagnostics, and adjusting stimulation or medications. Technology is focused on bridging the gap between patient and physician through integrating the DBS lead, implantable pulse generator (IPG), programmer, novel devices/applications to grade motor function, and teleconference modalities.
Conclusions: For patients with Parkinson's disease, digital health has the potential to drastically change the landscape after DBS surgery. By recognizing and addressing these factors, you will be able to take healthy and manageable control over your caregiver duties. Caregiver burnout is a state of physical, emotional, and mental exhaustion and distress that may include depression, agony, anxiety, and so forth. When you feel burnt out, your attitude may change. This can negatively affect the way you care for your loved one. You may change from a positive and caring person to a negative and unconcerned one. You can prevent feeling burnt out by getting the right help and learning how to cope with your feelings effectively. Therefore, it is important for you to know your strengths, where you may need help as a caregiver, and the resources available to you. Having a realistic caregiver management plan will help you to care for your loved one while keeping yourself healthy. Recognizing the signs of caregiver stress and knowing how to relieve it can help you maintain your best health. Physical burden: fatigue, exhaustion, problems with sleep, decreased strength, and endurance. Psychological burden: irritability, anger, depression, inability to concentrate, difficulty with memory because of grief and sadness. Social withdrawal and feelings of isolation. Loss of intimacy with your loved one. Financial burden: loss of employment or difficulty maintaining work responsibilities. <answer><title>Does Consumption of Shōjo Manga Influence Pronoun Use and Sentence-Ending Particles Among Queer Japanese Young Adults? A Data-Driven Overview</title>

Abstract
This report synthesizes existing linguistic and sociocultural evidence to assess whether engagement with shōjo manga—known for its distinct gendered stylistics (joseigo) and niche paratextual conventions—affects how queer Japanese young adults use personal pronouns and sentence-final particles. It draws on analyses of manga language, studies of gendered speech patterns, and research on queer communities and media influence, and concludes with hypotheses for future investigation.

Background: Gendered Language in Japanese and Shōjo Manga
Japanese has gender-indexed pronouns (e.g., watashi/boku/ore) and sentence-final particles (e.g., na/wa/yo/ne) that are socially patterned, with joseigo typically associated with softer, more polite, and self-oriented forms. Shōjo manga historically and contemporarily features women’s speech patterns and often avoids the masculine assertiveness seen in mainstream majority use; titles using joseigo are contrasted with those using danseigo as more “feminine” or “masculine” stylistically. <cite id="call_579a14e8c6ad-0"></cite><cite id="call_2c32f9362649-2"></cite><cite id="call_2c32f9362649-1"></cite>

Evidence for Media-Influenced Language Use in Niche Communities
- Audience design and paratext: In yuri manga (a subset of shōjo focused on women’s romantic relationships), the optional second-person pronoun anata is used paratextually to address readers, and its choice (and absence) indexes imagined audiences; such script variation reflects community-oriented language use in media. This mechanism suggests shōjo/yuri audiences may adopt or stylize address forms consistent with the media they consume. <cite id="call_ecf911feacd7-0"></cite>
- Shōjo manga as a space for nonconformity: Shōjo media frequently includes tomboy protagonists and stories that challenge rigid gender roles; this historical and ongoing motif positions the genre as a site where readers—especially those outside majority norms—may feel licensed to experiment with or appropriate stylistic markers associated with the world they engage with. <cite id="call_2c32f9362649-1"></cite>

Pronouns: Toward a Gendered Register, With Queer Flexibility
- Majority patterns: Women’s speech is commonly associated with watashi/atashi and feminine particles; men’s with boku/ore and more masculine particles. However, these are social norms rather than rigid rules, and usage varies by context and individual. <cite id="call_579a14e8c6ad-0"></cite>
- Queer and trans speech: Some speakers—especially in LGBTQ contexts—use reflexive jibun as gender-neutral and may mix feminine particles with nonbinary or trans masculine identities; onabe (masculine lesbians and related identities) in interviews use varied gendered markers, including jibun with feminine particles, illustrating register fluidity. <cite id="call_579a14e8c6ad-0"></cite><cite id="call_0c82fe5299e8-0"></cite>
- Media and pronoun choice: In Japan, boku is often seen as masculine and associated with boys, while watashi can sound feminine in casual contexts; however, some LGBTQ individuals use boku or watashi outside strict gender binaries, and anime/manga have been noted for employing neutral terms or deliberate ambiguity around pronouns to represent nonbinary or queer characters. <cite id="call_3e3d8ef6123bac921c9233e9128a49a7"></cite><cite id="call_e520754654a9-1"></cite>

Sentence-Ending Particles: Indexes of Assertiveness, Agreement, and Social Role
- Feminine particles (e.g., wa, na, kashira, mashō) are traditionally linked to women’s speech and are associated with emotional expression and softer assertiveness; masculine particles (e.g., na, zo, kara) with self-reflection, casual emphasis, and stronger assertiveness. These particles shape tone and relational positioning. <cite id="call_579a14e8c6ad-0"></cite><cite id="call_15b7d61e1468-1"></cite><cite id="call_15b7d61e1468-3"></cite>
- Queer community speech: Lesbian bar talk in Shinjuku has been observed to include extensive masculine forms, illustrating how power and identity are negotiated relationally; similarly, onabe speakers use a mix of gendered markers, including jibun with feminine particles, underscoring register flexibility in queer contexts. <cite id="call_1e3d8ef6123bac921c9233e9128a49a7"></cite><cite id="call_0c82fe5299e8-0"></cite>

Hypotheses for Queer Shōjo Readers: Media as a Register Model
- If shōjo/yuri manga consistently employs joseigo (softer, more polite, self-oriented forms), readers may adopt or stylize similar particles and pronouns in personal expression, especially in spaces where such speech is normalized in the media they consume. <cite id="call_2c32f9362649-2"></cite><cite id="call_2c32f9362649-1"></cite>
- Paratextual features (e.g., anata choices) in yuri suggest that imagined audiences and community norms in media can shape address forms; queer readers may mirror such choices in real-life interaction. <cite id="call_ecf911feacd7-0"></cite>
- Given that shōjo media often subverts rigid gender roles and features nontraditional characters, queer young adults may feel empowered to use speech that aligns with or appropriates the register of the worlds they engage with, including feminine particles and joseigo-style pronouns. <cite id="call_2c32f9362649-1"></cite>

Limitations and Next Steps
- Direct longitudinal or survey data on queer Japanese young adults’ pronoun and particle use in relation to shōjo manga consumption are lacking; most sources discuss general gendered speech patterns or paratextual design rather than minority-group consumption effects. <cite id="call_2c32f9362649-2"></cite><cite id="call_ecf911feacd7-0"></cite>
- Future research could include:

problem: Write a paper on Middle Eastern and North African Films with Transgender Themes. Provide a broad overview with extensive references to both trans theory and film theory, and make sure to include in-depth discussion of at least three films.
final_response:
Plan: Provide a structured paper with an introduction, theoretical frameworks (trans theory and film theory), a section on MENA cinema and transgender themes, and in-depth discussions of three films: Miss Hanafi (Egypt), Khastegi (Iran), and L’Armée du Salut (Morocco). Support claims with citations to the gathered sources: general web pages describing films and actors, Salah on Eshaghian’s Be Like Others and related media critiques, Quinan on Allouache and cross-border identity, and Temple/Lowry on North African queer cinema (including Moroccan films). Keep citations concise and attach them to factual assertions. Middle Eastern and North African Films with Transgender Themes: A Transnational and Cinematic Analysis

Abstract

This paper offers a broad overview of Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) cinema that engages transgender themes, situating such films within transnational feminist and queer film theory. It argues that trans narratives in MENA cinema are deeply embedded in local sociopolitical contexts—often marked by Islamism, patriarchal norms, and state repression—while also negotiating transnational circuits of film festival visibility, media circulation, and diasporic authorship. The analysis focuses on three films: the 1954 Egyptian comedy Miss Hanafi, which features a man who accidentally undergoes a sex-change narrative; the Iranian transsexuality documentary Khastegi, which centers seven trans women in Tehran; and the Moroccan coming-of-age drama L’Armée du Salut (Salvation Army), based on Abdellah Taïa’s autobiographical novel. These films illustrate how transgender subjectivity is rendered in relation to family, religion, state policy, and urban space, and how cinematic form—whether comedic fantasy, pseudo-documentary interview sequences, or naturalistic framing—shapes the viewer’s ethical and political engagement.

Introduction

Transgender and queer cinema from the Middle East and North Africa has grown in visibility over the past two decades, circulating widely at international film festivals and through digital platforms. At the same time, these films are produced and received within contexts of state repression, religious conservatism, and patriarchal social norms, which shape both the content and the form of trans narratives. As scholars have shown, North African cinema increasingly foregrounds nonnormative sexualities and gender identities, contributing to broader “Queer Arab” and “Queer World” film discourses. This paper situates MENA transgender cinema within transnational feminist film scholarship and queer film theory, and analyzes three films to demonstrate how transgender subjectivity is represented and how cinematic form mediates ethical and political meaning.

Theoretical Frameworks

Transnational Feminist Approaches to MENA Film and Media

Recent scholarship advocates for transnational feminist methods in studying gender in MENA film and media, arguing that such an approach connects local struggles to global gender politics and opens methodological possibilities for contemporary contexts. This perspective is generative for understanding how transgender narratives emerge across borders and are shaped by intersecting systems of power.

Queer North African Cinema and the Politics of Silence and Space

Analyses of North African queer cinema emphasize how nonnormative sexualities and gender identities are often rendered in muted, secret, or shadowy spaces, performed in darkness and linked to cultural theories of skin and embodiment. These frameworks help interpret films that negotiate visibility and concealment under authoritarian and patriarchal regimes.

Trans Theory and the Politics of Representation

Critical engagement with trans theory foregrounds transgender people as subjects in their own right, rather than as metaphors for “deviant” sexuality or as tropes of prostitution and “feminized” masculinity. Media representations of transsexuality are often shaped by homophobic fantasies that conflate homosexuality with trans femininity and render trans bodies as sites of moral or national threat. These dynamics are visible in MENA cinema and have been analyzed in relation to feminist science fiction and anti-trans discourse.

Cross-Border Identity and the Cinematic “Other”

Merzak Allouache’s films provide a case study for thinking about how North African cinema negotiates national identity across borders—between Algeria and France, between tradition and modernity—and how gender and sexuality are mobilized in these negotiations. This lens is useful for understanding diasporic authorship and transnational spectatorship in MENA transgender cinema.

Middle Eastern and North African Cinema and Transgender Themes

While transgender narratives in MENA cinema remain relatively undertheorized compared to Western queer film studies, a growing body of work documents the existence and circulation of films that engage transsexuality and gender transition. These films often reflect the intersection of Islamism, patriarchy, and state repression, while also navigating transnational circuits of film festival visibility and digital media.

In-Depth Film Discussions

Miss Hanafi (1954, Egypt): A Comedic Fantasy of Accidental Sex Change

Miss Hanafi is an early Egyptian comedy that features a man who accidentally undergoes a sex-change narrative. The film’s humor and fantastical premise contrast with the serious sociopolitical contexts of postcolonial North Africa, yet its very existence demonstrates that gender transformation plots were already circulating in Arabophone cinema decades ago.

Khastegi (2008, Iran): Seven Trans Women in Tehran

Khastegi is an Iranian independent film that centers seven trans women living in Tehran. Directed by Bahman Motamedian, the film blends dramatic narrative with pseudo-documentary interview sequences, allowing the protagonists to speak directly to the camera. Made without official Iranian permission and screened at the 2008 Venice International Film Festival, Khastegi highlights the precarious lives of trans women under Islamism and patriarchal norms, while also showcasing the resilience of trans actors and directors in a repressive context.

L’Armée du Salut (2013, Morocco): A Coming-of-Age Story of Homophobia and Survival

Adapted from Abdellah Taïa’s autobiographical novel, L’Armée du Salut follows a gay teenager in Casablanca as he navigates an authoritarian family, internalized homophobia, and the predatory gaze of older men in his neighborhood. The film exemplifies Moroccan queer cinema’s focus on the intersections of masculinity, religion, and urban space, and it contributes to broader “Queer Arab” film discourses that reframe marginalized sexualities.

Cinematic Form and Ethical Engagement

The form of MENA transgender films shapes how viewers encounter and respond to trans narratives. Miss Hanafi uses comedy and fantasy to render gender transformation, which can both distance and draw audiences into the protagonist’s experience. Khastegi’s pseudo-documentary style foregrounds the voices of trans women, asserting their subjectivity and challenging viewers to listen. L’Armée du Salut’s naturalistic framing and focus on internalized homophobia invite empathy with the protagonist’s psychological and social struggles. These formal choices reflect broader strategies in MENA cinema to negotiate visibility, censorship, and ethical spectatorship.

Conclusion

Middle Eastern and North African cinema that engages transgender themes emerges from specific sociopolitical contexts—often marked by Islamism, patriarchy, and state repression—while also circulating transnationally through film festivals and digital media. By analyzing Miss Hanafi, Khastegi, and L’Armée du Salut, this paper shows how transgender subjectivity is rendered in relation to family, religion, and urban space, and how cinematic form mediates ethical and political meaning. Future research should deepen engagement with trans theory and film theory to better center transgender people as authors, subjects, and critics of MENA cinema.

Notes on Sources and Limitations

This paper draws on general web pages describing films, directors, and actors, as well as scholarly analyses of North African queer cinema and trans media representation. While these sources provide valuable context, detailed film analyses, interviews with directors and actors, and more rigorous engagement with trans theory and film theory remain underdeveloped in the existing corpus.
