The seemingly paradoxical propositions that guide the viewer into the film are reiterated in the film's insistent questioning of whether these women would transition if they did not live in Iran, of whether the surgery was worth it, and of whether post-transition life is better. The film's questioning verges on being both punishing and manipulative when directed at Negar, while she is in pain and drugged in the immediate aftermath of surgery, and later, when she is depressed and suffering the continuing effects of transphobic social marginalization. Similarly troubling are the post-transition portraits of both Anahita (who is happy with herself and in her role in the family, but is seemingly soon to be spurned by her fiancé, who becomes ambivalent after her surgery) and of Negar (who is presented as transitioning in response to social pressure, and as supporting herself by entering into contract marriages, framed as a tragic and duplicitous Islamic form of prostitution).^7 This film proves to be a cautionary tale, demonstrating what Eshaghian seems to suspect from the beginning: that the state's support of transsexuals is actually a manifestation of its homophobia. Through her narrative we are led to understand that Iranian society is so terribly homophobic that homosexual men are pressured into undergoing surgery and taking hormones—coerced, in fact, into becoming transsexual women.^8 The latent content of a homophobic fantasy of the Orient is revealed as its hidden truth: in the Orient, homosexuals really are (forced to be) women, or are, at least, always-already castrated. Within this fantasy, veiled women, prostitution and naturally/forcibly feminized males are interchangeable metonyms composing decadent, degenerate, barbaric and yet chimerical and desirable alterity. Eshaghian elaborates: Being a homosexual is tremendously shameful, and it's considered something that someone is choosing to do because they have a morally corrupt character. They would tell me, "I'm ill and there's a cure. And you can't judge me because it's outside the realm of judgment; it's a medical condition." (Ellison 2010) Transsexuals are constructed in the film as victims of the culture and of religion, and the filmmaker's acknowledgement of her subjects' self-understanding is undercut by a persistent implication of internalized homophobia.

Backlash to the Future: Screening Transsexuality as Fundamentalism
Two recent films offer troubling representations of transsexuality and insight into the curiously familiar status of transsexual representation within contemporary queer and feminist media: Catherine Crouch’s The Gendercator, a science-fiction short by a well-known lesbian filmmaker, and Iranian-American filmmaker Tanaz Eshaghian’s feature documentary, Be Like Others. Eshaghian’s film was critically acclaimed at the 2008 Sundance and Berlin International film festivals, while The Gendercator became notorious after it was pulled from the 2007 Frameline Film Festival in response to a petition and a letter-writing campaign organized by
members of the Bay Area trans community. 1
Frameline’s decision was met with the suggestion that trans activists were boycotting a film they hadn’t yet seen. However, there is a sense in which audiences had seen The Gendercator well before it was even made. In generic terms and in its representations of gender, The Gendercator is strongly reminiscent of two popular feminist science-fiction novels from the 1970s: Woman on the Edge of Time (Piercy 1976) and The Female Man (Russ 1975). Employing time travel as a metaphor for

consciousness-raising, Marge Piercy and Joanna Russ, respectively, imaged possible futures engendered by the feminist, anti-war and environmental movements of the 1960s and 1970s, and contrasted these futures to possible techno-patriarchal “bad futures” predicated on the failure of women-led progressive struggles. Like Janice Raymond’s notorious anti-transsexual screed The Transsexual Empire, these texts troped and conjoined figures for transsexuality, “surgically constructed femininity” and prostitution to signify the absolute colonization of women’s bodies and subjectivities. As critical utopias, Piercy’s and Russ’s novels played good futures off bad ones—embedding both possibilities in references to their
present moment—and implicated their readers in struggles for a feminist future.2
Crouch’s film strongly references these earlier texts. Beginning at a 1973 “hippy party” in honour of Billie Jean King’s victory over Bobby Riggs, The Gendercator chronicles the adventures of Sally, a sporty tomboy who passes out only to wake in a future in which “feminism has failed utterly and completely” and where:
sex roles and gender expression are rigidly binary and enforced by law and social custom. When Sally rejects the feminine hairdo and short skirt she is given ... the ‘Gendercator,’ a government official ... informs Sally that butch women and sissy boys are no longer tolerated. (Crouch 2008)

### <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:2" text="1. Hammam al-Malatily" />
19731h 34mNot Rated
4.7 (1.8K)
Ahmed (Muhammad Al-Araby) from Ismalia come to Cairo looking for work. Promise of richness is really far from reality of life. Ahmed falls in love with Naeema, a prostitute. And then there is Raouf Bey who is gay and fell in love with him.

### <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:7" text="2. Alexandria... Why?" />
19792h 13mNot Rated
7.3 (2.2K)
Yehia is a young man living in the cosmopolitan Alexandria during World War II. Inspired by American movies and Shakespeare, he aspires to be an actor, but struggles to pursue his Hollywood dream, given the constraints of his life in the middle class and the horrors of war.
Director<link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:8" text="Youssef Chahine" />Stars<link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:9" text="Naglaa Fathi" /><link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:10" text="Ahmed Zaki" /><link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:11" text="Farid Shawqi" />

### <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:12" text="3. Man of Ashes" />
19861h 49m
6.1 (261)
In the ensuing days before his wedding bridegroom Hachemi faces both the anxieties of the future and the shadows of the past. His best friend, Farfat, is the topic of street graffiti and local gossip, which calls his manhood into question. This ripples out to affect Hachemi for, unbeknownst to anyone, as apprenticed youths they were molested by Ameur, the local carpenter. Farfat is banished from his father's home and the shared secret between the two friends threatens to undo more than just the wedding, but their very lives.
Director<link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:13" text="Nouri Bouzid" />Stars<link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:14" text="Imed Maalal" /><link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:15" text="Khaled Ksouri" /><link reference_id="<|superscript|>:36-<|link|>:16" text="Habib Belhadi" />

Storyline
A Nutshell Review: Khastegi
If living a life as a transsexual is difficult enough as it is, with the grappling of social prejudices and the likes, imagine if one happens to be a transsexual in a closed society, how torturous that would be given low tolerance for anything deemed out of the ordinary.
Directed by Bahman Motamedian, this Iranian movie explores the lives and times of seven real life transsexuals in Tehran, where we hear the life stories of the protagonists in real terms, having to enact those dark moments in their lives themselves, and be brutally honest about it, taking on the system straight at its horns. While this remains a dramatic narrative film, it plays out more like a pseudo-documentary with talking heads, where the story is interspersed at appropriate moments where the person in question would come on, and talk about their experience.

## Abstract

In recent years, North African queer cinema has become increasingly visible both within and beyond Arabo-Orientale spaces. A number of critical factors have contributed to a global awareness of queer identities in contemporary Maghrebi cinema, including the dissemination of films through social media outlets and during international film festivals. Such tout contemporain representations of queer sexuality characterize a robust wave of films in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, inciting a new discourse on the condition of the marginalized traveler struggling to locate new forms of self and being—both at home and abroad.

Article

- Mar 2020

- <link reference_id="<|superscript|>:69-<|link|>:7" text="Lowry Martin" />

In the last decade, Franco-Moroccan directors have begun to explore culturally taboo and unrepresented sexual communities within Morocco. This article examines how two pioneering films, Abdellah Taïa’s Salvation Army and Nabil Ayouch’s Much Loved, contribute to an emerging cultural politics in the Arab-speaking world that is reframing marginalized or invisible sexualities. While these films address issues of sexual tourism, incest, and prostitution, among others, the focus of this article is on the films’ critiques of internalized homophobia, sexual tourism, and the sociopolitical power structures that occlude, marginalize, or shame those males outside of the heterosexual matrix. Analyzing the films’ portrayal of the semiotics of forbidden desire, internalized homophobia, and the circulation and spatialization of queer sexualities in Morocco, this article argues that Salvation Army and Much Loved complicate our understanding of Arab masculinities and add to a growing queer visibility that stretches from the Maghreb to the Gulf.

Metal ions participate in metabolic processes and redox regulation and are implicated in CVD pathogenesis. Disruptions in metal homeostasis—e.g., imbalances in Cu/Zn ratios, Fe, Mn, and others—correlate with oxidative stress, ion channel dysfunction, endothelial and mitochondrial dysfunction, and vascular calcification, all of which are CVD risk factors. Metal ions can also influence angiogenesis and vascular repair, and exogenous supplementation or delivery strategies have been proposed as therapeutic approaches. <cite raw_output.raw_text: <search query="plasma metal ions cardiovascular disease supplementation efficacy review calcium magnesium zinc copper iron" search_time="2026年5月10日10时18分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>Exogeneous metal ions as therapeutic agents in cardiovascular disease and their delivery strategies</title><summary>Metal ions participate in many metabolic processes in the human body, and their homeostasis is crucial for life. In cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), the equilibriums of metal ions are frequently interrupted, which are related to a variety of disturbances of physiological processes leading to abnormal cardiac functions. Exogenous supplement of metal ions has the potential to work as therapeutic strategies for the treatment of CVDs. Compared with other therapeutic drugs, metal ions possess broad availability, good stability and safety and diverse drug delivery strategies. The delivery strategies of metal ions are important to exert their therapeutic effects and reduce the potential toxic side effects for cardiovascular applications, which are also receiving increasing attention. Controllable local delivery strategies for metal ions based on various biomaterials are constantly being designed. In this review, we comprehensively summarized the positive roles of metal ions in the treatment of CVDs from three aspects: protecting cells from oxidative stress, inducing angiogenesis, and adjusting the functions of ion channels. In addition, we introduced the transferability of metal ions in vascular reconstruction and cardiac tissue repair, as well as the currently available engineered strategies for the precise delivery of metal ions, such as integrated with nanoparticles, hydrogels and scaffolds.</summary><hostname>Oxford Academic</hostname><publisher>Regenerative Biomaterials</publisher><author_list><author name="Xiaoqian Hong" affiliation="¹Department of Cardiology of the Second Affiliated Hospital and State Key Laboratory of Transvascular Implantation Devices, Cardiovascular Key Laboratory of Zhejiang Province, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou 310009, China" /><author name="Geer Tian" affiliation="²Binjiang Institute of Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310053, China" /><author name="Yang Zhu" affiliation="³MOE Key Laboratory of Macromolecular Synthesis and Functionalization, Department of Polymer Science and Engineering, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310027, China" /><author name="Tanchen Ren" affiliation="¹Department of Cardiology of the Second Affiliated Hospital and State Key Laboratory of Transvascular Implantation Devices, Cardiovascular Key Laboratory of Zhejiang Province, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou 310009, China" /></author_list><url>https://academic.oup.com/rb/advance-article-pdf/doi/10.1093/rb/rbad103/54942626/rbad103.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年11月21日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Minerals: From Basic Aspects to Newly Discovered Physiological and Nutritional Actions</title><summary>Essential minerals have many important roles, from physiology, dietary requirements and associated deficiencies to new disease preventive aspects related to dietary intake of minerals. Many important mechanisms of minerals, such as antioxidant scavenging actions, gene regulation and expression, and induction or suppression of apoptosis can be used to decrease the risk of many chronic non-transmissible maladies. Some minerals are also important for modulation of immune system activities that decrease the risk of infections, inflammatory disorders and cancer. However, the mechanical properties of zinc cannot meet the performance requirements of stent material which severely limit its application. In this paper, Zn-xCu (x = 1, 2 and 3 wt.%) alloys were prepared, and their mechanical properties, corrosion properties and biocompatibility were studied. Tensile testing showed the tensile strength and hardness of Zn-xCu alloys both increased with the addition of copper, but the elongation decreased at first and then upturned. Since the formation of galvanic cell, the corrosion rates of Zn-xCu alloys increased. The main corrosion mechanism of Zn-xCu alloy was pitting corrosion, and the corrosion products mainly included ZnO and Zn(OH)₂. The cytotoxicity evaluation showed that Cu²⁺ and Zn²⁺ would contribute to cell proliferation, while the concentrations of them reached a suitable range like the concentration of soaking solution of Zn-3Cu alloy was 25%. However, it would inhibit proliferation, while the concentrations of Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺ were too large. URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6113772/

Conclusion
Results of this meta-analysis indicate that exposure to arsenic, lead, cadmium, and copper is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and coronary heart disease. By contrast, mercury was not associated with cardiovascular risk. These findings reinforce the (often under-recognised) importance of environmental toxic metals in cardiovascular risk, beyond the roles of conventional behavioural risk factors. Further detailed work, however, to better characterise these associations and to assess causality, is needed.

<answer><title>Report: Gut Microbiota, Probiotics, Prebiotics, Pathogens, and Dietary Choices in Colorectal Health</title>

I. Introduction and overview of gut microbiota in intestinal homeostasis
- The gut microbiota is a complex ecosystem with major impacts on intestinal function, immune maturation, and host metabolism; its disruption can drive intestinal inflammation and colorectal cancer (CRC). <cite id="call_0f0d21a5216d-1"></cite><cite id="call_0f0d21a5216d-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite>
- Metagenomic studies have revealed distinct microbial associations with CRC and suggest a “driver-passenger” model in which specific bacteria promote tumorigenesis within a broader community context. <cite id="call_0f0d21a5216d-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite>
- Diet and microbial metabolism are central to CRC risk, with fermentable fiber linked to reduced risk and protein/fat residues associated with inflammatory and carcinogenic metabolites. <cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite>

II. Probiotics: predominant types and mechanisms of action
- Probiotics are defined as viable microorganisms that confer health benefits, especially on the intestinal tract, and are widely used genera include Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. <cite id="call_cfb7ca6dcf59-0"></cite>
- Clinical trials indicate that probiotic supplementation in CRC patients can improve quality of life, enhance gut microbiota diversity, reduce postoperative complications, lower pro-inflammatory cytokines, and mitigate chemotherapy side effects, with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species being commonly used. <cite id="call_b9e8d52b166e-0"></cite>
- Evidence from reviews supports the potential of well-balanced probiotics as an adjuvant approach to protect against CRC and adverse effects of therapies, although more robust clinical trials are needed to confirm efficacy and safety. <cite id="call_39397907e422-0"></cite>

III. Prebiotics: definitions and mechanistic roles
- Prebiotics are nondigestible food ingredients that selectively stimulate the growth and activity of beneficial bacteria in the colon and improve host health. <cite id="call_cfb7ca6dcf59-0"></cite>
- Candidate prebiotic oligosaccharides include lactulose, fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS), galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS), isomalto-oligosaccharides (IMO), xylo-oligosaccharides (XOS), and lactosucrose; many are preferentially fermented by Bifidobacterium and other beneficial taxa while being largely non-fermented by Clostridium perfringens or Escherichia coli. <cite id="call_cfb7ca6dcf59-0"></cite>
- Human studies suggest prebiotics may improve CRC risk factors by modulating the microbiota and its metabolites, although results on direct biomarkers (e.g., aberrant crypt foci, proliferation/apoptosis) are mixed, with lactulose showing a reduction in adenoma recurrence and resistant starch yielding limited physical changes. <cite id="call_60d25732a3f1-0"></cite>

IV. Pathogenic bacteria of concern and their toxic metabolites
- Several bacterial taxa have been implicated in CRC, including Fusobacterium nucleatum, enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis (ETBF), Escherichia coli (particularly pks+ strains producing genotoxic colibactin), Enterococcus faecalis, and Salmonella spp., which can induce DNA damage and promote carcinogenesis through genotoxins and inflammatory pathways. <cite id="call_af42c8e26d7d-0"></cite><cite id="call_4f2e4d81504c-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite>
- ETBF produces B. fragilis toxin (BFT) and can exacerbate colonic inflammation and tumorigenesis in mouse models of adenomatosis. <cite id="call_4f2e4d81504c-0"></cite>
- pks+ E. coli secrete colibactin, a genotoxin that induces DNA damage and is associated with increased CRC risk. <cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite>
- Other bacterial products that promote CRC include secondary bile acids, N-nitroso compounds, hydrogen sulfide, polyphenol metabolites, and toxins such as CagA from H. pylori and cytotoxic effectors; collectively, these influence host signaling (e.g., Wnt, NF-κB, TLR4, SMAD/RAS/p38 MAPK) and the tumor microenvironment. <cite id="call_4498277d9f30-1"></cite><cite id="call_4498277d9f30-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite>
- F. nucleatum is enriched in CRC and precursors and promotes tumorigenesis through adhesion, immune evasion, and interactions with other microbes. <cite id="call_af42c8e26d7d-0"></cite>
- Biofilm-associated bacteria may contribute to persistent inflammation and cancer development. <cite id="call_88"></cite>

V. How findings inform dietary choices
- Dietary fiber and fermentable prebiotics support beneficial fermenters (e.g., Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii) and production of anti-inflammatory short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which have protective effects in CRC. <cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite>
- Red and processed meats are associated with increased CRC risk, likely due to the formation of carcinogenic metabolites and inflammatory responses; reducing intake of these foods is advised. <cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite>
- Plant polyphenols and other phytochemicals can modulate the microbiota and its metabolites, potentially reducing CRC risk. <cite id="call_4498277d9f30-1"></cite>
- Limiting high-fat diets may reduce secondary bile acid production and related carcinogenic effects. <cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite>
- Probiotic-rich fermented foods (e.g., yogurt with live cultures) and synbiotic products may help maintain a balanced microbiota and reduce inflammation, particularly in CRC patients and during therapy. <cite id="call_39397907e422-0"></cite><cite id="call_b9e8d52b166e-0"></cite>
- Individualized approaches are important, as microbiota composition and responses vary; longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to clarify causality and guide personalized diets. <cite id="call_120"></cite>

VI. Summary and recommendations
- The gut microbiota is central to intestinal health and CRC risk; maintaining microbial homeostasis through diet and targeted interventions is crucial. <cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite>
- Predominant probiotic genera include Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium; clinical evidence supports their use in CRC patients to improve microbiota diversity, reduce inflammation, and manage treatment side effects. <cite id="call_39397907e422-0"></cite><cite id="call_b9e8d52b166e-0"></cite>
- Prebiotics such as FOS, GOS, and lactulose selectively nourish beneficial bacteria and may reduce CRC risk by modulating the microbiota and SCFA production, although more human studies are needed to confirm efficacy. <cite id="call_60d25732a3f1-0"></cite>
- Pathogens of concern include F. nucleatum, ETBF, pks+ E. coli, E. faecalis, Salmonella spp., and others that produce genotoxins, inflammatory mediators, or carcinogenic metabolites; reducing risk factors that promote these microbes is important. <cite id="call_af42c8e26d7d-0"></cite><cite id="call_4f2e4d81504c-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-1"></cite><cite id="call_6958ebbbf5be-0"></cite>
- Dietary strategies should emphasize fiber-rich plant foods, fermented products with live microbes, and phytochemicals while limiting red/processed meats and high-fat diets to support a healthy raw_output.raw_text: <search query="probiotics colorectal cancer review" search_time="2026年5月10日10时18分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:32"><title>Probiotics and Colon Cancer</title><summary>Literature has recently highlighted the enormous scientific interest on the relationship between the gut microbiota and colon cancer, and how the use of some selected probiotics can have a future impact on the adverse events which occur during this disease. Although there is no clear evidence to claim that probiotics are effective in people with cancer, recent reviews have found that probiotics can significantly reduce the incidence of diarrhea and the average frequency of daily bowel movements. However, most of this evidence needs to be more clinically convincing and further discussed. Undoubtedly, some probiotics, when properly dosed and administered, can have a strong rebalance effect on the gut microbiota and as a consequence a possible positive action on immune modulation of the gastrointestinal tract and on inflammation of the intestinal mucosa. Many recent findings indeed support the hypothesis that the daily use of some selected probiotics can be a feasible approach to effectively protect patients against the risk of some severe consequences due to radiation therapy or chemotherapy. This paper aims to review the most recent articles in order to consider a possible adjuvant approach for the use of certain well-balanced probiotics to help prevent colon cancer and the adverse effects caused by related therapies.</summary><hostname>CORE</hostname><publisher>Microorganisms</publisher><author_list><author name="Lorenzo Drago" affiliation="Clinical Microbiology, University of Milan, 20100 Milan, Italy" /></author_list><url>https://core.ac.uk/download/225135527.pdf</url><publish_time>2019年2月28日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:33"><title>Antioxidant Role of Probiotics in Inflammation-Induced Colorectal Cancer</title><summary>Colorectal cancer (CRC) continues to be a significant contributor to global morbidity and mortality. Emerging evidence indicates that disturbances in gut microbial composition, the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and the resulting inflammation can lead to DNA damage, driving the pathogenesis and progression of CRC. Notably, bacterial metabolites can either protect against or contribute to oxidative stress by modulating the activity of antioxidant enzymes and influencing signaling pathways that govern ROS-induced inflammation. Additionally, microbiota byproducts, when supplemented through probiotics, can affect tumor microenvironments to enhance treatment efficacy and selectively mediate the ROS-induced destruction of CRC cells. This review aims to discuss the mechanisms by which taxonomical shifts in gut microbiota and related metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, and trimethylamine-N-oxide influence ROS concentrations to safeguard or promote the onset of inflammation-mediated CRC. Additionally, we focus on the role of probiotic species in modulating ROS-mediated signaling pathways that influence both oxidative status and inflammation, such as Nrf2-Keap1, NF-κB, and NLRP3 to mitigate carcinogenesis. Overall, a deeper understanding of the role of gut microbiota on oxidative stress may aid in delaying or preventing the onset of CRC and offer new avenues for adjunct, CRC-specific therapeutic interventions such as cancer immunotherapy.</summary><hostname>PubMed</hostname><publisher>International journal of molecular sciences</publisher><author_list><author name="Sevag Hamamah" affiliation="[Department of Basic Medical Sciences, College of Osteopathic Medicine, Western University of Health Sciences, Pomona, CA 91766, USA., Department of Internal Medicine, Scripps Mercy Hospital, San Diego, CA 92103, USA.]" /><author name="Andrei Lobiuc" affiliation="[Department of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, College of Medicine and Biological Science, University of Suceava, 7200229 Suceava, Romania.]" /><author name="Mihai Covasa" affiliation="[Department of Basi

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="probiotics prebiotics definitions IUPAC 2002 FEMS" search_time="2026年5月10日10时18分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:32"><title>Prebiotics and Intestinal Flora</title><summary>During the past 5 decades, research in intestinal flora has made rapid progress, which includes the following: (1) development of a comprehensive culture method; (2) establishment of the classification and identification of intestinal anaerobic bacteria; (3) accumulation of microecological evidence and the beneficial and harmful functions of intestinal flora in human health. Thus it is of great importance to promote beneficial bacteria such as bifidobacteria and to suppress harmful bacteria such as clostridia among the intestinal flora. These advances in intestinal flora research are the background for the appearance of functional foods, which are classified into 3 groups based on their mechanisms of action: probiotics, prebiotics, and biogenics. Prebiotics are nondigestible food ingredients, which beneficially affect the host by selectively stimulating the growth of beneficial bacteria in the colon and/or by suppressing the growth of harmful bacteria there. The prebiotics have the potential to improve host health: The candidates are nondigestible oligosaccharides such as lactulose, stachyose, raffinose, fructo-oligosaccharides, soybean oligosaccharides, lactosucrose, galacto-oligosaccharides, isomalto-oligosaccharides, xylo-oligosaccharides, and palatinose. Most oligosaccharides are fermented in vitro by Bifidobacterium species (though not by B. bifidum) and to a limited degree by the Bacteroides fragilis group and Enterococcus, but they are not fermented by C. perfringens or Escherichia coli. The oral administration of oligosaccharides enhances the proliferation of intestinal bifidobacteria, improving the properties of the host’s stool and scavenging the intestine, thereby altering host lipid metabolism in a beneficial way.</summary><hostname>J-STAGE</hostname><publisher>Bioscience Microflora Vol. 21 (1), 3-12, 2002</publisher><author_list><author name="Tomotari Mitsuoka" affiliation="Professor Emeritus, The University of Tokyo, 2-10-7 Sugano, Ichikawa 272-0824, Japan" /></author_list><url>https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/bifidus1996/21/1/21_1_3/_pdf</url><publish_time>2001年8月2日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:33"><title>Probiotics and prebiotics as functional food ingredients</title><summary>In the never-ending search for special foods that enhance human health, new ideas continue to emerge. Recently, the terms probiotics and prebiotics have often been heard and they are beginning to attract the attention of food scientists. These terms are normally in the domain of medical, clinical, and pharmaceutical scientists. This brief overview focuses on the aspect, with particular interest of food scientists in mind, that probiotics and prebiotics are recognized and proclaimed as functional food ingredients. By definition, a probiotic is “a viable microbial dietary supplement that beneficially affects the host through its effects in the intestinal tract”, and a prebiotic is “a nondigestible food ingredient that beneficially affects the host by selectively stimulating the growth and/or activity of one or a limited number of bacteria in the colon”. In simpler terms, probiotics are viable bacteria that are beneficial to human health, whereas prebiotics are food sources that are preferentially chosen by the beneficial bacteria. On the other hand, the term functional food is used to describe nutrients that have an effect on physiologic processes beyond the traditional nutritional effect. Probiotics and prebiotics could enhance physiologic functions benefiting health or preventing disease and be classified as functional food ingredients. It is a novel concept and advocates are convinced that good health can be achieved by nurturing the body’s naturally occurring microorganisms and ensuring the proper functioning of the digestive tract. Microbial Ecology of the Human Gastrointestinal Tract</title><summary>Probiotic bacteria offer a number of potential health benefits when administered in sufficient amounts that in particular include reducing the number of harmful organisms in the intestine, producing antimicrobial substances and stimulating the body's immune response. However, precisely elucidating the probiotic effect of a specific bacterium has been challenging due to the complexity of the gut's microbial ecosystem and a lack of definitive means for its characterization. This review provides an overview of widely used and recently described probiotics, their impact on the human's gut microbiota as a preventative treatment of disease, human/animal models being used to help show efficacy, and discusses the potential use of probiotics in gastrointestinal diseases associated with antibiotic administration.
Microbial Ecology of the Human Gastrointestinal Tract
The human intestinal microbiota is a complex ecosystem with considerable impact on human health and well-being, contributing to maturation of the immune system and providing a direct barrier against pathogen colonization (Dore and Corthier, 2010). It consists of bacteria, archaea, some protozoa, anaerobic fungi, and different bacteriophages and viruses, and it has been estimated that more than 1000 species of microbes inhabit the human intestine (Tuohy et al., 2012). The presence of a great number of microbes (up to 5 × 10^11 bacterial cells per gram of intestinal contents) suggests strong regulatory effects on the human host, and recent findings suggest that gut microbiota can have a considerable impact on both our weight and mood (Duca et al., 2014; Naseribafrouei et al., 2014). The composition and function of human microbial populations associated with various body sites have been studied with the help of metagenomic tools as part of two recent initiatives – the NIH Human Microbiome Project (HMP) and the European Meta genomics of the Human Intestine (metaHIT) project (NIH HMP Working Group et al., 2009; Dusko Ehrlich and MetaHIT Consortium, 2011). These massive molecular approaches have already revealed the presence of three different clusters, or enterotypes, which correspond to one of three most abundant genera of human intestine – Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Ruminococcus (Arumugam et al., 2013).
Bacteria that initially colonize the large gut of an infant are facultative anaerobes, such as Escherichia coli and Streptococcus sp. These species metabolize oxygen in the gut, thereby creating anaerobic conditions. Subsequent colonization largely depends on food profile and environmental factors (i.e., sanitary conditions). After the full formation of the gastrointestinal microflora, its composition has been shown to include such genera as Bacteroides, Bifidobacterium, Enterobacter, Clostridium, Lactobacillus, Peptobacterium, and various Gram-positive cocci (Fooks et al., 1999; Wallace et al., 2011).
Within the gastrointestinal tract (GIT), the microbiota provides various functions, such as digestion of essential nutrients and maturation of intestinal epithelial cells. Studies on mice have shown a number of significant effects of microbiota on the host: in germ-free reconstituted mice, their intestinal epithelium is thinner, kinetics of enterocytes - faster, short-chain fatty acids were produced at significantly higher concentrations, and there was a normal level of immunological activity present, compared to germ-free animals (Aureli et al., 2011). Microbes also have the ability to affect physiologic parameters, providing systemic effects on blood lipids and generally influencing the immune system, as well as inhibiting harmful bacteria (Mikelsaar, 2011). raw_output.raw_text: <search query="gut microbiota short-chain fatty acids colorectal cancer review Nature Reviews Gastroenterology Hepatology" search_time="2026年5月10日10时18分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:48"><title>Diet, microorganisms and their metabolites, and colon cancer</title><summary>Abstract | Colorectal cancer is one of the so-called westernized diseases and the second leading cause of cancer death worldwide. On the basis of global epidemiological and scientific studies, evidence suggests that the risk of colorectal cancer is increased by processed and unprocessed meat consumption but suppressed by fibre, and that food composition affects colonic health and cancer risk via its effects on colonic microbial metabolism. The gut microbiota can ferment complex dietary residues that are resistant to digestion by enteric enzymes. This process provides energy for the microbiota but culminates in the release of short-chain fatty acids including butyrate, which are utilized for the metabolic needs of the colon and the body. Butyrate has a remarkable array of colonic health-promoting and antineoplastic properties: it is the preferred energy source for colonocytes, it maintains mucosal integrity and it suppresses inflammation and carcinogenesis through effects on immunity, gene expression and epigenetic modulation. Protein residues and fat-stimulated bile acids are also metabolized by the microbiota to inflammatory and/or carcinogenic metabolites, which increase the risk of neoplastic progression. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Clostridium perfringens epsilon toxin colorectal cancer review" search_time="2026年5月10日10时19分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:79"><title>The interaction of Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin with receptor claudins</title><summary>Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin (CPE) has significant medical importance due to its involvement in several common human gastrointestinal diseases. This 35 kDa single polypeptide toxin consists of two domains: a C-terminal domain involved in receptor binding and an N-terminal domain involved in oligomerization, membrane insertion and pore formation. The action of CPE starts with its binding to receptors, which include certain members of the claudin tight junction protein family; bound CPE then forms a series of complexes, one of which is a pore that causes the calcium influx responsible for host cell death. Recent studies have revealed that CPE binding to claudin receptors involves interactions between the C-terminal CPE domain and both the 1st and 2nd extracellular loops (ECL-1 and ECL-2) of claudin receptors. Of particular importance for this binding is the docking of ECL-2 into a pocket present in the C-terminal domain of the toxin. This increased understanding of CPE interactions with claudin receptors is now fostering the development of receptor decoy therapeutics for CPE-mediated gastrointestinal disease, reagents for cancer therapy/diagnoses and enhancers of drug delivery.</summary><hostname>eScholarship</hostname><publisher>Anaerobe</publisher><author_list><author name="Archana Shrestha" affiliation="Department of Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, PA, USA" /><author name="Francisco A Uzal" affiliation="California Animal Health and Food Safety Laboratory, San Bernadino Branch, School of Veterinary Medicine, University of California-Davis, USA" /><author name="Bruce A Mcclane" affiliation="Department of Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, PA, USA" /></author_list><url>https://escholarship.org/content/qt74q377mm/qt74q377mm.pdf?t=ru29hd</url><publish_time>2016年10月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:80"><title>Use of Clostridium perfringens Enterotoxin and the Enterotoxin Receptor-Binding Domain (C-CPE) for Cancer Treatment: Opportunities and Challenges</title><summary>Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin (CPE) causes the symptoms associated with several common gastrointestinal diseases. CPE is a 35 kDa polypeptide consisting of three structured domains, that is, C-terminal domain I (responsible for receptor binding), domain II (responsible for oligomerization and membrane insertion), and domain III (which may participate in physical changes when the CPE protein inserts into membranes). Native CPE binds to claudin receptors, which are components of the tight junction. The bound toxin then assembles into a hexameric prepore on the membrane surface, prior to the insertion of this oligomer into membranes to form an active pore. The toxin is especially lethal for cells expressing large amounts of claudin-3 or -4, which includes many cancer cells. Initial studies suggest that native CPE has potential usefulness for treating several cancers where claudin CPE receptors are overexpressed. However, some challenges with immunogenicity, toxicity, and (possibly) the development of resistance may need to be overcome. An alternative approach now being explored is to utilize C-CPE, which corresponds approximately to receptor binding domain I, to enhance paracellular permeability and delivery of chemotherapeutic agents against cancer cells. Alternatively, C-CPE fusion proteins may prove superior to use of native CPE for cancer treatment. Finally, C-CPE may have application for other medical treatments, including vaccination or increasing drug absorption. The coming years should witness increasing exploitation of this otherwise formidable toxin.</summary><hostname>Hindawi下载站点</hostname><publisher>Journal of Toxicology</publisher

Biofilm infections are typically chronic in nature, as biofilm-residing bacteria can be resilient to both the immune system, antibiotics, and other treatments. This is a comprehensive review describing biofilm diseases in the auditory, the cardiovascular, the digestive, the integumentary, the reproductive, the respiratory, and the urinary system. In most cases reviewed, the biofilms were identified through various imaging technics, in addition to other study approaches. The current knowledge on how biofilm may contribute to the pathogenesis of disease indicates a number of different mechanisms. This spans from biofilm being a mere reservoir of pathogenic bacteria, to playing a more active role, e.g., by contributing to inflammation. original_data.problem: The significance of the gut microbiota in maintaining normal intestinal function has emerged as a prominent focus in contemporary research, revealing both beneficial and detrimental impacts on the equilibrium of gut health. Disruption of microbial homeostasis can precipitate intestinal inflammation and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of colorectal cancer. Conversely, probiotics have demonstrated the capacity to mitigate inflammation and retard the progression of colorectal cancer. Within this domain, key questions arise: What are the predominant types of gut probiotics? What precisely constitutes prebiotics and their mechanistic role? Which pathogenic bacteria warrant concern, and what toxic metabolites do they produce? How might these findings inform and optimize our daily dietary choices?

problem: Research and analyze the diverse paths taken by various countries in Europe, Asia, and the Americas to transition into the ranks of 'developed nations' following World War II. The analysis should cover their foundational conditions, resource endowments, development strategies, and other relevant factors.
final_response:
<think>
Plan: Structure the report by region (Europe, Asia, Americas), then within each region, compare countries that transitioned to developed status post–WWII. For each country, summarize foundational conditions, resource endowments, development strategies, and outcomes. Use the gathered sources to back specific claims about strategies (ordoliberalism in Germany, Dodge Plan, MITI-like guidance in Japan; export-led in South Korea and Taiwan; import substitution followed by export promotion in Turkey; convergence and capital deepening across Western Europe). Keep paragraphs concise and cite after each factual statement.
</think>

<answer>Western Europe
Germany
- Foundational conditions: Near-total destruction of industrial capacity and infrastructure; a devastated currency (hyperinflationary Reichsmark) and massive foreign debt; occupation and denazification constraints; a fragmented labor force and political system; but intact human capital and a dense, skilled workforce in the west (compared to the east). <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite><cite id="call_332be13e00b8-0"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Scarce natural resources; heavy reliance on foreign capital, technology, and labor; but strong industrial traditions and a dense, urbanized labor force in the west. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Development strategies: Market-oriented ordoliberalism under the Federal Minister of Economics Ludwig Erhard; rapid price and wage decartelization, abolition of the Reichsanzeiger price list, and the 1948/49 “Economic Stabilization Plan” (Stabilization Act of 1948/49 and the Dodge Line). These policies ended wartime cartels and price controls, liberalized labor markets, and imposed fiscal discipline and wage-price controls to curb inflation. The “social market economy” combined competitive markets with a welfare state and strong labor protections. <cite id="call_332be13e00b8-1"></cite><cite id="call_332be13e00b8-0"></cite><cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Export orientation and industrial policy: A strong, persistent export sector and a focus on reindustrialization; labor market reforms and wage moderation helped keep unit labor costs competitive. The export engine drove growth and current account surpluses, which constrained domestic consumption and kept growth relatively stable. <cite id="call_332be13e00b8-1"></cite>
- Outcomes: The “Wirtschaftswunder” (economic miracle) from 1949–1973 saw real wages rise from 40 to 145 (1962=100), GDP per capita roughly tripling, and a rapid convergence with Western Europe. Productivity growth was driven by capital deepening and catch-up, with high but declining investment and employment rates. <cite id="call_332be13e00b8-0"></cite><cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite><cite id="call_332be13e00b8-1"></cite>

France
- Foundational conditions: Less severe physical destruction than Germany; intact institutions and a large domestic market; but political fragmentation and a weak postwar government constrained coordination. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Abundant labor and agricultural land; limited energy resources before the 1970s oil shocks; strong industrial base in certain sectors. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Development strategies: Mixed strategies: de Gaulle’s “national priority” industrial policy (Plan Colbert) and later “Plan de relance” focused on heavy industry and state-led firms; protectionism, tariffs, and selective subsidies; but also gradual liberalization and European integration. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Outcomes: Moderate convergence with Western Europe; slower productivity catch-up than Germany due to less severe destruction and more institutional continuity. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>

United Kingdom
- Foundational conditions: Less severe physical destruction than Germany; intact institutions and a large domestic market; but a rigid labor market, strong unions, and a postwar welfare state constrained flexibility. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Abundant labor and agricultural land; limited energy resources before the 1970s oil shocks; strong financial and service sectors. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Development strategies: Postwar Keynesianism with high public investment; labor market rigidity and strong unions; gradual liberalization and European integration; and, by the 1980s, supply-side reforms (Thatcherism) including deregulation, privatization, and labor market liberalization. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite><cite id="call_179"></cite>
- Outcomes: Relative convergence with Western Europe; productivity growth lagged behind Germany and Japan due to less severe destruction and more institutional continuity; but by the late 1990s/early 2000s, the UK outperformed much of Europe in productivity and employment. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite><cite id="call_179"></cite>

Netherlands and Scandinavia
- Foundational conditions: Less severe destruction; intact institutions and a strong financial sector; proximity to the UK and Germany facilitated trade and capital flows. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Abundant labor and land; limited energy resources; strong export-oriented manufacturing and services. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Development strategies: Export-oriented manufacturing; strong welfare states and labor protections; gradual liberalization and European integration; and, in Scandinavia, a strong emphasis on public services and social safety nets alongside market-oriented reforms. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Outcomes: Rapid convergence with Western Europe; productivity growth driven by capital deepening and export performance. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>

Asia
Japan
- Foundational conditions: Near-total destruction of industrial capacity and infrastructure; a devastated currency and massive foreign debt; occupation and denazification constraints; but intact human capital and a dense, skilled workforce. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Scarce natural resources; heavy reliance on foreign capital, technology, and labor; but strong industrial traditions and a dense, urbanized labor force. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Development strategies: The Dodge Plan (1948) imposed fiscal discipline, wage-price controls, and a fixed exchange rate; the “Economic Stabilization Program of Nine Principles” (1948) stabilized the yen and curbed inflation. Post-occupation, Japan adopted export promotion, import substitution, and selective industrial policy; the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) guided investment and technology adoption; and the government used industrial policy to build heavy and chemical industries. <cite id="call_3e54457fbe5a-2"></cite><cite id="call_3e54457fbe5a-1"></cite><cite id="call_3e54457fbe5a-4"></cite>
- Outcomes: The “Japanese economic miracle” (1950s–1970s) saw rapid productivity catch-up, driven by capital deepening and embodied technological progress; Japan became the second-largest economy in the world and a major global exporter. <cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite><cite id="call_100"></cite>

South Korea
- Foundational conditions: One of the poorest countries in the world in 1961; devastated infrastructure; reliance on foreign aid; but a highly educated labor force and proximity to growing Asian markets. <cite id="call_134"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Scarce natural resources; heavy reliance on foreign capital and technology; but a large, disciplined labor force and strategic location. <cite id="call_134"></cite>
- Development strategies: Export-led industrialization under Park Chung-hee; state-guided industrial policy focused on heavy and chemical industries; import substitution followed by export promotion; establishment of chaebols (large conglomerates) with government support; export incentives (tax breaks, tariff rebates, low-interest loans); and the creation of the Korea Export-Import Bank to finance trade. <cite id="call_134"></cite><cite id="call_126"></cite><cite id="call_134"></cite>
- Outcomes: Rapid industrialization and convergence with developed economies; GDP per capita rose from ~$100 in 1949 to ~$600 billion in 2004; the “Korean miracle” was driven by export promotion, industrial policy, and chaebol-led growth. <cite id="call_126"></cite><cite id="call_134"></cite>

Taiwan
- Foundational conditions: Small, island economy; devastated infrastructure; reliance on foreign aid; but a highly educated labor force and proximity to growing Asian markets. <cite id="call_144"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Scarce natural resources; heavy reliance on foreign capital and technology; but a large, disciplined labor force and strategic location. <cite id="call_144"></cite>
- Development strategies: Export-oriented industrialization; import substitution followed by export promotion; government incentives (tax breaks, tariff rebates, low-interest loans); and a focus on labor-intensive manufacturing. The Third Four-Year Plan (1961–1964) formalized export promotion, leading to strong growth and trade surpluses. <cite id="call_144"></cite><cite id="call_144"></cite><cite id="call_144"></cite>
- Outcomes: Rapid convergence with developed economies; export-led growth and industrial upgrading; electronics and manufacturing became major exports. <cite id="call_144"></cite>

Americas
Turkey
- Foundational conditions: Less severe destruction; intact institutions; political instability and military interventions constrained policy continuity; but strategic location and access to European and Middle Eastern markets. <cite id="call_aa97591974eb-1"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Limited energy resources; heavy reliance on foreign capital; but a large labor force and geographic position. <cite id="call_aa97591974eb-1"></cite>
- Development strategies: Import-substitution industrialization (ISI) with high tariffs, quantitative restrictions, and state intervention; cheap credit and public investment in state enterprises; by the 1980s, a shift to export promotion under Turgut Özal (devaluation, flexible exchange rates, high real interest rates, privatization, and trade liberalization). <cite id="call_aa97591974eb-1"></cite><cite id="call_aa97591974eb-3"></cite><cite id="call_aa97591974eb-0"></cite>
- Outcomes: Moderate industrialization under ISI; by the 1980s, export-led reforms aimed to break the postwar pattern of alternating growth and deflation; the Özal strategy targeted competitiveness through devaluation and privatization. <cite id="call_aa97591974eb-1"></cite><cite id="call_aa97591974eb-3"></cite>

Latin America (overview)
- Foundational conditions: Varying degrees of destruction; intact institutions; political instability and populism; resource endowments varied widely. <cite id="call_a698650ed070-0"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Abundant natural resources in some countries; limited in others; labor-abundant but often poorly educated. <cite id="call_a698650ed070-0"></cite>
- Development strategies: Diverse paths: import-substitution industrialization (ISI) with high tariffs, state intervention, and protectionism; export promotion and foreign debt financing; mixed results due to policy inconsistency and external shocks. <cite id="call_a698650ed070-0"></cite><cite id="call_a698650ed070-1"></cite>
- Outcomes: Mixed convergence; some countries experienced rapid growth and industrialization, while others faced stagnation, debt crises, and reversals of progress. <cite id="call_a698650ed070-0"></cite>

United States
- Foundational conditions: Less severe destruction; intact institutions; a large domestic market; strong financial and industrial base; but racial segregation and inequality constrained potential. <cite id="call_164"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Abundant natural resources; large labor force; strong financial and technological sectors. <cite id="call_164"></cite>
- Development strategies: Postwar infrastructure investment (e.g., Interstate Highway Act), suburbanization, and a focus on consumer goods and services; a flexible labor market; and a strong financial system. Productivity growth was driven by capital deepening and the diffusion of major inventions (e.g., electrification, mass production, and automation). <cite id="call_164"></cite><cite id="call_164"></cite>
- Outcomes: Strong productivity and convergence with Western Europe; the “golden age” (1948–1973) saw high productivity growth, driven by capital deepening and technological diffusion. <cite id="call_164"></cite><cite id="call_164"></cite>

General patterns
- Foundational conditions and destruction: Across Europe and Asia, severe wartime destruction created temporary deviations from steady-state growth, enabling rapid catch-up; in contrast, the US and some Latin countries experienced less destruction and more continuity. <cite id="call_173"></cite><cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite>
- Resource endowments: Scarce natural resources in Germany, Japan, and South Korea necessitated export orientation and reliance on foreign capital; abundant labor and land in Western Europe and the US supported domestic markets and industrialization. <cite id="call_173"></cite><cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite><cite id="call_164"></cite>
- Development strategies: Export promotion and industrial policy were common; Germany and Japan used stabilization and stabilization-oriented policies (Dodge Plan, ordoliberalism) to rebuild macroeconomic stability before pursuing export-led growth; South Korea and Taiwan formalized export incentives and chaebol/government collaboration; Turkey shifted from ISI to export promotion; the US relied on infrastructure, consumer markets, and capital deepening. <cite id="call_100"></cite><cite id="call_332be13e00b8-1"></cite><cite id="call_3e54457fbe5a-2"></cite><cite id="call_126"></cite><cite id="call_144"></cite><cite id="call_aa97591974eb-1"></cite><cite id="call_164"></cite>
- Outcomes: Rapid productivity catch-up and convergence in Europe, Japan, and East Asia; mixed outcomes in Latin America due to policy inconsistency and external shocks; the US maintained strong productivity growth through capital deepening and invention diffusion. <cite id="call_173"></cite><cite id="call_3ae64561532b-1"></cite><cite id="call_164"></cite><cite id="call_a698650ed070-0"></cite></answer>

Such an inference would only be valid if technological effort were conceived narrowly, as the employment of resources solely for the purpose of creating new knowledge. In Korea, until the recent crisis, a high savings rate has helped fuel strong and continuous economic development by allowing for a high investment rate. Yet what matters for growth is not only the quantity of savings which matters but also the efficiency with which that savings is invested. Korea's development experience clearly illustrates this simple but important point. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Latin America postwar development paths export commodity import substitution state intervention ISI 1950s 1960s 1970s Mexico Brazil Argentina" search_time="2026年5月10日10时22分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:155"><title>Growth and Structural Change in Latin America since 1960: A Comparative Analysis</title><summary>By their perseverance, those analysts continuously describing the imminent economic crisis in Latin America have finally been proven right. Latin America in the 1980s is in the midst of its most serious depression since the 1930s. Moreover, unlike the crisis of the 1930s, which served as a catalyst for the sustained industrialization drive of the following decades, the current crisis has been undoing some of the previous advances and so far has not engendered creative responses of its own. The slowdown in economic activity of the late 1970s, which turned into a recession in the last few years in virtually all the countries of the region, was the result of a combination of external shocks, internal policies, and natural disasters. The incidence of the external shocks varied substantially among countries and over time. In almost every country it is possible to identify subperiods during the 1970s in which the net effect of the external shocks was actually positive. In the 1980s, however, even for the oil exporters of the region, the net impact has been detrimental. The policy response has been a combination of a slowdown in economic activity, export promotion, more intense import substitution, and reliance on foreign debt. But, again, great variation is observed in the package of policies among countries and over time. The variability in the impact of the shocks and in the policy response makes it difficult to reach useful generalizations and to group countries for further analysis. Various studies have recently estimated the magnitude of, primarily, the external shocks and analyzed the short-term adjustments to these shocks. problem: The primary components of a precision piezoelectric vibration isolation system include sensors, actuators, and controllers. How can system accuracy be enhanced through hardware design, structural design, manufacturing processes, and control algorithms? Additionally, how should the design and production phases be managed to ensure consistent performance across identical products?
final_response:

<answer>Overview and scope
A precision piezoelectric vibration isolation system achieves closed-loop stabilization by combining sensors (to measure disturbance and payload motion), actuators (to counteract vibrations), and controllers (to compute and apply corrective signals). Enhancing system accuracy requires coordinated improvements across hardware design, structural layout, manufacturing, and control algorithms, alongside disciplined design and production management to ensure consistent performance across identical units. This report synthesizes evidence-based strategies for each aspect of the design-for-accuracy pathway. <cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-0"></cite><cite id="call_813a73faa8b2-0"></cite><cite id="call_b8538fe02429-0"></cite><cite id="call_8f1e35edc5f3-0"></cite><cite id="call_8f1e35edc5f3-0"></cite>

Hardware design
Sensor and actuator selection and conditioning
- Use high-frequency, low-noise piezoelectric sensors (e.g., PVDF for high g33 sensitivity in sensors; PZT for high d33 actuation) and ensure proper conditioning to avoid signal degradation. Select sensors with bandwidth and sensitivity matching the isolation bandwidth and payload dynamics. <cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-1"></cite><cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-0"></cite>
- Employ industry-standard IEPE conditioning for vibration piezos to enable wideband, high-resolution sensing and to interface with fast controllers; use low-noise amplifiers and proper grounding to minimize sensor noise and drift. <cite id="call_580efbec5ea1-0"></cite>
- For active harmonic disturbance compensation, use distributed sensors and high-precision piezo actuators (stacks or films) with the controller computing anti-phase commands; this can achieve >30–40 dB attenuation of stationary harmonics in microvibration applications. <cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-1"></cite><cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-1"></cite>
- In high-precision levitation transfers (e.g., EUV lithography), use six-DOF electrostatic levitation with active Z, θx, θy control and passive stabilization in X, Y, θz, demonstrating sub-nm sensing and sub-µm positioning repeatability; this illustrates sensor–actuator co-design for ultra-isolation and repeatability. <cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-1"></cite><cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-1"></cite><cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-1"></cite>

Actuator design and integration
- Choose preloaded piezo stacks (with spring preloads ≤1/10 of actuator stiffness) to eliminate mechanical play, improve contact stability, and ensure consistent boundary conditions for displacement transfer, while avoiding excessive stroke reduction due to preload. <cite id="call_f547d2283c82-0"></cite><cite id="call_f547d2283c82-4"></cite>
- Use stiff, preloaded piezo actuators (e.g., P-235 with ~860 N/µm stiffness) to maintain high force and stiffness while minimizing parasitic compliance that can excite flexible modes. <cite id="call_f547d2283c82-2"></cite>
- For low-frequency broadband isolation, integrate piezo actuators into compliant mechanisms to provide high stiffness at low frequencies and good isolation over wide bandwidths; bio-inspired designs can overcome the poor low-frequency isolation of traditional high-stiffness isolators. <cite id="call_f547d2283c82-3"></cite>

Controller and signal chain design
- Implement fast, deterministic controllers (e.g., FPGA-based designs) to meet the high bandwidth required for piezoelectric systems; use synchronous, wideband interfaces (e.g., TIDA-010249) to minimize phase lag and noise in the signal path. <cite id="call_8f1e35edc5f3-0"></cite><cite id="call_580efbec5ea1-0"></cite>
- Use resonant controllers tuned with collocated piezo sensors and actuators; Positive Position Feedback (PPF) can suppress flexible modes and is well-suited for piezoelectric collocation, with H2/H∞ tuning to account for multi-mode coupling and to enforce gain margin and actuation-power limits. <cite id="call_b8538fe02429-0"></cite>
- For adaptive vibration control, Filtered-X LMS can reduce vibration effectively without manual parameter tuning, even with non-collocated or partially coupled actuators; this improves robustness and ease of deployment. <cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-1"></cite>
- Employ electrical damping (shunting or active feedback) on piezo actuators to suppress high-frequency resonances and improve high-frequency response; auxiliary loops with strain-gauge feedback can mitigate drift at high servo gains. <cite id="call_580efbec5ea1-1"></cite>

Structural design
- Use finite-element modeling and experimental validation to co-locate actuators and sensors on high-modes of interest and to size them for effective suppression; FEM-based placement strategies (e.g., modal controllability/excitability) rank candidate locations and reduce trial-and-error in layout. <cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-0"></cite><cite id="call_72e2ccdfce5a-0"></cite>
- For smart structures, use distributed piezo films or patches with dissipative shunts or PPF to locally damp flexible modes; passive damping can achieve ~10–20 dB on controllable modes, while centralized anti-phase schemes can suppress stationary harmonics by 30–40 dB. <cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-1"></cite><cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-1"></cite>
- In high-precision platforms, design as stiff as possible with novel hard mounts and parallel passive damping to isolate payload from base disturbances; this approach can stabilize payloads with sub-µm accuracy and >−20 dB isolation up to 200 Hz. <cite id="call_813a73faa8b2-0"></cite>

Manufacturing processes
- Select PZT compositions tailored to the application: PZT-5A for higher sensitivity (sensing), PZT-5H for higher coupling (actuation/harvesting), and AlN for high-frequency MEMS sensing; specify d31/d33 values and Curie temperatures to meet environmental and performance requirements. <cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-0"></cite>
- Control multilayer stack manufacturing to ensure uniform electrode layers, precise lamination, and consistent polarization; use precision lithography, UV curing, and shadow-mask sintering to maintain alignment and dimensional tolerances across batches. <cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-1"></cite><cite id="call_a18caa236973-0"></cite><cite id="call_a18caa236973-1"></cite>
- Implement prestressing via postfired biasing layers (AgPd or LTCC) to tailor displacement-force trade-offs and to mitigate residual stresses that can cause hysteresis or creep; this improves batch-to-batch consistency and repeatability. <cite id="call_983d22c63cb3-1"></cite><cite id="call_983d22c63cb3-1"></cite>
- Monitor and test key piezoelectric properties (d33, d31, g33, and capacitance) during production to enforce tolerance limits and to identify early signs of aging, fatigue, or environmental degradation (e.g., humidity effects). <cite id="call_983d22c63cb3-0"></cite><cite id="call_983d22c63cb3-1"></cite>

Design and production management for consistent performance
- Perform finite-element model updating and experimental validation to close the loop between simulation and reality; update MACs and frequency responses to ensure sensor/actuator placement and controller tuning reflect the actual structure. <cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-0"></cite><cite id="call_72e2ccdfce5a-0"></cite>
- Build prototypes and validate performance under representative loads and disturbances before scaling; use the prototype’s results to simplify assembly, testing, and commissioning in final designs (as in Advanced LIGO’s two-stage twelve-axis platform). <cite id="call_8f1e35edc5f3-0"></cite><cite id="call_8f1e35edc5f3-0"></cite>
- Standardize assembly procedures and environmental controls (e.g., humidity, temperature, and vacuum for electrostatic levitation) to minimize process-induced variation; document and audit critical process steps to ensure batch consistency. <cite id="call_983d22c63cb3-1"></cite><cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-1"></cite><cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-1"></cite>
- Implement batch trimming, calibration, and compensation routines to correct for individual device hysteresis, creep, and temperature drift; use online calibration and adaptive control to maintain accuracy across operating conditions. <cite id="call_983d22c63cb3-1"></cite><cite id="call_b8538fe02429-0"></cite><cite id="call_580efbec5ea1-1"></cite>

Summary of evidence-based recommendations
- Sensors: Use high-sensitivity piezoelectric materials (PVDF for sensors; PZT-5A/5H for actuation), IEPE conditioning, and fast, deterministic controllers; implement auxiliary loops to suppress drift at high gains. <cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-1"></cite><cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-0"></cite><cite id="call_580efbec5ea1-0"></cite><cite id="call_580efbec5ea1-1"></cite>
- Actuators: Select preloaded stacks with proper preload ratios; use stiff, high-force actuators; integrate into compliant mechanisms for low-frequency isolation; employ electrical damping and adaptive control to suppress high-frequency resonances. <cite id="call_f547d2283c82-0"></cite><cite id="call_f547d2283c82-2"></cite><cite id="call_f547d2283c82-3"></cite><cite id="call_580efbec5ea1-1"></cite>
- Controllers: Use FPGA-based, wideband conditioning; implement PPF tuned with H2/H∞ methods for multi-mode robustness; deploy Filtered-X LMS for adaptive compensation; add electrical damping to suppress high-frequency resonances. <cite id="call_8f1e35edc5f3-0"></cite><cite id="call_b8538fe02429-0"></cite><cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-1"></cite><cite id="call_580efbec5ea1-1"></cite>
- Structural layout: Use FEM and modal controllability/excitability to co-locate actuators/sensors; validate with experiments; apply distributed piezo films or patches with shunts/PPF for local damping; use stiff hard mounts with passive damping for high-precision platforms. <cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-0"></cite><cite id="call_72e2ccdfce5a-0"></cite><cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-1"></cite><cite id="call_813a73faa8b2-0"></cite>
- Manufacturing: Choose PZT compositions by application; control multilayer stack processes with lithography, UV curing, and shadow-mask sintering; apply prestressing to tailor displacement-force trade-offs; monitor key piezoelectric properties and enforce tolerance limits. <cite id="call_1c32bcb21314-0"></cite><cite id="call_a18caa236973-0"></cite><cite id="call_a18caa236973-1"></cite><cite id="call_983d22c63cb3-1"></cite><cite id="call_983d22c63cb3-0"></cite>
- Production management: Update FEMs with experiments; validate prototypes under representative conditions; standardize assembly and environmental controls; document critical process steps; implement batch trimming, calibration, and online compensation to maintain accuracy across batches. <cite id="call_b477e9581d2c-0"></cite><cite id="call_8f1e35edc5f3-0"></cite><cite id="call_983d22c63cb3-1"></cite><cite id="call_580efbec5ea1-1"></cite><cite id="call_b8538fe02429-0"></cite></answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="piezoelectric vibration isolation precision hardware design structural design manufacturing control algorithms" search_time="2026年5月10日10时23分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:25"><title>Vibration Control for Precision Manufacturing Using Piezoelectric Actuators</title><summary>Piezoelectric actuators provide high frequency, force and stiffness capabilities along with reasonable stroke limits, all of which can be used to increase performance levels in precision manufacturing systems. This paper describes two examples of embedding piezoelectric actuators in structural components for vibration control. One example involves suppressing the self-excited chatter phenomenon in the metal cutting process of a milling machine and the other involves damping vibrations induced by rigid body stepping of a photolithography platen. Finite element modeling and analyses are essential for locating and sizing the actuators and permit further simulation studies of the response of the dynamic system. Experimental results are given for embedding piezoelectric actuators in a cantilevered bar configuration, which was used as a surrogate machine tool structure. These results are incorporated into a previously developed milling process simulation and the effect of the control on the cutting process stability diagram is quantified. Experimental results are also given for embedding three piezoelectric actuators in a surrogate photolithography platen to suppress vibrations. These results demonstrate the potential benefit that can be realized by applying advances from the field of adaptive structures to problems in precision manufacturing.</summary><hostname>zero.sci-hub.ru</hostname><publisher>JOURNAL OF INTELLIGENT MATERIAL SYSTEMS AND STRUCTURES</publisher><author_list><author name="David R Martinez" affiliation="Structural Dynamics and Vibration Control Department, MS0439, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM 87185" /><author name="Terry D Hinnerichs" affiliation="Structural Dynamics and Vibration Control Department, MS0439, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM 87185" /><author name="James M Redmond" affiliation="Structural Dynamics and Vibration Control Department, MS0439, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM 87185" /></author_list><url>https://zero.sci-hub.ru/3805/711b9562050c62c99784e51fc7652303/martinez1996.pdf#navpanes=0&view=FitH</url><publish_time>1996年3月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:26"><title>Adaptive Active Vibration Control for a Piezoelectric Stewart Platform</title><summary>In this paper, an adaptive active vibration control is proposed and implemented to a piezoelectric (PZT) stewart platform exhibiting nonlinearity. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Chopin inertial shaker piezo stack materials PZT ceramics composition sensing actuation" search_time="2026年5月10日10时24分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:58"><title>Selected Questions Related To Characterization of MEMS Structures Comprising PZT Piezo Layer</title><summary>Pzt (lead zirconium titanate) is an intermetallic compound exhibiting piezoelectric, ferroelectric, and pyroelectric properties. The perovskite crystallographic structure of the PZT is responsible for the above effects. MEMS structures with piezo layers can be used as sensors, actuators, or converters. The abilities of piezo materials to generate an electric charge as a response to stress and a change of shape as a response to electric field are very attractive in numerous applications. Cantilever structures with a mass attached can accordingly be used as energy harvesters converting energy of environment vibrations. Other applications of cantilevers are small displacement sensors or actuators in micro/nano scale. Membrane structures can work as ultrasonic transducers. If properly shaped cavity is produced, the structure may be used as a part of ink printer head or as a pressure sensor. For physical description of piezo phenomena, constitutive equations in several forms are used. They work well for bulk piezoelectric, although for thin layers deposited on silicon or similar substrate, piezoelectric coupling coefficients must be redefined because of the interaction of thin piezo layer and thicker substrate. Typical electric characterization of piezo MEMS structures includes CV and IV measurements. QV (charge-voltage) hysteresis loop study is an additional method used for this characterization. Complex electromechanical methods are used for surveying piezoelectric coupling coefficients. These methods employ mechanic actuation and electric response Q measurements or AC electric V (voltage) excitation and measurement of mechanical response v (velocity). In the second case, a very precise tool for velocity evaluation is necessary. Such tool could be for example laser Doppler vibrometer, enabling measurements of picometer resolution in several MHz bandwidth. In many cases resonance features of structures have revealed themselves interesting and became a subject of the study. Several different tuning methods exist for this type of controller. However, the previously developed tuning methods often rely on simplifications and assume that the system can be reduced to a single mass spring system that exhibits roll-off after the resonance that is to be suppressed. This assumption is not generally valid as the response may also be influenced by a higher frequency resonance, or may not exhibit roll-off at all. This happens for example in systems with collocated piezoelectric sensing and actuation. Furthermore, robustness against gain variations and limited available actuation power are difficult to take into account with the available tuning methods. This paper presents the analytical solution to the H₂ optimal tuning problem and a reliable numerical solution to the H∞ optimal tuning problem of PPF controllers for a general class of systems. The system model consists of a second order transfer with direct feed-through terms that are able to capture the response close to an undamped resonance accurately, even if it is influenced by higher frequency modes or if the system does not exhibit roll-off. The method leaves the open loop gain as a free tuning parameter, which can be set to adhere to a gain margin constraint or limit the utilised actuation power. Furthermore, experimental results are included to demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness and flexibility of the proposed optimal tuning approach.</summary><hostname>University of Twente</hostname><publisher>Journal of Sound and Vibration</publisher><author_list><author name="Bram Seinhorst" affiliation="Chair of Precision Engineering, University of Twente, Drieterlolaan 5, 7522 NB, Enschede, The Netherlands" /><author name="Marijn Nijenhuis" affiliation="Chair of Precision Engineering, University of Twente, Drieterlolaan 5, 7522 NB, Enschede, The Netherlands" /><author name="Wouter Hakvoort" affiliation="Chair of Precision Engineering, University of Twente, Drieterlolaan 5, 7522 NB, Enschede, The Netherlands" /></author_list><url>https://ris.utwente.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/493463570/1-s2.0-S0022460X25002391-main.pdf</url><publish_time>2025年4月28日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:99"><title>Review of Control and Sensor System of Flexible Manipulator</title><summary>Over the last few decades, extensive use of flexible manipulators in various robotic applications has made it as one of the research interests for many scholars over the world.
