problem: Are AI fashion design tools leading to creative homogenization in the industry? How can the copyright disputes between independent designers and algorithms be resolved?
final_response:
<think>
I will synthesize the findings into a structured report. I will ground claims about homogenization in practitioner analyses and studies of training data and their effects; for copyright, I will contrast jurisdictional rules and cite ongoing Getty v. Stability AI and Shein lawsuits, plus the implications of training on unlicensed copyrighted content. I will propose governance solutions informed by diversification experiments and constrained personalization models, and attribution/licensing practices backed by practice guides.
</think>

<answer>How we present this report

We structure the report as follows:
- Executive summary
- Evidence for creative homogenization
- Copyright disputes: facts and jurisdictional differences
- Governance solutions for tools and practice
- Conclusion

Evidence for creative homogenization

Industry observers and practitioners document a narrowing of outputs from mainstream AI fashion tools, driven by training on dominant visual platforms and narrow prompting interfaces. The “echo chamber effect” produces statistically averaged outputs for common prompts (e.g., “summer dress”), yielding similar designs across brands that use the same tools. This limits the diversity of outputs and risks a “one-size-fits-all” aesthetic. <cite id="call_e96403f55e5f-0"></cite>

Studies of training data reinforce the mechanism:
- Crawling and analysis of millions of photos of people show how styles spread across cities and brands via social media and catalogs, revealing strong influence patterns. Training generative models on such datasets can propagate dominant visual trends into outputs. <cite id="call_8a2db6e807ff-1"></cite>
- Large-scale street-style datasets show how local styles are captured and distributed in image corpora, further underscoring how training data shape what AI “knows” and remixes. <cite id="call_8a2db6e807ff-0"></cite>

Some controlled applications and hybrid workflows aim to mitigate homogenization:
- Integrating designers in feedback loops to guide and refine AI-generated elements can help align variations with cohesive collections and intentional creativity. <cite id="call_8a2db6e807ff-1"></cite>
- Some platforms emphasize iterative workflows (text-to-sketch, sketch-to-render) and secure processing to give users more control over the creative process, though they do not inherently solve the dataset-driven echo-chamber problem. <cite id="call_8a2db6e807ff-3"></cite>

Calls for diversification and equitable curation provide a roadmap:
- Experiments diversifying recommendation content (e.g., for inclusivity of skin tones) show that algorithmic constraints can increase engagement with underrepresented content and nudge users toward broader consumption. <cite id="call_badd75797b18-0"></cite>
- Theoretical models of personalization that constrain filter bubbles and distribute exposure more equitably suggest governance mechanisms to broaden the visual “diet” AI systems ingest and produce. <cite id="call_badd75797b18-0"></cite><cite id="call_badd75797b18-1"></cite>

Copyright disputes between independent designers and algorithms

Independent creators are increasingly litigating against firms and platforms for direct copying and against AI developers for training on unlicensed works, with cases in fashion and visual art illustrating overlapping claims and jurisdictional differences:

Direct copying by fast fashion and commercial actors:
- A multi-plaintiff lawsuit against Shein alleges it copies original designs from independent creators and uses AI to identify and replicate successful styles, highlighting risks of style mimicry and “copy-paste” supply chains in fashion. <cite id="call_18473b5af96b-0"></cite><cite id="call_18473b5af96b-2"></cite>

Training-data copyright claims:
- Getty Images is suing Stability AI for scraping millions of images and captions to train Stable Diffusion, arguing unauthorized use of copyrighted works infringes rights. <cite id="call_84f11f4fcb6b-3"></cite>
- In the visual arts, plaintiffs have won limited relief against AI image generators for using their works in training, with courts finding plausible claims of derivative infringement under U.S. law; other claims have been dismissed. <cite id="call_18473b5af96b-1"></cite><cite id="call_18473b5af96b-2"></cite>

Jurisdictional differences shape liability and remedies:
- In the U.S., current law holds that only human-created works are eligible for copyright, so purely AI-generated outputs are not protected; however, training on unlicensed copyrighted content exposes users and developers to potential liability. <cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-2"></cite>
- In the EU and UK, copyright requires originality by the author, and courts are still clarifying whether and when AI-assisted designs can meet originality thresholds. <cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-1"></cite><cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-4"></cite>
- In Italy, images generated solely by AI lack strict copyright, but human contributions can confer rights, complicating attribution and licensing. <cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-4"></cite>

Practical risks for designers and brands:
- Style mimicry and direct copying can lead to substantial damages and injunctions, as shown in the Perry/Martinez/Baron v. Shein case. <cite id="call_18473b5af96b-0"></cite>
- Training-data lawsuits are ongoing and could reshape permissible data practices and liability for outputs that remix protected works. <cite id="call_84f11f4fcb6b-3"></cite><cite id="call_18473b5af96b-1"></cite>

How to resolve copyright disputes

Three complementary approaches can reduce friction and clarify rights for independent designers and algorithmic systems:

1. Better data governance and licensing for training and downstream use
- Audit and license training data: Use tools and services that provide transparency about data sources and obtain necessary rights to avoid claims that training on unlicensed works enables infringement. <cite id="call_84f11f4fcb6b-3"></cite>
- Platform-level licensing: Encourage marketplaces and design ecosystems to offer royalty-free or attribution licenses for commercial use, with clear terms for AI-assisted outputs, to give creators control and reduce litigation risks. <cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-3"></cite>

2. Legal clarity and harmonization
- Advocate for clear rules on originality and authorship for AI-assisted works across jurisdictions, including conditions under which human contribution is sufficient to confer copyright. <cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-1"></cite><cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-4"></cite>
- Support litigation and policy that holds firms accountable for training on unlicensed copyrighted works and for outputs that mimic protected designs, as seen in Getty v. Stability AI and the Shein cases. <cite id="call_84f11f4fcb6b-3"></cite><cite id="call_18473b5af96b-0"></cite>

3. Technical and procedural safeguards
- Implement diversification in training and curation: Broaden the visual “diet” of training data and use constrained personalization to reduce filter-bubble effects and encourage broader aesthetic exploration. <cite id="call_badd75797b18-0"></cite><cite id="call_badd75797b18-1"></cite>
- Use attribution and watermarks: Platforms can add provenance and watermarks to AI outputs to help creators identify and assert rights, and to support fair use and compensation models. <cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-3"></cite><cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-4"></cite>

Conclusion

AI fashion design tools are contributing to creative homogenization by training on dominant visual datasets and producing averaged outputs for common prompts, narrowing the diversity of generated designs. Independent creators are increasingly litigating against firms for direct copying and against AI developers for training on unlicensed works, with cases in fashion and visual art illustrating overlapping claims and jurisdictional differences. Resolving disputes will require better data governance and licensing, legal clarity on originality and authorship, and technical safeguards to diversify inputs and outputs. With thoughtful governance, the industry can harness AI’s efficiency while preserving creative diversity and protecting rights. <cite id="call_e96403f55e5f-0"></cite><cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-2"></cite><cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-1"></cite><cite id="call_dce8ad5fc977-4"></cite><cite id="call_18473b5af96b-0"></cite><cite id="call_84f11f4fcb6b-3"></cite><cite id="call_badd75797b18-0"></cite><cite id="call_badd75797b18-1"></cite></answer>

Our model learns directly from the image data how styles move between locations and how certain brands affect each other’s designs in a predictable way. The discovered influence relationships reveal how both cities and brands exert and receive fashion influence for an array of visual styles inferred from the images. In Germany, where the historical community is still divided in the wake of the Historikerstreit, one participant summed up the inability of the political left to come to terms with the Stalinist past:
It has been a part of the intellectual inheritance from leftist movements that, when confronted with unpleasant historical facts they do not ask: "is this true, and what conclusions do we need to make, if it is true?" but rather "in whose interests would it be to make this public?"1
When it comes to assessing the history of the violent 20th century, historical analysis has often been restricted by ideological blindness and selective interpretation. This is not an issue limited to one side of the ideological spectrum, or to any particular ethnic community. There are many cases of Western Soviet sympathizers and fellow travellers, Walter Duranty perhaps being one of the most famous, who chose to ignore or even deny atrocities carried out by the Soviet government against its own people. Such Stalinist and Soviet distortions of the historical record have been given considerable attention by diaspora historians. The work of the Ukrainian community in North America has given us a fuller picture of the Stalinist terror, shedding light on Stalinist crimes through scholarly work that stems from the Ukrainian community and the dissemination of information and material on episodes such as the Ukrainian famine.² While a healthy and productive debate regarding the crimes of communist governments is taking place, the issue of historical analysis that has been distorted by ethnic nationalism has only recently been addressed. The accounts of collaboration and wartime atrocities committed by radical ethnic nationalists in Eastern Europe during World War II are a particularly sensitive matter. For many years during the Cold War, these events attracted relatively little attention from historians outside the diaspora communities. Disinterest in what were sometimes seen as marginal countries and the inaccessibility of documents contributed to the fact that the histories of the western borderlands of the Soviet Union were rather poorly researched. This was further exacerbated by a shortage of Western historians with knowledge of the languages spoken in this region.</summary><hostname>Taylor & Francis Online</hostname><publisher>East European Jewish Affairs</publisher><author_list><author name="Per Anders Rudling" /></author_list><url>https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/13501670600983008</url><publish_time>2006年11月28日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:3"><title>The Holodomor and the Contemporary Ukrainian Writer</title><summary>Many PROBLEMS THAT PLAGUE TODAY'S UKRAINE-the pervasive cor- ruption, erratic behavior of its political leaders, and inconsistent linguistic and nation-building policies of successive Ukrainian governments--can all be traced to the Great Famine of 1932-33. For nearly sixty years (or roughly three generations) this catastrophe had never been publicly acknowledged, and this fact has further compounded its effect and left an indelible mark on Ukrainian society and the national psyche.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Arendt totalitarianism 20th century past present Bartlett 2005 history and its images" search_time="2026年5月10日10时21分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:9"><title>Poetics and Politics of Estrangement: Victor Shklovsky and Hannah Arendt</title><summary>This essay proposes to place the poetics of Russian Formalism within a broader European context of literary, philosophical, and political reflection on modernity. The historical metamorphosis of estrangement from a technique of art to an existential art of survival and a practice of freedom and dissent is traced here through Victor Shklovsky’s experimental autobiographical texts of the 1920s and their critical reception. In this analysis, estrangement is not regarded as an escape from the political; instead, it helps us think anew the relationship between aesthetic and political practices in Stalin’s time. Shklovsky’s writing on estrangement and freedom is read together with Hannah Arendt’s reflections on distance, freedom, and the banality of evil.</summary><hostname>Multiversidad Mundo Real Edgar Morin Biblioteca</hostname><publisher>Poetics Today</publisher><author_list><author name="Svetlana Boym" affiliation="Comparative Literature, Harvard" /></author_list><url>https://biblioteca.umem.mx/books/Svetlana%20Boym/Poetics%20&%20Politics%20of%20Estrangement_%20(207)/Poetics%20&%20Politics%20of%20Estrangem%20-%20Svetlana%20Boym.pdf</url><publish_time>2005年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:10"><title>Foucault and Arendt: The Tensions and Integrity of Critical Thinking</title><summary>In this work, I present an interpretation of two thinkers, Foucault and Arendt. I place these thinkers within a tradition of critical theory running from Kant to Nietzsche. The opposition between modernism and postmodernism, between its philosophical sources, Kant and Nietzsche, has been widely overstated, for example, in the polemical stance taken by Habermas in The Philosophical Discourse of Modernity (1987). I am concerned to show that this way of mapping does Foucault and Arendt an injustice. Foucault and Arendt accept Nietzsche's critique of reason and Western thought and attack Kant's official philosophy, an analytical philosophy of truth. For them, critique is based as much on a serious and sustained interrogation of historical experience as it is on a deconstruction of metaphysical philosophy. Recognizing the problems of attaching labels to Foucault's work and that of Arendt, I focus on the tensions and complexity of their work. There are tensions in Foucault's thought between totalizing/detotalizing impulses, discursive/extra-discursive theorization, macro/micro perspectives, and domination/resistance relations as well as between ethical-political commitments and archaeological detachment. There are also tensions in Arendt's thought between creative rupture and exercise in retrieval, between agonism and consensus as well as between existential engagement and philosophical withdrawal. problem: How did Netflix manage to successfully adapt One Hundred Years of Solitude, a notoriously difficult book to bring to the screen?
final_response:
<think>
I will synthesize a data-driven report grounded in the gathered evidence: the García Márquez family’s involvement and language choice; the chronological serialization across 8 episodes covering the novel’s first 6–7 chapters; the Colombian shoot with major locations; the construction of multiple Macondo sets spanning ~70 soccer fields; casting scale (10,000+ candidates, 70% non-professional); writers’ compression strategy with a narrator; and the focus on naturalized magical realism without heavy CGI. I will cite specific sources for each claim.
</think>

<answer><title>How Netflix Managed to Successfully Adapt One Hundred Years of Solitude: A Data-Driven Report</title>

Executive summary
Netflix’s 2024–2026 series adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude achieved scale and cultural authenticity by securing the García Márquez family’s blessing, shooting in Colombia in Spanish with Colombian actors, and serializing the narrative across 16 episodes (first 8 released December 2024). The first season alone covers the novel’s first 6–7 chapters in chronological order, builds three towns including a 540,000-m² Macondo near Alvarado, Tolima, and casts thousands of performers while preserving Márquez’s magical realism through naturalized visuals rather than heavy special effects. These choices helped navigate the book’s notorious difficulty and contributed to its reception as a respectful, immersive take on Macondo and the Buendía family. <cite id="call_149dc3b9f8df-1"></cite><cite id="call_149dc3b9f8df-2"></cite><cite id="call_416e5afd8e33-2"></cite><cite id="call_3395ab493b02-3"></cite><cite id="call_e30ba0385ea4-3"></cite><cite id="call_b60277331ba6-2"></cite>

1. Securing the García Márquez family’s blessing and language choice
The García Márquez family’s support was central to the project’s cultural legitimacy. The series was produced in Spanish and with Colombian actors, honoring a key condition reportedly expressed by Márquez himself, who had long refused to sell the rights for fear of distortion. After his death in 2014, his sons—Rodrigo García and Gonzalo García Barcha—served as executive producers, ensuring the adaptation aligned with the family’s vision and Márquez’s stated preferences. <cite id="call_80c85bd9db2d-1"></cite><cite id="call_149dc3b9f8df-3"></cite><cite id="call_80c85bd9db2d-4"></cite>

2. Chronological serialization and structural compression
Rather than the novel’s non-linear, multi-generational structure, the series adopts a chronological narrative (shot in order), with the first season covering the novel’s first 6–7 chapters—Macondo’s founding, José Arcadio Buendía’s alchemical obsession, the family’s early conflicts, and the arrival of Melquíades and the Gypsies. This framing compresses the source material into 8 episodes, providing a clear temporal anchor for viewers while preserving the core mythic arc. The writers, José Rivera, Natalia Santa, and Camila Brugés, explicitly designed the series to proceed chronologically and included a narrator to guide the audience through Márquez’s dense world. <cite id="call_3395ab493b02-3"></cite><cite id="call_416e5afd8e33-2"></cite><cite id="call_b60277331ba6-2"></cite><cite id="call_b60277331ba6-1"></cite>

3. Filming in Colombia and location scouting
To ground the series in the novel’s cultural and geographical context, production was entirely in Colombia, with locations including Cali, Villavicencio, Girardot, Palomino, Santa Marta, Barranquilla, and La Guajira. The show’s landscapes—from the Caribbean coast to Tolima’s mountains and the Magdalena River region—help visually evoke Macondo’s shifting environment and the novel’s real Colombian history. <cite id="call_149dc3b9f8df-3"></cite><cite id="call_e30ba0385ea4-1"></cite><cite id="call_1f27889508d6-3"></cite>

4. Building multiple towns to realize Macondo and its evolution
Production involved constructing three different towns to reflect Macondo’s developmental stages: an early village of mud huts and bamboo representing José Arcadio and Úrsula’s youth, a full-scale Macondo near Alvarado, Tolima (covering ~540,000 m²), and additional sets for later seasons. The Tolima Macondo included ceramic-named streets and faithful 19th-century costumes, immersing viewers in the novel’s world while leveraging Colombia’s natural terrain (including mountains resembling the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta). <cite id="call_149dc3b9f8df-3"></cite><cite id="call_e30ba0385ea4-3"></cite><cite id="call_e30ba0385ea4-4"></cite><cite id="call_e30ba0385ea4-1"></cite>

5. Casting scale and diversity
To reflect Macondo’s community feel, the casting process visited music and dance schools across Colombia (Montería, Santa Marta, Bogotá, Medellín) and attracted over 10,000 candidates. Approximately 70% of the cast were non-professional actors, reinforcing the series’ grounded, ensemble-driven tone. This approach helped portray the Buendía family’s relationships and the town’s social fabric with a sense of realism and cultural specificity. <cite id="call_149dc3b9f8df-1"></cite><cite id="call_e30ba0385ea4-3"></cite>

6. Narrative and stylistic choices for cinematic translation
The series naturalizes magical realism within a largely realistic aesthetic, avoiding flashy CGI for effects (e.g., ghosts without halos or music cues). This pragmatic approach respects the source material’s tone while making it accessible on screen. The decision to serialize the story chronologically and use a narrator also addresses the novel’s complex timelines and nested storytelling, helping viewers follow the Buendía saga without sacrificing the book’s lyrical depth. <cite id="call_b60277331ba6-2"></cite><cite id="call_b60277331ba6-3"></cite><cite id="call_b60277331ba6-1"></cite>

7. Critical reception and reported successes
Early reviews note that the series succeeds in translating Macondo’s atmosphere and the family’s emotional realities onto screen, even as some viewers find the timeline and relationships challenging. By anchoring the story in Colombia, using a narrator, and focusing on naturalized magical realism, the adaptation is widely seen as a respectful, immersive take on Márquez’s masterpiece. <cite id="call_3395ab493b02-3"></cite><cite id="call_b60277331ba6-2"></cite><cite id="call_b60277331ba6-1"></cite>

Conclusion
Netflix’s adaptation of One Hundred Years of Solitude succeeded by securing the García Márquez family’s blessing, shooting in Colombia in Spanish with Colombian actors, and structurally compressing the novel’s first 6–7 chapters into a chronological 8-episode season. The production built multiple towns—including a large-scale Macondo near Alvarado, Tolima—to realize the novel’s geography and period detail, while a broad, mostly non-professional cast helped ground the family saga. Writers José Rivera, Natalia Santa, and Camila Brugés, alongside director Alex García López, translated Márquez’s dense, multi-generational narrative into cinematic storytelling that prioritized naturalized magical realism over heavy special effects. These choices addressed the book’s notorious difficulty and contributed to the series’ reception as a culturally authentic and immersive adaptation. <cite id="call_149dc3b9f8df-1"></cite><cite id="call_149dc3b9f8df-2"></cite><cite id="call_416e5afd8e33-2"></cite><cite id="call_3395ab493b02-3"></cite><cite id="call_e30ba0385ea4-3"></cite><cite id="call_e30ba0385ea4-4"></cite><cite id="call_b60277331ba6-2"></cite><cite id="call_b60277331ba6-1"></cite><cite id="call_3395ab493b02-3"></cite></answer>

The series masterfully blends adventure, politics, and psychological drama into a complex web of storytelling. The magical realism that so vividly permeates the book is beautifully translated into the series, giving viewers a unique glimpse into the inner workings of the plot and characters. The story follows the life of a dreamy-eyed Colombian man, José Arcadio Buendía, who sets out to establish a utopian town, Macondo. But what begins as an idealistic vision devolves into a state of narcissistic isolation that precipitates deviant behavior and sets the town against religious and governmental forces. This dynamic reflects an old psychiatric idea that masturbation—understood symbolically as a mindless circularity of libidinal energy—can lead to madness. José, a puer figure, goes mad and fails to hold the center of his family compound as the town slowly descends into chaos. Alchemically, he is bound to a tree at the center of the family compound, but sadly, fixation does not bring transformation. He fails to bring order to his family or peace to his utopian town. The series explores how the inability to integrate “warring opposites”—conservative and liberal, idealism and pragmatism—fuels the inevitable collapse of Macondo. Márquez’s novel and the series emerge out of Colombia’s struggle between the bloody confrontation between political parties, a situation similar to the problems facing the West today. Macondo, in Márquez’s words, is not “a place, but a state of mind.”</summary><hostname>Taylor & Francis Online</hostname><publisher>Jung Journal</publisher><author_list><author name="Thom F. With streaming providers like YouTube and Netflix shifting to high-fidelity audio formats such as stereophonic sound and Dolby Atoms, ensuring proper audio and video adaptation has become a critical aspect of modern streaming platforms. Additionally, Variable Bitrate (VBR) encoding has gained great popularity in encoding audio and video content, given its higher quality-to-bits ratio. However, the considerable variability in network bandwidth, in combination with VBR features such as significantly fluctuating audio/video chunk sizes and diverse content complexity, makes existing ABR schemes formidable to make optimal bitrate selection due to their overlook of audio adaptation or oblivious to VBR features. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="ADAS liability shared control driver human-machine interface legal case law proposed guidelines" search_time="2026年5月10日10时26分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>Burges Salmon response to joint Law Commission and Scottish Law Commission preliminary consultation paper dated 8 November 2018 on Automated Vehicles</title><hostname>Amazon S3</hostname><publisher>Burges Salmon response to joint Law Commission and Scottish Law Commission preliminary consultation paper dated 8 November 2018 on Automated Vehicles</publisher><url>https://s3-eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/lawcom-prod-storage-11jsxou24uy7q/uploads/2019/06/AV033-Burges-Salmon-LLP.pdf</url><publish_time>2019年2月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>European Tort Law 2017</title><hostname>Universität Hamburg Fakultät für Rechtswissenschaft</hostname><publisher>European Tort Law</publisher><author_list><author name="Ernst Karner" /><author name="Barbara C Steininger Eds" /></author_list><url>https://www.jura.uni-hamburg.de/media/die-fakultaet/personen/wurmnest-wolfgang/wurmnest-goemann-yb-2017-european-tort-law.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:3"><title>DRIVING MISS DAISY: AN AUTONOMOUS CHAUFFEUR SYSTEM</title><hostname>Houston Law Review</hostname><publisher>HOUSTON LAW REVIEW</publisher><url>https://houstonlawreview.org/article/4050.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:4"><title>Highly Automated Driving on Highways based on Legal Safety DISSERTATION</title><summary>Vehicle automation is proposed as one of the solutions to make transport safer, more com- fortable and more environmentally friendly. It is gradually being introduced through Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS). ADAS started as Anti-lock Braking Systems (ABS) and have now extended to Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) and Lane Keeping Assist Systems (LKAS). This work aims to contribute to this evolution, by discussing how driving systems can share the road with human drivers. It presents the legal safety concept for the design of a highly automated driving system for highways. The legal safety concept proposes to base driving system design on traffic rules. This allows fully automated driving in traffic with human drivers, without necessarily changing equipment on other vehicles or infrastructure. The driving system uses traffic rules to predict legal or non- legal trajectories of objects in its perception zone and worst-case objects outside its perception zone. If all objects respect traffic rules, accidents will be avoided. If not, driving defensively will avoid most accidents. Today, international law allows highly automated driving, but not yet fully automated driving. The driving system interacts with the human driver, via human rules. The HAVEit project (European Seventh Framework Programme) and ABV project (French National Research Agency) propose human rules based on the horse-rider metaphor (H- metaphor). If needed, the driving system takes over control in order to avoid accidents. If the human driver cannot continue driving, the driving system brings the vehicle to a safe standstill on the emergency lane. The consequences of these human rules on driving system design are explored. System rules form the third set of rules of the legal safety concept. With system rules, system components respect the limitations of other system components. The requirements on perception, control and Human-Machine Interface (HMI) components of the legal safety system are discussed. The decision component, which is the central component of the legal safety system, is completely worked out from requirements to design. The legal safety system has been implemented on PC and automotive Electronic Control Units (ECUs). INTRODUCTION
1.1
Burges Salmon is an independent UK law firm with a market-leading transport law practice across all modes include rail, road transport and highways, aviation and airports and marine and ports.
1.2
Burges Salmon has been actively partnering in Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAV) research and development projects and trials since 2014. These include the Innovate UK-funded projects VENTURER, FLOURISH, Capri, RoboPilot and MultiCAV.
1.3 Burges Salmon has published the following legal reports in conjunction with AXA on CAV issues relating to insurance, safety, civil and criminal liability, data and cybersecurity:
(a)
VENTURER Year 1 Report 20161
(b)
FLOURISH Year 1 Report 20172
(c) “Are we ready to ‘handover’ to driverless technology” (VENTURER, April 2018)3
(d) “Driverless cars: liability frameworks and safety by design” (VENTURER, June
2018)4
(e) FLOURISH Year 2 Report 20185
1.4 More generally on highway safety, we produced a report in April 2018 for the RAC Foundation6: ‘A Highways Accident Investigation Branch - What Lessons can be learned from the Rail Industry and the Cullen Inquiry?’. Subsequent to that report the RAC Foundation received funding from DfT to run a pilot on highways accident data analysis.
1.5 We welcome the 3 year joint project of the Law Commission of England and Wales and Scottish Law Commission to review the legal framework for automated vehicles and we are pleased to submit our response to the preliminary consultation below.
1.6 Should the Law Commissions wish to explore any part of our responses further then we are happy to assist further where we can.
2 GENERAL CORE THEMES
2.1
Automated vehicles present a challenge to a framework of driving laws and rules which have, from their inception in the 19th Century and subsequent development, rested on the fundamental basis that ‘driving’ is solely a human activity. Application and enforcement of those driving laws focuses on individual and indivisible human actors. Applicable legal criteria and tests of expected standards or criminalised behaviours relating to vehicle ownership and use have also been constructed around the language and lenses of human behaviours and standards – reasonableness, due care and attention, careless, unfit, wanton or furious. The law has, logically, focused on individual actions looking at the behaviour of a defined individual against a defined obligation falling wholly upon the individual.
2.2
The introduction of automated vehicles that are truly capable of driving themselves will create a new class of non-human activity that is more analogous to automated processes of products.
2.3
Further, the performance of these products is likely, amongst other things, to:

VENTURER brings together a rich partnership of public, private and academic experts in order to establish the South West region of the UK as a world class test site facility for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles.

VENTURER will focus on
the people as well as the technology side of the trials to understand the blockers and drivers to wide scale adoption of autonomous vehicle capability.
These trials will go hand in hand with developing an understanding of the insurance and legal implications of increased vehicle autonomy. VENTURER will also establish a realistic simulation environment.
The three year project began in July 2015 and is based in the Bristol and South Gloucestershire region, with an independent test site established as part of a sustainable and ongoing facility.

Foreword
AXA is proud to be a partner in the VENTURER project. We understand that the integration of semi-autonomous, highly autonomous and fully autonomous vehicles into the UK motor market has the potential to disrupt and fundamentally alter the current motor insurance model but at the same time transform society for the better.
Through our involvement in this project, we hope to gain an understanding of the risk modelling that will be necessary to underwrite insurance policies for cars with higher levels of automation by, for example, exploring the issues of where liability will fall during the use of such vehicles. It will also give us advanced notice of safety and assistance features making their way on to the existing car market, enabling us to reflect these aspects in reduced pricing for our customers at an earlier stage.
Whilst we see autonomous vehicles as a massive step forward in terms of road safety, motor vehicle accidents will still happen and we will need to be able to determine the cause - the driver or the car.
Motor insurance has been compulsory in the UK for almost 90 years and it exists to protect road users and pedestrians. That protection is incredibly important when you consider that over 90 per cent of all motor accidents are caused by human error.
At the time of publication of this report, media outlets were talking about ‘the first fatality in a self-driving car’ (a Tesla Model S driven in Florida in May 2016). The Tesla Autopilot is a driver assistance feature in beta testing phase where the driver is advised to keep alert and have their hands on the wheel at all times, so it is not a true autonomous vehicle in that sense. It is a reminder however that robust legal and insurance frameworks need to be in place, taking into account clear liability positions on driver and vehicle across scenarios.
So, on the one hand these vehicles will radically change the way we do business and that in itself is obviously a reason to be involved. On the other hand though, driverless technology is exciting from an insurance perspective because it has the potential to significantly reduce the number of accidents on the roads and the injuries and deaths caused by those accidents. It is thought that the reduction could be as much as 50 per cent and that can only be good news for road safety.
Insurers are also very mindful of the wider role that they play in society and driverless technology represents an opportunity to reduce fuel consumption, reduce congestion and to offer mobility solutions to those currently unable to or unwilling to drive.

Introduction
As the VENTURER project’s 3 year trials formally conclude, we have pleasure in presenting Burges Salmon and AXA’s third legal and insurance report.
At the time of writing, the Automated and Electric Vehicles Bill (AEV Bill) has only just completed its committee stage has not yet been finalised, but we expect the content of this report to remain equally valid after its enactment1.
This report will consider legal and insurance issues for automated vehicles (AVs) in the context of a number of collision scenarios, with particular focus on the mechanics and limitations of machine to human handover arising from VENTURER’s research. Questions as to “who is liable?” and “who will pay?” in the event of an accident involving a self-driving vehicle have been understandably asked for as long as the concept of self-driving vehicles has existed. From time to time, the questions become more vocal as questions take on real world significance through events involving AVs in testing or advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS).
This report aims to help demystify the legal and insurance analysis around a number of example scenarios and, where possible, offer practical commentary or recommendations and identify further areas for reform, investigation or consultation (particularly in light of VENTURER findings).

LATIN telemedicine - expanded umbrella of cost-effective ami coverage for 100 million people</title><summary>Background
AMI is a unique entity where the immediate diagnosis can be made by a single test, the EKG. Despite this matchless attribute of easy diagnosis, developing (and some developed) countries lack resources and efficient pathways for urgent and reliable diagnosis of AMI. With Latin Telemedicine Infarct Network (LATIN), we have previously presented Telemedicine as a pragmatic solution for urgent and accurate diagnosis of AMI. In this work, we reveal pathways of scalable population-based AMI management models.
Purpose
To utilize telemedicine as a foundation pillar for creating cost-effective and global models of AMI management.
Methods
LATIN pilot tested the hypothesis of remote guidance of AMI management and expanded access by creating a hub and spoke, STEMI systems of care that exploited regional resources. A highly efficient, web-based, cloud-computing prototype was developed and scrupulously monitored with a new metric of time to telemedicine diagnosis (TTD). STEMI systems of care were created to efficiently triage the diagnosed patients for being treated with thrombolysis, pharmaco-invasive management or Primary PCI. This stratagem had enormous provincial variability and was constrained mainly by ambulance structure. Telemedicine and IT costs were forced lower and enabled a cost-effective process to hugely provide access to 100 million patients located in poorer regions of Colombia, Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina. Education and training have formed the mantra for LATIN and stakeholder development, and ambulance systems development has remained immutable goals.
Results
Almost 800,000 patients were successfully screening through LATIN with a cost for accurate STEMI diagnosis of < $3, a tele accuracy that exceeded 95% and with TTD <4 minutes. A total of 8,440 (1.1%) of patients were diagnosed with AMI in this manner and 3,924 (46.5%) urgently reperfused, mainly with Primary PCI (3,048, 77.8%). D2B times have been lowered now to 51 minutes but this is fortuitous, as several PCI-capable facilities are small, and direct transfer to the catheterization laboratory is easy. Door in and Door out times and transport times remain high as a large number of patients are denied by insurance and other payers for treatment. Overall, mortality is 5.2%.

problem: I would like a detailed analysis of the Saint Seiya franchise (anime/manga). The analysis should be structured around the different classes of armor (Cloths, Scales, Surplices, God Robes, etc.), such as Bronze Saints, Silver Saints, Gold Saints, Marina Generals, Specters, God Warriors, etc. For each significant character within these categories, provide details on their power level, signature techniques, key appearances/story arcs, and final outcome/fate within the series.
final_response:
<think>
Summarize the series’ armor hierarchy and major characters across Bronze, Silver, Gold, Marina Generals, Specters, and God Warriors, using the gathered sources to extract class descriptions, representative Saints and their Cloths, signature techniques, key arcs, and fates. For each class, list several significant members and fill in the requested details, citing Fandom pages and other summaries that describe their roles, armors, attacks, story arcs, and outcomes. Avoid speculation; if a source only mentions general class traits or a character’s arc without specific power levels or techniques, state that clearly.
</think>

<answer>Below is a structured, data-driven analysis of Saint Seiya’s major warrior classes and representative characters, based on canon sources across the franchise’s series and supplementary materials.

Armor hierarchy and class definitions
- Bronze Saints: The lowest rank of Athena’s army; initiates in the mysteries of Cosmo who mainly serve as backup for Silver Saints on missions. Their Cloths cover only vital points and are relatively light and less durable. Bronze Saints can ascend through training and earn promotions to Silver or Gold. The Pegasus Bronze Cloth, for example, is light and has wings but is frequently damaged and repaired by Aries Mu or later by the Sculptor’s tools; its evolution into a God Cloth requires Athena’s blood and is a rare miracle by the wearer’s Cosmo<cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-0"></cite><cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-1"></cite><cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-2"></cite><cite id="call_8eb9271fbd45-2"></cite><cite id="call_4f05a75d5f92-0"></cite>.
- Silver Saints: Middle-tier soldiers who act as eyes and ears of the Sanctuary and commanders over groups of Bronze Saints. They wear more durable armors than Bronze Saints and can train new Saints; some even master the seventh sense. The Silver Cloths are second most powerful of Cloths and are said to be five times stronger and faster than Bronze Saints. Examples include Camelopardalis Silver Saint (used by the Sanctuary in Saint Seiya Ω) and Caelum, which was originally a Bronze Cloth in early materials but became a Silver Saint in Ω<cite id="call_a2a42d2a5bb0-4"></cite><cite id="call_a2a42d2a5bb0-2"></cite><cite id="call_a2a42d2a5bb0-3"></cite><cite id="call_4f05a75d5f92-0"></cite>.
- Gold Saints: The elite warriors who guard the twelve houses of the Sanctuary and serve as Athena’s most trusted protectors. They wear the most powerful Cloths, which are said to have absorbed the light of the Sun since the days of Myth and can even recreate that might when combined. The Gold Cloths almost completely cover the body, leaving only small portions exposed, and provide near-absolute protection; they are the pinnacle of the Saints’ armors. In some continuations, the number of Gold Cloths increases to thirteen to include Ophiuchus<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-1"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-3"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-4"></cite>.
- Marina Generals (Posiedon’s Army): The highest-ranking soldiers of Poseidon’s navy, each guarding a specific ocean and its pillar in a manner analogous to how the Gold Saints guard Athena’s Sanctuary. They wear specialized armors and wield immense power comparable to or superior to the fabled Gold Saints of Athena. Notable examples include Sea Horse Baian (trusted guardian of the Mammoth Pillar), Scylla Io, Chrysaor Krishna, Kraken Isaak, Siren Sorrento, and Sea Dragon Kanon (who later defected to Hades). Their attacks include barriers, divine breath, and devastating whirlwinds, and they play pivotal roles in defending the seas against Athena’s Saints<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-0"></cite><cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-3"></cite><cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-4"></cite>.
- Specters (Hades’ Army): The 108 warriors of the Underworld who serve as Hades’ standing army and staff. Each Specter is bound to a specific Evil Star and wields a Surplice armor corresponding to their destined star. They are not the dead who live in the Underworld but rather warriors resurrected to fight for Hades. Their power is formidable, and they play key roles in invading the Sanctuary and challenging Athena’s Saints; notable Specters include the Sea Dragon Unity and the music-based Siren Sorrento (whose mental attacks exemplify the strength of music-type Specters) and the Sea Magus Chi Mei Sei Land Bright Star<cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-1"></cite><cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-2"></cite><cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-4"></cite><cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-3"></cite><cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-2"></cite>.
- God Warriors (Asgard’s Army): Warriors who protect Odin and Asgard and wear God Robes rather than Cloths. They appear primarily in the anime and are said to possess strength comparable to Gold Saints, though their power can be pushed beyond typical training levels. They are awakened or enhanced by Hilda’s power and the Odin Sapphires, and their role in battles against Loki and the forces of Hades culminates in a bittersweet ending where the Gold Saints ultimately prevail and send their Cloths to aid the Bronze Saints in Elysium<cite id="call_5bdd3239be21-0"></cite><cite id="call_5bdd3239be21-1"></cite><cite id="call_5bdd3239be21-2"></cite>.

Representative characters and details
Bronze Saints
- Pegasus Seiya (Bronze Pegasus Cloth): Signature technique is the rapid-fire Pegasus Meteor Fist; his Cloth has wings and evolves into a God Cloth during the Sanctuary Arc when Athena smears her blood on it, granting flight and enhanced dimensional travel. In the Sanctuary Arc, his God Cloth allows him to confront Hades directly, suffering grave wounds from Hades’ sword. The Pegasus Cloth has multiple versions (Kyū Cloth, Shin Cloth, New Cloth, Myth Cloth EX/Final Bronze Cloth), with repairs often handled by Aries Mu or later by Athena’s blood<cite id="call_e371b3a6a3b8-3"></cite><cite id="call_e371b3a6a3b8-2"></cite><cite id="call_e371b3a6a3b8-0"></cite><cite id="call_e371b3a6a3b8-4"></cite>.
- Cygnus Hyoga (Bronze Cygnus Swan Cloth): Known for his ice-based abilities; signature techniques include the Ice Meteor Fist and the defensive Ice Wall. His Cloth is light and has a swan motif; he later becomes the future Gold Saint of Aquarius and is recognized as such after a duel with Camus<cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-1"></cite><cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-2"></cite><cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-4"></cite>.
- Draco Shiryu (Bronze Dragon Cloth): Calm and collected, his Cloth is heavy and dragon-themed; he later becomes the future Gold Saint of Libra and is recognized as such by Dohko<cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-1"></cite><cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-2"></cite><cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-4"></cite>.
- Andromeda Shun (Bronze Andromeda Cloth): Wears a unitard-like Surplice when not in armor; his Cloth has multiple versions (New Cloth, Final Cloth) repaired by Shion with Athena’s blood during the Sanctuary Arc. His signature technique is the Andromeda Spiral, and he is known for his pacifistic, self-sacrificing nature; he later becomes the future Gold Saint of Virgo<cite id="call_e6e8e822de7f-1"></cite><cite id="call_e6e8e822de7f-0"></cite><cite id="call_4f05a75d5f92-0"></cite><cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-1"></cite>.
- Phoenix Ikki (Bronze Phoenix Cloth): His Cloth has self-repairing properties from ash and fire; signature techniques include the Phoenix Meteor Fist and the Phoenix God’s Will. He later becomes the future Gold Saint of Sagittarius and is recognized as such by Aiolos; in Saint Seiya Omega, he temporarily loses his hearing due to a barrier set by Shion<cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-1"></cite><cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-2"></cite><cite id="call_4f05a75d5f92-0"></cite><cite id="call_e02660b89ba1-2"></cite>.

Silver Saints
- Camelopardalis Silver Saint: Used by the Sanctuary in Saint Seiya Omega; details on techniques and arcs are sparse in general sources, but the series notes that Camelopardalis was originally a Bronze Cloth in early materials and became a Silver Saint in Omega<cite id="call_a2a42d2a5bb0-3"></cite><cite id="call_a2a42d2a5bb0-1"></cite>.
- Caelum: Originally a Bronze Cloth in some sources but designated as a Silver Saint in Saint Seiya Omega; details on techniques and arcs are limited to series placement<cite id="call_a2a42d2a5bb0-1"></cite><cite id="call_a2a42d2a5bb0-3"></cite>.

Gold Saints
- Aries Mu (Gold Aries Cloth): Specialized in repairing Cloths and wielding the Sculptor’s tools; his Cloth is said to be among the strongest and is used to mend damaged armors across the series<cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-1"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite>.
- Taurus Saga (Gold Taurus Cloth): Known for his immense strength and the technique Poseidon’s Rage; he is one of the most feared Gold Saints and plays a central role in defending the Sanctuary<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite>.
- Gemini Shura (Gold Gemini Cloth): Twin-wielding powerhouse with the Twin Drills; his Cloth is highly mobile and balanced, reflecting the Gemini constellation<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite>.
- Libra Dohko (Gold Libra Cloth): Master of the Dragon Shiryu and future Pope; his Cloth embodies balance and wisdom, and he is a key strategist in the Sanctuary<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite>.
- Sagittarius Aiolos (Gold Sagittarius Cloth): Mentor to Seiya; his Cloth is associated with the bow and arrow, and he is known for the Shooting Star and Shooting Star Barrage<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite>.
- Aquarius Camus (Gold Aquarius Cloth): Ice master with the Aquarius Meteor Fist; he is the future master of Hyoga and a central figure in the Sanctuary’s defense<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite>.
- Pisces Deathmask (Gold Pisces Cloth): Dual-wielding swords with the Deathmask Slash; he is one of the most feared Gold Saints and a key defender of the Sanctuary<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite>.
- Virgo Shaka (Gold Virgo Cloth): The most powerful Gold Saint, wielding the God’s Will and the God’s Will Final; he is a central antagonist in the original series and later becomes a guardian of the Sanctuary<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite>.
- Ophiuchus Shura (Gold Ophiuchus Cloth): The 13th Zodiac Saint; his Cloth is associated with the serpent-eagle and he is a pivotal figure in the Sanctuary’s defense and the series’ lore<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-1"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite>.

Marina Generals
- Sea Horse Baian: Guardian of the Mammoth Pillar; his power is said to be equal to or superior to the fabled Gold Saints of Athena. Techniques include the Rising Billows (a massive whirlwind) and God Breath; he is a loyal warrior of Poseidon and a major obstacle for Athena’s Saints<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-3"></cite><cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-4"></cite>.
- Scylla Io: A formidable general of Poseidon’s navy; details on her techniques and role in battles are limited to general descriptions of Marina Generals<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite>.
- Chrysaor Krishna: A powerful general associated with the sword; details on his techniques and arcs are sparse in general sources<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite>.
- Limnade Caça: A Marina General guarding a specific ocean; details on his techniques and role are limited to general descriptions<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite>.
- Kraken Isaak: A Marina General known for his immense strength; details on his techniques and arcs are limited to general descriptions<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite>.
- Siren Sorrento: A Marina General whose music-based abilities exemplify the strength of music-type warriors; her mental attacks are a notable aspect of her combat style<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite><cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-2"></cite>.
- Sea Dragon Kanon: A Marina General who later defects to Hades; his betrayal and role in the conflict against Athena’s Saints are pivotal in several arcs<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-4"></cite>.
- Sea Dragon Unity: A combined form of Marina Generals under the Sea Dragon’s command; details on techniques and arcs are limited to general descriptions<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite>.

Specters
- Sea Magus Chi Mei Sei Land Bright Star: A Specter associated with music and light; details on techniques and arcs are limited to general descriptions of Specters and their Evil Stars<cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-3"></cite>.
- Sea Magus Chi Shin Sei Land Advance Star: Another music-type Specter; details on techniques and arcs are limited to general descriptions<cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-3"></cite>.
- Siren Sorrento (also listed as a Marina General): Her music-based mental attacks exemplify the strength of music-type Specters; details on her role in battles are noted in analyses of Specter power<cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-2"></cite><cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite>.
- Sea Horse Baian (also a Marina General): His power is comparable to or superior to the fabled Gold Saints of Athena; details on his role in battles are noted in general descriptions of Marina Generals<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-3"></cite><cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-4"></cite>.

God Warriors
- Seven God Warriors of Asgard: Warriors protecting Odin and Asgard; they wear God Robes and are exceptionally strong, with power comparable to Gold Saints. Some show abilities beyond typical training, awakened or enhanced by Hilda and the Odin Sapphires. Their role culminates in battles against Loki and the forces of Hades, with the Gold Saints ultimately prevailing and sending their Cloths to aid the Bronze Saints in Elysium<cite id="call_5bdd3239be21-0"></cite><cite id="call_5bdd3239be21-1"></cite><cite id="call_5bdd3239be21-2"></cite>.

Fates and key arcs
- Bronze Saints: Many Bronze Saints ascend through training and earn promotions to Silver or Gold ranks; those who attain Gold status often become future leaders or strategists (e.g., Shiryu becomes Libra’s future Gold Saint and later Pope, Hyoga becomes Aquarius’ future Gold Saint). In the Sanctuary Arc, several Bronze Saints are deployed to Elysium and are aided by the Gold Saints’ Cloths<cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-1"></cite><cite id="call_4f05a75d5f92-0"></cite><cite id="call_e6e8e822de7f-1"></cite>.
- Silver Saints: Act as commanders and trainers; some may ascend to Gold ranks or become key figures in defending the Sanctuary. In Omega, Silver Saints like Camelopardalis are part of the Sanctuary’s forces and play roles in the broader conflict<cite id="call_a2a42d2a5bb0-3"></cite><cite id="call_a2a42d2a5bb0-1"></cite>.
- Gold Saints: Serve as the Sanctuary’s elite defenders and often become future leaders (e.g., Shion becomes Pope, Shaka becomes a guardian). In the final battle against Hades, Gold Saints wield their ultimate forms and send their Cloths to aid the Bronze Saints in Elysium<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite><cite id="call_5bdd3239be21-2"></cite>.
- Marina Generals: Defend Poseidon’s oceans and pillars; some defect to Hades (e.g., Kanon), while others remain loyal and play pivotal roles in battles against Athena’s Saints<cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-1"></cite><cite id="call_ca4cc96d3529-4"></cite>.
- Specters: Invade the Sanctuary and challenge Athena’s Saints; their defeat culminates in the Gold Saints’ victory and the sending of Cloths to Elysium<cite id="call_4088b31d97b3-1"></cite><cite id="call_5bdd3239be21-2"></cite>.
- God Warriors: Participate in battles against Loki and Hades; their role is bittersweet, with the Gold Saints ultimately prevailing and aiding the Bronze Saints in Elysium<cite id="call_5bdd3239be21-2"></cite>.

Armor evolution and special forms
- God Cloths: Evolve when Athena’s blood is smeared on a Cloth, granting wings and near-absolute protection; they are miracles by the wearer’s Cosmo and can withstand extreme attacks, with Athena’s Cloth (Kamui) being the most powerful<cite id="call_8eb9271fbd45-0"></cite><cite id="call_8eb9271fbd45-3"></cite><cite id="call_8eb9271fbd45-2"></cite>.
- Final Cloth: Refers to Cloths repaired by Athena’s blood during the Sanctuary Arc against Hades; they are stronger and more durable, with examples like the Andromeda Final Cloth and the Pegasus Final Bronze Cloth<cite id="call_e6e8e822de7f-1"></cite><cite id="call_e6e8e822de7f-0"></cite><cite id="call_e371b3a6a3b8-2"></cite>.
- New Cloth: Repaired after the Sanctuary Arc with the blood of Gold Saints; examples include the Pegasus New Cloth<cite id="call_e371b3a6a3b8-2"></cite>.
- Kyū Cloth and Shin Cloth: Earlier versions of the Pegasus Cloth, with repairs handled by Aries Mu or later by Athena’s blood<cite id="call_e371b3a6a3b8-2"></cite><cite id="call_e371b3a6a3b8-4"></cite>.
- Myth Cloth EX: A collectible representation of the Final Bronze Cloth of Pegasus Seiya, highlighting the evolution and design changes<cite id="call_e6e8e822de7f-4"></cite>.

Class comparisons and lore
- Gold vs. Silver vs. Bronze: Gold Cloths are the most powerful and provide near-absolute protection; Silver Cloths are second-tier and more durable than Bronze Cloths; Bronze Cloths cover only vital points and are the lightest and least durable<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-2"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-0"></cite><cite id="call_9a8d05e11df3-1"></cite>.
- Gold Cloths and the Sun’s Light: The Gold Cloths have absorbed the light of the Sun since the days of Myth and can recreate that might when combined, underscoring their divine origin and power<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-1"></cite>.
- Ophiuchus and the 13th Zodiac: In some continuations, the number of Gold Cloths increases to thirteen to include Ophiuchus, reflecting expanded lore and canon<cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-1"></cite><cite id="call_14ede4adcfec-3"></cite>.

Note: While the above provides a structured overview and representative details, some characters and arcs are described with limited specificity in the sources, and certain power levels or techniques are not quantified beyond general descriptions. For precise battle metrics or detailed technique breakdowns, dedicated analyses of specific arcs and character profiles would be necessary.</answer>

problem: For a research project titled 'Analysis and Study of Singles Badminton Player Actions Using Sports Videos,' please refine and optimize the following four research components: 1) Object Detection and Tracking within Badminton Videos; 2) Recognition of Technical Actions performed by Singles Players; 3) Recognition of Tactical Intent behind Singles Players' Actions; 4) Prediction of Singles Players' Subsequent Actions.

I will synthesize a data-driven report for the research project, structuring each of the four components with concrete model choices, processing pipelines, datasets, and performance targets, and back each specific claim with citations from the already retrieved sources.

<answer><title>Analysis and Study of Singles Badminton Player Actions Using Sports Videos: Optimized Research Plan</title>

Object Detection and Tracking within Badminton Videos
- Core pipeline: Combine robust object detectors with efficient trackers and specialized models for small fast objects. Detect shuttlecock and racket with a lightweight, improved YOLO variant (e.g., GhostNet-based YOLOv5) tuned for singles play, and track detected entities with DeepSORT for real-time multi-target association. For shuttlecock, use TrackNet or TrackNetV2 to produce heatmaps across consecutive frames, achieving high accuracy and substantially increased FPS for real-time processing in match videos. Use MediaPipe for pose estimation to augment player tracking and action context. <cite id="call_258cacaa5ff9-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-3"></cite><cite id="call_d45d1a28c128-2"></cite><cite id="call_8d77c20ed3de-0"></cite>
- Shuttlecock refinement: Fuse detections from TrackNet/YOLOv7 with a shot refinement algorithm to resolve misses and false positives and precisely identify the hitting moment; this approach improves shuttlecock accuracy, recall, and F1 in large rally sets. <cite id="call_8d77c20ed3de-0"></cite><cite id="call_54312587ca64-0"></cite>
- Player detection/pose: Use improved YOLOv5 variants (e.g., GhostNet compression) for lightweight detection on embedded platforms and MediaPipe for 3D joint coordinates to support skeleton-based models for fine-grained action recognition. <cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-3"></cite><cite id="call_10116ec796e0-0"></cite>
- Evaluation datasets: Benchmark shuttlecock tracking on 55k+ frames from diverse match videos and leverage ShuttleSet/Bad­mintonDB for rally/stroke-level annotations to validate tracking timing and hit detection. <cite id="call_8d77c20ed3de-0"></cite><cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-0"></cite>

Recognition of Technical Actions performed by Singles Players
- Feature modalities: Fuse RGB features from ViTs with skeleton-based spatiotemporal information (MediaPipe joints) and optionally integrate shuttlecock trajectory and hit cues; hybrid RGB+pose models achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in badminton action recognition. <cite id="call_e05a829e6f29-0"></cite><cite id="call_54312587ca64-0"></cite><cite id="call_54312587ca64-1"></cite>
- Fine-grained stroke recognition: Deploy a skeleton-based transformer (TemPose) with temporal and interaction layers and optionally inject shuttlecock position into transformer layers to capture detailed motion and improve recognition accuracy; NTU RGB+D competitiveness demonstrates versatility. <cite id="call_54312587ca64-1"></cite><cite id="call_54312587ca64-0"></cite><cite id="call_54312587ca64-1"></cite><cite id="call_54312587ca64-1"></cite>
- Lightweight embedded detection: For real-time embedded applications, use GhostNet-compressed YOLOv5 with smoother activation and CBAM attention to maintain high FPS while improving accuracy on limited platforms. <cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-3"></cite>
- Shot-type transformer: For rally-level stroke-type classification, apply the Badminton Stroke-type Transformer (BST) that segments racket swings, runs pose estimation, and leverages shuttlecock trajectories; this approach outperforms prior state of the art on ShuttleSet. <cite id="call_54312587ca64-0"></cite>

Recognition of Tactical Intent behind Singles Players’ Actions
- Tactical ontology and multimodal fusion: Use ShuttleSet with computer-aided labeling to capture stroke types, hitting locations, and rally context; integrate player position, pose, and shuttlecock trajectory for multimodal shot captioning and tactical event modeling. <cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-1"></cite>
- Wearable strategy analysis: Combine IMU (racket/wrist) and UWB localization to recognize strategies and classify thirteen shots plus non-shot activities; this pipeline achieves strong strategy recognition accuracy when fusing sensor streams. <cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-0"></cite>
- Ontology-driven mappings: Formalize match-to-shot event hierarchies (MatchEvent–SetEvent–RallyEvent–ShotEvent) and link participants, spatio-temporal extents, and tactics to enable structured tactical analysis and forecasting. <cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-4"></cite>
- Fine-grained motion recognition: Use TemPose to prioritize frames and poses relevant to tactical decisions and to model variable-length multi-person actions with minimal non-human context. <cite id="call_54312587ca64-1"></cite>

Prediction of Singles Players’ Subsequent Actions
- Event-driven spatiotemporal transformers: Adapt basketball event-driven modeling (CourtMotion) to singles badminton by processing skeletal data through GNNs and then a Transformer with attention heads for passes/shots/steals; this yields trajectory prediction gains and improves shot prediction and assist attribution. <cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-3"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-1"></cite>
- Next-action forecasting: Build axial/sequential transformers that jointly predict action totals and future events at multiple time steps, inspired by football forecasting; apply this to rally-level shot types and rally outcomes with temporal dynamics captured by attention. <cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-3"></cite><cite id="call_72ea02717c0f-0"></cite>
- Trajectory generation and counterfactuals: Use generative multi-agent models (e.g., VRNN-based GNNs) to forecast diverse future trajectories and answer conditional tactical questions (e.g., “what if the player changes shot selection?”). <cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-1"></cite>
- Shot forecasting benchmarks: Participate in stroke forecasting challenges (e.g., ShuttleSet22) to benchmark temporal models and refine attention mechanisms for rally-to-shot anticipation. <cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-2"></cite>

Datasets and Evaluation
- Shuttlecock tracking and hit detection: Evaluate TrackNet/TrackNetV2 on 55k+ frames from diverse match videos and refine with YOLOv7 swing detection to improve accuracy, recall, and F1; TrackNet reports 99.7% precision, 97.3% recall, and 98.5% F1 on tennis, while TrackNetV2 achieves 96.3% accuracy, 97.0% precision, and 98.7% recall with 31.8 FPS. <cite id="call_8d77c20ed3de-0"></cite><cite id="call_8d77c20ed3de-0"></cite>
- Shot-type recognition: Benchmark BST on ShuttleSet and report improvements over prior methods; deploy hybrid ViT+pose models to reach 98.68% accuracy for fine-grained stroke recognition. <cite id="call_54312587ca64-0"></cite><cite id="call_e05a829e6f29-0"></cite>
- Tactical datasets: Use ShuttleSet (36,492 strokes, 3,685 rallies) and BadmintonDB (9 matches with rally/stroke outcomes) for stroke-level annotations and player-specific match analysis; BFMD provides dense rally/hit captions with multimodal cues. <cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-1"></cite>
- Sensor fusion for tactics: Demonstrate shot classification (90.9%) and strategy recognition (80%) using IMU and UWB localization; use wearable datasets (e.g., MultiSenseBadminton) for physiological/gaze signals to complement video analysis. <cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-2"></cite>

Implementation Roadmap
1. Tracking pipeline: Detect shuttlecock and racket with improved YOLOv5; track with DeepSORT; refine hits with TrackNet/YOLOv7 and shot refinement; add MediaPipe pose for player context. <cite id="call_258cacaa5ff9-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-3"></cite><cite id="call_8d77c20ed3de-0"></cite><cite id="call_54312587ca64-0"></cite>
2. Action recognition: Fuse RGB (ViT) and skeleton (MediaPipe) features; use LSTM or TemPose to model temporal dependencies; deploy lightweight variants for embedded inference. <cite id="call_e05a829e6f29-0"></cite><cite id="call_54312587ca64-1"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-3"></cite>
3. Tactical intent: Annotate strokes with ShuttleSet; integrate player position/pose and shuttlecock trajectory; apply CourtMotion-style GNN+Transformer with event heads for shot/assist prediction. <cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-1"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-3"></cite>
4. Action prediction: Train axial/sequential transformers to forecast rally outcomes and shot types; use generative GNN models for conditional trajectory forecasts; benchmark on ShuttleSet22. <cite id="call_72ea02717c0f-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-1"></cite><cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-2"></cite>

Expected Outcomes and Contributions
- Reliable shuttlecock tracking and precise hit detection with TrackNet/TrackNetV2 and refinement pipelines, validated on large match datasets. <cite id="call_8d77c20ed3de-0"></cite><cite id="call_8d77c20ed3de-0"></cite>
- State-of-the-art stroke recognition via hybrid ViT+pose and skeleton-based transformers, with lightweight variants for embedded deployment. <cite id="call_e05a829e6f29-0"></cite><cite id="call_54312587ca64-1"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-3"></cite>
- Structured tactical analysis using ShuttleSet ontologies and multimodal fusion, enabling shot-type forecasting and strategy profiling. <cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-1"></cite>
- Temporal models that jointly predict rally outcomes and shot types, with conditional generation for counterfactual tactical evaluation. <cite id="call_72ea02717c0f-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-1"></cite><cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-2"></cite>

Notes on Uncertainty
- Some sensor fusion and strategy recognition results are from single-study setups; generalizability across players and conditions should be validated in future work. <cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-0"></cite>
- Transformer-based forecasting models (e.g., axial transformers, CourtMotion) are demonstrated in basketball/football; direct adaptation to singles badminton will require tuning for single-player dynamics and rally structure. <cite id="call_72ea02717c0f-0"></cite><cite id="call_4bbca20e7013-1"></cite>
- ShuttleSet22 provides a forecasting benchmark; participation will clarify model strengths and limitations in stroke anticipation. <cite id="call_5d442bc66f4d-2"></cite></answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="badminton singles shuttlecock tracking deep learning monocular" search_time="2026年5月10日10时27分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:84"><title>TrackNet: A Deep Learning Network for Tracking High-speed and Tiny Objects in Sports Applications</title><summary>Ball trajectory data are one of the most fundamental and useful information in the evaluation of players’ performance and analysis of game strategies. Although vision-based object tracking techniques have been developed to analyze sport competition videos, it is still challenging to recognize and position a high-speed and tiny ball accurately. In this paper, we develop a deep learning network, called TrackNet, to track the tennis ball from broadcast videos in which the ball images are small, blurry, and sometimes with afterimage tracks or even invisible. The proposed heatmap-based deep learning network is trained to not only recognize the ball image from a single frame but also learn flying patterns from consecutive frames. TrackNet takes images with the size of 640×360 to generate a detection heatmap from either a single frame or several consecutive frames to position the ball and can achieve high precision even on public domain videos. The network is evaluated on the video of the men’s singles final at the 2017 Summer Universiade, which is available on YouTube. The precision, recall, and F1-measure of TrackNet reach 99.7%, 97.3%, and 98.5%, respectively. To prevent overfitting, 9 additional videos are partially labeled together with a subset from the previous dataset to implement 10-fold cross validation, and the precision, recall, and F1-measure are 95.3%, 75.7%, and 84.3%, respectively. A conventional image processing algorithm is also implemented to compare with TrackNet. Our experiments indicate that TrackNet outperforms conventional method by a big margin and achieves exceptional ball tracking performance. The dataset and demo video are available at https://nol.cs.nctu.edu.tw/ndo3je6av9/</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><author_list><author name="Yuchuan Huang" affiliation="Department of Computer Science, College of Computer Science, National Chiao Tung University, 1001 University Road, Hsinchu City 30010, Taiwan" /><author name="Ino Liao" affiliation="Department of Computer Science, College of Computer Science, National Chiao Tung University, 1001 University Road, Hsinchu City 30010, Taiwan" /><author name="Chinghsuan Chen" affiliation="Department of Computer Science, College of Computer Science, National Chiao Tung University, 1001 University Road, Hsinchu City 30010, Taiwan" /><author name="Tsu Ik" affiliation="Department of Computer Science, College of Computer Science, National Chiao Tung University, 1001 University Road, Hsinchu City 30010, Taiwan" /><author name="Wenchih Peng" affiliation="Department of Computer Science, College of Computer Science, National Chiao Tung University, 1001 University Road, Hsinchu City 30010, Taiwan" /></author_list><url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.03698</url><arxiv_url>https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.03698</arxiv_url><arxiv_id>1907.03698</arxiv_id></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:85"><title>Tracking Fast Moving Objects by Segmentation Network</title><summary>Abstract—tracking Fast Moving Objects (FMO), which appear as blurred streaks in video sequences, is a difficult task for standard trackers, as the object position does not overlap in consecutive video frames and texture information of the objects is blurred. Up-to-date approaches tuned for this task are based on background subtraction with a static background and slow deblurring algorithms. In this article, we present a tracking-by-segmentation approach implemented using modern deep learning methods that perform near real-time tracking on real-world video sequences. We have developed a physically plausible FMO sequence generator to be a robust foundation for our training pipeline and demonstrate straightforward network adaptation for different FMO scenarios with varying foreground.</summary><hostname>Sci-Hub</hostname><publisher>2020 25

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="badminton player action recognition deep learning singles" search_time="2026年5月10日10时27分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:100"><title>Self-Attention-Based Deep Convolution LSTM Framework for Sensor-Based Badminton Activity Recognition</title><summary>Sensor-based human activity recognition aims to classify human activities or behaviors according to the data from wearable or embedded sensors, leading to a new direction in the field of Artificial Intelligence. When the activities become high-level and sophisticated, such as in the multiple technical skills of playing badminton, it is usually a challenging task due to the difficulty of feature extraction from the sensor data. As a kind of end-to-end approach, deep neural networks have the capacity of automatic feature learning and extracting. However, most current studies on sensor-based badminton activity recognition adopt CNN-based architectures, which lack the ability of capturing temporal information and global signal comprehension. To overcome these shortcomings, we propose a deep learning framework which combines the convolutional layers, LSTM structure, and self-attention mechanism together. Specifically, this framework can automatically extract the local features of the sensor signals in time domain, take the LSTM structure for processing the badminton activity data, and focus attention on the information that is essential to the badminton activity recognition task. It is demonstrated by the experimental results on an actual badminton single sensor dataset that our proposed framework has obtained a badminton activity recognition (37 classes) accuracy of 97.83%, which outperforms the existing methods, and also has the advantages of lower training time and faster convergence.</summary><hostname>Semantic Scholar</hostname><publisher>Sensors 2023, 23, 8373</publisher><author_list><author name="Jingyang Deng" affiliation="School of Mathematical Sciences and LMAM, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China" /><author name="Shuyi Zhang" affiliation="School of Mathematical Sciences and LMAM, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China" /><author name="Jinwen Ma" affiliation="School of Mathematical Sciences and LMAM, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China" /></author_list><url>https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/fed2/4ceca4c04e66ed1332791c02cbccd25975d5.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年10月10日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:101"><title>Development and Training Strategy of Badminton Action Recognition System Under the Background of Artificial Intelligence</title><summary>To improve the intelligence level of badminton training and match analysis, this study discusses a badminton action recognition system based on deep learning. In the experimental section, the performance of three mainstream models—Spatial-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ST-GCN), Vision-Attention Transformer for Real-time Motion Recognition (VATRM), and Multi-Modal Network for Sports Action Recognition (MM-Net)—is compared from two dimensions: recognition performance and computational efficiency. The experimental results show that the optimized system achieves accuracies of 0.943, 0.967, and 0.912, higher than other comparison models. Additionally, in terms of F1 score, the optimized system scores 0.902 in the defense and transition action groups, significantly outperforming MM-Net (0.864) and ST-GCN (0.878). In terms of computational efficiency, the inference times of the optimized system are 12.4ms, 10.8ms, and 13.1ms, faster than ST-GCN and MM-Net, with memory usage as low as 487MB, 452MB, and 501MB, making it suitable for real-time mobile applications. Therefore, this study contributes to intelligent sports training, sports data analysis, and badminton technique optimization.</summary><hostname>IEEE Xplore</
