problem: Research for me how to improve the Static Noise Margin of SRAM (Static Random Access Memory) through advancements in chip manufacturing processes, to make SRAM storage signals more stable and less susceptible to bit flips?
final_response:
<think>
I will synthesize the gathered evidence into a structured report focused on manufacturing-process-driven improvements for SRAM static noise margin (SNM). I will organize the report around technology platform choices (bulk vs. SOI), device architecture (FinFETs, UTB SOI, FD-SOI, double gate), process design techniques (body bias, β-ratio tuning, back-gating), and process-variation-aware design (corner strategies, monitors). For each section, I will back key claims with citations to the sources already retrieved, prioritizing localized studies and measured results. I will also include practical guidance and quantitative examples (percentage SNM gains, yield improvements, write-current boosts) where available.
</think>

<answer>SRAM Static Noise Margin (SNM) and Bit-Flip Robustness by Manufacturing-Process Advancements
Overview and Motivation
As CMOS scales below 32nm, SRAM stability degrades due to increased dopant fluctuations, gate-edge and fin-line-edge roughness (LER), SCE, and mismatch. These variations worsen SNM variability and raise single-event upset (SEU) and thermal challenges, pushing yield and reliability concerns. Process innovations—such as SOI platforms, advanced FinFET designs, and variation-aware biasing—directly improve electrostatic control, suppress VTH fluctuations, and stabilize SRAM signals. Below is a structured, data-driven review of process-based SNM and bit-flip resilience improvements.

Technology Platform Choices: SOI vs. Bulk
SOI platforms (including FD-SOI and UTB SOI) provide superior electrostatic integrity and reduced SCE compared to bulk CMOS, which translates to more stable SRAM SNM and better yield at aggressive nodes.
- Elimination of channel dopants and suppression of RDF- and LER-induced variations in FD-SOI improve SNM while boosting write current and SRAM yield. For the same cell area (~0.07µm²), comparable SNM can be achieved with ~30% higher write current, and yield is enhanced by >2σ. <cite id="31"></cite>
- Intrinsic-channel SOI (IC-SOI) mitigates dopant-induced VTH fluctuations critical at 25nm and below; optimized back bias further suppresses VTH variations for single-gate IC-SOI FETs. <cite id="23"></cite>

FinFET Architectures and LER Mitigation
FinFETs inherently improve gate control and SCE suppression, enhancing SRAM stability at sub-50nm nodes. However, fin LER and other stochastic shape fluctuations introduce device mismatch and SNM variability that must be addressed in process and design.
- FinFET SRAMs demonstrate excellent stability and leakage control down to LG=20nm, but LER-induced fin shape fluctuations cause increased average VTH and reduced average ION, increasing SNM variability. Ensemble Monte Carlo and TCAD studies quantify these impacts and propose equivalent-fin-width modeling and sensitivity-aware design to reduce expensive Monte Carlo simulations for FinFET-SRAM integration. <cite id="41"></cite>
- In 55nm FinFET SRAMs, resist- vs. spacer-defined fins show that spacer-defined fins have ~2.5× higher SNM variability at VDD=1.2V due to short-range LER, highlighting the importance of process control over fin geometry for SRAM yield. <cite id="3102ed852a87-2"></cite>
- Non-correlated fin LER (across fins) has a larger impact on characteristics fluctuation than correlated LER in trapezoidal bulk FinFETs, emphasizing the need for uniform lithography and spacer processes to minimize SRAM cell-to-cell mismatch. <cite id="3102ed852a87-3"></cite>

Process Design Techniques for SNM and Yield
Beyond device architecture, process tuning and circuit-level design choices directly raise SNM and reduce bit-flip susceptibility.
- Body biasing load, access, and driver transistors in SOI SRAMs suppresses VTH variations and improves pull-up drive, demonstrably increasing write and read margins. At 65nm SOI, Advanced ABC technology increases SNM by 27% at 32nm and 49% at 22nm nodes. <cite id="30"></cite>
- Back-gating in UTB SOI SRAMs (pull-up transistors with positive back-gate bias; pull-down/pass-gate with negative bias) increases pull-up strength and decreases pass-gate strength, significantly improving RSNM variation without substantial RSNM loss. <cite id="2b486562f10b-0"></cite>
- Beta-ratio tuning (increasing NMOS/PMOS current matching) modestly raises SNM and has limited effect on SNM variability in subthreshold UTB SOI; thus, back-gating is more effective than β-ratio alone for subthreshold SRAMs. <cite id="2b486562f10b-0"></cite>
- Negative bit-line (VBL) and boosted word-line (VWL) biases are more effective than lowering cell supply to improve write SNM (WSNM), with negative VBL providing larger WSNM gains. <cite id="2b486562f10b-0"></cite>
- Independent gate operation in FinFETs enables asymmetric gate control to tune pull-up/pull-down strengths for margin enhancement, a key enabler of stable SRAM at sub-20nm nodes. <cite id="1bd2c1cf0d9f-3"></cite>

Process-Corner and Variability-Aware Design
To ensure robust SNM across PVT corners and process tails, SRAMs must be designed and characterized under worst-case process corners and yield-aware conditions.
- Process-corner SNM behavior varies by cell: SS corners raise NMOS VTH and lower PMOS VTH, reducing SNM; FF corners lower NMOS VTH and raise PMOS VTH, increasing SNM. FS and SF corners have mixed impacts, with FS generally improving write ability while degrading read stability. <cite id="5af81c6203b2-2"></cite>
- Yield-aware design shows that to achieve 99% yield, SNM must be set conservatively in the high-sigma tail; conversely, a modest SNM reduction can significantly improve yield, underscoring the need for process-margin budgets and yield modeling. <cite id="5af81c6203b2-3"></cite>
- SRAM-specific SOMM (Stochastic Operational Mismatch Margin) corners provide a more accurate way to capture mismatch-induced margin degradation than traditional PVT corners, guiding layout and process tuning for yield. <cite id="5af81c6203b2-0"></cite>

On-Chip Body-Bias Monitors and Dynamic Biasing
To counter process-induced VTH shifts and SCE tails, on-die body-bias monitors enable real-time PVT compensation, improving SNM and reducing bit-flip risk without large standby current penalties.
- Independent N- and P-process monitors correct die-as-fabricated process corners, reducing delay and leakage standard deviation by ~74% in ring oscillators and improving SRAM yield. <cite id="35c1ce42670a-2"></cite>
- In FD-SOI and multi-Vt FinFETs, back-bias selection at 6σ yield minimizes minimum operating voltage (Vmin) while maintaining sufficient SNM, balancing performance and reliability. <cite id="35c1ce42670a-1"></cite>
- Mixed body-bias generation circuits that fix Ids and Vt across temperature improve SRAM SNM and enable sub-1V operation; a 4-kb SRAM prototype showed ~100mV lower VDD at -40°C with stable margins. <cite id="adfa2067caa9-0"></cite>

Practical Guidance for Process Engineers
To improve SRAM SNM and bit-flip robustness through manufacturing processes:
1. Choose SOI platforms (UTB or FD-SOI) to suppress SCE and RDF, reduce LER sensitivity, and stabilize SRAM margins. FD-SOI can deliver ~30% higher write current with comparable SNM and >2σ yield improvement for aggressive nodes. <cite id="31"></cite>
2. Optimize FinFET geometry and lithography to minimize fin LER and shape fluctuations; prefer resist-defined fins over spacer-defined to reduce SNM variability at 55nm and below. <cite id="3102ed852a87-2"></cite>
3. Implement process-tunable back-gating in UTB SOI and asymmetric gate biasing in FinFETs to raise pull-up strength and lower pass-gate impact, improving RSNM variation and WSNM without large current penalties. <cite id="2b486562f10b-0"></cite>
4. Tune β-ratio and supply/bias schemes (negative VBL, boosted VWL) to complement body biasing and maximize SNM under supply/voltage constraints. <cite id="2b486562f10b-0"></cite>
5. Use SOI body bias monitors and dynamic biasing to correct local PVT corners and SCE tails, improving SNM stability across temperature and process windows. <cite id="35c1ce42670a-2"></cite>
6. Characterize SRAM under SOMM and standard PVT corners, and apply yield-aware margin budgets to balance SNM and area/power targets. <cite id="5af81c6203b2-0"></cite><cite id="5af81c6203b2-2"></cite><cite id="5af81c6203b2-3"></cite>
7. Monitor and control fin geometry uniformity and spacer processes to reduce cell-to-cell mismatch and hold/read stability degradation from non-correlated fin LER. <cite id="3102ed852a7-3"></cite>

Summary of Process-Driven SNM Improvements
- SOI platforms (UTB, FD-SOI): Suppressed SCE and RDF; improved SNM consistency and yield. <cite id="31"></cite><cite id="23"></cite>
- FinFET architectures: Better gate control and leakage; stable margins at sub-20nm, but require LER-aware design. <cite id="1bd2c1cf0d9f-3"></cite><cite id="41"></cite>
- Body biasing (load, access, driver): 27–49% SNM gains at 32–22nm SOI; back-gating reduces RSNM variation. <cite id="30"></cite><cite id="2b486562f10b-0"></cite>
- Beta-ratio tuning: Modest SNM lift; back-gating more effective in subthreshold. <cite id="2b486562f10b-0"></cite>
- Supply/bias schemes: Negative VBL/boosted VWL improve WSNM more than lower VDD. <cite id="2b486562f10b-0"></cite>
- Process-corner design: SS lowers SNM; FF raises it; FS/SF require careful margin planning. <cite id="5af81c6203b2-2"></cite>
- Yield-aware design: Trade SNM for yield or vice versa using yield models and SOMM corners. <cite id="5af81c6203b2-3"></cite><cite id="5af81c6203b2-0"></cite>
- On-die body bias monitors: Reduce delay/leakage variation and stabilize SRAM margins across PVT. <cite id="35c1ce42670a-2"></cite>

By integrating these process innovations—SOI platforms, FinFET architectures with LER-aware lithography, back-gating and β-ratio tuning, dynamic body biasing with monitors, and yield-aware corner strategies—SRAM SNM and bit-flip robustness can be significantly improved across advanced nodes.</answer>

Abstract
This paper presents that Advanced Actively Body-bias Controlled (Advanced ABC) technology contributes to enhancing operation margins of SRAMs. Significant enhancement of Static Noise Margin (SNM) is successfully realized by using a body bias of load transistors while suppressing threshold-voltage variations for the first time. It is demonstrated that the write and read margins of 65nm-node SOI SRAMs are improved by the Advanced ABC technology. Furthermore, it is found that the SNM is enhanced by 27% for 32nm and 49% for 22nm node. It is summarized that this technology is one of ountermeasures for emerging generations. c
Introduction
Silicon technology faces scaling barriers. This is because increase of performance variations due to dopant fluctuations and size fluctuations drastically reduces operation margins especially for ultra-high-density SRAMs [1]. It is reported that high-speed and low-voltage operation is demonstrated by using ABC technology [2-3]. To enhance operation margins for 32nm node and beyond LSTP devices, we developed Advanced ABC technology with the body bias of load, access and driver transistors. We demonstrate robustness of the Advanced ABC technology by investigating operation margins.
Experiments
The partially depleted SOI technology is fabricated with hybrid trench isolation featuring full trench isolation and partial trench isolation. We used 2M-bit SRAMs with 65nm SOI process to verify the Advanced ABC technology. The cell size of the SRAM is \(0.54 um^{2}\) . The thickness of the SOI is 100nm. The SNM depending on technology node is also analyzed by using simulations.
Results and Discussion
A. Investigation of transistor characteristics with body bias
Figure 1 shows transistor characteristics for partially depleted SOI NMOSFETs with high-stress SiN liner. The drain voltage is 1.2V. The body bias considering dynamic threshold voltage improves the drain current by 23% at the off current of 0.1nA/um. Figure 2 shows threshold-voltage lowering depending on the body bias. The differences of threshold voltages are indicated as global variations. The gate length is 33nm. The drain voltage is 0.05V. The difference of the threshold voltages at the body bias of 0.6V is reduced by 15% due to the difference of the body effects. As the body effects of high threshold voltage are larger than those of low one, the difference is reduced at forward bias. It is demonstrated that the forward body bias is effective ay to reduce the variations of the threshold voltages. w
B. Analysis of operation margins of Advanced ABC SRAM
The variations of the transistor performance spoil operation of SRAMs. To resolve the issue, we developed an Advanced ABC SOI SRAM as shown in Fig. 3 and 4. The body potential of the load transistors is changed to improve the read margin. The body bias is executed only during the read operation and is controlled through well taps. The body potential of the access and driver transistors is changed to improve the write margin. *1Changhwan Shin, 1Min Hee Cho, 3,1Yasumasa Tsukamoto, 2Bich-Yen Nguyen, 1Borivoje Nikolić, and 1Tsu-Jae King Liu
1Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720 USA 2
SOITEC, 1010 Land Creek Cove, Austin, Texas, 78746, USA
3Renesas Technology Corp., 4-1 Mizuhara, Itami, Hyogo, 664-0005 Japan
*Phone: +1-510-643-2638, Fax: +1-510-643-2636, E-mail: shinch@eecs.berkeley.edu
Abstract
The performance and yield of 6-T SRAM cells implemented in thin-BOX FD-SOI technology vs. bulk technology are compared via 3dimensional (3D) atomistic process and device simulations and analytical modeling for SRAM yield estimation. Performance is enhanced due to the elimination of channel dopants, and variation due to gate-LER and RDF are suppressed, for FD-SOI technology. For the same cell area \((~ 0.07 \mu m^{2})\) ), comparable SNM can be achieved with 30% higher write current, and SRAM yield is enhanced by \(>2 sigma\)
Introduction
Continued bulk MOSFET and SRAM cell area scaling are becoming increasingly difficult due to increased random variation in transistor performance with decreasing gate length ( \((L_{GATE})\) , caused by gate line-edge roughness (LER) and random dopant fluctuations (RDF) [1]. The use of a lightly doped (fully depleted) SOI MOSFET structure with a thin (~10 nm-thick) buried oxide (BOX) and a heavily doped substrate has been reported to be effective for suppressing this variation [2]. The thin-BOX structure (vs. a thick-BOX structure) has been shown to be optimal for SRAM in sub-50nm technology nodes [3]. In this work, the benefits of thin-BOX FD-SOI technology vs. bulk MOSFET technology for improving 6-T SRAM cell yield at the 22nm technology node are assessed, via 3-dimensional (3D) atomistic process and device simulations and analytical modeling for SRAM yield estimation.
Thin-BOX FD-SOI MOSFET Design
Fig. 1a shows a cross-sectional view of an n-channel thin-BOX FD-SOI MOSFET structure simulated in this work. Device parameters are summarized in Table I, and were selected according to [4] for superior short-channel effect control and to allow for effective backbiasing. The structure is fabricated using an implantation-free process to avoid dopant straggling and damage-induced defects in the thin body region [4], to reduce RDF-induced variations. The process uses a lowtemperature, zero-silicon-loss epitaxial growth process to form (faceted) in-situ-doped \((10^{20} ~cm^{-3})\) ) raised-source/drain regions – from which dopants are diffused to form the lightly doped source/drain extensions – to reduce series resistance with minimal increase in sidewall gate capacitance [4]. The gate work function ( \((\Phi_{M})\) ) was selected to achieve the LOP ITRS specification for off-state leakage current ( \((I_{OFF})\) , ~3nA/μm. For comparison, planar bulk MOSFETs with uniform channel doping profile ( \(10^{18} ~cm^{-3}\) boron), doped poly-Si gate (Ф \((\Phi_{M}=\) 4.05eV), and comparable \(I_{OFF}\) were also simulated. Fig. 2 shows the transfer characteristics for n-channel FD-SOI and bulk MOSFETs. The FD-SOI MOSFET exhibits steeper sub-threshold slope (due to negligible depletion capacitance) and higher drive current (due to higher carrier mobility). Table II provides a summary comparison of device performance parameters. A simple analytical model was fit to the simulated current-voltage data (Fig. 2), to allow for fast estimation of SRAM metrics such as read static noise margin (SNM) [5] and write current (Iw) [6].

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="FinFET SRAM Static Noise Margin process variation yield electrostatic integrity double gate stacked gate STT Vt variation SOI UTB SNM variability" search_time="2026年5月10日10时43分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:40"><title>First observation of FinFET specific mismatch behavior and optimization guidelines for SRAM scaling</title><summary>Vₜ-mismatch, and thus SRAM scalability, is greatly improved in narrow SOI FinFETs, with respect to planar bulk, because of their undoped channel and near-ideal gate control. We show by simulations and by measurements that in FinFETs, unlike planar bulk, β-mismatch becomes dominant, leading to radically different SRAM characteristics. By careful process tuning, we demonstrate a substantial reduction in β-mismatch. We show the impact of this novel mismatch behavior on SRAM performance and yield under various optimization strategies and thereby provide guidelines for SRAM design in a FinFET technology.</summary><hostname>Sci-Hub</hostname><author_list><author name="T Mrelle" affiliation="NXP-TSMC Research Center, Kapeldreef 75, 3001 Leuven, Belgium" /><author name="G Curatola" affiliation="IMEC, Belgium" /><author name="A Nackaerts" /><author name="N Collaert" affiliation="IMEC, Belgium" /><author name="Mjh Van Dal" /><author name="G Doornbos" affiliation="NXP Semiconductors, The Netherlands" /><author name="Ts Doorn" affiliation="NXP Semiconductors, The Netherlands" /><author name="P Christie" /><author name="G Vellianitis" /><author name="B Duriez" /><author name="R Duffy" /><author name="Bj Pawlak" /><author name="Fc Voogt" affiliation="NXP Semiconductors, The Netherlands" /><author name="R Rooyackers" affiliation="IMEC, Belgium" /><author name="L Witters" affiliation="IMEC, Belgium" /><author name="M Jurczak" affiliation="IMEC, Belgium" /><author name="Rjp Lander" /></author_list><url>https://zero.sci-hub.se/2241/eb416cf89f1f85dc05351dfc8cef2e43/merelle2008.pdf#navpanes=0&view=FitH</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:41"><title>Fin shape fluctuations in FinFET: Correlation to electrical variability and impact on 6-T SRAM noise margins</title><summary>Threshold voltage (V_T) and drive current (I_ON) variability of low stand-by power (LSTP)-32 nm FinFETs subject to fin line-edge roughness (LER) is investigated through Technology Computer-Aided Design (TCAD) simulations featuring quantum-corrected hydrodynamic transport. Statistical results provided by an ensemble Monte Carlo (MC) approach highlight an increase in the average V_T and a decrease in the average I_ON with respect to sensitivity analysis based predictions. Correlations of fin shape fluctuations to electrical performance are investigated, thus assessing further limitations of sensitivity analysis and proposing better alternatives to the expensive MC approach. An equivalent fin width is calculated, which allows reducing the spread in I_ON scatter plots and highlights relative importance of LER in different fin regions. Simplified device instances with linearly varying fin width are simulated to better assess the impact of local thinning/thickening in the channel, source and drain extensions. Asymmetries in the device behavior are observed upon swapping the taper direction and the critical role of extensions is identified. Moreover, the impact of LER on noise margins of FinFET-based Static Random Access Memories (SRAMs) is investigated, considering the hold, read and write operating modes. Results are compared to published data on fabricated cells with similar device features. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="body bias SRAM SNM write disturbance body drivability PSV body bias monitor test die mode latch-up considerations" search_time="2026年5月10日10时43分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:58"><title>Mixed Body Bias Techniques With Fixed Vt and Ids Generation Circuits</title><summary>There remains a need to improve sub-1-V CMOS VLSIs with respect to variation in transistor behavior. In this paper, to minimize variation in delay and the noise margin of the circuits in processors, we propose several mixed body bias techniques using body bias generation circuits. In these circuits, either the saturation region of the current between source and drain (Ids) or the threshold voltage (Vt) of PMOS/NMOS is permanently fixed, regardless of temperature range or variation in process. A test chip that featured these body bias generation circuits was fabricated using a 130-nm CMOS process with a triple-well structure. The mixed body bias techniques which keep the Ids of the MOS in the decoder and I/O circuits of a register file fixed and maintain the Vt of the MOS in both the memory cell and domino circuits of the register file fixed resulted in positive temperature dependence of delay from -40 °C to 125 °C, 85% reduction of the delay variation compared with normal body bias (NBB) at VDD = 0.8 V. In addition, the results using these techniques show a 100-mV improvement in lower operating voltage compared with NBB at -40 °C on a 4-kb SRAM.</summary><hostname>Semantic Scholar</hostname><publisher>IEEE JOURNAL OF SOLID-STATE CIRCUITS, VOL. 40, NO. 1, JANUARY 2005</publisher><author_list><author name="Masaya Sumita" affiliation="Semiconductor Company, Matsushita Electric Industrial Company, Ltd., Kyoto 617-8520, Japan" /><author name="Shiro Sakiyama" /><author name="Masayoshi Kinoshita" /><author name="Yuta Araki" /><author name="Yuichiro Ikeda" /><author name="Kohei Fukuoka" /></author_list><url>https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Mixed-body-bias-techniques-with-fixed-V-sub-t-and-I-Sumita-Sakiyama/0bfbc0f3a1e1cab3bce0de122f5576a2489a7025</url><publish_time>2005年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:59"><title>High Performance Process Variations Aware Technique for Sub-threshold 8T-SRAM Cell</title><summary>The demand of low power high density integrated circuits is increasing in modern battery operated portable systems. Sub-threshold region of MOS transistors is the most desirable region for energy efficient circuit design. The operating ultra-low power supply voltage is the key design constraint with accurate output performance in sub-threshold region. Degrading of the performance metrics in Static random access memory (SRAM) cell with process variation effects are of major concern in sub-threshold region. In this paper, a boot-strapped driver circuit and a bootstrapped driver dynamic body biasing technique is proposed to assist write operation which improves the write-ability of sub-threshold 8T-SRAM cell under process variations. The bootstrapped driver circuit minimizes the write delay of SRAM cell. The bootstrapped driver dynamic body bias increases the output voltage levels by boosting factor therefore increasing in switching threshold voltage of MOS devices during hold and read operation of SRAM latch. The increment in threshold voltage improves the static noise margin and minimizing the process variation effects. - Product progress and commercial status vary from early-stage pilots to established deployments; some firms (e.g., Intuitive Surgical) are enterprise incumbents; others (e.g., Nimbro@Home) are academic research platforms <cite id="call_4baf1a06f601-1"></cite><cite id="call_50f2a28d66b3-2"></cite>
- Venture funding trends (e.g., $7.2B in 2024) are reported, but firm-level details (especially for non-profiled startups) are sparse; humanoid focus highlighted but not quantified <cite id="call_5a047d9804a6-0"></cite>
- LLM/agent stacks are increasingly integrated (e.g., Nimbro@Home, Helm.ai), but many firms’ technical paths and product progress are described at the stack level rather than concrete products <cite id="call_50f2a28d66b3-2"></cite><cite id="call_751c6e9b88d6-4"></cite></answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Embodied AI survey 2024 robotics startups" search_time="2026年5月10日10时46分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>미국 AI로봇 생태계 분석: 로봇AI 기술 중심으로</title><summary>This study explores the emerging AI robot industry, approached in this research as a domain shaped by the convergence of the AI and robotics sectors. Major U.S. firms are classified into four types based on their technology stacks and business models: (1) vertically integrated, (2) AI platform-driven, (3) robot body-specialized, and (4) robot AI-specialized. Vertically integrated and AI platform-driven firms lead the U.S. and global ecosystems, collaborating with hardware makers and investing in general-purpose RFM companies. U.S. AI firms are expected to strengthen cooperation with Chinese and Korean partners to complement limited robot body capabilities. The evolution of robot intelligence is expected to follow four directions: (1) improved operational accuracy through advanced control intelligence, (2) greater generality via large vision-language-action models, (3) broader applicability across diverse robot forms, and (4) integration of physical, cognitive, and social intelligence for human-robot coexistence. To support this multidirectional evolution, a new robot intelligence architecture must be developed alongside continued technological innovation.</summary><hostname>ETRI</hostname><publisher>전자통신학회논문</publisher><author_list><author name="김상민" affiliation="기술경쟁연구실 책임연구원" /></author_list><url>https://ettrends.etri.re.kr/ettrends/217/0905217023/088-101.%20%EA%B9%80%EC%84%B1%EB%AF%BC_217%ED%98%B8_%EC%B5%9C%EC%A2%85.pdf</url><publish_time>2025年3月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Embodied Perception Interaction, and Cognition for Wearable Robotics: A Survey</title><summary>Wearable robotics, encompassing exoskeletons and other assistive devices, have emerged as promising tools for constructing and augmenting human capabilities in various domains, including healthcare, rehabilitation, and assistive technologies. This review explores the domains of perception, interaction, and cognition in wearable robotics, with a focus on advancing embodied intelligence in these systems. Perception involves the recognition of human motion intentions through sensory signal acquisition, multimodal fusion, and intent recognition. Interaction encompasses various modes of human-robot interaction, ranging from physical interaction control relying on interaction force to human-in-the-loop control methods reliant on human physiological or biomechanical feedback signals. Cognition extends beyond motor function reconstruction, focusing on the cognitive reconstruction of humans, facilitated by sensory feedback and human-machine interface technologies. Several challenges hinder their seamless integration into wearable robotics, including difficulties in signal processing and integration, robot control, bidirectional information transfer, and interface design. Future research efforts should prioritize addressing these challenges to advance embodied intelligence in wearable robotics, leveraging artificial intelligence algorithms to empower exoskeleton technology, designing ergonomic interfaces for enhanced wearer comfort and safety, developing advanced signal processing techniques for accurate interpretation of human biological signals, and integrating multimodal sensing for comprehensive interaction.</summary><hostname>IEEE Xplore</hostname><publisher>IEEE Transactions on Cognitive and Developmental Systems</publisher><author_list><author name="Xiaoyu Wu" /><author name="Jiale Liang" /><author name="Yiang Yu" /><author name="Guoxin Li" /><author name="Gary G. Yen" /><author name="Haoyong Yu" /></author_list><url>https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10682963</url><publish_time>2024年9月18日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:3"><title>Towards Robust and Secure Embodied AI: A Survey on Vulnerabilities and Attacks</title><summary>Embodied AI systems, including robots and autonomous vehicles

problem: 在微电子工艺中，金属薄膜的生长可以使用多种设备，物理气相沉积设备，化学气相沉积设备，电子束蒸发沉积设备，原子层沉积设备和分子束外研设备。为我调研在如今先进制程的芯片工艺中金属薄膜的生长运用到了上面哪几种设备？分别用来沉积什么金属薄膜？为什么选择它们呢？
final_response:
<think>
Plan: Provide a concise, structured report on which deposition technologies are used for metal layers in modern chip manufacturing (focusing on copper, tungsten, cobalt, tantalum/TaN, and tantalum nitride), and explain why. Use sources already retrieved to back claims about ALD conformality, CVD superconformality, sputter seed/barriers, and e-beam niche roles. Keep formatting light with bullet lists and short paragraphs.
</think>

<answer>在先进制程（如3nm及以下）的芯片后端金属化中，主要使用以下设备沉积关键金属薄膜，每种设备对应特定功能层，选择它们是因为工艺需求（如高深宽比填充、界面控制、电阻率、均匀性）与技术优势（如PVD的高沉积速率、ALD的原子级控制、CVD的超级 conformality）的匹配：

物理气相沉积（PVD）设备
- 功能：溅射
- 用途：沉积阻挡/粘附层（如钴、钌）和铜的种子层，以及钨的成核层
- 为什么选它：
  - 提供高沉积速率和良好的台阶覆盖，适合大面积和高深宽比结构的初始成核层（如钨接触孔）<cite id="call_3c67efb9884c-3"></cite><cite id="call_3c67efb9884c-0"></cite>。
  - 在先进节点中，钴作为低电阻率（~6.24 μΩ·cm）屏障材料，其粘附层和种子层依赖溅射以实现良好的铜电镀填充特性，特别是在高深宽比接触中表现更好<cite id="call_3c67efb984c-0"></cite><cite id="call_3c67efb984c-1"></cite>。
  - 溅射靶材在3nm节点需达到原子级工程（纯度7n、晶粒<50μm、缺陷趋近于零），以支撑先进制程的均匀性和可靠性<cite id="call_3c67efb984c-2"></cite>。

化学气相沉积（CVD）设备
- 功能：碘催化CVD、氯化物/羰基CVD、等离子体增强CVD（PECVD）
- 用途：沉积铜（互连）和钨（接触塞/通孔填充）
- 为什么选它：
  - 碘催化CVD铜实现“超级 conformal”填充，可定量建模并适用于细线宽互连，避免电镀中的空洞缺陷，是先进节点铜互连的关键工艺<cite id="call_286af0df168f-1"></cite>。
  - 钨CVD使用WF6与H2/SiH4还原，配合成核层（如脉冲CVD或ALD成核）和高压力沉积，可填充高深宽比接触孔，是钨接触塞的主流方案<cite id="call_9ebcb9f8c4c2-1"></cite><cite id="call_9ebcb9f8c4c2-3"></cite>。
  - 氯化物/羰基CVD适用于钼、镍、钨等金属，提供灵活的前驱体选择以适应不同金属沉积需求<cite id="call_286af0df168f-2"></cite>。
  - PECVD允许低温沉积，对热敏感基板重要，也可用于有机涂层，扩展了CVD在先进工艺中的应用边界<cite id="call_286af0df168f-4"></cite>。

电子束蒸发（电子束蒸发）设备
- 功能：蒸发源
- 用途：沉积金属粘附层、铜种子层（某些方案）及高熔点金属（如铂、金）
- 为什么选它：
  - 在半导体制造中用于金属化层沉积，尤其适合高熔点金属，且能提供高纯度和良好均匀性，适用于特定粘附层和种子层需求<cite id="call_36a35fdc816f-0"></cite><cite id="call_36a35fdc816f-2"></cite>。
  - 在电子束蒸发系统中，对金属化层的厚度和成分控制精确，确保互连的电性能，是先进制程中某些金属沉积的补充手段<cite id="call_36a35fdc816f-0"></cite>。

原子层沉积（ALD）设备
- 功能：原子层沉积（含等离子体增强）
- 用途：沉积阻挡层（如TaN）、粘附层（如Co）、铜种子层及钨的成核层
- 为什么选它：
  - ALD提供亚埃级厚度控制、超高 conformality 和 pinhole-free 膜层，特别适合复杂3D结构（如高深宽比通孔），是先进节点低接触电阻和可靠互连的关键技术<cite id="call_b885a049ad09-0"></cite><cite id="call_b885a049ad09-1"></cite>。
  - ALD TaN 已广泛用于14nm及以下节点，相比PVD可降低接触电阻（28%左右），并改善通孔填充；PEALD TaN 在32nm线宽下显著降低电阻，尽管其本征电阻率较高，但通过工艺优化（如PVD后处理）可进一步提升性能<cite id="call_2b5db3031620-3"></cite><cite id="call_2b5db3031620-4"></cite><cite id="call_2b5db3031620-2"></cite>。
  - ALD铜在钴粘附层上可实现连续、纳米晶种子层，改善铜在SiO2、Si3N4和TaN上的成核，确保电连续性<cite id="call_2b5db3031620-1"></cite>。
  - ALD钨在接触孔中通过SiH4或B2H6成核，结合CVD填充，可解决高深宽比结构的填充挑战，是先进节点钨接触塞的成熟方案<cite id="call_9ebcb9f8c4c2-1"></cite>。

分子束外延（MBE）设备
- 功能：分子束外延
- 用途：沉积金属薄膜（如高纯度单晶金属层）
- 为什么选它：
  - MBE是超高真空下的物理沉积方法，适用于单晶外延生长，沉积速率慢（1–300 nm/min）但能实现高度取向的单晶薄膜，适合特定高纯度金属层或界面控制需求<cite id="call_5672f90817be-0"></cite><cite id="call_5672f90817be-3"></cite>。
  - 在半导体制造中，MBE可用于沉积高纯度金属层（如用于接触或互连的特定金属），但因其沉积速率慢和设备成本高，通常用于研究或特定高要求的界面层，而非主流互连金属沉积<cite id="call_5672f90817be-4"></cite>。

总结：先进节点互连金属沉积的典型设备组合是
- PVD（溅射）：钴/钌屏障粘附层和铜种子层，钨成核层；
- CVD（碘催化、氯化物/羰基、PECVD）：铜互连和钨接触塞填充；
- ALD（含PEALD）：TaN阻挡层、钴粘附层、铜种子层、钨成核层；
- 电子束蒸发：高熔点金属粘附层或特定种子层；
- MBE：高纯度单晶金属层（研究/特定界面）。
选择依据是：PVD提供高沉积速率和良好台阶覆盖；CVD实现超级 conformal 填充；ALD控制原子级厚度和保形性；电子束蒸发适用于特定高熔点金属；MBE用于单晶外延需求。这些设备协同满足先进节点对低电阻率、高填充、低接触电阻和复杂3D结构的严苛要求<cite id="call_3c67efb9884c-3"></cite><cite id="call_286af0df168f-1"></cite><cite id="call_9ebcb9f8c4c2-1"></cite><cite id="call_b885a049ad09-0"></cite><cite id="call_5672f90817be-4"></cite>。
</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="2023 2024 copper interconnect ALD CVD sputter cobalt tantalum tungsten 3nm 2nm manufacturing process report TSMC N3 Samsung 3nm metal deposition" search_time="2026年5月10日10时49分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:27"><title>(Invited) Current and Future Applications of ALD in Micro-Electronics</title><summary>This paper describes the status of current and future applications of Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) and Plasma Enhanced ALD (PEALD) in the field of Micro-electronics. Substantial expansion of the ALD market is expected in the coming decade, both in IC manufacturing, but also in adjacent non-IC applications. Several techniques will be described that work around the relatively slow deposition rate of ALD.</summary><hostname>IOPscience</hostname><publisher>ECS Transactions</publisher><author_list><author name="Ivo J Raaijmakers" affiliation="ASM, PO Box 60615, 1320AE Almere, the Netherlands" /></author_list><url>https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1149/1.3633649/meta</url><publish_time>2011年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:28"><title>ALD as Enabling Technology for the Next Generation of Microprocessors</title><summary>As dimensions of microprocessor components continue to shrink, new and enabling technologies are required to enable the next generation of (sub)nanometer size features and components. With this aim, the industry has long aspired to gain molecular and even atomic-level control over architectural assembly. Building from the basic principles of chemistry and physics, one of today’s technological forefronts in self-assembly and atomic-scale placement is being realized via ALD. Herein, the advances in ALD/CVD with a focus on BEOL interconnect development will be reviewed. Architectural, materials, and integration platforms (barrier, adhesion, seed) will be reviewed. original_data.problem: 在微电子工艺中，金属薄膜的生长可以使用多种设备，物理气相沉积设备，化学气相沉积设备，电子束蒸发沉积设备，原子层沉积设备和分子束外研设备。为我调研在如今先进制程的芯片工艺中金属薄膜的生长运用到了上面哪几种设备？分别用来沉积什么金属薄膜？为什么选择它们呢？
original_data.additional_instructions: Please write a well structured, data-driven report on the given research question, and add citations when needed.

problem: Summarize the global investments, key initiatives, and outputs related to Artificial Intelligence (AI) by major international consulting firms (e.g., Big Four, Accenture, MBB, IBM, Capgemini). Cover aspects such as AI-driven products/services, client case studies, application scenarios, strategic directions, and talent development programs.
final_response:
<think>
I will synthesize a structured report on global AI investments, products/services, case studies, talent programs, and strategic directions across Big Four (PwC), MBB (McKinsey, BCG, Deloitte), and other consultancies (Accenture, Bain). I will cite specific documents already retrieved, and where evidence is sparse, I will note uncertainty without inventing new sources.
</think>

<answer><title>Global AI Investments, Products, and Outputs by Major International Consulting Firms</title>

Overview and investment scale
- Financial services is a leading sector for AI investment, with 2023 global outlays hitting $35 billion and projected to reach $97 billion by 2027; the focus is shifting from efficiency to revenue growth via AI. <cite id="call_26f7e9146523-0"></cite>
- McKinsey estimates that generative AI alone could add $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion annually across 63 use cases, roughly 15–40% more than prior AI value, with implications across industries including banking, high tech, and life sciences. <cite id="call_f39eb192ddf8-1"></cite>
- Accenture reports investing $3 billion in AI to accelerate client reinvention, building on over 1,450 patents and hundreds of client solutions at scale. <cite id="call_b539dcf0202f-0"></cite>

Big Four firms

PwC
- Products and services:
  - Proprietary AI-assisted financial statement disclosure checking (leveraging cloud-based machine learning and advanced statistics) to augment audit procedures and support sustainability/climate reporting, reducing turnaround times and improving quality. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-0"></cite>
  - Low-code AI solutions for ESG reporting automation (e.g., CSRD.ai Manager on SAP BTP), streamlining data collection, KPI calculation, and report generation to meet evolving compliance requirements. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-2"></cite>
  - Conversational interfaces and natural language processing for reporting automation, enabling requestors to interact via chatbots and retrieve data mapped against banking-specific ontologies. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-1"></cite>
  - Generative AI chatbots tailored to advisory workflows (e.g., a GPT-4–based tool developed with Harvey), deployed across tax, legal, and HR to accelerate deal-making and internal processes. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-4"></cite>
- Case studies and client outcomes:
  - Banking and financial services pilots highlight a phased approach to responsible AI, starting with secure environments, prioritized use cases (e.g., private ChatGPT apps, customer service/sales solutions, and software development lifecycle tools), and scaling into workflows, with data quality as the top concern for generative AI. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-3"></cite>
  - ESG reporting automation demonstrably improves efficiency and accuracy, enabling audit-grade ESG reporting and confident compliance with evolving standards. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-2"></cite>

McKinsey & Company
- Products and services:
  - Digital McKinsey offers AI-enabled transformations and digital-first solutions, including frameworks and tools for deploying generative AI responsibly and at scale. <cite id="call_fa45eba75081-0"></cite>
  - McKinsey Analytics provides data-driven insights to assess AI impact, feasibility, and market dynamics, supporting clients in deploying AI across sectors. <cite id="call_d2d3d5078690-0"></cite>
  - Collaboration with Salesforce to develop generative AI solutions for field service (e.g., diagnostics and resolution support), evaluating 30+ use cases to enhance customer service and first-time issue resolution. <cite id="call_fa45eba75081-2"></cite>
- Case studies and client outcomes:
  - A global bank’s contact-center and KYC pilots illustrate real business impact, with rigorous selection and risk prioritization yielding measurable results in customer service and compliance operations. <cite id="call_fa45eba75081-0"></cite>
  - Internal productivity tools (e.g., a generative AI assistant for McKinsey consultants) report high adoption (72%), time savings (up to 30%), and high monthly prompt volumes (500,000+), underscoring rapid uptake and tangible efficiency gains. <cite id="call_fa45eba75081-1"></cite>
  - Field service pilots show AI tools can significantly speed diagnosis and resolution, improving customer experience and first-time fix rates. <cite id="call_fa45eba75081-2"></cite>

MBB firms

BCG
- Products and services:
  - BCG’s Henderson Institute explores AI’s economic impacts and workforce implications, including learning and development in the age of generative AI and the emergence of future AI talent pools. <cite id="call_d1938c196ca1-4"></cite>
  - Industry-specific reports (e.g., asset management) detail AI’s role in boosting efficiency, personalization, and unlocking private market potential, with strategic guidance for adoption and scaling. <cite id="call_d1938c196ca1-0"></cite>
- Case studies and client outcomes:
  - Public-sector pilots in the GCC estimate generative AI could yield over $65 billion in annual productivity gains by 2033, highlighting opportunities in citizen services and workforce productivity. <cite id="call_d1938c196ca1-3"></cite>
  - Asset management industry analyses show AI can transform the value chain, enhance personalization, and unlock private market potential, with firms increasingly prioritizing AI investments. <cite id="call_d1938c196ca1-0"></cite>

Deloitte
- Products and services:
  - Deloitte’s Center for Technology, Media & Telecommunications provides research and insights on AI’s workforce effects, including how AI augments human performance and reshapes skills and roles. <cite id="call_edc21cb52e4e-0"></cite>
  - Reports on emerging technologies in actuarial science detail AI applications for risk modeling, fraud detection, pricing, and underwriting, with practical use cases across insurance and finance. <cite id="call_edc21cb52e4e-1"></cite>
  - Global Human Capital Trends reports examine how new technologies (including AI) are blurring the boundary between humans and machines, emphasizing human-centric, augmented work models. <cite id="call_0f563a479206-0"></cite>
- Case studies and client outcomes:
  - Luxury industry pilots show limited adoption of analytical AI but growing testing of generative AI use cases, with barriers including expertise, data management, IP concerns, and strategic prioritization. <cite id="call_e91618a737ca-0"></cite>
  - Insurance case studies demonstrate that prioritizing AI with clear governance and business alignment can deliver seamless digital-first experiences, countering the common “95% haven’t seen measurable impact” challenge. <cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-0"></cite>

Accenture
- Products and services:
  - Accenture’s AI offerings span generative AI R&D via the Generative AI Center of Excellence, large language model and AI agent experimentation, and hundreds of client solutions across marketing, retail, security, and back-office operations. <cite id="call_b539dcf0202f-0"></cite>
  - AI democratization initiatives (e.g., “AI for Everyone”) aim to make AI accessible for business transformation and operational reinvention, emphasizing practical adoption and outcomes. <cite id="call_b539dcf0202f-3"></cite>
- Case studies and client outcomes:
  - Financial services industry reports indicate that 32–39% of work has high automation potential and 34–37% high augmentation potential, with firms increasingly allocating budgets to AI to drive both efficiency and revenue growth. <cite id="call_26f7e9146523-0"></cite>
  - Software developer productivity studies (e.g., GitHub Copilot field experiments) show generative AI can increase completed tasks by ~26%, improving coding productivity across large firms. <cite id="call_26f7e9146523-0"></cite>
  - Accenture’s Technology Vision surveys highlight broad executive optimism about generative AI’s long-term value, with 97% of respondents viewing it as a “game-changer” and prioritizing near-term exploration and investment. <cite id="call_b539dcf0202f-4"></cite>

Other consultancies

Bain & Company
- Products and services:
  - Digital practice and AI/GenAI offerings include frameworks for scaling generative AI, responsible AI governance, and pilot-to-scale roadmaps tailored to industries such as insurance, pharma, and financial services. <cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-1"></cite>
  - Industry-specific insights and case studies provide ROI-focused guidance on AI adoption, including productivity and cost-savings targets and implementation best practices. <cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-2"></cite>
- Case studies and client outcomes:
  - Insurance pilots demonstrate that disciplined AI implementation can deliver measurable outcomes in customer experience, automation, and human expertise integration, helping firms beat the “95%” adoption gap. <cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-0"></cite>
  - Pharma sector surveys indicate strong executive confidence in GenAI value, with 40% of executives incorporating expected savings into 2024 budgets and 60% setting productivity/cost-saving targets. <cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-2"></cite>
  - Banking pilots report potential cost reductions within 2–3 years, improved customer satisfaction, and indirect employee engagement gains from generative AI assistants in branch settings. <cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-3"></cite>
  - Software development studies show that AI-based coding assistants can meet/exceed goals for speed-to-market and code quality, with strong executive satisfaction rates. <cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-4"></cite>

Across firms: common strategic directions
- Governance and responsible AI: Establish secure environments, prioritize use cases, and embed AI into workflows while refining governance and data quality practices. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-3"></cite>
- Workforce augmentation and reskilling:
  - McKinsey and Deloitte emphasize human-centric, augmented work models where AI handles up to 60–70% of worker activities, with implications for skills, roles, and transitions. <cite id="call_edc21cb52e4e-0"></cite><cite id="call_f39eb192ddf8-1"></cite>
  - Upskilling imperatives and boundaryless workforce strategies highlight the need to build adjacent skills and prepare for accelerated automation curves. <cite id="call_0f563a479206-0"></cite>
- Industry focus and ROI:
  - Financial services, consumer goods, insurance, pharma, and public-sector clients report measurable efficiency, customer experience, and productivity gains, alongside strategic investments to capture revenue opportunities. <cite id="call_26f7e9146523-0"></cite><cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-0"></cite><cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-2"></cite><cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-3"></cite>
- Collaboration and ecosystems:
  - Partnerships with cloud providers (Salesforce, SAP), open models (Harvey, GPT-4), and industry consortia support tailored pilots, secure environments, and scalable integrations. <cite id="call_fa45eba75081-2"></cite><cite id="call_163ef662c3af-4"></cite>

Talent development programs
- Upskilling and reskilling:
  - Deloitte underscores the “Upskilling Imperative” to build future-ready workforces for the AI age, addressing skills gaps and preparing workers for augmented roles. <cite id="call_0f563a479206-1"></cite>
  - McKinsey’s internal tools and frameworks show high adoption and productivity gains, reinforcing the value of AI literacy and tool fluency among consultants. <cite id="call_fa45eba75081-1"></cite>
- Learning and development:
  - BCG Henderson Institute analyses highlight the growing importance of human skills (problem framing, collaboration, creativity) amid AI integration and the need to cultivate tomorrow’s AI leaders. <cite id="call_d1938c196ca1-4"></cite>
- Workforce transformation:
  - Global Human Capital Trends emphasize boundaryless work models where AI enhances team performance, requiring new HR and leadership approaches to redeploy worker time and capabilities. <cite id="call_0f563a479206-0"></cite>

Application scenarios and use cases
- Customer experience and sales/marketing:
  - Chatbots, personalization tools, and content generation improve engagement, satisfaction, and conversion, with measurable impacts in banking, insurance, and consumer-facing sectors. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-3"></cite><cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-0"></cite>
- Operational efficiency:
  - RPA/AI in claims processing, pricing, and KYC reduces errors, speeds cycles, and improves fraud detection, with pilots reporting cost reductions and faster turnaround. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-3"></cite><cite id="call_26f7e9146523-0"></cite>
- Software engineering and R&D:
  - Coding assistants and prompt engineering tools accelerate development, improve code quality, and shorten time-to-market, with strong executive satisfaction and productivity lifts. <cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-4"></cite>
- Reporting and compliance:
  - AI-assisted disclosure checking and ESG reporting automation reduce manual effort, enhance accuracy, and support sustainability reporting at audit-grade standards. <cite id="call_163ef662c3af-0"></cite><cite id="call_163ef662c3af-2"></cite>
- Field service and support:
  - Diagnostic AI tools improve first-time resolution, reduce call times, and elevate customer experience in industrial and consumer service contexts. <cite id="call_fa45eba75081-2"></cite>

Conclusion
Major international consulting firms are investing heavily in AI research, products, and client transformations, with a clear emphasis on generative AI, responsible governance, and workforce augmentation. Evidence from PwC, McKinsey, BCG, Deloitte, and Accenture shows measurable efficiency, customer experience, and productivity gains across financial services, insurance, pharma, and public-sector clients, alongside strategic initiatives to reskill and prepare for AI-driven work models. While firm-specific details on pricing, proprietary models, and full internal productivity metrics are not widely published, the aggregated case studies and reports indicate a strong industry consensus on AI’s value and the importance of disciplined implementation and governance. <cite id="call_26f7e9146523-0"></cite><cite id="call_f39eb192ddf8-1"></cite><cite id="call_b539dcf0202f-0"></cite><cite id="call_163ef662c3af-3"></cite><cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-0"></cite><cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-2"></cite><cite id="call_c4eb7b2ac68b-3"></cite><cite id="call_edc21cb52e4e-0"></cite><cite id="call_0f563a479206-0"></cite><cite id="call_d1938c196ca1-4"></cite></answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Accenture AI Global Impact Report 2023 investments client cases AI products services" search_time="2026年5月10日10时49分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services</title><summary>This paper, the first in a series on artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, draws on insights from roundtable discussions with over 100 financial services executives worldwide, as well as from the latest external research on AI. As exploration of AI's far-reaching impact continues, the aim of this paper is to provide an overview of the state of AI in financial services, along with key open questions and potential risks to be considered by business leaders, policy-makers and customers. Key insights: Financial services businesses with their data-rich and language-heavy operations are uniquely positioned to capitalize on the developments of AI and have been doing so for years. More recently, with the developments of generative AI (genAI), research indicates that 32-39% of the work performed across capital markets, insurance and banking businesses has high potential to be fully automated and 34-37% holds high augmentation potential. This has driven a significant increase in new AI investment. In 2023, financial services firms spent $35 billion on AI, with projected investments across banking, insurance, capital markets and payments businesses expected to reach $97 billion by 2027. With this sizeable investment, financial services are one of the most heavily invested industries in AI, with prominent use cases across the enterprise where automation and machine learning are streamlining tasks, reducing operational costs and improving accuracy. With much of the existing AI adoption in financial services largely focused on driving efficiency, the attention of business leaders is now shifting towards revenue growth opportunities. Backend applications will continue to be important; in addition, approximately 70% of financial services executives believe AI will directly contribute to revenue growth in the coming years. The rapid maturing of AI, coupled with an expanding list of applicable uses, is pushing the industry towards reinvention at an unprecedented - and often uncomfortable - speed and scale. As technological developments accelerate, the integration of various emerging innovations, such as small language models, AI agents and quantum computing will drive both innovation and uncertainty across financial services. This shift will continue to challenge business leaders, policy-makers and regulators. Looking ahead, financial services stakeholders must increase collaboration to address key risks such as data transparency, privacy, cybersecurity and the spread of misinformation, while also closing policy gaps that could hinder the use and innovation of AI. Overcoming these challenges is essential to ensuring that AI can be leveraged effectively and responsibly across the industry, now and in the future.</summary><hostname>SSRN</hostname><publisher>World Economic Forum</publisher><url>https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm?abstractid=3366846</url><publish_time>2025年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>The Effects of Generative AI on High Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers</title><summary>This study evaluates the impact of generative AI on software developer productivity by analyzing data from three randomized controlled trials conducted at Microsoft, Accenture, and an anonymous Fortune 100 electronics manufacturing company. This would increase the impact of all artificial intelligence by 15 to 40 percent. This estimate would roughly double if we include the impact of embedding generative AI into software that is currently used for other tasks beyond those use cases. 2. About 75 percent of the value that generative AI use cases could deliver falls across four areas: Customer experience, marketing and sales, software engineering, and R&D. Across 16 business functions, we examined 63 use cases in which the technology can address specific business challenges in ways that produce one or more measurable outcomes. Examples include generative AI’s ability to support interactions with customers, generate creative content for marketing and sales, and draft computer code based on natural-language prompts, among many other tasks. 3. Generative AI will have a significant impact across all industry sectors. Banking, high tech, and life sciences are among the industries that could see the biggest impact as a percentage of their revenues from generative AI. Across the banking industry, for example, the technology could deliver value equal to an additional $200 billion to $340 billion annually if the use cases were fully implemented. In retail and consumer packaged goods, the potential impact is also significant at $400 billion to $660 billion a year. 4. Generative AI has the potential to change the anatomy of work, augmenting the capabilities of individual workers by automating the capabilities of individual workers by automating some of their individual activities. Current generative AI and other technologies have the potential to automate work activities that absorb 60 to 70 percent of employees’ time today. In contrast, we previously estimated that technology has the potential to automate half of the time employees spend working.¹ The acceleration in the potential for technical automation due to generative AI’s increased ability to understand and natural language, which is required for work activities that account for 25 percent of total work time. Thus, generative AI has more impact on knowledge work associated with occupations that have higher wages and educational requirements than on other types of work. 5. The pace of workforce transformation is likely to accelerate, given increases in the potential for technical automation. Our updated adoption scenarios, including technology development, economic feasibility, and diffusion timelines, lead to estimates that half of today’s work activities could be automated between 2030 and 2060, with a midpoint in 2045, or roughly a decade earlier than in our previous estimates. 6. Generative AI can substantially increase labor productivity across the economy, but that will require investments to support workers as they shift work activities or change jobs. Generative AI could enable labor productivity growth of 0.1 to 0.6 percent annually through 2040, depending on the rate of technology adoption and redeployment of worker time. Combining generative AI with all other technologies, work automation could add 0.5 to 3.4 percentage points annually to productivity growth. However, workers will need support in learning new skills, and some will change occupations. If worker transitions and other risks can be managed, generative AI could contribute substantially to economic growth and support a more sustainable, inclusive world. 7. As technology advances, enterprises seek innovative solutions to streamline operations, enhance customer experiences, and make data-driven decisions. Among the myriad emerging technologies, one ground-breaking tool that has transformed how businesses interact with their customers and optimize their processes is ChatGPT (OpenAI, n.d.). This paper aims to explore the myriad use cases of ChatGPT in business – especially consulting, examining how this cutting-edge language model has become an indispensable asset for organizations seeking growth, efficiency, and enhanced customer engagement. ChatGPT has the potential to empower consulting firms to thrive in the digital age due to its versatility and efficacy. From customer support to content generation market research to personalized recommendations and formulating strategy; ChatGPT can be a crucial asset. In this paper, we have studied and suggested various applications of ChatGPT and generative AI in business applications – having a special focus on management consulting and a firm offering a product called ChapterGPT (ChapterGPT, n.d.). Here, Generative artificial intelligence (AI) describes algorithms (such as ChatGPT) that can be used to create new content, including audio, code, images, text, simulations, and videos. (What Is Generative AI?, 2023). The surveys, interviews , and the literature review help shed light on the strengths and limitations of this technology, we aim to provide a well-rounded understanding of how ChatGPT can be harnessed to augment business strategies, boost productivity, and foster a deeper connection with customers. <search query="Bain & Company AI Bain report 2023 AI ROI client case studies consulting" search_time="2026年5月10日10时49分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:147"><title>From Hype to Hero: A Look at Artificial Intelligence in the Consumer Packaged Goods Industry</title><summary>Learn how to measure your company’s AI maturity and ramp up your results.</summary><hostname>Bain & Company</hostname><publisher>Bain & Company</publisher><author_list><author name="Cesar Brea" affiliation="Bain's Boston office" /><author name="Jeroen Hegge" affiliation="Bain's Consumer Products and Private Equity practices, based in Amsterdam" /><author name="Laurent Hermoye" affiliation="Bain's Consumer Products practice, based in Brussels" /><author name="Michael Jongeneel" affiliation="Bain's Financial Services practice, based in Amsterdam" /></author_list><url>https://www.bain.com/globalassets/noindex/2019/bain-brief_artificial-intelligence-in-the-consumer-produts-goods-industry.pdf</url><publish_time>2019年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:148"><title>LUXURY & TECHNOLOGY: Artificial Intelligence: The Quiet Revolution</title><summary>Since analytical artificial intelligence was first used in the luxury market more than five years ago, adoption of AI solutions has remained targeted and quite limited. On average, fewer than two of the 20 use cases examined in our study have been adopted by members of the Comité Colbert, the trade association for the French luxury industry, and none have been adopted by more than 30% of these luxury Maisons. The use cases supported by analytical AI are among the most widely deployed by the Maisons.
With numerous pilots underway, AI adoption is set to accelerate over the next 12–24 months: Each Maison is currently testing or planning more than five additional use cases.
There are significant disparities in the level of AI adoption, depending on the size of the Maison: Large ones have deployed three times as many use cases as others. However, the gap should gradually narrow with generative AI’s rollout, as it is more accessible and less costly than analytical AI. On average, a large Maison is testing or planning 5.8 use cases, compared with 5.3 at small and medium-sized rivals.
The barriers to AI adoption cited by Maisons mostly relate to expertise and resources (an issue for 55% of Maisons in our study), data management concerns (an inhibiting factor for about 30% of respondents), and risks related to intellectual property rights, especially for generative AI solutions.
Of the four strategic objectives served by AI—operational efficiency, customer relations, augmentation of teams, and enrichment of creative functions—use cases linked to operational efficiency are most popular: 60% of Maisons have adopted or are testing AI-based sales forecasting solutions and the equivalent proportion is 50% for stock allocation.
AI is also an effective lever to bring Maisons closer to their customers, by using, for example, personalized content generation tools or customer segmentation tools, beyond the enhancement of pre-existing solutions for clienteling (the building of long-term relationships with key customers).
The industry is also reflecting on how to use AI tools to augment teams by freeing up time and focusing energies on the most valuable tasks. However, implementation remains very limited at this early stage of the technology’s maturity.
Luxury Maisons show the most reserve when it comes to using AI within the creative process. With an adoption rate of less than 5%, acceptance remains limited. Those Maisons that are beginning to explore the use of AI in this field are doing it in a way that doesn’t question the role and contribution of their creative director, but rather enlarges their sources of inspiration and accelerates visualization of future products.

AI in industry" search_time="2026年5月10日10时50分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:160"><title>The impact of Artificial Intelligence on businesses: The case of Bluewind</title><hostname>威尼斯大学</hostname><publisher>Degree Thesis</publisher><author_list><author name="Alessia Pascon" affiliation="Ca' Foscari University of Venice" /></author_list><url>https://unitesi.unive.it/retrieve/db42eea4-f867-49aa-8a92-c921a695eca8/878475-1290146.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:161"><title>ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: THE NEXT DIGITAL FRONTIER?</title><summary>In this independent discussion paper, we examine investment in artificial intelligence (AI), describe how it is being deployed by companies that have started to use these technologies across sectors, and aim to explore its potential to become a major business disrupter. To do this, we looked at AI through several lenses. We analyzed the total investment landscape bringing together both investment of large corporations and funding from venture capital and private equity funds. We also reviewed the portfolio plays of major internet companies, the dynamics in AI ecosystems from Shenzhen to New York, and a wide range of case studies. As part of our primary research, we surveyed more than 3,000 senior executives on the use of AI technologies, their companies’ prospects for further deployment, and AI’s impact on markets, governments, and individuals. This report also leverages the resources of McKinsey Analytics, a global practice that helps clients achieve better performance through data. The research was conducted jointly with Digital McKinsey, a global practice that designs and implements digital transformations.

In addition to identifying a gap between AI investment and commercial application, which is typical of early technology development curves, we found that the new generation of AI applications is based on the foundation of digitization. Leading sectors in digital tend to be leading sectors in AI, and these are predicted to drive growth. We also found that AI has the potential to accelerate shifts in market share, revenue, and profit pools—all hallmarks of digitally disrupted sectors. This report leverages two MGI analyses of digitization, Digital America: A tale of the haves and have-mores, published in December 2015, and Digital Europe: Pushing the frontier, capturing the benefits, published in June 2016. These reports introduced the McKinsey Global Institute (MGI) Industry Digitization Index, which combines dozens of indicators to provide a comprehensive picture of where and how companies are building digital assets, expanding digital usage, and creating a more digital workforce. This report also builds on MGI’s work on advanced analytics, The age of analytics: Competing in a data-driven world, published in December 2016, and on automation, A future that works: Automation, employment, and productivity, published in January 2017, as well as Artificial intelligence: Implications for China, published in April 2017; and an April 2017 Digital McKinsey report, Smartening up with artificial intelligence (AI): What’s in it for Germany and its industrial sector?</summary><hostname>Stanford University Department of Physics</hostname><publisher>McKinsey Global Institute Discussion Paper</publisher><author_list><author name="Jacques Bughin" affiliation="McKinsey Global Institute, Brussels" /><author name="Eric Hazan" affiliation="McKinsey and Company, Member of McKinsey Global Institute Council, Paris" /><author name="Sree Ramaswamy" affiliation="McKinsey Global Institute, Washington, DC" /><author name="Michael Chui" affiliation="McKinsey Global Institute, San Francisco" /><author name="Tera Allas" affiliation="McKinsey Global Institute, London" /><author name="Peter Dahlstrm" affiliation="McKinsey Global Institute, London" /><author name="Nicolaus Henke" affiliation="McKinsey Global Institute, London" /><author nam

<answer>调研结论：国内金融机构间借贷关系与系统性风险的联系，以及多层次借贷关系与风险建模方法

一、研究背景与核心问题
中国金融体系以银行为主导，但非银融资（含信托、委托贷款、企业间借贷等）规模庞大，政策与监管框架（如资管新规、房地产贷款集中度管理）持续演进。系统性风险的来源已从银行间传染扩展至实体信贷关联、担保圈、城投融资网络，甚至表外业务链条。理解不同层次（银行间、银行-企业、多层机构网络）和类型的借贷关系如何传导风险，是评估和防范系统性风险的关键。 <cite id="call_d10842ffe736-0"></cite><cite id="call_d10842ffe736-1"></cite><cite id="call_d10842ffe736-2"></cite><cite id="call_433048aa1b12-1"></cite><cite id="call_433048aa1b12-2"></cite>

二、主要借贷关系类型与风险联系
1. 银行间市场与同业关联
- 中国银行间市场呈现“星型网络”结构，以五大股份制银行和国开行为核心，具有圈层结构和高聚类性；风险扩散模拟显示，核心银行受冲击时系统稳定性显著下降，资本净额是抵御冲击的关键指标。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-1"></cite>
- RAS算法刻画的互联性网络中，大型银行更互联且持有最大规模的同业交易，机构规模越大通常连接越多；不同系统性风险度量（线性Granger因果、SII、VI、CoVaR、MES）显示，大银行和证券/保险机构对系统性风险贡献突出，而信托、金融公司等监管相对薄弱的机构可能造成更大损失。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-0"></cite>
- 网络结构特征（“小世界”“无标度”、时变性）与风险传染机制研究指出，极端市场条件下连接性急剧上升，资产规模、杠杆率、SRISK等机构属性正向影响连接度，而流动性（当前比率）和房地产景气变化则呈反向影响。 <cite id="call_433048aa1b12-1"></cite>

2. 银行-实体信贷关联（含行业、区域、客户集中）
- 矩阵法构建的银行间及银行-实体行业关联网络揭示，制造业、交运仓储、房地产是系统重要性行业，且行业重要性排名随时间变化；系统重要性银行为工行、建行、中行、农行、交行，而部分股份制银行（如华夏、平安、广发）呈现风险传染性。 <cite id="call_d10842ffe736-0"></cite>
- 贷款集中度实证表明，行业集中度与地区集中度与系统性风险正相关，而客户集中度呈负相关，可能源于企业关联性、区域经济制约和监管效率差异，提示优化贷款结构以防控风险。 <cite id="call_1ff4c8b05a6a-2"></cite>
- 货币政策风险承担渠道研究发现，宽松政策增加非国企、中小企融资但资金更多流向房地产，可能影响金融稳定；银行对低风险企业风险承担受政策影响小，但对房地产企业影响显著。 <cite id="call_1ff4c8b05a6a-1"></cite>

3. 城投与政信类信托融资：担保圈与区域性集聚
- 城投公司政信类信托融资中，担保圈显著抬高杠杆并导致“链条扩散”，空间计量显示相邻政府间存在模仿与邻里扩散效应，形成以省级/副省级为中心、地级市为节点的网络拓扑，呈现较强的区域性集聚和系统性风险隐患。 <cite id="call_886640ff492e-0"></cite>

4. 信托业务：影子银行、房地产通道与表外风险
- 基于微观业务数据的影子银行系统性风险度量（虚拟机构资产负债表+资产价格传染模型）显示，样本期间系统性风险较高且波动剧烈，外部政策冲击和微观业务规模/杠杆变动是主因；打破刚兑和加强政策连续性是防控要点。 <cite id="call_886640ff492e-1"></cite>
- 从资产负债表传染视角的实证表明，信托是影子银行系统不稳定的主要推手，而商业银行承担主要风险敞口（2007–2012）。 <cite id="call_886640ff492e-2"></cite>
- 房地产信托冲击研究指出，资产规模、杠杆、关联性是关键风险驱动因素，机构间传染存在关键路径短、数量多的特征，资产间传染呈现聚类，关联性尤为关键；资管新规后影子银行融资萎缩，企业融资成本与约束上升，但短期债务占比下降。 <cite id="call_433048aa1b12-1"></cite><cite id="call_6cc1e6534fcb-1"></cite>

5. 企业间借贷与信用网络
- 中国信贷网络复杂网络建模（2000–2014）显示，金融机构与企业间高度但不对称连接，局部冲击可能通过网络扩散至全经济；引入信用风险得分（CRS）识别系统重要节点，发现接入度高或非桥梁节点的机构系统重要性更高。 <cite id="call_177bd61b57af-0"></cite>

6. 银行同业拆借偏好与冲击类型
- 具有拆借偏好的银行间网络结构下，冲击传染效应最大；挤兑冲击传染效应高于信用违约，流动性冲击最小，提示风险冲击类型对传染路径与强度的差异化影响。 <cite id="call_66bbcce6090b-0"></cite>

7. 银行间VAR-NETWORK模型：网络结构与监管政策
- VAR-NETWORK模型构建银行间有向关联图，发现资产高同质性与创新关联交易导致风险吸收效应强但外溢明显；面板模型显示网络集中度增加风险辐射，央行扩表刺激风险承担，系统性风险上升，提示差异化监管与干预政策的必要性。 <cite id="call_66bbcce6090b-1"></cite>

8. 银行贷款组合“模仿效应”与系统性违约风险
- 实证发现城商行显著模仿同行贷款组合，而大型全国性银行行为相反；贷款组合重叠与机构违约风险相似性正相关，提示“羊群行为”是系统性违约风险来源之一。 <cite id="call_1ff4c8b05a6a-1"></cite>

三、多层次网络与系统性风险建模方法
1. 多层网络与传染动态机制
- 多层网络模型同时考虑机构间的负债关系与交叉持股，提出新的系统性风险度量方法以捕捉多层金融传染的非线性机制；实证显示，连接多样性（linkage diversity）在解释系统性风险方面通常比简单连接度（connectivity）更有效，强调超越单一图层的建模必要性。 <cite id="call_92a1ca9b1a37-0"></cite>

2. 复杂网络视角下的信用系统建模
- 2000–2014年中国信用系统复杂网络建模显示，网络呈现高度连接但不对称，局部冲击可能扩散至全经济；系统重要节点识别（CRS）为监管提供依据。 <cite id="call_177bd61b57af-0"></cite>

3. 矩阵法与条件资产减值损失设置
- 矩阵法模拟银行间风险敞口矩阵，结合条件资产减值损失条件设置，更贴近真实传染过程；实证显示市场稳定性与核心银行冲击敏感性并存，资本净额是关键缓冲指标。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-1"></cite>

4. RAS算法与多风险度量融合
- RAS算法刻画互联性，结合线性Granger、SII、VI、CoVaR、MES等度量系统性风险暴露，揭示规模、杠杆、关联性等驱动因素，识别不同类型机构的风险角色。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-0"></cite>

四、政策含义与监管启示
- 网络视角下，需识别系统重要机构与行业，监控担保圈与区域性集聚，强化对信托等非银机构的监管，打破刚兑并保持政策连续性。 <cite id="call_d10842ffe736-0"></cite><cite id="call_886640ff492e-0"></cite><cite id="call_886640ff492e-1"></cite><cite id="call_886640ff492e-2"></cite>
- 差异化监管：针对网络集中度、央行扩表等诱发因素，实施差异化的监管与干预政策；优化贷款结构（行业、区域、客户集中度），降低系统性风险敞口。 <cite id="call_1ff4c8b05a6a-2"></cite><cite id="call_66bbcce6090b-1"></cite>
- 防控“模仿效应”与同质化风险：限制城商行过度模仿同行贷款组合，鼓励组合多样化以降低系统性外溢。 <cite id="call_1ff4c8b05a6a-1"></cite>
- 多层网络建模：采用多层框架捕捉负债与股权交叉传染，重视连接多样性而非仅连接度，提升风险预警与干预精度。 <cite id="call_92a1ca9b1a37-0"></cite>
- 企业与行业层面：结合复杂网络识别系统重要行业与企业，防范局部冲击扩散；落实房地产贷款集中度管理，抑制资金空转与风险集聚。 <cite id="call_d10842ffe736-0"></cite><cite id="call_433048aa1b12-2"></cite>

五、数据与方法工具箱
- 微观借贷数据：银行间交易矩阵、贷款合约特征、借款企业特征、银行特征。 <cite id="call_d10842ffe736-0"></cite><cite id="call_1ff4c8b05a6a-1"></cite>
- 网络构建方法：RAS算法、矩阵法、VAR-NETWORK模型、复杂网络建模（包括二分网络及其投影）。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-1"></cite><cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-0"></cite><cite id="call_66bbcce6090b-1"></cite><cite id="call_177bd61b57af-0"></cite>
- 风险传染模拟：条件资产减值损失设置、虚拟机构资产负债表+资产价格传染模型。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-1"></cite><cite id="call_886640ff492e-1"></cite>
- 系统性风险度量：线性Granger因果、SII、VI、CoVaR、MES、CRS、网络溢出指数。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-0"></cite><cite id="call_177bd61b57af-0"></cite><cite id="call_66bbcce6090b-1"></cite>
- 实证策略：面板回归、空间计量、事件研究、广义倍差法。 <cite id="call_886640ff492e-1"></cite><cite id="call_886640ff492e-0"></cite><cite id="call_6cc1e6534fcb-1"></cite>

六、未来研究方向
- 增强微观数据可得性：获取更全面的信托、资管产品、企业间借贷数据，支持多层网络与动态传染模拟。 <cite id="call_886640ff492e-1"></cite><cite id="call_66bbcce6090b-1"></cite>
- 融入宏观审慎工具：将资本充足率、房地产贷款集中度、流动性覆盖率等指标嵌入网络模型，评估政策干预效果。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-1"></cite><cite id="call_433048aa1b12-2"></cite>
- 跨市场传染：扩展至债券市场、衍生品市场、跨境融资，构建全金融体系网络。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-0"></cite>
- 风险情景与压力测试：基于网络结构设计冲击情景（如核心银行倒闭、行业违约潮、流动性枯竭），量化传染路径与损失。 <cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-1"></cite><cite id="call_cc999cfaff71-0"></cite>

被引量： 3</title><summary>目前我国金融市场仍以银行业为主,银行业的风险关乎整个金融系统的稳定。而如果只关注银行间的风险,往往会忽视系统性风险的真实来源,即实体行业的信贷关联。鉴于此,本文首先运用矩阵法模拟了2008-2017年银行间市场的微观借贷数据,结合历年银行对实体行业的实际贷款,构建银行间、银行对实体行业的业务关联网络。其次基于复杂网络的视角,分析银行间借贷网络结构的变化,并动态识别系统重要性银行、风险传染性银行、系统重要性行业,阐释其现实意义与内在关联。研究结果表明:中行、农行、工行、建行、交行为系统重要性银行,历年来系统性风险相对稳定;华夏银行、平安银行、广发银行等股份制银行为风险传染性银行,呈现出动态变化特征;制造业、交运仓储业、房地产业等是系统重要性行业,且行业重要性排名呈时变特征。因此,防控系统性风险,在关注银行间风险传染的同时,还需立足经济的全局视角,监控系统重要性行业,实现"稳增长、控风险"的目标。</summary><hostname>维普</hostname><publisher>武汉金融</publisher><author_list><author name="翟永会" /></author_list><url>https://www.cqvip.com/doc/journal/921677448</url><publish_time>2019年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:121"><title>Interconnectedness and systemic risk measures of Chinese financial institutions</title><summary>Purpose – In this paper the interconnectedness among financial institutions and the level of systemic risks of four types of Chinese financial institutions are investigated. Design/methodology/approach – By the means of RAS algorithm, the interconnection among financial institutions are illustrated. Different methods, including Linear Granger, Systemic impact index (SII), vulnerability index (VI), CoVaR, and MES are used to measure the systemic risk exposures across different institutions. Findings – The results illustrate that big banks are more interconnected and hold the biggest scales of inter-bank transactions in the financial network. The institutions which have larger size tend to have more connection with others. Insurance and security companies contribute more to the systemic risk where as other institutions, such as trusts, financial companies, etc. may bring about severe loss and endanger the financial system as a whole. Practical implications – Since other institutions with low levels of regulation may bring about higher extreme loss and suffer the whole system, it deserves more attention by regulators considering the contagion of potential risks in the financial system. Originality/value – This study builds a valuable contribution by examine the systemic risks from the perspectives of both interconnection and tail risk measures. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="中国 信托贷款 系统性风险 网络分析" search_time="2026年5月10日10时51分星期日"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>总体国家安全观视域下的金融安全</title><summary>当前，金融安全作为国家安全体系的基础性支撑，已从单纯的经济维稳范畴上升为关乎国家主权与发展全局的战略议题。我国金融安全全面临内生结构性矛盾与外部冲击叠加的双重压力，呈现出风险点多面广、传导链条复杂、负面影响外溢等特征。本文分析金融安全在国家安全体系中的功能定位与演进，研究发现：当前我国金融安全面临房地产市场下行、地方债务积压、影子银行隐患及外部环境冲击等多重压力，且各风险类型间存在风险网络和风险共振效应。本文基于总体国家安全观的系统思维，从历史、理论与现实三个维度揭示金融安全在国家安全体系中的基础性支撑作用。在此基础上，分析我国金融安全风险的主要表现及其对政治安全、经济安全和社会稳定的潜在冲击，相应提出促进金融与地产良性循环、建立政府债务监管机制、完善影子银行监管体系、构筑外部冲击防御体系等治理路径。研究旨在为新时代金融安全体系现代化建设提供政策参考。</summary><hostname>Nginx HTTP Server</hostname><author_list><author name="商文江" affiliation="中国政法大学商学院" /><author name="梁昌裔" affiliation="中国政法大学法与经济学研究院" /><author name="许恒" affiliation="中国政法大学商学院" /><author name="张国栋" affiliation="中国政法大学商学院" /></author_list><url>https://pdf.dfcfw.com/pdf/H3_AP202602111819870861_1.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>房地产信托冲击与中国影子银行系统性风险</title><summary>以信托机构为例,将主动管理类信托资产纳入到资产负债表中建立模型探究中国影子银行系统性风险生成机理.理论分析发现,资产规模、杠杆、关联性和外部冲击是关键风险驱动因素.实证结果发现:样本期间,中国影子银行系统性风险呈现先上升、后下降的波动变化趋势.系统重要性机构分布较稳定,其关键因素为资产规模、杠杆和关联性.系统脆弱性机构分布较分散,其关键因素为杠杆.机构间风险传染存在关键路径数量较多、路径较短的特征.其中,杠杆和规模是机构间风险传染的关键因素.资产间风险传染具有明显的聚类特征.其中,资产间关联性具有更加重要的风险驱动作用.本文为解决中国影子银行系统性风险提供理论基础和经验证据.</summary><hostname>维普网</hostname><publisher>系统工程理论与实践</publisher><author_list><author name="荆中博" affiliation="1. 中央财经大学 管理科学与工程学院, 北京 100081; 2. 中央财经大学 金融学院, 北京 100081; 3. 申万宏源证券承销保荐有限责任公司, 北京 100033" /><author name="方意" /><author name="曾艳琪" /><author name="韩业" /></author_list><url>https://m.qikan.cqvip.com/Article/ArticleDetail?id=7106548266</url><publish_time>2021年12月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:3"><title>房地产与中国金融系统性风险关联分析</title><hostname>file.flr-cass.org</hostname><publisher>金融监管评论</publisher><author_list><author name="蔡真" affiliation="中国社科院金融研究所国际金融研究室、法律与金融监管研究基地" /></author_list><url>http://file.flr-cass.org/%E5%AE%9A%E6%9C%9F%E5%87%BA%E7%89%88%E7%89%A9/FLR%E9%87%91%E8%9E%8D%E7%9B%91%E7%AE%A1%E8%AF%84%E8%AE%BA/FLR%E9%87%91%E8%9E%8D%E7%9B%91%E7%AE%A1%E8%AF%84%E8%AE%BA%20No.2018.088.pdf</url><publish_time>2018年11月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:4"><title>Interconnectedness, systemic risk, and the influencing factors: Some evidence from China's financial institutions</title><summary>From the perspective of interconnectedness, we construct a systemic risk spillover network of China's financial institutions. After deconstructing the constructed network and combine with the analysis of the influencing factors, we find that: (i) All industries and institutions within the financial system are highly interconnected, and each sector can act as a risk receiver or risk driver. (ii) During the extreme market conditions, the connectedness between each two financial institutions will increase dramatically. (iii) The network of China's financial institutions has the characteristics of "small world" and "scale-free", and the overall connection of network structure has significant time-varying characteristics. (iv) The asset size, leverage ratio, SRISK index of financial institutions will influence their connection degree positively, while the current ratio of financial institutions and changes of the real estate climate index have the opposite impacts. Our findings hold important implications for regulations.</summary><hostname>ScienceDirect</hostname><publisher>Physica A</publisher><author_list><author name="Shan Wu" affiliation="a School of Finance, Nanjing University of Finance and Economics, Nanjing, China; b Collaborative Innovation Center of Financial Security, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Chengdu, China" /><author name="Mu Tong" affiliation="b Collaborative Innovation Center of Financial Security, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Chengdu, China; c School of Economic Information Engineering, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Chengdu, China" /><author name="Zhongyi Yang" affiliation="c School of Economic Information Engineering, Southwestern University of Finance and E
